For it was said, "Bhikkhus, I allow the establishing of such a boundary spanning across a river where there is a permanent boat or a permanent bridge." If it is not at the direct crossing point but is slightly upstream or downstream, it is also proper. The Elder Karavika Tissa, however, said, "It is proper even if it is within the distance of a gāvuta."

A monk establishing this boundary spanning across a river should stand on one bank and proclaim the marker (nimitta) at the upper riverbank. From there, encompassing himself as much as the desired limit, he should proclaim the marker at the lower riverbank at the end of that limit. Then, he should proclaim the marker on the opposite bank directly facing the [first] marker. From there, by the power of the desired limit, he should proclaim markers up to the riverbank directly facing the first proclaimed marker upstream, bring it back, and connect it with the first proclaimed marker. Then, having brought the monks standing within all the markers into the hatthapāsa...
192:
...the boundary should be established with the kammavācā. Monks who are in the river and do not come [to the act] do not invalidate the formal act. At the conclusion of the establishment, excluding the river, both the opposite bank and this bank within the markers become a single boundary. The river, however, is not counted as part of the baddhasīmā (bound boundary); it is simply a separate nadīsīmā (river boundary).

If there is an island in the river and one wishes to include that island within the boundary, one should, following the previous method, proclaim the markers on the bank where one is standing and then proclaim markers at the near and far edges of the island. Then, one should proclaim a marker on the opposite bank directly facing the marker on this bank of the river, and from there, following the previous method, proclaim markers up to the point directly facing the first proclaimed marker upstream. Then, one should proclaim markers at the far and near edges of the island, bring them back, and connect them with the first proclaimed marker. Then, having brought all the monks on both banks and the island into the hatthapāsa, the boundary should be established with the kammavācā. Monks who are in the river and do not come do not invalidate the formal act. At the conclusion of the establishment, excluding the river, the two banks and the island within the markers become a single boundary. The river, however, is just a nadīsīmā.

If the island is longer than the extent of the vihārasīmā (monastery boundary) either upstream or downstream, one should proclaim a marker at the near edge of the island directly facing the marker of the vihārasīmā extent. From there, encompassing the tip of the island, one should again proclaim a marker at the far edge directly facing the marker at the near edge of the island. After that, following the previous method, starting from the facing marker on the opposite bank, one should proclaim the markers on the opposite bank and the markers at the far and near edges of the island and connect them with the first proclaimed marker. A boundary established by proclaiming in this way has the shape of a mountain (pabbata-saṇṭhāna). If the island is longer than the extent of the vihārasīmā in both directions, upstream and downstream, one should encompass both tips of the island and proclaim the markers, following the previous method, to complete the connection of markers. A boundary established by proclaiming in this way has the shape of a mudiṅga drum (mudiṅga-saṇṭhāna). If the island is small and within the extent of the vihārasīmā, the markers should be proclaimed on the island according to the very first method. A boundary established by proclaiming in this way has the shape of a paṇava drum (paṇava-saṇṭhāna). Thus far, the binding of a boundary should be understood.

When does a boundary established in this way cease to be a boundary? It ceases to be a boundary when the Saṅgha abolishes the boundary. How is it to be abolished?
193:
"Monks, a monk who designates a boundary should first designate the samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā (boundary of common communion), and afterwards, the avippavāsa-sīmā (boundary of non-separation from the three robes) should be designated. Monks, a monk who abolishes a boundary should first abolish the avippavāsa-sīmā, and afterwards, the samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā should be abolished." According to these words, it should be understood that the avippavāsa-sīmā is to be abolished first, and the samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā is to be abolished afterwards.

How is it abolished? A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha thus:

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. That avippavāsa-sīmā which was designated by the Saṅgha as one not to be separated from the three robes—if the Saṅgha is ready, the Saṅgha should abolish that avippavāsa-sīmā. This is the motion.

Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. That avippavāsa-sīmā which was designated by the Saṅgha as one not to be separated from the three robes—the Saṅgha is abolishing that avippavāsa-sīmā. Whichever venerable one approves of the abolition of this avippavāsa-sīmā, let him be silent. Whichever does not approve, let him speak.

The Saṅgha has abolished that avippavāsa-sīmā. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I understand it." (Thus he should inform).

In this way, the avippavāsa-sīmā is first abolished.

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. That boundary which was designated by the Saṅgha as a samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha (common communion and single Uposatha), if the Saṅgha is ready, the Saṅgha should abolish that samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha boundary. This is the motion.

Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. That boundary which was designated by the Saṅgha as a samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha—the Saṅgha is abolishing that samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha boundary. Whichever venerable one approves of the abolition of this samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha boundary, let him be silent. Whichever does not approve, let him speak."
194:
"The Saṅgha has abolished that samānasaṃvāsa-ekūposatha boundary. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I understand it." (Mahāvagga, 146) — In this way, the boundary is abolished.

A monk who abolishes a boundary should know the proper conduct. This is the conduct (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā, 144): Standing in a khaṇḍasīmā (partial boundary), one should not abolish an avippavāsa-sīmā; likewise, standing in an avippavāsa-sīmā, one should not abolish a khaṇḍasīmā. A monk standing in a khaṇḍasīmā should only abolish a khaṇḍasīmā; likewise, one standing in another boundary should only abolish that other boundary. Boundaries are abolished for two reasons: either to make a small boundary large for the expansion of the monastery, or to make a large boundary small to provide space for other monks' dwellings. In such abolition, if they know both the khaṇḍasīmā and the avippavāsa-sīmā, they will be able to both abolish and establish them. Even if they know the khaṇḍasīmā but not the avippavāsa-sīmā, they will still be able to abolish and establish them. Monks who do not know the khaṇḍasīmā but know only the avippavāsa-sīmā might be able to abolish them by standing in places free from doubt, such as the courtyard of a cetiya, the courtyard of a Bodhi tree, or an Uposatha hall, but they will certainly not be able to re-establish them. If they were to establish them, they would cause an overlapping of boundaries (sīmāsambheda), making a monastery boundary a non-monastery boundary; therefore, they should not be abolished. Those monks who know neither of the two will be able to neither abolish nor establish them. A boundary becomes a non-boundary either through a kammavācā (formal act) or through the disappearance of the Dispensation (Sāsana). Monks who do not know the boundary cannot perform the kammavācā; therefore, it should not be abolished. Only after knowing it well should it be abolished and established. This is the decision regarding the baddha-sīmā (bound boundary).

Abaddha-sīmā (unbound boundaries) are of three types: gāmasīmā (village boundary), sattabbhantarayasīmā (seven-inter-space boundary), and udakukkhepasīmā (water-splash boundary). Among these three, whatever is the extent of a village's land is called a gāmasīmā. By taking the village, the city and the town are also included (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā, 147). In those cities and villages, whatever area the village-headmen receive taxes from, whether that area is small or large, it is counted only as a gāmasīmā. The same method applies to city boundaries and town boundaries. Even within a single village land, if the king demarcates a certain area saying, "Let this be a separate village (visuṃgāma)," and gives it to someone, that area also becomes a visuṃgāma-sīmā. Therefore, that visuṃgāma-sīmā and other boundaries...
195: The boundaries of natural villages, towns, and market towns are just like fixed boundaries (baddha-sīmā); however, they do not provide protection from the offense of being separated from the three robes (ticīvara-vippavāsa). In a forest where there is no village, a boundary extending seven abbhantaras all around is called a sattabbhantara-sīmā. Here, a forest without a village is found in forest tracts such as the Viñjhāṭavī, or in the middle of the ocean, or on small islands in the ocean where fishermen do not go. 'Seven abbhantaras all around' means seven abbhantaras in every direction from the monks standing in the middle; diametrically, it is fourteen abbhantaras. In this context, one abbhantara is twenty-eight cubits (hattha) in length. This boundary expands according to the size of the assembly; therefore, the measurement of the abbhantara should be made starting from the edge of the assembly all around. If two groups of the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha separately, another abbhantara should be left between the two seven-abbhantara boundaries for the sake of an outskirt (upacāra). 'Monks, every river is not a baddha-sīmā, every ocean is not a baddha-sīmā, every natural lake is not a baddha-sīmā'—having thus rejected the status of fixed boundaries for rivers and so on, it was further said: 'Monks, in a river, in the ocean, or in a natural lake, the area defined by the splash of water all around a man of average strength is where they are of common communion and have a single Uposatha.' This is called a water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā). In that statement, a river has the characteristics already mentioned in the signs of a river; the ocean is also well-known. A hole (pool) that is not made by anyone digging, but is self-formed and remains filled with water coming from all around, and where water remains during the rainy season as described for a river, is called a natural lake (jātassara). Even a hole dug by water breaking out from a river or the ocean attains this characteristic; this too is simply a jātassara. In these rivers and so on, the area defined by the splash of water all around a man of average strength is called a water-splash boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā). How should the water-splash be performed? Just as gamblers throw a wooden ball, so a man of average strength should take water or sand in his hand and throw it with all his strength. The place where the water or sand thus thrown falls is called one water-splash. A monk standing outside the reach of that water-splash invalidates the formal act (kamma). As far as the assembly expands, so far the boundary expands; the water-splash from the edge of the assembly is the measure. This udakukkhepa-sīmā, in these rivers and so on...
196: ...is obtained only within these rivers and so on, not outside. Therefore, in a river or a natural lake, the area that the water overflows for the four months of the natural rainy season, and in the ocean, the area where the natural waves descend and stay—from that point onwards is the allowable ground (kappiya-bhūmi). Standing on that ground, it is proper to perform formal acts such as the Uposatha. Even in times of drought or in the summer when rivers and natural lakes are dry, that overflow area remains the allowable ground. However, if people dig a well or cultivate a field in a dried-up natural lake, that place becomes village territory (gāmakhetta). The water-splash boundary does not extend outside the area called the allowable ground; it only extends within. Therefore, within those rivers and so on, the limit of the water-splash should be determined all around starting from the edge of the assembly; this is the summary here. This is the detailed explanation: If a river is not very long and the Saṅgha sits everywhere from the source to the mouth, there is no need for the water-splash boundary; the entire river is sufficient for those monks. The statement made by Mahāsumatthera, 'In a river flowing for one yojana, one should abandon the upper half-yojana and perform the formal act in the lower half-yojana,' was rejected by Mahāpadumatthera. For the Blessed One said, 'The inner robe of a bhikkhunī who crosses at any place while covering the three circles gets wet'—this was stated as the measure of a river, not a yojana or a half-yojana. Therefore, by the power of this Pali text, it is proper to perform Saṅgha acts starting from the source of a river that has the characteristics previously mentioned. If, however, many monks perform formal acts separately in this river, all of them should leave another water-splash between their own and others' water-splash limits for the sake of a boundary interval (sīmantarika); it is said that more than that is proper, but less is not. The same method applies to natural lakes and the ocean. When monks go to perform a formal act in a river, if the river water is full to the brim, they should wear a water-cloth (udakasāṭika) and perform the act only within the river. If they are unable to do so, they may also perform it while staying on a boat. However, it is not proper to perform it on a moving boat. Why? Because the boundary is only the extent of the water-splash. A boat passes that boundary very quickly; in such a case, the motion (ñatti) would be in one boundary and the proclamation (anusāvanā) would be in another. Therefore, having stopped the boat with an oar or...
197:
A Sangha act should be performed by suspending from a rock or by tying to a tree growing within the river. It is permissible for monks standing on a platform (scaffolding) constructed within the river or on a tree growing within the river to perform the act.

If a branch of the tree or an aerial root extending from it rests upon a monastery boundary (vihāra-sīmā) or a village boundary (gāma-sīmā) outside the riverbank, the act should be performed only after clearing the boundary or cutting the branch. It is not permissible to perform the act by tying a boat to a branch or an aerial root of a tree growing outside the riverbank that has entered into the river; those performing the act must either clear the boundary or cut the branch to remove its connection to the bank. It is absolutely not permissible to perform the act with a boat tied to a stake driven into the riverbank.

When a bridge is built across a river, if both the bridge and the bridge pillars (supports) are located only within the river, it is permissible for monks standing on that bridge to perform the act. If the bridge or the bridge pillars rest upon the bank, it is not permissible; it should be performed only after clearing the boundary. Alternatively, if the bridge pillars are within the river and the bridge itself exists in the open space above both banks, it is permissible.

If there is a stone slab or a small island within the river, the area that is submerged by water throughout the four months of the normal rainy season, as previously mentioned, is reckoned as the river itself. An area submerged by a torrent during a period of excessive rain should not be taken as such. This is because such an area is reckoned only as a village boundary (gāma-sīmā).

When those who draw a canal from a river create a dam in the river, if that water flows either over the dam or by breaking through it, it is permissible to perform the act in all such places where the water flows. If the current is cut off by a dam or by a stone embankment and the water no longer flows, it is not permissible to perform the act in that place where the water does not flow. It is also not permissible to perform it on the dam itself. If some part of the dam is submerged by water like the aforementioned stone slab or island, it is permissible there. This is because that place is reckoned as the river itself.

When a lake is created by destroying a river, if the water comes and fills the lake because a levee is built below, it is not permissible to perform the act in this lake. However, it is permissible in the place where the water flows above. Below the lake, it is permissible starting from the place where the excess water discharged descends into the riverbed and flows.

In the winter and summer seasons when it does not rain, it is also permissible in a dry river; however, it is not permissible in a canal drawn from a river. If that canal breaks over time and becomes a riverbed, reaching the state of a river, it is permissible. If some river overflows and flows covering a village or town boundary (nigama-sīmā), it is indeed a river; it is permissible to perform the act there. If it overflows a monastery boundary (vihāra-sīmā), it is reckoned only as a monastery boundary.
198:
In the ocean as well, it is not permissible for monks performing a Sangha act to do so in a place where rising water or normal waves come with force and submerge it. However, in a place where normal waves subside and remain steady, that area is called the 'inner ocean' starting from the edge of the water; the act should be performed by those standing there. If the force of the waves is troublesome, it should be performed while standing in a boat or on a platform. The decision regarding these boats and so on should be understood in the same manner as mentioned for the river. If there is a stone slab in the ocean and waves sometimes come and submerge that stone slab and sometimes do not, it is not permissible to perform the act on that stone slab. This is because that stone slab is reckoned only as a village boundary (gāma-sīmā). If, however, it is always submerged by normal water whether waves come or not, it is permissible.

If there is an island or a mountain, and if that island is in a remote place where fishermen do not go, it is reckoned only as a forest boundary (arañña-sīmā). Within the limit of a round-trip journey that those fishermen can make in a day, however, it is reckoned as a village boundary; in that place, it is not permissible to perform the act without clearing the village boundary. If the ocean overflows and stays upon a village boundary or a town boundary (nigama-sīmā), it is indeed the ocean; it is permissible to perform the act in that ocean. If it overflows a monastery boundary, it is reckoned only as a monastery boundary.

Monks performing a Sangha act in a natural lake (jātassara) should not perform the act in a lake that dries up and has no water for drinking or for washing hands and feet as soon as the rain stops in the rainy season as mentioned before; this lake is not called a jātassara, but is reckoned only as village land (gāma-khetta). However, if water remains in the rainy season as mentioned, this lake alone is called a jātassara. In whatever part of that lake water remains throughout the four months of the rainy season, it is permissible to perform the act in that jātassara lake. If the water is deep, it is permissible for monks standing on a platform that has been constructed, or on a platform tied to a tree growing within the lake. The decision regarding stone slabs and islands within this jātassara lake is the same as mentioned for the river.

A jātassara lake that is sufficient for performing the act during a time of normal rainfall is permissible for performing a Sangha act even if it dries up and becomes waterless during a time of drought or in the summer and winter seasons. The statement mentioned in the Andhaka Commentary, 'Every jātassara lake that is dry and waterless belongs only to the village land (gāma-khetta),' should not be accepted. If, however, they dig a hole or a pond etc. for the sake of water in this jātassara lake, that place is not a jātassara and is reckoned as a village boundary. The same rule applies even when gourds, cucumbers, etc., are planted. If they fill that jātassara lake with earth and make it dry land...
199:
If an embankment is built on one side, making that natural lake into a large reservoir, the entire lake becomes an artificial lake (ajātassara) and is classified as a village boundary (gāmasīmā). A salt lake (loṇī) is also classified as a natural lake (jātassara). It is permissible to perform Sangha acts in a place where there is water throughout the four months of the rainy season. This is the decision regarding unbound boundaries (abaddhasīmā).

## In the Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha,
## the discussion on the decision regarding boundaries is concluded.
## 25. Discussion on the Decision Regarding Uposatha and Pavāraṇā

In this matter of Uposatha and Pavāraṇā (according to the Nidānavatthanā of the Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-aṭṭhakathā), there are three kinds of Uposatha based on the day: the fourteenth-day Uposatha (cātuddasī), the fifteenth-day Uposatha (pannarasī), and the harmony Uposatha (sāmaggi-uposatha). Among these Uposathas, in the three seasons of winter (hemanta), summer (gimha), and the rainy season (vassāna), by performing two on the third and seventh fortnights (pakkha) of each season, there are six fourteenth-day Uposathas. The remaining days are fifteenth-day Uposathas. Thus, there are twenty-four Uposathas in a year. This is the regular practice. When there is a suitable reason, it is also permissible to perform the Uposatha on another fourteenth day.

For monks who have completed the first rains-retreat (purimavassa), the full moon day of the first Kattika month (Pubbakattika) is the Pavāraṇā day. If those same monks postpone the Pavāraṇā because of harassment by quarrelsome people, then either the fourteenth day of the waning moon of the Kattika month or the full moon day of the second Kattika month (Pacchimakattika) becomes the Pavāraṇā day. For monks who have completed the second rains-retreat (pacchimavassa), the full moon day of the second Kattika month is the Pavāraṇā day. These three are the Pavāraṇā days. This is also the regular practice. When there is a suitable reason, it is also permissible to perform Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth days preceding the two Kattika full moon days.

However, when a divided Saṅgha is reunited according to the method mentioned in the Kosambakakkhandhaka, and the Saṅgha performs the act of communal harmony (saṅghasāmaggi) to settle that legal issue (adhikaraṇa), the Uposatha should be performed at that very moment. Because of the statement, "The Pātimokkha should be recited," any day other than the fourteenth or fifteenth can be called an Uposatha day. For monks who have completed the rains-retreat, this very day within the month of Kattika is called the Harmony Pavāraṇā day (sāmaggi-pavāraṇā). Thus, the Uposatha should be performed on these three types of days. When performing it, if it is the fourteenth-day Uposatha, one should say, "Today is the fourteenth-day Uposatha." If it is the harmony Uposatha,
200:
## 25. Discussion on the Decision regarding Uposatha and Pavāraṇā

'Today is the Uposatha of harmony (sāmaggī),' it should be said. On the fifteenth day, however, according to the method found in the Pali text, it should be said: 'Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha.'

Three other types of Uposatha are also taught based on the performer: Uposatha by the Saṅgha, Uposatha by a group (gaṇa), and Uposatha by an individual (puggala). Based on the method of performance, there are three other types of Uposatha: Suttuddesa-uposatha, Pārisuddhi-uposatha, and Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha. Among these, Suttuddesa-uposatha is the recitation of the Pātimokkha taught in the manner beginning with 'Suṇātu me bhante saṅgho.' Of the remaining two types of Uposatha, Pārisuddhi-uposatha is first of all twofold: by way of announcing in the presence of others and by way of mutual announcement. Among these, the Pārisuddhi-uposatha performed in the presence of others is also twofold: performed in the presence of those who have already performed Pavāraṇā and those who have not.

Among these two, on the day of Mahāpavāraṇā (the full moon of Assayuja), a monk who entered the later rains, or one who did not enter the rains, or one whose rains were broken, should give his physical presence to those who have performed Pavāraṇā. On the full moon of Kattika, a monk who did not enter the rains or whose rains were broken should do the same. He should say three times: 'Venerable sirs, I am pure; may you hold me to be pure.' Except for Pavāraṇā day, at other times, when the resident monks have just finished reciting the Pātimokkha, if other monks of equal status or fewer arrive before the whole assembly has risen, or after some have risen, or after all have risen, those arriving monks should announce their purity in the presence of the resident monks in the manner already described.

Pārisuddhi-uposatha performed by way of mutual announcement is twofold: with a motion (ñatti) and without a motion. Among these, in a monastery where three monks reside, when they assemble on the Uposatha day, one monk should say: 'Listen to me, sirs, today is the fourteenth-day Uposatha' or 'the fifteenth-day Uposatha,' and then set the motion: 'If it is suitable to the sirs, let us perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha mutually.' Then the senior monk, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder, squatting, and raising his joined palms, should say three times: 'Friends, I am pure; may you hold me to be pure.' The remaining monks should say 'Venerable sir' and speak in the same manner. This is how it is done with a motion. Where two monks reside, the purity should be announced in the same manner but without a motion. This is Pārisuddhi-uposatha.
201:
If there is only one monk, after performing all the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇīya) and knowing that no other monks are coming, he should say: 'Today my Uposatha is the fourteenth-day' or 'the fifteenth-day,' and then say: 'I resolve (adhiṭṭhāmi).' This is Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha. In this way, three types of Uposatha should be known by the method of performance. By this much, nine types of Uposatha have been explained. Among those nine, when an Uposatha endowed with the three characteristics—the fifteenth-day by date, Saṅgha-uposatha by performer, and Suttuddesa by method—is occurring, a monk who goes elsewhere for the purpose of residing, other than for Saṅgha business or due to danger, without performing the Uposatha on that day, whether to a monastery without monks, a place that is not a monastery, or a monastery or place with monks of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka), commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

A monk who arrives at the assembly place after having performed Uposatha elsewhere while the Saṅgha is assembling for Uposatha, if he cannot attend in person, must give his consent (chanda). A monk who is ill or busy with duties, when giving his purity (pārisuddhi), must also give his consent. How? In the presence of one monk, he should make it known by body, speech, or both: 'I give my consent, carry my consent, report my consent.' Thus is consent given. An ill or busy monk who has not yet performed Uposatha must give his purity. How? In the presence of one monk, he should make it known by body, speech, or both: 'I give my purity, carry my purity, report my purity.' Thus is purity given. The monk giving purity must also give consent. For the Blessed One said: 'Monks, I allow a monk giving purity on that Uposatha day to also give consent if there is business for the Saṅgha to perform.' In this regard, giving purity completes the Uposatha act for both the Saṅgha and oneself, but not the remaining Saṅgha business. Giving consent completes the Uposatha act and the remaining business for the Saṅgha only, but for oneself, the Uposatha remains unperformed. Therefore, a monk giving purity must also give consent. By the method previously mentioned, it is proper for one monk to carry pure consent, or purity, or this combined consent and purity, even for many monks. If that monk, on the way, meets another monk and gives the consent or purity of those from whom he received it, as well as his own consent and purity, it reaches only that monk.
202:
Apart from this, the consent and purity (chandapārisuddhi) of other monks is called 'cat-chain-like consent and purity' (biḷālasaṅkhalikā chandapārisuddhi). This consent and purity does not 'come' [on its own]. Therefore, one must go to the place of assembly oneself and inform them. If one intentionally fails to inform them, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, the consent and purity is considered to have arrived as soon as the monk carrying it enters the forearm's length (hatthapāsa).

It is not proper to perform any Sangha act (saṅghakamma) with 'stale' (pārivāsiya) consent. In this context, there are four types of staleness: assembly-stale (parisapārivāsiya), night-stale (rattipārivāsiya), consent-stale (chandapārivāsiya), and intention-stale (ajjhāsayapārivāsiya). Among these, assembly-stale refers to when monks have assembled for some business, but then a rain cloud arises, or a military display (ussāraṇā) occurs, or people come crowding in, and the monks leave, saying, 'There is no opportunity for us; let us go elsewhere,' without relinquishing their consent. This is called assembly-stale. Although it is assembly-stale, because the consent was not relinquished, it is proper to perform the act.

Furthermore, monks assemble at night, saying, 'Let us perform the Uposatha and so on,' and they request one monk, saying, 'Let us listen to the Dhamma until everyone has assembled.' While that monk is preaching the Dhamma, dawn breaks. If they were sitting with the intention, 'Let us perform the fourteenth-day Uposatha,' it is proper to perform it as a fifteenth-day Uposatha. If they were sitting to perform a fifteenth-day Uposatha, it is not proper to perform the Uposatha on the first day of the following fortnight (which is not an Uposatha day), but it is proper to perform other Sangha business. This is called night-stale (rattipārivāsiya).

Furthermore, monks are sitting with the intention, 'Let us perform some Sangha act such as rehabilitation (abbhāna).' Among them, a monk who is an expert in astrology says, 'Today the stars are harsh; do not perform this act.' Based on his words, those monks relinquish their consent and remain sitting there. Then, another monk arrives and says, 'The goal eludes the fool who waits for the stars,' and adds, 'What is the use of stars? Perform it.' This is both consent-stale (chandapārivāsiya) and intention-stale (ajjhāsayapārivāsiya). In such a case of staleness, it is not proper to perform the act without bringing the consent and purity again.

If a certain monk is sick and unable to give consent and purity, he should be carried into the midst of the Sangha on a couch or a chair. If the monks attending to the sick one think, 'If we move the patient from his place, his illness will increase or he will pass away'...
203:
That monk should not be moved from his place; the Sangha should go there and perform the Uposatha. If there are many such sick monks, the Sangha should stand in a line so that everyone is within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa). If they are far apart and the Sangha is insufficient [to bridge the gap], the Uposatha should not be performed on that day. The Uposatha must not be performed by a divided (vagga) Sangha; if it is performed, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If four monks reside in a monastery and, having brought the consent and purity of one, the [other] three perform the purity-uposatha (pārisuddhi-uposatha); or if three monks reside and, having brought the consent and purity of one, the [other] two recite the Pātimokkha—that Uposatha act is an unlawful and divided (adhamma-vagga) Uposatha act. If all four assemble and perform the purity-uposatha, or if three or two monks [assemble and] recite the Pātimokkha, that Uposatha act is an unlawful and united (adhamma-samagga) Uposatha act. If among four monks, the purity of one is brought and three recite the Pātimokkha; or if among three monks, the purity of one is brought and two perform the purity-uposatha—that Uposatha act is a lawful and divided (dhamma-vagga) Uposatha act. If all four residing in the same monastery assemble and recite the Pātimokkha; or if three perform the purity-uposatha; or if two perform the purity-uposatha with each other—that Uposatha act is a lawful and united (dhamma-samagga) Uposatha act.

Regarding Pavāraṇā acts: if five monks reside in a monastery and, having brought the pavāraṇā of one, the [other] four perform the pavāraṇā by setting a group motion (gaṇañatti); or if four or three monks reside and, having brought the pavāraṇā of one, the [other] three or two perform the pavāraṇā by setting a Sangha motion (saṅghañatti)—all these are unlawful and divided (adhamma-vagga) pavāraṇā acts. If all five persons assemble together and perform pavāraṇā by setting a group motion; or if four, three, or two residents assemble together and perform pavāraṇā by setting a Sangha motion—all these are unlawful and united (adhamma-samagga) pavāraṇā acts. If among five persons, the pavāraṇā of one is brought and four perform pavāraṇā by setting a Sangha motion; or if among four or three persons, the pavāraṇā of one is brought and three or two perform pavāraṇā by setting a group motion—all these are lawful and divided (dhamma-vagga) pavāraṇā acts. If all five persons assemble together and perform pavāraṇā by setting a Sangha motion; or if four or three persons assemble together and perform pavāraṇā by setting a group motion; [if] two...
204:
Monks invite one another; a monk living alone performs the Pavāraṇā by determination (adhiṭṭhāna-pavāraṇā); all this is called the Pavāraṇā act in accordance with the Dhamma and in harmony.

In this Pavāraṇā act, if it is the 14th day Pavāraṇā, one should determine: "Today is my 14th day Pavāraṇā." If it is the 15th day Pavāraṇā, one should determine: "Today is my 15th day Pavāraṇā." A monk giving his Pavāraṇā [to another] should make the meaning known by body, by speech, or by both body and speech, saying: "I give my Pavāraṇā; please convey my Pavāraṇā; please invite on my behalf." After the Pavāraṇā has been given in this way, the monk conveying the Pavāraṇā should approach the Saṅgha and invite thus: "Venerable Sirs, the bhikkhu Tissa invites the Saṅgha by what is seen, heard, or suspected. May the Saṅgha speak to him out of compassion; seeing [the offense], he will make amends. For the second time... For the third time... the bhikkhu Tissa invites the Saṅgha... he will make amends." If [the monk] is senior to oneself, one should say: "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Tissa..." By doing so, the invitation has been made on behalf of that monk.

The monk giving Pavāraṇā should also give his consent (chanda); the giving of consent should be understood as previously mentioned. Here too, the giving of consent is for the remaining formal acts. Therefore, if the one giving Pavāraṇā gives his consent, when the Pavāraṇā is announced in the manner mentioned, both the monk giving Pavāraṇā and the Saṅgha have performed the invitation. If he gives only the Pavāraṇā but not the consent, when that monk's Pavāraṇā is announced and the Saṅgha has invited, the invitation is well-performed for all, but other formal acts may be invalidated. If he gives only the consent but not the Pavāraṇā, the Saṅgha's Pavāraṇā and the remaining formal acts are not invalidated, but that monk remains uninvited. On the Pavāraṇā day, a monk who arrives after having performed the Pavāraṇā by determination outside the boundary (sīmā) should also give his consent; by doing so, the Saṅgha's Pavāraṇā act is not invalidated.

If five monks entered the early Vassa (purimikā) and five monks entered the late Vassa (pacchimikā), after the early Vassa monks have performed the Pavāraṇā by setting forth the motion (ñatti), the late Vassa monks should perform the Pārisuddhi Uposatha in their presence. Two motions should not be set forth in a single Uposatha hall. If there are four, three, two, or one monk who entered the late Vassa, the same method applies. If there are four in the early Vassa and four, three, two, or one in the late Vassa, the same method applies. If there are three in the early Vassa and three, two, or one in the late Vassa, the same method applies. This is the defining characteristic (lakkhaṇa) in this matter.
205:
If the monks who entered the late Vassa are fewer than or equal to those who entered the early Vassa, and they complete the group for Saṅgha-pavāraṇā, the motion (ñatti) should be set forth by way of Saṅgha-pavāraṇā. However, if there is one monk in the late Vassa and there are four monks [in the early Vassa] with him, it is not proper to perform Pavāraṇā by setting forth a Saṅgha motion for the four monks. But by way of a group motion (gaṇa-ñatti), that monk is a group-completer (gaṇapūraka); therefore, the early Vassa monks should perform Pavāraṇā by setting forth the motion by way of a group, and the remaining [late Vassa] monk should perform the Pārisuddhi Uposatha in their presence. If there are two in the early Vassa and two or one in the late Vassa, the same method applies. If there is one in the early Vassa and one in the late Vassa, one monk should perform Pavāraṇā in the presence of the other, and the other should perform the Pārisuddhi Uposatha. If the monks who entered the late Vassa are more than those who entered the early Vassa by even one, the Pātimokkha should be recited first, and afterwards the fewer early Vassa monks should perform Pavāraṇā in the presence of those [late Vassa] monks.

On the Pavāraṇā day of the full moon of Kattika (the end of the four-month period), if the monks who entered the late Vassa are more than or equal to those who entered the first Vassa and have already performed the Mahāpavāraṇā, the Pavāraṇā should be performed by setting forth the Pavāraṇā motion. After they have performed Pavāraṇā, the remaining [early Vassa] monks should perform the Pārisuddhi Uposatha. If the monks who performed the Mahāpavāraṇā are many and the monks who entered the late Vassa are few or only one, after the Pātimokkha has been recited, that [late Vassa] monk should perform Pavāraṇā in the presence of those [early Vassa] monks. Should that Pātimokkha be recited in its entirety or only in part? It is proper to recite even a part. Thus, the Blessed One said:

“Monks, there are these five recitations of the Pātimokkha. Having recited the Introduction (nidāna), the rest should be made known by [the phrase] 'to be heard.' This is the first recitation of the Pātimokkha. Having recited the Introduction and the four Pārājikas, the rest should be made known by 'to be heard.' This is the second recitation of the Pātimokkha. Having recited the Introduction, the four Pārājikas, and the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, the rest should be made known by 'to be heard.' This is the third recitation of the Pātimokkha. Having recited the Introduction, the four Pārājikas, the thirteen Saṅghādisesas, and the two Aniyatas, the rest should be made known by 'to be heard.' This is the fourth recitation of the Pātimokkha. The fifth is recitation in full.”
206:
Among those five ways of reciting the Pātimokkha (Mahāvibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 150), the instruction to recite the Nidāna (Introduction) and announce the remaining parts by the word 'heard' (suta) means: After reciting this Nidāna—"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me... for that monk, the confession of the offense leads to comfort"—one should announce the remaining parts by the word 'heard' as follows: "Venerable sirs, the Nidāna has been recited. I ask the venerable ones therein: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask... thus I record this. The four Pārājika rules have been heard by the venerable ones... they should be practiced without dispute."

In this manner, the remaining four Pātimokkuddesa (sections of Pātimokkha recitation) should also be understood. Because of the words (Mahāvagga 150), "I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha in brief when there is an obstacle. Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in brief when there is no obstacle; whoever should so recite it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," the Pātimokkha must not be recited in brief without an obstacle.

These are the ten obstacles: obstacle from a king, obstacle from thieves, obstacle from fire, obstacle from water, obstacle from humans, obstacle from non-humans, obstacle from wild beasts, obstacle from reptiles, obstacle to life, and obstacle to the holy life (brahmacariyantarāya).

Among those obstacles, if a king arrives while the monks are sitting down to perform the Uposatha, this is called an obstacle from a king (rājantarāya). If thieves arrive, this is an obstacle from thieves (corantarāya). If a forest fire approaches or fire breaks out in the monastery, this is an obstacle from fire (aggyantarāya). If it rains or a flood comes, this is an obstacle from water (udakantarāya). If many people arrive, this is an obstacle from humans (manussantarāya). If a spirit seizes a monk, this is an obstacle from non-humans (amanussantarāya). If wild beasts such as tigers or bears arrive, this is an obstacle from wild beasts (vāḷantarāya). If reptiles such as snakes bite a monk, this is an obstacle from reptiles (sarīsapantarāya). If a monk becomes ill, or passes away, or if enemies seize him wishing to kill him, this is an obstacle to life (jīvitantarāya). If people seize one or many monks wishing to make them fall away from the holy life, this is an obstacle to the holy life (brahmacariyantarāya).

When such obstacles exist, the Pātimokkha should be recited in brief, or the first uddesa should be recited. Or the first two, three, or four uddesas may be recited. In this regard, if an obstacle arises before an uddesa—starting from the second one—is finished, that unfinished uddesa should also be announced by the word 'heard' (suta). However, if the Nidāna-uddesa is not yet finished, there is no such thing as announcing it by the word 'heard'.
207:
In the act of Pavāraṇā (Invitation) as well, if there is an obstacle, it is proper to perform Pavāraṇā by inviting twice (dvevācika), inviting once (ekavācika), or by those of equal seniority inviting together (samānavassika). In this matter, the one who sets forth the motion (ñatti) should say, "If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should perform Pavāraṇā by inviting twice." In the Pavāraṇā of inviting once, he should say, "...should perform Pavāraṇā by inviting once." In the Pavāraṇā of those of equal seniority, he should say, "...those of equal seniority should perform Pavāraṇā together."

In this samānavassika Pavāraṇā, many monks of equal seniority are allowed to perform Pavāraṇā together. If the motion that encompasses all forms of Pavāraṇā is set forth as: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the Pavāraṇā day on the fifteenth. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should perform Pavāraṇā," then it is proper to perform Pavāraṇā by inviting three times, twice, or once; however, the samānavassika (equal seniority) method is not proper. If the motion says, "...should perform Pavāraṇā by inviting three times," then only inviting three times is proper, and other forms are not. If it says, "...by inviting twice," then inviting twice and three times are proper, while inviting once and the samānavassika method are not. If it says, "...by inviting once," then inviting once, twice, and three times are proper, and only the samānavassika method is not. If it says, "...samānavassika," then all forms of Pavāraṇā are proper.

By whom should the Pātimokkha be recited? According to the words (Mahāvagga 154), "Monks, I allow the Pātimokkha to be the responsibility of the Elder (Thera)," the Pātimokkha should be recited by the Elder of the Saṅgha. According to the words (Mahāvagga 155), "Monks, whichever monk there is competent and capable, I allow the Pātimokkha to be his responsibility," it may also be recited by a more junior monk. In this regard, although it is true that a junior but competent monk is allowed to recite the Pātimokkha, the meaning here is: if the Elder does not know five, four, or three sections (vaggas) of the Pātimokkha by heart, but two uddesas are memorized perfectly and clearly without break, the recitation remains the responsibility of the Elder. However, if he cannot recite even this much clearly, it becomes the responsibility of a competent monk. Therefore, one should either recite it oneself or request another to do so.

According to the words (Mahāvagga 154), "Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in the midst of the Saṅgha without being requested; whoever should recite it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," one must not recite the Pātimokkha without being requested. Not only the Pātimokkha, but the Dhamma also should not be taught [without request], because of the words (Mahāvagga 150), "Monks, the Dhamma should not be taught in the midst of the Saṅgha without being requested; whoever should teach it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
208:
In this matter, the exhortation (ajjhesanā) pertains to the monk appointed by the Saṅgha to preach the Dhamma, or to the Elder of the Saṅgha (Saṅghatthera). Therefore, if there is no monk specifically exhorted to preach the Dhamma, one may preach either by asking permission from the Saṅghatthera or by being requested by that Elder. If there are many Dhamma preachers (dhammakathika) in the monastery, the Saṅghatthera should have them speak in turns. A monk who is told, "You preach the Dhamma; give the gift of Dhamma," should preach the Dhamma using all three methods. If told, "Recite the Pali (osārehi)," he only has the right to recite the Pali. If told, "Expound the meaning (kathehi)," he only has the right to expound the meaning. If told, "Chant in the Sarabhañña style," he only has the right to chant in the Sarabhañña style. Furthermore, the Saṅghatthera should not make a request while sitting on a high seat. If it is a case of a preceptor (upajjhāya) and a co-resident (saddhivihārika), and the preceptor, sitting on a high seat, says, "Recite," the student should recite while focusing on his study (sajjhāya). If there are junior monks present, he should recite with the thought, "I shall recite for them."

If the Saṅghatthera in a monastery only allows his own pupils to preach and does not exhort others who have melodious voices, the others should say, "Venerable Sir, please let such-and-such a monk preach." If he says, "Let him preach," or remains silent, it is proper to let him preach. If he objects, he should not be allowed to preach. If the listening of Dhamma has already begun before the Saṅghatthera arrives, there is no need to stop and ask permission when he arrives later. However, one who is about to expound the meaning after reciting the Pali should do so either after asking permission or without stopping. The same rule applies if the Elder arrives while the meaning is being expounded.

In the case of preaching to those sitting nearby, the Saṅghatthera alone is the authority. Therefore, the Elder himself should preach, or he should tell another monk, "Preach." However, he should not say this while sitting on a high seat. To laypeople, however, it is permissible to say, "Do preach." If laypeople ask a monk they know, that monk should preach after asking permission from the Elder. If the Saṅghatthera is asked, "Venerable Sir, these people are asking a question," and he says, "Explain it," or remains silent, the monk has the right to explain. The same rule applies to giving thanks (anumodanā) in a house and similar occasions. If the Saṅghatthera grants permission, saying, "You may preach in the monastery or in a house even without asking me," it is appropriate and he has the right to preach everywhere. Even when performing one's own recitation (sajjhāya), the Elder must be asked for permission. If another senior Elder (older than the one who gave permission) arrives while one is reciting after having asked permission from one Elder, there is no need to ask again. However, if he arrives while one has stopped with the thought, "I shall rest," one must ask permission when starting again. If the recitation was started before the Saṅghatthera arrived...
209:
The same rule applies to a monk who is reciting his studies. If one Saṅghatthera has given permission, saying, "Recite as you please even without asking me," it is proper to recite as one pleases; however, if another Elder arrives, one must ask him before reciting.

In a monastery where all the monks are ignorant (bāla) and unskilled (abyatta), and do not know how to recite the Pātimokkha, what should be done? Those monks should immediately send one monk to a nearby residence, saying, "Go, friend, and return after learning the Pātimokkha either in brief or in detail." If they succeed in this way, it is well. If they do not succeed, all those monks must go every fortnight to a residence where such monks (who know the Pātimokkha) reside, for the purpose of performing the Uposatha. If they do not go, they incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This applies only during the summer and winter seasons. During the rainy season (vassāna), however, one must not enter the Vassa without a reciter of the Pātimokkha. If the one who entered the Vassa leaves, disrobes, or passes away, and if there is another reciter available, it is proper to stay for the later Vassa (pacchimikā). If there is no one, they must go elsewhere; if they do not go, they incur a dukkaṭa offense. If the reciter leaves, disrobes, or passes away during the later Vassa, they should stay for the full two months (from the day after the full moon of Poṭṭhapāda to the full moon of Kattika).

In a monastery where those ignorant and unskilled monks reside, if a monk arrives who is of great learning (bahussuta), an heir to the traditions (āgatāgama), a bearer of the Dhamma (dhammadhara), a bearer of the Vinaya (vinayadhara), a bearer of the Mātikā (mātikādhara), wise, skilled, sagacious, conscientious (lajjī), scrupulous (kukkuccaka), and desirous of training (sikkhākāma), those monks should support him with the four requisites, assist him, win him over with pleasant speech, and serve him with bathing powder, clay, tooth-sticks, and water for washing the face. If they do not support, assist, win him over, or serve him with powder, clay, tooth-sticks, and water, all of them incur a dukkaṭa offense. In this matter, neither senior nor junior monks are exempt; everyone must serve him in turns. An offense is incurred by a monk who does not serve during his turn. That distinguished monk, however, should not consent to (accept) services such as the sweeping of his precinct or the giving of tooth-sticks by the great Elders. Even if he does not consent, the great Elders should come for the evening and morning attendance (to serve). That monk, knowing of their coming, should go to the great Elders first for attendance. If that monk has co-residents as attendants, he should say, "I have attendants; may the Venerable ones remain unconcerned." Otherwise, if in that very monastery one or two monks who are perfect in their duties say, "We will perform the duties for the Elder; let the rest of the Venerable ones live at ease," then no offense is incurred by any of them.
210:
According to the words beginning with "If a monk has an offense, he should reveal it" (Mahāvagga, 134), a monk with an offense should not perform the Uposatha. Therefore, a monk who remembers an offense on the Uposatha day must confess it. One who wishes to confess should approach another monk, place the upper robe over one shoulder, sit in a squatting position, raise the hands in salutation (añjali), and say: "Friend, I have fallen into an offense of such-and-such a name; I confess it." If he is junior (to the receiver), he should say: "Venerable sir, I..."

Saying "I confess that offense" is well-said even if one says "I confess it before you" or "I confess it before your reverences" according to what is appropriate for oneself. The receiver should also say, according to what is appropriate for himself: "Venerable sir, do you see that offense?" or "Friend, do you see that offense?" Then the confessor should say: "Friend, I see it" or "Venerable sir, I see it." Again, the receiver should say: "Venerable sir, restrain yourself in the future" or "Friend, restrain yourself in the future." When this is said, the confessor should say: "Friend, it is well; I will restrain myself well" or "Venerable sir, it is well; I will restrain myself well."

If there is doubt (vematika) regarding an offense, he should approach another monk, place the upper robe over one shoulder, sit in a squatting position, raise the hands in salutation, and say: "Friend, I have doubt regarding an offense of such-and-such a name; when I am free from doubt, I will remedy that offense." Having said this, the Uposatha should be performed and the Pātimokkha should be listened to. The Uposatha should not be obstructed because of that doubt.

According to the words "Monks, a common (sabhāga) offense should not be confessed; for him who confesses it, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Monks, a common offense should not be received; for him who receives it, there is an offense of wrongdoing" (Mahāvagga, 169), if both persons have fallen into an offense through the same basis, such as eating at the wrong time, such a common offense should neither be confessed nor received. However, it is proper for a monk who has fallen into an offense due to eating at the wrong time to confess in the presence of a monk who has fallen into an offense due to eating food that has not been made allowable.

If the entire Saṅgha has fallen into a light offense (lahuka-āpatti) through a common basis such as eating at the wrong time, what should be done in that case? Those monks should immediately send one monk to a nearby monastery, saying: "Friend, go, that..."
211:
"...remedy the offense and return; we will remedy the offense in your presence." If they obtain such a means for purification from that offense, it is well. If they do not obtain it, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha (make a formal announcement): "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This entire Saṅgha has fallen into a common offense. When we see another monk who is pure and free from offense, we will remedy that offense in his presence" (Mahāvagga, 171). Having said this, the Uposatha should be performed.

If there is doubt, he should say: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This entire Saṅgha has doubt regarding a common offense. When we are free from doubt, we will remedy that offense" (Mahāvagga, 171). Having said this, the Uposatha should be performed.

If, in this Saṅgha, some monk, thinking "It is proper to confess that common offense," confesses in the presence of another monk, that confession is indeed well-confessed. However, due to the act of confession, the confessor, and due to the act of receiving, the receiver, both incur an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Since that wrongdoing is of a different basis (nānāvatthuka), they should confess it to each other. By doing so, those two monks become free from offense. In their presence, the remaining monks should confess or announce their common offenses. If those monks perform the Uposatha without doing so, they incur an offense of wrongdoing prescribed for performing the Uposatha while having an offense, according to the method beginning with "Friends, announce your purity."

If any monk remembers an offense while the Pātimokkha is being recited, that monk should say to a nearby monk: "Friend, I have fallen into an offense of such-and-such a name; having risen from here, I will remedy that offense." The nearby monk should be one of the same category (sabhāga). For if it is said to a monk of a different category (visabhāga), there may be disputes, quarrels, schisms in the Saṅgha, etc. Therefore, without telling him, one should perform the Uposatha with the intention: "I will rise from here and remedy it."

If any monk has doubt regarding an offense while the Pātimokkha is being recited, he should likewise say only to a nearby monk of the same category: "Friend, I have doubt regarding an offense of such-and-such a name; when I am free from doubt, I will remedy that offense." Having said this, the Uposatha should be performed and the Pātimokkha should be listened to. The Uposatha should not be obstructed because of that doubt.
212:
“Monks, I allow the sweeping of the Uposatha hall,” based on this and other such statements (Mahāva. 159)—

“Sweeping, lighting the lamp, [setting out] water, and [arranging] the seats; these four are called the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa) of the Uposatha.” (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 168)—

The Uposatha should be performed only after completing these four kinds of preliminary duties as stated.

By whom should these preliminary duties be performed? “Monks, I allow a senior monk (thera) to command a junior monk (nava). Monks, a junior monk who is commanded by a senior monk and is not ill must not fail to sweep; if he does not sweep, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” based on this and other such statements, it should be performed by the monk commanded by the senior monk. The senior monk who gives the command should not command someone who is performing some other task, or someone who is always alone, or someone who is carrying out the burdens of the Saṅgha, or anyone among the intoning chanters (sarabhāṇaka), Dhamma preachers (dhammakathika), and so on, to sweep the Uposatha hall. However, the remaining monks should be commanded in rotation. If the commanded monk cannot find even a temporary broom, he should sweep by breaking off a suitable (kappiya) tree branch. For a monk who cannot find even such a branch, performing it by any available suitable means is indeed proper.

As for the monk commanded to arrange the seats, if there are no seats in the Uposatha hall, they should be brought from the communal (saṅghika) dwellings and arranged, and then returned after the Uposatha. If there are no seats, it is proper to spread out mats or leaves. If even mats are unavailable, suitable tree branches should be broken and spread out. For a monk who cannot find anyone to make things suitable, performing it by any available suitable means is indeed proper.

The senior monk who commands the lighting of the lamp should say, “In such and such a place, there is oil, a wick, or a lamp-bowl; take it and light it.” If oil and other supplies are not available, they should be sought. For a monk who cannot find them after searching, performing it by any available suitable means is indeed proper. Alternatively, a fire should also be lit in a lamp-bowl.

“Consent (chanda), purity (pārisuddhi), announcing the season (utu), counting the monks, and exhortation (ovāda); these [five] are called the preliminary tasks (pubbakicca) of the Uposatha.” (Mahāva. 168)—

These four [types of] preliminary tasks as stated should be performed after the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa). Indeed, the Uposatha should not be performed without performing those preliminary tasks.
213:
“If it is the appropriate time for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha” (Mahāva. 143). In accordance with this statement, when the Uposatha act is appropriate for the Saṅgha, it should be performed at that time. That which is called the appropriate time (pattakalla) is comprised of four factors. Therefore, the Teachers of the Commentaries said:

“It is an Uposatha day, as many monks as are eligible for the act are present, common offenses (sabhāgāpatti) do not exist, and excluded persons are not present therein; this is called the appropriate time (pattakalla).” (Mahāva. Aṭṭha. 168).

In that verse, “Uposatha” refers to any one of the three Uposatha days. Only when it is such an Uposatha day does this Uposatha act of the Saṅgha become what is called an act at the appropriate time (pattakalla); it is not so if it is not the day. As it was said: “Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day” (Mahāva. 183).

“As many monks as are eligible for the act” means as many monks as are suitable and appropriate for that Uposatha act, which at the minimum limit is four monks of regular standing (pakatatta), who have not left the arm’s reach (hatthapāsa) and are staying within a single boundary (sīmā). Only when those four monks are staying within a single boundary without leaving the arm’s reach does that Uposatha act of the Saṅgha become what is called an act at the appropriate time (pattakalla); it is not so if there are fewer than four. As it was said: “Monks, I allow the recitation of the Pātimokkha to four [monks]” (Mahāva. 168).

In the phrase “common offenses (sabhāgāpatti) do not exist,” it refers to when the entire Saṅgha incurs a light offense (lahukāpatti) due to a common basis such as eating at the wrong time; such an offense with a common basis is called a common offense (sabhāgā). Whether such common offenses do not exist or even if they do exist, it is still considered appropriate (pattakalla).

In the phrase “excluded persons are not present therein,” based on the statement, “Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly that includes laypeople” (Mahāva. 154), it includes laypeople; and by the method stated as “Monks, the Pātimokkha should not be recited in an assembly where a bhikkhunī is sitting” (Mahāva. 183), it includes a bhikkhunī, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), a female novice (sāmaṇerī), one who has renounced the training, one who has committed an ultimate offense (pārājika), one suspended for not seeing an offense, one suspended for not atoning for an offense, one suspended for not relinquishing a sinful view, a pandaka, one living by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka), one who has gone over to another sect (titthiyapakkantaka), an animal (such as non-humans like devas, nāgas, garuḍas), ...
214:
A matricide, a patricide, a killer of an Arahant, a violator of a bhikkhunī, a schismatic, one who sheds the blood of a Buddha, and a hermaphrodite—these twenty persons and the one previously mentioned, totaling twenty-one persons, are to be known as those who must be excluded. They should be excluded by keeping them outside the hatthapāsa (physical reach). Among these, if the Saṅgha performs the Uposatha while the three types of suspended persons (ukkhittaka) are present, they incur a pācittiya offense. If any of the remaining eighteen persons are present, they incur a dukkaṭa offense. Here, 'animal' (tiracchānagata) refers to non-humans (amanussa) such as devas, nāgas, and garuḍas whose higher ordination is prohibited. Heretics (titthiya) are included under the term 'laypeople' (gahaṭṭha). These persons must also be excluded. Thus, it should be understood that the Uposatha is valid (pattakalla) only when it is comprised of these four factors. All these decisions should also be applied to the Pavāraṇā ceremony. According to the words: 'Monks, the reciter of the Pātimokkha should not intentionally fail to make the assembly hear; whoever does not make them hear, commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Monks, I allow the reciter of the Pātimokkha to strive, thinking, "How can I make them hear?" There is no offense for one who strives' (Mahāvagga, 154), the reciter of the Pātimokkha must strive to make the assembly hear.

## Thus ends the Manual of Vinaya Decisions Extracted from the Pali (Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha).
## The Discussion on the Decisions regarding Uposatha and Pavāraṇā is finished.

## 26. Discussion on the Decisions regarding Entering the Rainy Season Retreat (Vassūpanāyika)

In the term 'Vassūpanāyika', there are two types of entering the rainy season retreat: the Early Vassa (purimikā) and the Late Vassa (pacchimikā). Among these, the Early Vassa should be entered on the day after the full moon of Āsāḷha, which is the first day of the waning moon (paṭipada). The Late Vassa should be entered on the day after the full moon following the Āsāḷha full moon (i.e., the full moon of Sāvaṇa), which is the first day of the waning moon. A monk entering the Vassa should prepare the monastery, set out drinking and utility water, complete the duties of respect (sāmīcikamma) such as worshipping the cetiya, and then enter the Vassa by reciting once, twice, or thrice: 'I enter the Vassa in this monastery for these three months.' Even if he fails to enter the Vassa due to forgetfulness, if he has the intent (ālaya) thinking 'I will reside here,' the lodging he has taken is considered well-taken; his Vassa is not broken, and he is entitled to perform the Pavāraṇā. This is because even without a verbal recitation, the Vassa is entered merely by having the intent (ālaya). Here, the arising of the thought 'I will reside for the Vassa here' is indeed called intent (ālaya).
215:
'Monks, one who does not wish to enter the Vassa on the day of entering the Vassa should not intentionally cross over the monastery boundary; whoever crosses over, commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)' (Mahāvagga, 186). According to these words, if one crosses the monastery boundary (sīmā) on the day of entering the Vassa with the intention of not entering the Vassa, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense for each monastery. If on that day he enters and crosses the precincts (upacāra) of a hundred monasteries, he incurs a hundred offenses. However, if he crosses a monastery and turns back without entering the precinct of another monastery, he incurs only one offense. A monk who is unable to enter the Early Vassa due to some obstacle must enter the Late Vassa.

'Monks, one should not enter the Vassa without a lodging (senāsana); whoever enters, commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)' (Mahāvagga, 204). According to these words, a monk who does not have a lodging roofed with one of the five types of roofing and fitted with a door should not enter the Vassa. According to the words: 'Monks, one should not enter the Vassa in a chavakuṭikā; whoever enters, commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa),' etc., it is not permissible to enter the Vassa in a chavakuṭikā, under an umbrella, or in a large pot. In this context, a chavakuṭikā is a hut made of an eight-legged couch or similar items. While it is not permissible to enter the Vassa in such a place, it is permissible to enter the Vassa in another small hut constructed in a cemetery. Regarding the umbrella, it is permissible to enter the Vassa if the umbrella is placed on four posts, screened around, and fitted with a door; this is called an umbrella-hut (chattakuṭī). Regarding the pot, it is permissible to enter the Vassa by making a small hut with a large pot-shard in the same manner as described for the umbrella.

'Monks, one should not enter the Vassa in a tree hollow; whoever enters, commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).' According to these words, it is not permissible to enter the Vassa in a plain tree hollow. However, it is permissible to enter the Vassa if a small hut with a plank roof is made inside a large tree hollow and fitted with an entrance door. It is also permissible to cut a tree and make a small hut with a plank roof on top of the stump. According to the words: 'Monks, [one should not enter the Vassa] in the fork of a tree,' etc., it is not permissible to enter the Vassa in a plain tree fork. However, one should enter the Vassa by binding a platform (aṭṭaka) on a large tree fork, making a small hut with a plank roof on it, and fitting it with a door.

'Monks, I allow you to enter the Vassa in a cattle pen (vaja),' etc. According to these words, it is permissible to enter the Vassa in a cattle pen, a caravan (sattha), or a boat (nāva). In this context, 'vaja' refers to the dwelling place of herdsmen. If a monk who has gone along with the cattle pen when it moves breaks his Vassa, there is no offense, as it is said: 'Monks, I allow you to go wherever the cattle pen goes' (Mahāvagga, 203).
216:
A monk entering the rains retreat (vassa) in a caravan (sattha) should say to the lay supporters on the day of entering the vassa: "It is proper to obtain a hut (kuṭī)." If they build and provide one, he should enter that hut and say three times: "I enter the rains retreat here." If they do not provide one, he should enter the rains retreat under a wagon (sakaṭa) that stands in the form of a hall (sālā). If he does not obtain even such a wagon, he should make a mental resolution (ālaya). It is not proper to enter the rains retreat among the caravan (among the people themselves). What is called 'ālaya' is the mere arising of the thought (without verbal recitation): "I will reside in this caravan for the three months of the rains."

If the day of Pavāraṇā occurs while the caravan is still on the journey, the Pavāraṇā should be performed in that very caravan. If the caravan reaches the monk's desired destination during the rains and then moves on, he should remain at the desired destination and perform Pavāraṇā together with the monks there. If the caravan stops at a village along the way before reaching the destination during the rains, or if it disperses, he should remain in that village and perform Pavāraṇā with the monks; it is not proper to go elsewhere without performing Pavāraṇā.

A monk entering the rains retreat on a boat (nāvā) should also enter the retreat only in a hut (on the boat). If he cannot find one after searching, he should make a mental resolution (ālaya). If the boat remains at sea for the entire three months of the rains, the Pavāraṇā should be performed on that very boat. If the boat reaches the shore and the monk wishes to go elsewhere, he must not go; he should stay in the village where the boat docked and perform Pavāraṇā with the monks. Even if the boat travels elsewhere along the coast, if the monk wishes to stay in the village first reached, let the boat go; the monk should stay in that village and perform Pavāraṇā with the monks. Thus, in these three places—the cattle-pen (vaja), the caravan (sattha), and the boat (nāvā)—there is no offense for the breaking of the rains retreat, and one receives the opportunity to perform Pavāraṇā.

Because of the words, "Monks, having entered the rains retreat, one should not set out on a journey without having resided for either the first three months or the last three months; for him who sets out, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)," a monk who has entered the first rains (purimikā) must not set out on a journey without residing for the first three months, and one who has entered the later rains (pacchimikā) must not set out without residing for the later months. If a monk who has entered the rains sets out on a seven-day business (sattāhakaraṇīya) on that very day even before dawn, there is no offense if he can return within seven days. What then need be said of one who stays for two or three days and then sets out on a seven-day business, returning within seven days (there is no offense).

"Monks, I allow you to go on the seven-day business when sent for by seven classes of persons, but not when not sent for. For a monk, a nun, a female trainee..."
217:
"...for a male novice, a female novice, a male lay follower, or a female lay follower." According to these words, if any of the five fellow-dhamma-practitioners (sahadhammikas) has built—either for the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, or for their own benefit—a monastery (vihāra), a half-roofed house (aḍḍhayoga), a long mansion (pāsāda), a flat-roofed mansion (hammiya), a cave (guhā), an enclosure (pariveṇa), a gatehouse (koṭṭhaka), an assembly hall (upaṭṭhānasālā), a fire room (aggisālā), an allowable hut (kappiyakuṭi), a toilet (vaccakuṭi), a cloister (caṅkama), a cloister hall (caṅkamanasālā), a well (udapāna), a well-shed (udapānasālā), a sauna (jantāghara), a sauna-shed (jantāgharasālā), a lotus pond (pokkharaṇī), a pavilion (maṇḍapa), a park (ārāma), or the site for a park (ārāmavatthu), and sends word saying, "May the venerable ones come; I wish to give gifts, to hear the Dhamma, and to see the monks," then one should go on a seven-day business (sattāhakaraṇīya); but one should not go if not sent for. Similarly, if a male or female lay follower has built any of the monasteries etc. for the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, or has built for their own benefit any of the dwellings, beds, or houses etc., or specifies any other business to be done, or becomes ill and sends a messenger to the monks saying, "May the venerable ones come; I wish to give gifts, to hear the Dhamma, and to see the monks," then one should go on a seven-day business; but one should not go if not sent for.

According to the words, "Monks, I allow you to go on a seven-day business to the seven classes of persons even if not invited, much more so if invited: for a monk, a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, a female novice, and for one's mother and father," one should go even if not invited for the following reason: "I will search for, or inquire about, or nurse with food for the sick (gilānabhatta), or food for the attendant (gilānupaṭṭhākabhatta), or medicine for these sick fellow-dhamma-practitioners such as monks, and for one's sick parents." If invited, what need is there to say? However, in the Andhaka Commentary (Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā), it is said, "It is proper to go even if not invited to those who nurse one's parents, whether they are relatives or non-relatives." Since that statement is found neither in the (Mahā) Commentary nor in the Pali, it should not be accepted.

If a monk's brother or another relative is sick and sends a messenger to the monk saying, "I am sick; may the venerable one come; I wish for the venerable one's arrival," then one should go on a seven-day business; but one should not go if not sent for. If a person who is devoted to the monks and lives with them in the same monastery becomes sick and sends a messenger to the monks saying, "I am sick; may the monks come; I wish for the monks' arrival," then one should go on a seven-day business; but one should not go if not sent for.
218:
If dissatisfaction (anabhirati), remorse (kukkucca), or wrong view (diṭṭhigata) arises in a monk, a nun, a female trainee (sikkhamānā), a male novice (sāmaṇera), or a female novice (sāmaṇerī), one may go with the intention: 'I will dispel or cause to be dispelled the dissatisfaction; I will remove or cause to be removed the remorse; I will clear away or cause to be cleared away the wrong view; or I will give a Dhamma talk,' even if not invited, provided it is for a seven-day business. If invited, it goes without saying. If a certain monk has committed a grave offense (garu-āpatti) and is worthy of probation (parivāsa), sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanā), penance (mānatta), or rehabilitation (abbhāna), one may go even if not invited, thinking: 'I will exert effort in giving probation, etc., I will recite the formal act, or I will be one who completes the quorum (gaṇapūraka).' If invited, it goes without saying. The same rule applies to nuns who are worthy of penance, sending back to the beginning, or rehabilitation. If a male novice wishes to be ordained or to ask about his years (vassa), or if a female trainee wishes to be ordained or her training is impaired, or if a female novice wishes to take up the training or ask about her years, one may go even if not invited. If invited, it goes without saying.

If the Sangha wishes to carry out a formal act against a monk or a nun—be it an act of censure (tajjaniya-kamma), subordination (niyassa-kamma), banishment (pabbājaniya-kamma), reconciliation (paṭisāraṇīya-kamma), or suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma)—one may go even if not invited, thinking: 'How might the Sangha not carry out the act, or change it to a lighter one?' If invited, it goes without saying. Even if the act has already been carried out, one may go even if not invited, thinking: 'How might he conduct himself properly, show humility (literally: drop his bristles), perform the duties of one undergoing penance (nettāraṃ vatteyya), and how might the Sangha revoke that act?'

According to the words, 'I allow you, monks, to go on Sangha business' (Mahāvagga 199), it is also proper to go for Sangha business connected with lodgings. In this regard, whatever needs to be done for the Uposatha halls, etc., for the lodgings, or for the shrines (cetiya), umbrellas, railings (vedikā), etc.—even down to a monk's private lodging—all is intended as Sangha business. Therefore, one may go to bring building materials, etc., for its completion, or to provide food and wages to carpenters and so on. Furthermore, in this matter, this method not directly mentioned in the Pāli (pāḷimuttaka-naya) should also be known: one should not go for the purpose of listening to the Dhamma without being invited. However, if in a large monastery an agreement (katikā) was made beforehand, saying, 'We shall assemble on such and such a day' for the purpose of performing duties, it is considered as being invited, and it is proper to go.
219:
If it is agreed, 'We should assemble on such and such a day,' it is indeed called being invited; it is proper to go. It is not proper to go with the thought, 'I will wash my belongings (robes).' However, if the teacher (ācariya) or preceptor (upajjhāya) sends one, it is proper. If the monastery is not too far, but one cannot reach it and return on the same day, it is proper to go (using the seven-day rule). Although one is not permitted to go for the sake of recitation (uddesa), inquiry (paripucchā), etc., one is permitted to go with the thought, 'I will see my teacher.' If the teacher says to that monk, 'Do not go today yet,' it is proper (to stay). One is not permitted to go to visit a family of supporters or a family of relatives.

If, after the monks have entered the rains retreat (vassūpagata), the alms-village is destroyed by bandits, what should be done then? One should go to wherever the villagers have moved. If the village splits into two, one should go where the majority of people are. If the majority are faithless and lack devotion, one should go where there are people with faith and devotion. In this case, if the village has moved to a place not far away, one should go to that village for alms and return to stay in the monastery itself. If they have moved far away, one should spend the dawn by returning within seven days. If that is not possible, one should stay in a suitable place in that very village. If the people offer food by tickets (salākabhatta), etc., as they did before, they should be told, 'We no longer stay in that monastery.' But if they say, 'We do not give to the monastery or the palace; we give only to you; please stay and eat wherever you like,' then one may eat as one pleases; that food belongs only to those monks.
