If they say, 'Please have it brought to the place where you stay and eat,' then it should be brought to the place of residence and eaten according to seniority (vassaggena). If, at the time of Pavāraṇā, they offer rains-residence gifts (vassāvāsika), they should be accepted if the monks spent the dawn within the seven-day limit. Monks whose rains retreat was broken (chinnavassa) should say, 'We did not stay in that monastery; we are those whose rains retreat is broken.' If the donors say, 'Let the venerable ones who have come to our monastery accept it,' then it should be accepted. As for distributable goods (vebhaṅgiya-bhaṇḍa) such as robes brought here with the thought, 'Let not the property deposited in the monastery be destroyed,' one should go to that very monastery, ask permission (apaloketvā), and distribute them. The same rule applies to the produce from fields, lands, etc., entrusted to lay attendants (kappiyakāraka) with the instruction, 'Provide the four requisites to the venerable ones from this.' Whether the communal distributable goods are inside the monastery or outside the boundary (sīmā), it is not proper to distribute them by asking permission from monks staying outside the boundary. However, even if the goods are in both places, it is indeed proper to distribute them by asking permission from the monks staying within the boundary.
220:
If monks who have entered the Rains Retreat are harassed by wild beasts, which might seize or pursue them; or if they are harassed by snakes and reptiles, which might bite or pursue them; or if they are harassed by thieves, who might rob or strike them; or if they are harassed by spirits (pisāca), who might possess or harm (oppress) them; thinking, "This is indeed a danger," they may depart. There is no offense for breaking the retreat.

If the village where they collect alms is burnt by fire or swept away by water, and the monks suffer for lack of almsfood, thinking, "This is indeed a danger," they may depart. Even if the retreat is broken, there is no offense. If the lodgings (senāsana) are burnt by fire or swept away by water, and the monks suffer for lack of lodgings, thinking, "This is indeed a danger," they may depart. Even if the retreat is broken, there is no offense.

If monks who have entered the Rains Retreat do not obtain a sufficient amount of either coarse or fine food as they desire, thinking, "This is indeed a danger," they may depart. If they obtain a sufficient amount of coarse or fine food as they desire, but do not obtain suitable food (sappāya), thinking, "This is indeed a danger," they may depart. If they obtain a sufficient amount of coarse or fine food as they desire and obtain suitable food, but do not obtain suitable medicines, thinking, "This is indeed a danger," they may depart. If they obtain a sufficient amount of coarse or fine food as they desire, obtain suitable food, and obtain suitable medicines, but do not obtain a proper attendant (upaṭṭhāka), thinking, "This is indeed a danger," they may depart. In all these cases, there is no offense for breaking the retreat.

If a woman invites a monk who has entered the Rains Retreat, saying, "Come, Bhante, I will give you silver, or gold, or a field, or a plot of land, or a bull, or a cow, or a male slave, or a female slave; or I will give you my daughter to be your wife, or I myself will be your wife, or I will bring you another wife," and if that monk thinks, "The Blessed One has said that the mind is easily changed; this might be a danger to my holy life (brahmacariya)," he may depart. There is no offense for breaking the retreat. In the same manner as described, if a courtesan invites him, or a widow invites him, or a eunuch (paṇḍaka) invites him, or relatives invite him, or kings invite him, or thieves invite him, or drunkards invite him, the same rule applies. If a monk who has entered the Rains Retreat sees an ownerless treasure, and if that monk thinks, "The Blessed One has said that the mind is easily changed; this might be a danger to my holy life (brahmacariya)," he may depart. There is no offense for breaking the retreat.
221:
If a monk who has entered the Rains Retreat sees many monks striving to cause a schism in the Saṅgha, or hears that "many monks are striving to cause a schism in the Saṅgha," and if that monk thinks, "The Blessed One has said that a schism in the Saṅgha is a very grave matter; let not the Saṅgha be divided while I am present," he may depart. Even if the retreat is broken, there is no offense. If a monk who has entered the Rains Retreat hears that "in such and such a monastery, many monks are striving to cause a schism in the Saṅgha," and if that monk thinks, "Those monks are my friends; I will say to them, 'Friends, the Blessed One has said that a schism in the Saṅgha is a grave matter; do not let a schism in the Saṅgha be pleasing to you.' They will follow my words, they will listen, they will pay attention," he may depart. Even if the retreat is broken, there is no offense. However, once the Saṅgha has already been divided, there is no purpose in going.

If any monk, having been told, "Stay for the retreat here for these three months," gives his word but then fails to fulfill it, he commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). It is not only in failing to fulfill that specific promise that he commits a wrongdoing; if he fails to fulfill various promises such as, "Accept alms for these three months; we shall both stay for the retreat here; we shall learn the texts together," he also commits an offense of wrongdoing. Such a wrongdoing occurs when one initially has a pure mind but later fails to fulfill the promise. However, if one gives his word with an impure mind from the very beginning, he commits an offense of expiation (pācittiya). The statement that failing to fulfill the promise results in a wrongdoing means that a wrongdoing is incurred along with the pācittiya.

Monks who have entered the Rains Retreat, setting aside the regular major and minor duties to be performed during the retreat, should be told, "Bind brooms." If broom-sticks and broom-twigs are easily available, each monk should bind six or five hand-brooms, or two or three long-handled brooms. If they are difficult to find, two or three hand-brooms and one long-handled broom should be bound. The novices (sāmaṇeras) should each make five torches. In the living quarters, a dye-finish (kāsāva-paribhaṇḍa) should be applied. While performing these duties, monks should not teach the texts, nor have them taught; they should not engage in recitation, nor perform ordinations (as novices or monks), nor give dependence (nissaya), nor listen to Dhamma. This is because all these are impediments (papañca). Saying, "We shall practice the monk's Dhamma without impediments," let them all undertake the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). Without taking sleep, let them spend the time standing or walking. Let them practice the vow of silence (mūgavata). May those monks who go on the seven-day business (sattāha-karaṇīya) also receive their allocated goods. Such an unrighteous duty...
222:
One should not perform such an unrighteous practice as saying, "Let the monks who have departed also receive the distributed goods." Rather, this should be done: The Pariyatti Dhamma establishes the threefold Saddhamma (True Dhamma); therefore, teach and have others taught, and perform recitations with respect. Without causing disturbance to those living in the meditation houses (padhānaghara), sit within the monastery and teach, have others taught, perform recitations, and fulfill the hearing of the Dhamma. When giving the novice ordination (pabbajjā), do so after careful investigation; when giving the higher ordination (upasampadā), do so after careful investigation; when giving dependence (nissaya), do so after careful investigation. For even a single son of good family, having obtained the novice and higher ordinations, can establish the entire Dispensation (Sāsana). Undertake as many ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) as you are able to according to your own strength. Throughout this entire rainy season (vassa), one should be diligent and exert effort during the whole day, as well as during the first and last watches of the night. The ancient Great Elders (Mahātheras), having cut off all impediments (palibodha), fulfilled the practice of solitary dwelling during the rainy season. Knowing the proper measure in speech, it is appropriate to speak on the ten subjects of talk (dasavatthukathā), the ten talks on foulness (asubhakathā), the ten talks on recollections (anussatikathā), and the thirty-eight subjects of meditation (ārammaṇakathā). It is proper to perform duties for visiting monks and to give to those who have departed on a seven-day business (sattāha-karaṇīya) after they have asked for leave; such duties should be performed.

Furthermore, monks should be exhorted: "Do not speak words of contention, slander, or harshness. Reflecting on your virtues (sīla) every day, do not neglect the Four Protections (caturārakkha), and dwell with much systematic attention (manasikāra)." The duty of using the tooth-stick should be explained. When worshipping a shrine (cetīya) or a Bodhi tree, when offering perfumes and flowers, or when putting the alms-bowl into its bag, one should not speak. The duty of the alms-round should be explained. Within the village, one should not speak with people about matters concerning requisites or unsuitable matters. One should dwell with guarded faculties. The duties of the Khandhakas and the Sekhiyas should be fulfilled. In this way, many kinds of talk leading out of suffering (niyyānika-kathā) should be explained.

## Thus in the Pālimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha,
## The Discussion on the Decision regarding the Commencement of the Rainy Season is finished.
223:
## 27. Discussion on the Decision regarding the Duties toward Preceptors and Others

Regarding duties (vatta), there are many kinds, such as: the duty toward the preceptor (upajjhāya-vatta), the duty toward the teacher (ācariya-vatta), the duty toward the guest (āgantuka-vatta), the duty toward the resident (āvāsika-vatta), the duty toward the departing monk (gamika-vatta), the duty regarding the refectory (bhattagga-vatta), the duty regarding the alms-round (piṇḍacārika-vatta), the duty regarding the forest-dweller (āraññika-vatta), the duty regarding the lodging (senāsana-vatta), the duty regarding the sauna (jantāghara-vatta), and the duty regarding the latrine (vaccakuṭi-vatta). Among these, the duty toward the preceptor should first be understood thus: The co-resident (saddhivihārika) should rise early, remove his sandals, place his upper robe over one shoulder, and offer the tooth-wood and face-washing water to the preceptor. In offering the tooth-wood, he should present three kinds—large, medium, and small—and whichever of these the preceptor takes for three days, from the fourth day onwards, he should offer only that kind. If the preceptor takes any kind without a fixed preference, then he should offer whatever is available. The one offering face-washing water should also present both cold and hot water, and whichever the preceptor uses for three days, from the fourth day onwards, he should offer only that kind of face-washing water. If he uses both, then both should be presented. Having placed the water at the face-washing place, he should sweep starting from the latrine. When the elder has gone to the latrine, the courtyard should be swept; by sweeping thus, the courtyard is not left neglected. Before the elder comes out of the latrine, the seat should be prepared. When the preceptor has performed his bodily needs and come to sit on that seat, if there is congee (yāgu), the vessel should be washed and the congee offered. When he has finished drinking the congee, water should be given, the vessel received, placed low, and washed carefully without clattering, then put away. When the preceptor rises from the seat, the seat should be removed. If that place is dirty, being strewn with any rubbish, that place should be swept. If there is no other rubbish but only water drops, it should be wiped with the hand.

If the preceptor wishes to enter the village for alms, the lower robe for the village should be given, and the dwelling robe should be received. The waist-belt should be given. The double-layered outer robes should be given. The bowl should be washed and given along with water. If the preceptor desires an attendant monk (pacchāsamaṇa), the attendant, covering the three circles, should dress neatly, fasten the waist-belt, put on the double-layered outer robes, fasten the button, wash and take the bowl, and become the preceptor's attendant. He should walk neither too far nor too close. In this regard, it should be understood that if he can reach the preceptor in one or two strides when the preceptor turns back to look, he is walking at a distance that is neither too far nor too close.
224:
If the preceptor (upajjhāya), while collecting alms, receives congee or rice and the bowl becomes hot or heavy, the student should give his own bowl to the teacher and take the teacher's bowl. One should not interrupt the preceptor while he is speaking. From here on, wherever a prohibition is made with the word 'na' (not), it should be understood that a dukkaṭa offense is incurred for all such duties. If the preceptor speaks in a way that borders on an offense, he should be restrained. When restraining him, it should be done as if asking a question: "Venerable Sir, is it proper to speak like this? Does it not lead to an offense?" One should not say, "Old man, do not speak like this," with the intention of restraining him.

If the village is nearby, or if there is a sick monk in the monastery, one should return from the village earlier. If the village is far and there is no one else coming with the preceptor, one should leave the village with him, wrap the bowl with the robe on the way, and return earlier than the preceptor. Upon arriving earlier, one should prepare the seat, and place the water for washing feet, the footstool, and the foot-scrubber nearby. One should go out to meet him and take the bowl and robe. Give him the robe for changing and take the village-entry robe. If the robe is damp with sweat, it should be dried in the sun for a moment. Do not leave the robe in the sun for long. The robe should be folded. When folding the robe, one should fold it by moving the corner about four finger-breadths away. Why? To prevent a crease from forming in the middle. If folded with the edges even, a crease forms in the middle, and from there it always breaks and becomes weak. This was said to prevent such weakness. Therefore, to prevent it from breaking tomorrow at the same place it was folded today, it should be folded daily by moving it four finger-breadths. The waist-band should be placed inside the fold of the robe.

If there is alms-food and the preceptor wishes to eat, one should offer water and present the food. The preceptor should be asked about drinking water. When asking, one should ask up to three times: "Venerable Sir, may I bring drinking water?" If there is still time, one should eat after the preceptor has finished. If time is short, one should place the water near the preceptor and eat oneself. After he has eaten, give him water, take the bowl, hold it low, and wash it carefully without bumping it. After making it dry, dry it in the sun for a moment. Do not leave the bowl in the sun for long. The bowl and robe should be stored. The bowl...
225:
When storing the bowl, one should hold the bowl with one hand and feel under the couch or under the bench with the other hand before placing it. The bowl should not be placed on the ground without a covering such as a mat or a piece of leather. However, if the ground is prepared with a black finish, or plastered, or is free of dust, it is proper to place it on such ground. It is also proper to place it on clean sand. It is not proper on dust, dirt, or gravel. In such places, one should spread a leaf or a bowl-stand and place it on top.

When storing the robe, one should hold the robe with one hand and wipe the robe-pole or robe-rope with the other hand, then place the robe with the edge on the far side and the fold on the near side. This was said for the purpose of inserting the hand under the robe-pole etc., and placing it gently with the hand facing forward. If one holds the edge and throws the fold over the robe-pole, the fold might hit the wall; therefore, it should not be done that way. When the preceptor has risen, the seat should be put away, and the water for washing feet, the footstool, and the foot-scrubber should be stored. If that place is dirty, it should be swept and cleaned.

If the preceptor wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared. If he needs cold water, cold water should be prepared. If he needs hot water, hot water should be prepared.

If the preceptor wishes to enter the sauna (jantāghara), the bath powder should be kneaded with water, and the clay should be moistened. Taking the sauna-stool, one should follow behind the preceptor and give him the stool. Take his robe and place it in a smoke-free area. Give him the powder and the clay. If one is able, one should enter the sauna. When entering, one should smear the face with clay and cover oneself in front and behind before entering. One should not sit crowding the elder monks, nor should one deny a seat to the junior monks. In the sauna, one should perform duties for the preceptor. Duties in the sauna mean all tasks such as providing embers, clay, and hot water. When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-stool and cover oneself in front and behind before leaving.

In the water too, one should perform duties such as scrubbing the preceptor's limbs. After he has bathed, one should come out first, dry one's own body, put on the under-robe, and then wipe the water from the preceptor's body. Give him the under-robe and the double-robe (saṅghāṭi)...
226:
The saṅghāṭi (outer robe) should be handed over. The sauna-bench should be brought first and the seat prepared. Water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-scrubber should be placed nearby. The upajjhāya (preceptor) should be asked if he wants drinking water, for thirst often arises in the sauna due to the heat. If he wishes to be taught the Pali, it should be taught. If he wishes to ask about the Commentaries, they should be answered.

If the dwelling where the upajjhāya stays is dirty, if one is able and not overcome by any illness, it should be cleaned. A saddhivihārika who is not ill, even if he has sixty years of standing (vassa), must perform all duties for the upajjhāya. For one who does not perform them out of disrespect, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Regarding the rules containing the word 'na' (prohibitions), even if one is ill, if one performs the forbidden act, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

When cleaning the dwelling, first the bowl and robes should be taken out and placed to one side. The sitting mat and the coverlet should be taken out and placed to one side. The mattress and pillow should be taken out and placed to one side. The bed should be lowered and carefully taken out, without scraping or knocking against the door-posts or the door-leaves, and placed to one side. The chair should be lowered and carefully taken out, without scraping or knocking against the door-posts or the door-leaves, and placed to one side. The bed-supports should be taken out and placed to one side. The spittoon should be taken out and placed to one side. The backrest should be taken out and placed to one side. The floor covering should be noted as to how it was laid, then taken out and placed to one side.

If there are cobwebs in the dwelling, they should first be removed starting from the ceiling. The window-slits and corners should be wiped. If the wall treated with red ochre is moldy, it should be wiped with a cloth that has been moistened and wrung out. If the floor treated with black coloring is moldy, it should be wiped with a cloth that has been moistened and wrung out. If the floor is untreated earth, it should be sprinkled with water and swept, thinking, 'Let not the dwelling be soiled with dust.' The rubbish should be collected and thrown away to one side.

The floor covering should be dried in the sun, cleaned, shaken out, brought back, and laid down exactly as it was laid before. It is for this purpose that it was said: 'The floor covering should be noted as to how it was laid, then taken out and placed to one side.' If, however, it was laid by someone who did not know how to do it first, it should be laid leaving a space of about two or three finger-breadths from the wall all around. In this dwelling, this is...
227: The duty of preparing [the room]: If a mat is very large, it should be cut, the edge folded back, tied, and then spread out. If one does not know how to fold and tie the edge, it should not be cut. The bed-legs should be dried in the sun, wiped, and placed in their proper positions. The bed (mañca) should be dried in the sun, cleaned, shaken out, lowered, and carried carefully without scratching or striking the doorframe, and then spread out as it was prepared. The chair (pīṭha) should be dried in the sun, cleaned, shaken out, lowered, and carried carefully without scratching or striking the doorframe, and then spread out as it was prepared. The bolster and pillow should be dried in the sun, cleaned, shaken out, carried, and spread out as they were prepared. The sitting mat and the floor-covering should be dried in the sun, cleaned, shaken out, carried, and spread out as they were prepared. The spittoon should be dried in the sun, wiped, carried, and placed in its proper position. The leaning board should be dried in the sun, wiped, carried, and placed in its proper position. The alms-bowl and robes should be stored. When storing the alms-bowl, one should hold the bowl with one hand and feel under the bed or chair with the other hand before placing the bowl; the bowl should not be placed on the bare ground without a base. When storing the robe, one should hold the robe with one hand and wipe the robe-rail or robe-cord with the other hand; then, placing the edge on the far side and the fold on the near side, the robe should be laid down. If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed. If dusty winds blow from the west, north, or south, the southern windows should be closed. If it is the cold season, the windows should be opened during the day and closed at night. If it is the hot season, they should be closed during the day and opened at night. If there is dirt, the courtyard should be swept, the porch should be swept, the service hall should be swept, the fire-room should be swept, and the latrine should be swept. Drinking water and water for use should be set out. Water should be poured into the pot for washing. If dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arises in the preceptor (upajjhāya), the co-resident (saddhivihārika) should take him elsewhere, or another monk should be told, "Please take the elder elsewhere," or a Dhamma talk should be given to him. If doubt (kukkucca) arises in the preceptor, the co-resident should dispel it himself or have it dispelled by another.
228:
A Dhamma talk should be given to that preceptor. If a wrong view arises in the preceptor, the resident pupil should resolve it; or he should tell another, "Please make the elder give up his wrong view," or a Dhamma talk should be given to him. If the preceptor has committed a grave offense and is deserving of probation (parivāsa), the resident pupil should make an effort, approaching various monks and requesting them to grant the probation. If he is capable himself, he should grant it himself. If he is not capable, he should have another grant it. If the preceptor is deserving of being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanā), or is deserving of penance (mānatta) or rehabilitation (abbhāna), he should make an effort in the same manner as mentioned.

If the Sangha desires to carry out a formal act against the preceptor—whether an act of censure (tajjaniyakamma), an act of subordination (niyassakamma), an act of banishment (pabbājaniyakamma), an act of reconciliation (paṭisāraṇiyakamma), or an act of suspension (ukkhepaniyakamma)—the resident pupil should make an effort, thinking, "By what means might the Sangha not carry out the act against the preceptor, or how might it be changed to a lighter act?" If the resident pupil knows, "The Sangha desires to carry out an act of suspension against the preceptor," he should approach each monk and request, "Venerable sirs, please do not carry out the act against our preceptor." If they still carry it out, he should request, "Please carry out only a light act, such as an act of censure or an act of subordination." If they still carry it out, then he should request the preceptor, "Venerable sir, please conduct yourself properly." Having thus made him conduct himself properly, he should request the monks, "Venerable sirs, please revoke the act that has been carried out."

If the preceptor's robe needs to be washed, the resident pupil should wash it; or he should make an effort, thinking, "How might the preceptor's robe be washed?" If the preceptor's robe needs to be made, or the dye needs to be boiled, or the robe needs to be dyed, the resident pupil should do it all; or he should make an effort, thinking, "How might the preceptor's robe be dyed?" When dyeing the robe, he should dye it by turning it over well, and he should not leave until the drips have ceased.

Without asking the preceptor, he should not give a bowl to anyone, nor should he receive a bowl from anyone. He should not give a robe to anyone, nor should he receive a robe from anyone. He should not give a requisite to anyone, nor should he receive a requisite from anyone. He should not cut the hair for anyone, nor should he have his hair cut by anyone.
229: He should not have (his hair) cut. He should not perform personal services for anyone (who is incompatible with the teacher), nor should he have personal services performed by anyone. He should not perform chores for anyone, nor should he have chores performed by anyone. He should not become the attendant monk of anyone, nor should he take anyone as an attendant monk. He should not fetch almsfood for anyone, nor should he have almsfood fetched by anyone. Without asking the preceptor, he should not enter a village. If he wishes to enter for almsfood or for some other business, he should enter only after asking permission. If the preceptor, having risen early, wishes to go to a distant place for alms, he should go after saying, "You young monks, enter for alms." If he has gone without saying so, the pupil, having gone to the teacher's compound and not seeing the preceptor, is allowed to enter the village. If he sees him even while entering the village, he is allowed to enter only after asking permission from the place where he saw him. Without asking the preceptor, he should not go to a cemetery to stay there or to contemplate a corpse. He should not depart for another region. If he wishes to depart, he should explain the reason and ask permission up to three times. If he grants permission, it is well. If he does not grant permission, yet for the pupil living in dependence on that preceptor, his recitation, inquiry, or meditation subject does not prosper, or if the preceptor is foolish and incompetent and refuses permission to go merely out of a desire to keep the pupil near him—in such cases, it is allowed to go even if the teacher forbids it. If the preceptor is ill, he should be cared for as long as he lives; he should wait until he recovers; he should not go anywhere. If there is another monk as an attendant, he should seek medicine, hand it over to that monk, and say, "Venerable sir, this monk will care for you," and then he may go. This is the duty towards a preceptor (upajjhāyavatta). This same duty is called the duty towards a teacher (ācariyavatta) because it is to be performed by a pupil (antevāsika) for his teacher (ācariya). Here, there is a difference only in name. Among those duties, if the duties up to the dyeing of robes are not performed, it is a loss for the preceptor and the teacher. Therefore, for one who does not perform them, whether he is free from dependence (nissayamuttaka) or not, there is an offense. From the giving of a bowl to anyone onwards, there is an offense only for one who is not yet free from dependence. If the preceptor or the teacher accepts the performance of the duties, even if there are many resident pupils and pupils, there is an offense for all of them. If the preceptor or the teacher says, "I have an attendant; you should apply yourselves only to your own recitation, reflection, and so on," there is no offense for the resident pupils and others. Whether the preceptor or the teacher accepts or does not accept...
230:
If the preceptor or the teacher says, "I have those who attend to me; you should only strive in your own recitation, reflection, and so forth," then there is no offense for the co-residents. If the teacher, being like a fool, does not know [whether duties are performed], and among many co-residents, one monk who is accomplished in duties says, "I will perform the duties of the preceptor or the teacher; you may remain unconcerned," and thus takes the burden upon himself and excuses the others, then from the time he takes the burden, there is no offense for the other students. Among these pupils, the pupil in dependence (nissaya-antevāsika) must perform all the duties of the teacher for as long as he lives in dependence on the teacher. The pupils of the teacher who gave the going-forth (pabbajjā), the teacher who gave the higher ordination (upasampadā), and the teacher who teaches the Dhamma (dhamma-antevāsika) must perform the duties from the beginning until the dyeing of robes, even if they are released from dependence. However, there is no offense for these three types of pupils in such matters as giving a bowl without asking permission.

Among these pupils, the pupil of the teacher who gave the going-forth and the pupil of the teacher who gave the higher ordination are burdens for the teacher for as long as they live. As for the pupil in dependence and the pupil in Dhamma, for as long as they live nearby, the teachers and preceptors must also support and assist the pupils and co-residents; they must be constantly looked after through instruction, questioning, advice, and repeated admonition. If the pupils or co-residents do not have a bowl, a robe, or any other requisite, and if the teacher has an extra bowl, robe, or requisite, it must be given. If he does not have any, he must make an effort to seek them by righteous means. If the pupils or co-residents are ill, all duties must be performed, starting from providing a tooth-stick to pouring water into the rinsing jar, as mentioned in the duties of a preceptor; if they do not do so, there is an offense. Therefore, teachers and preceptors must also conduct themselves properly toward their pupils and co-residents. Whoever does not conduct himself properly toward teachers, preceptors, and so forth, incurs an offense.

## The Discussion on the Duties of Preceptors and Others is Finished.

Now, the duties of a visiting monk (āgantuka-vatta) and others should be known. When a visiting monk reaches the vicinity of the monastery precincts (upacāra-sīmā), he should remove his sandals, lower them, shake them out, hold them with the sandal-stick, lower his umbrella, uncover his head, place his robe on his shoulder, and enter the monastery (ārāma) properly and without haste. Upon entering the monastery, he should observe, "Where do the resident monks (āvāsika) assemble?" If the resident monks are assembled in the attendance hall, a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree, he should go there, set down his bowl in a suitable place, set down his robe in a suitable place, take an appropriate seat and sit down. He should ask about the drinking water and the utility water: "Which is the drinking water, and which is the utility water?"
231:
If he needs drinking water, he should take and drink it. If he needs utility water, he should take it and wash his feet. When washing the feet, water should be poured with one hand and the feet should be washed with the other hand. One should not pour water with the same hand used for washing, nor wash the feet with the same hand used for pouring. He should ask for the cloth for wiping sandals and wipe the sandals. When wiping the sandals, he should first wipe with a dry cloth and then with a wet cloth. The sandal-wiping cloth should be washed and spread out in a certain place.

If the resident monk is senior, he should be paid homage. If he is junior, he should be made to pay homage. He should ask about the lodging: "Which lodging is assigned to me?" He should ask whether the lodging has been occupied before or not. He should ask about the time for alms-round: "Is the alms-resort village near or far? Should one wander for alms early in the morning or during the day?" He should ask about the unsuitable resorts (agocara) and the suitable resorts (gocara). An "unsuitable resort" means a village of those with wrong views, or a village where alms are restricted, where alms are given to only one or two monks. He should ask about the families designated as learners (sekha). He should ask about the place for excrement and the place for urine. He should ask about the drinking water and utility water: "In this pond, do they only drink the drinking water, or do they also use it for bathing and so forth?" He should ask about the walking staff. He should ask about the agreements (katika) of the Sangha. In some places, there are wild beasts or non-human beings (amanussa); therefore, he should ask, "At what time should one enter, and at what time should one leave?" If the dwelling is unoccupied (secluded), he should knock on the door, wait for a moment, open the bolt, open the door, and look inside while standing outside.

If that dwelling is dirty, or if a couch is placed upon a couch, or a chair upon a chair, or if the bedding is piled up on top, if he is able, the entire dwelling should be cleaned. If he is unable, he should look after the place where he himself stays. A monk who is able to clean the entire dwelling should, according to the method mentioned in the duties of a preceptor, take out the floor coverings, couches, chairs, and so forth, clean the dwelling, and then bring them back in and arrange them in their original places.
232: If winds with dust blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed. If winds with dust blow from the west, north, or south, the southern windows should be closed. If it is the cold season, the windows should be opened during the day and closed at night. If it is the hot season, they should be closed during the day and opened at night. If there is dirt, the courtyard should be swept, the gatehouse should be swept, the service hall should be swept, the fire-room should be swept, the toilet should be swept, drinking water and water for use should be set out, and water should be poured into the foot-washing jar. This is the Duty of an Incoming Monk (Āgantuka-vatta). In the Duty of a Resident Monk (Āvāsika-vatta), a resident monk, seeing an incoming monk who is senior to him, should prepare a seat, and place water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-scrubber nearby. He should go out to meet him and receive his bowl and robes. He should ask him about drinking water. If the one being asked drinks all the water brought once, he should be asked, "Shall I bring more?" He should also be fanned with a fan. The one fanning should fan once on the top of the feet, once in the middle of the body, and once on the head. If the guest says, "That is enough," he should fan more gently. If he says "Enough" again, he should fan even more gently than that. At the third time of saying so, the fan should be put away. The feet of that incoming monk should also be washed. If he has oil of his own, he should rub them with oil. If he does not have any, he should rub them with the incoming monk's oil. If he is able, the sandals should be wiped. The one wiping the sandals should first wipe them with a dry cloth, and later with a wet cloth. The sandal-wiping cloth should be washed and put aside in one place. The incoming monk should be paid homage. The lodging should be pointed out, saying, "This lodging falls to you." Whether it has been occupied or not should be told. The alms-resort should be told, the non-alms-resort should be told, the families designated as learners (sekha) should be told. The place for defecation should be told, the place for urination should be told, the drinking water should be told, the water for use should be told, the walking sticks should be told. The Saṅgha's agreement and regulations should be told, saying, "At this time one should enter, at this time one should depart." If the incoming monk is junior, the resident monk, while still sitting, should say, "Place the bowl here, place the robe here, this is the seat, sit down."
233: Drinking water should be told, water for use should be told, the sandal-wiping cloth should be told. The incoming monk should be made to pay homage. The lodgings and so forth should also be told while still sitting. If a senior monk arrives, preparing the seat and so forth should be done even by stopping the sewing of robes or new construction work. While sweeping the courtyard of a Cetiya, one should put down the broom and begin to perform the duty for that incoming monk. For a wise incoming monk will say, "Sweep the Cetiya courtyard first." While providing medicine to a sick person, if the sick person is not very ill, one should perform the duty without yet providing the medicine. But if it is a very ill person, one should only provide the medicine. For a wise incoming monk will say, "Provide the medicine first." This is the Duty of a Resident Monk (Āvāsika-vatta). In the Duty of a Departing Monk (Gamika-vatta), a departing monk should store all wooden items such as couches and stools, clay items, and dyeing vessels and so forth, either in the fire-room or in another secure place, close the doors and windows, hand over the lodging, and then depart. If there is no monk, it should be handed over to a novice. If there is no novice, it should be handed over to a monastery attendant (ārāmika). If there is no monk, novice, or monastery attendant, he should prepare a couch on four stones, place another couch on top of that couch, place a stool on top of the stool, pile the bedding on top, store the wooden and clay items, close the doors and windows, and then depart. If the monastery leaks, if he is able, he should cover it all. Or he should take care, thinking, "How might the monastery be covered?" If he succeeds in this way, it is good. If he does not succeed, he should prepare a couch on four stones in a place where it does not leak, place another couch on top of that couch, place a stool on top of the stool, pile the bedding on top, store the wooden and clay items, close the doors and windows, and then depart. If the monastery leaks, if he is able, the bedding should be carried to the village. Or he should take care, thinking, "How might the bedding be carried to the village?" If he succeeds in this way, it is good. If he does not succeed, he should prepare a couch on four stones in the open, place another couch on top of that couch, place a stool on top of the stool, pile the bedding on top, store the wooden and clay items...
234:
After putting away what needs to be stored, covering it with grass or leaves, one should depart with the thought: "Indeed, may the parts (of the dwelling) remain intact." This is the duty of a traveling monk (Gamika-vatta).

Regarding the duty in the dining hall (Bhattagga-vatta): If the mealtime is announced within the monastery, one should dress properly, covering the three circles (the navel and both knees), fasten the waist belt, fold the double robe (saṅghāṭi), fasten the button, wash and take the alms-bowl, and enter the village carefully and without haste.

One should not overtake the elder monks and walk in front of them. One should enter the house well-covered, well-restrained, with eyes downcast, and making little noise. One should not enter the house with the body swaying, nor with loud laughter. One should not enter the house swaying the body, swaying the arms, or swaying the head. One should not enter the house with hands on the hips, nor with the head covered, nor by walking on the toes (squatting).

One should sit in the house well-covered, well-restrained, with eyes downcast, and making little noise. One should not sit in the house with the body swaying, nor with loud laughter. One should not sit in the house swaying the body, swaying the arms, or swaying the head. One should not sit in the house with hands on the hips, nor with the head covered, nor with the arms clasped around the knees. One should not sit by pushing against the elder monks. If the seat is equal to the seat of a Mahāthera, and if there are many seats, one should sit leaving one or two seats vacant. One should not sit on the seats prepared by counting the monks until the Mahāthera says, "Please sit." If the Mahāthera does not say so, one should say, "Venerable sir, this seat is high." One should sit only when told, "Please sit." If, even after being informed in this way, he does not speak, there is no offense for the junior monk who sits; the offense is only for the Mahāthera. This is because a junior monk commits an offense by sitting in such a seat without asking, and an elder monk commits an offense by not giving permission when asked. Junior monks should not be denied a seat. One should not sit in the house after spreading out the double robe (saṅghāṭi).

When the water for washing the bowl is given, one should hold the bowl with both hands and receive the water. As for the water of donation, one should place the bowl on the stand in front and receive it. One should wash the bowl by holding it low, without making the sound of water, and without striking it. If there is a receptacle for the water, one should hold it low and pour the water into the receptacle, thinking, "May I not splash the one receiving the water with water..."
235:
...pour the water, thinking: "May I not splash the one receiving the water; may I not splash the monks nearby; may I not splash the double robe (saṅghāṭi)." If there is no receptacle, one should hold it low and pour the water on the ground, thinking: "May I not splash the monks nearby; may I not splash the double robe (saṅghāṭi)."

When almsfood is being offered, one should hold the bowl with both hands and receive the food. One should receive food in such a measure that there is space for the curry. If there is ghee, oil, or side dishes, the elder monk should say, "Prepare it equally for all." This should be said not only regarding ghee and such, but also regarding the rice. However, if the items like ghee are so little that they are only enough for one or two monks, saying "Prepare it equally for all" would cause distress to the people. Therefore, one should take such items only once or twice and not take the remainder. Almsfood should be received respectfully, with attention focused on the bowl, with a proportionate amount of curry, and only up to the edge of the bowl. As long as all the monks have not yet received their food, the elder monk should not begin eating. This instruction refers to a dining hall with a limited number of monks where the people wish to pay respects only after serving all the monks. In a large dining hall where some are eating in one area while water is being served in another, one may eat as one pleases.

Almsfood should be eaten respectfully, with attention focused on the bowl, in successive order, and with a proportionate amount of curry. One should not eat by pressing down the top of the rice. One should not cover up curry or side dishes with rice out of a desire to get more. A monk who is not ill should not ask for food for his own sake and eat it. One should not look at another's bowl with a critical mind. One should not make an extra-large mouthful. One should make a round, even mouthful. The mouth should not be opened until the mouthful has reached it. While eating, the whole hand should not be put into the mouth. One should not speak with the mouth full of food. One should not eat by tossing food into the mouth, nor by biting off mouthfuls, nor by stuffing the cheeks, nor by shaking the hands, nor by scattering grains of rice, nor by sticking out the tongue, nor by making a smacking sound (capu-capu), nor by making a slurping sound (suru-suru), nor by licking the hands, nor by scraping the bowl, nor by licking the lips.
236:
One should not hold a drinking water cup with hands soiled with food. An elder should not accept water for washing hands until all the monks have finished their meal. However, if the laypeople say, 'Venerable sirs, please wash your bowls and hands,' or if the monks say, 'You may take the water,' then it is permissible to accept it. When water is being given, one should hold the bowl with both hands to receive the water. The bowl should be washed while keeping it low, without making the sound of splashing water and without striking the bowl. If there is a water receptacle, one should keep it low and pour the water into the receptacle, reflecting: 'May I not splash water on the receptacle, may I not splash water on the nearby monks, and may I not splash water on the outer robe (saṅghāṭi).' If there is no water receptacle, one should keep it low and pour the water onto the ground, reflecting: 'May I not splash water on the nearby monks, and may I not splash water on the outer robe.' One should not discard bowl-washing water that contains rice grains inside the house.

When rising to leave the place of the meal, the junior monks should depart first, and the elder monks should depart later. This is said because if the houses are cramped, there would be no space for the great elders to exit. Junior monks who depart in this manner should stand at the door of the house and proceed in order only after the elders have exited. However, if the great elders are seated at the front of the house and the junior monks are inside the house, they should exit in order starting from the elders' seats. They should proceed in a spaced-out line so that people can pass between them, without their bodies touching one another.

Based on the words, 'Bhikkhus, I allow an elder monk to give thanks (Anumodanā) in the refectory,' the Saṅghatthera (the most senior monk of the group) should perform the Anumodanā in the refectory. The remaining monks should not depart, leaving that single monk alone.

Based on the words, 'Bhikkhus, I allow four or five senior and junior monks to wait in the refectory,' when the Saṅghatthera is seated to perform the Anumodanā, four monks should sit in descending order of seniority. If a junior elder is seated, the great elder and three monks in descending order should sit. If the fifth monk is seated, four monks in ascending order should sit. (Note: 'Descending' refers to junior monks, and 'ascending' refers to senior monks.) Even if the Saṅghatthera urges a junior monk below him to perform the Anumodanā, starting from the Saṅghatthera...
237:
...four monks must certainly remain seated. If the monk reciting the Anumodanā says, 'Venerable sirs, please proceed; there is no need to wait,' then it is permissible to leave. If the great elder says, 'Let us go, friends,' and the reciting monk says, 'Please proceed,' it is also permissible to leave. It is also permissible to leave after intending, 'We will wait outside the village,' and having gone outside the village, telling one's own pupils, 'You wait for the arrival of that monk who is reciting the Anumodanā.' If laypeople, of their own accord, ask only a single monk to recite the Anumodanā, there is no offense for that reciting monk, nor is it the responsibility of the great elder. Only when people ask for a discourse while the monks are seated nearby should the elder be asked for permission. The rule here is that only the monk urged by the great elder to recite the Anumodanā should be waited for. According to the words, 'Bhikkhus, when there is a necessary business, I allow one to go after asking permission from the monk nearby,' if one is pressed by the need to pass stool or urine, etc., one should go after asking permission from the monk nearby. This is the duty regarding the refectory (Bhattaggavatta).

Regarding the duty of the alms-round (Piṇḍacārikavatta): A monk on alms-round, thinking, 'I shall now enter the village,' should dress neatly, covering the three circles (the knees and the navel), fasten the waistband, wear the double outer robe, attach the fastener, wash and take the alms-bowl, and enter the village properly and without haste. He should go from house to house in order, being well-covered; everything should be understood here in the same manner as described in the Bhattaggavatta.

When entering a house, he should take note: 'I will enter by this way, and exit by this way.' He should not enter too hurriedly. He should stand neither too far nor too near, nor should he stand for too long, nor should he turn back too quickly. While standing, he should observe: 'Do they wish to give alms or not?' If they put down their work, rise from their seat, touch a ladle, touch a vessel, or set it down, he should stand, knowing, 'They wish to give.' When alms are being given, he should lift the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) with his left hand, offer the bowl with his right hand, and receive the alms by holding the bowl with both hands. Whether the donor is a woman or a man, he should not look at their face while the alms are being poured. He should observe: 'Do they wish to give curry or not?' If they touch a ladle, touch a vessel, or set it down, he should stand, knowing, 'They wish to give.' After the alms have been given, he should cover the bowl with his outer robe and turn back properly without haste.
238:
The monk who returns first from the alms-round in the village should prepare the seats. He should set out the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-scrubber. He should wash and set out the refuse bowl (avakkārapāti), and prepare the drinking water and the utility water. The monk who returns last from the alms-round in the village, if there are leftovers from the monks who returned earlier and he wishes to eat, he may eat. If he does not wish to eat, he should discard them in a place without grass or into water without living beings. That monk should put away the seats, the foot-washing water, the footstool, and the foot-scrubber. He should wash and put away the refuse bowl, put away the drinking water and utility water, and sweep the dining hall. A monk who sees that the drinking water pot, the utility water pot, or the toilet water pot is empty should fill it. If it is too heavy for him alone, he should summon a companion with a hand signal and lift it together; he should not break his silence for that reason.

## This is the Duty of the Alms-Collector.

In the Duty of the Forest-Dweller, a monk living in the forest should rise early, place his bowl in its bag, sling it over his shoulder, place his robe on his shoulder, put on his sandals, put away wooden and clay utensils, close the doors and windows, and depart from his dwelling. Thinking, "Now I will enter the village," he should take off his sandals, place them down, shake them out, put them in the bag, and sling it over his shoulder. Covering the three circles, he should dress neatly, fasten the waistband, put on the double outer robe, fasten the buckle, wash and take his bowl, and enter the village properly and without haste. The entire procedure for going, such as walking well-covered and in order from house to house, should be understood here in the same way as described in the Duty of the Dining Hall.

When entering a house, he should note, "I will enter by this way, I will exit by this way." The entire procedure for alms-gathering should be understood in the same way as described in the Duty of the Alms-Collector. The forest-dwelling monk should prepare drinking water and utility water. If there are not enough vessels, he should use the drinking water vessel for utility water as well. If he cannot find a vessel, he should use a bamboo tube. If he cannot find even that, he should ensure there is a water pit or well nearby. Fire should be prepared; the fire-drilling sticks (araṇisahita) should be prepared. If the fire-drilling sticks are available, it is permissible even if he does not light a fire. Just as for the forest-dweller, a monk traveling through a wilderness should also desire to have fire-drilling sticks. However, for a monk living in a group (gaṇavāsī), it is permissible even without those fire-drilling sticks.
239:
A walking staff should be carried. All the constellations, or at least a part of them, should be learned; he must be one who is skilled in the directions. This is the duty of a forest-dweller.

In the lodging duty, in whichever dwelling he stays, if that dwelling is dirty, he should clean it if he is able. When cleaning the dwelling, he should first take out the bowl and robes and set them aside; he should take out the sitting mat (nisīdana) and set it aside; he should take out the mattress and pillow and set them aside. He should lower the bed (mañca) and, without scraping or knocking it against the doorposts or door-frames, take it out carefully and set it aside. He should lower the chair (pīṭha) and, without scraping or knocking it against the doorposts or door-frames, take it out carefully and set it aside. The bed-legs should be taken out and set aside. The spittoon should be taken out and set aside. The leaning board should be taken out and set aside. He should take note of how the floor covering was laid, then take it out and set it aside. If there are cobwebs in the dwelling, he should first remove them from the ceiling. The windows and corners should be wiped. If the wall treated with red ochre is stained, he should moisten a cloth, wring it out, and wipe it. If the floor treated with black coloring is stained, he should moisten a cloth, wring it out, and wipe it. If the floor is untreated, he should sprinkle it with water and sweep it, thinking, "Let not the dwelling be soiled by dust." He should collect the rubbish and discard it in one place.

One should not shake out the bedding near other monks; one should not shake out the bedding near the dwelling; one should not shake out the bedding near the drinking water; one should not shake out the bedding near the utility water; one should not shake out the bedding in the courtyard on the windward side. The bedding should be shaken out on the leeward side.

After sun-drying, cleaning, and shaking out the floor covering, he should bring it back and lay it as it was laid before. After sun-drying and wiping the bed-legs in one place, he should bring them back and place them in their original positions. After sun-drying, cleaning, and shaking out the bed in one place, he should lower it and, without scraping or knocking it against the doorposts or door-frames, bring it back carefully and set it as it was set before. After sun-drying, cleaning, and shaking out the chair in one place, he should lower it and, without scraping or knocking it against the doorposts or door-frames, bring it back carefully and set it as it was set before...
240:
The prepared bolsters and pillows should be sunned in a certain place, cleaned, dusted, brought back, and laid out as they were. The floor coverings and mats should also be sunned, dusted, brought back, and laid out as they were. The spittoon should also be sunned in a certain place, cleaned, brought back, and placed in its usual spot. The back-rest board should also be sunned in a certain place, cleaned, and placed in its usual spot.

The bowl and robes should be put away. A monk putting away the bowl should hold the bowl with one hand, feel under the couch or under the bench with the other hand, and then place the bowl. The bowl should not be placed on the bare ground. A monk putting away the robe should hold the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-pole or robe-line with the other hand, and then place the robe with the edges on the outside and the fold towards himself.

If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed. If dusty winds blow from the west, north, or south, the southern windows should be closed. If it is the cold season, the windows should be opened during the day and closed at night. If it is the hot season, the windows should be closed during the day and opened at night.

If it is dirty, the courtyard should be swept, the porch should be swept, the attendance hall should be swept, the fire-room should be swept, and the toilet should be swept. If there is no drinking water, drinking water should be provided. If there is no utility water, utility water should be provided. If there is no water in the foot-washing jar, water should be poured into the foot-washing jar.

If one lives in the same dwelling with a senior monk (vuḍḍha), one should not give a lesson, ask a question, recite, preach the Dhamma, light a lamp, extinguish a lamp, open windows, or close windows without asking the senior monk. Since a door is for general use, there is no need to ask permission regarding the door; however, the rest, such as giving lessons, should be done only after asking permission. One may ask permission daily. Alternatively, if when one says, "Venerable sir, let it be as if I have already asked permission," the senior monk accepts saying "Very well," or if the senior monk himself says, "Live as you please," then it is also permissible. It is also permissible through the intimacy of being like-minded (sabhāga). If one walks on the same walkway (caṅkama) with a senior monk, one should turn when the senior monk turns, and one should not brush against the senior monk with the corner of one's robe. This is the duty regarding lodgings (senāsanavatta).
241:
In the duties regarding the fire-room (jantāghara), the one who goes first to the fire-room, if the ashes have accumulated, should discard the ashes. If it is dirty, the fire-room should be swept, the surrounding area should be swept, the courtyard should be swept, the porch should be swept, and the fire-room hall should be swept. The bathing powder should be kneaded, the clay should be moistened, and water should be poured into the water trough.

One entering the fire-room should smear the face with clay and enter the fire-room covering both the front and the back. One should not sit crowding the elder monks, and newly ordained monks should not be denied a seat. If one is able, one should perform services for the elder monks in the fire-room. One leaving the fire-room should take the fire-room stool and leave the fire-room covering both the front and the back. If one is able, one should also perform services for the elder monks at the water. One should not bathe in front of the elder monks, nor should one bathe upstream from them. One who has finished bathing and is ascending should give way to those who are descending. The one who leaves the fire-room last, if there is mud in the fire-room, should wash it; after washing the clay bowl and putting away the fire-room stool, one should extinguish the fire, close the door, and then depart. This is the duty regarding the fire-room (jantāghara-vatta).

In the duties regarding the toilet (vaccakuṭi), the one who goes to the toilet should cough while standing outside; the one sitting inside should also cough in return. Having placed the robe on the robe-rail or the robe-cord, one should enter the toilet properly and without haste. One should not enter too hurriedly, nor should one enter with the lower robe lifted up. Standing on the toilet footrests, one should then lift the robe. One should not defecate while groaning, nor should one defecate while chewing a tooth-stick. One should not defecate outside the cesspit bowl, nor should one urinate outside the urinal bowl. One should not spit into the urinal bowl. One should not wipe oneself (after defecating) with split wood, rough wood, knotted wood, thorny wood, hollow wood, or rotten wood. However, there is no offense for one who has entered without taking a wiping-stick (kanu-taṃ). The used wiping-stick should not be dropped into the toilet pit. Standing on the toilet footrests, one should cover oneself. One should not leave too hurriedly, nor should one leave with the robe lifted up. Standing on the rinsing footrests, one should then lift the robe. One should not rinse with a 'capu-capu' splashing sound. One should not leave water remaining in the rinsing bowl. This is said with reference to a public place. Since others will come to that place, water should not be left remaining. In a part of a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha...
242:
...if it is a place designated for one's own constant use or a private place, it is permissible (to leave water). It is also permissible for one who has taken a purgative and must enter repeatedly. While standing on the rinsing footrests, one must remain covered.

If the toilet is soiled with excrement or if the exterior is smeared with excrement, one should fetch water and wash it. If there is water but no vessel, it is considered as having no water. If there is a vessel but no water, this also is considered as having no water. If both are absent, it is certainly a case of no water; in such a case, one should depart after wiping with wood or something else. If the basket for wiping-sticks is full, the wiping-sticks should be discarded. If there is rubbish, the toilet should be swept, the surrounding area should be swept, the courtyard should be swept, and the porch should be swept. If there is no water in the rinsing jar, water should be poured into the rinsing jar.

According to the words, "Bhikkhus, when there is water, one should not remain without rinsing after defecating; whoever does not rinse, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa)" (Cūḷavagga, 373), an offense is committed by a monk who does not perform the act of rinsing when water is available. If there is water but no private place, one should take water with a vessel and rinse elsewhere. If there is no vessel, it should be taken with an alms-bowl. If even an alms-bowl is not available, it is considered as having no water. For a monk who goes thinking, "This place is too open, there will be other water ahead," and the time for alms-round arrives before he finds water, it is proper to depart after wiping with wood or something else; it is then permissible both to eat and to give thanks (anumodanā). According to the words, "Bhikkhus, one should not defecate in the toilet according to seniority; whoever does so, there is an offense of wrongdoing. Bhikkhus, I allow defecating according to the order of arrival" (Cūḷavagga, 373), one entering the toilet must enter according to the order of arrival. In these three places—the toilet, the urinal, and the bathing place—the order of arrival alone is the standard. This is the duty regarding the toilet (vaccakuṭi-vatta).

## Thus ends the Discussion on the Decision of the Duties of Preceptors and others
## in the Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha.
243: ## 28. Discussion on the Decision for the Distribution of the Four Requisites. The distribution of the four requisites means the distribution of the four requisites such as robes and so on. In that distribution of robes, first, the robe-receiver, the robe-storer, the storekeeper, the storehouse, the robe-distributor, and the distribution of robes should be known. Regarding the distribution of those requisites (Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā 340-342), "Monks, I allow you to appoint a monk endowed with five factors as a robe-receiver: one who would not go to a wrong course through favoritism, would not go to a wrong course through hatred, would not go to a wrong course through delusion, would not go to a wrong course through fear, and would know what is received and what is not" (Mahāvagga 342). According to these words, a robe-receiver endowed with these five factors should be appointed. In that appointment, one is said to go to a wrong course through favoritism if he receives [robes] first for his own relatives and so on even though they arrived later, or if he receives them by showing affection to certain donors, or if, being greedy by nature, he diverts them to his own side. One is said to go to a wrong course through hatred if he receives [robes] later for one who arrived first out of anger, or if he receives them while showing contempt for poor people, or if he causes an obstacle to the gains of the Saṅgha by saying, "Is there no place to keep things in your house? Take your property and go back." One who is unmindful and lacks clear comprehension is said to go to a wrong course through delusion. One is said to go to a wrong course through fear if he receives [robes] first for powerful rulers even though they arrived later out of fear, or if he is terrified, thinking, "This position of robe-receiver is very difficult." Knowing "I have received this and that; I have not yet received this and that" is called knowing what is received and what is not. Therefore, a monk should be appointed who does not go to a wrong course through favoritism and so on, who receives [robes] according to the order of arrival without making a distinction between those with relatives and those without, or between the wealthy and the poor; who is endowed with virtue, conduct, and great and small duties; who is mindful, wise, and learned; and who is able to inspire faith in the donors while performing the appreciation (anumodanā) with clear and smooth speech and with well-rounded syllables and phrases. Such a monk should be appointed. And he should be appointed in this way: First, the monk should be requested. Having requested him, a competent and able monk should inform the Saṅgha (proclaim the motion)— "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named so-and-so as the robe-receiver. This is the motion (ñatti)."
244:
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named [so-and-so] as the Robe-Receiver. If the appointment of the monk named [so-and-so] as the Robe-Receiver is pleasing to the venerable ones, let them be silent. If it is not pleasing, let them speak. The monk named [so-and-so] has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the Robe-Receiver. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore they are silent. Thus I understand it.” (Mahāvagga, 342) —

In this way, by this kammavācā or by apalokana (announcement), it is proper to make the appointment in the midst of the entire Saṅgha within the monastery or in a khaṇḍasīmā. A person thus appointed should not stay at the edge of the monastery or in a meditation dwelling. He should stay in a place such as the entrance area of the monastery where people coming and going can easily see him, keeping a fan by his side, and being well-dressed in his inner and outer robes.

Regarding the Robe-Depositor (cīvaranidahaka), because of the words: “Monks, I allow you to appoint a monk who possesses five qualities as a Robe-Depositor: one who does not follow the path of favoritism (chandāgati), does not follow the path of malice (dosāgati), does not follow the path of delusion (mohāgati), does not follow the path of fear (bhayāgati), and knows what is deposited and what is not,” a monk possessing these five qualities [should be appointed as follows]:

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named [so-and-so] as the Robe-Depositor. This is the motion (ñatti).

Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The Saṅgha appoints the monk named [so-and-so] as the Robe-Depositor. If the appointment of the monk named [so-and-so] as the Robe-Depositor is pleasing to the venerable ones, let them be silent. If it is not pleasing, let them speak.

The monk named [so-and-so] has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the Robe-Depositor. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore they are silent. Thus I understand it.” (Mahāvagga, 342) —

In this way, by this kammavācā or by apalokana, the appointment should be made in the manner already described.
245:
Regarding the Storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika), in accordance with the words: “Monks, I allow you to appoint a monk who possesses five qualities as a Storekeeper: one who does not follow the path of favoritism, does not follow the path of malice, does not follow the path of delusion, does not follow the path of fear, and knows what is secure and what is insecure” (Mahāvagga, 343), a monk possessing these five qualities should be appointed by kammavācā or by apalokana in the following manner: “Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monk named [so-and-so] as the Storekeeper,” and so forth.

In appointing this Storekeeper, a place that has no defects in the roof, etc., is called a secure (gutta) place. However, in a monastery where the roofing grass or roofing tiles have fallen in some place, causing leaks from that hole or allowing entry to rats and so forth, or if there is a hole in the walls, etc., or if termites are rising—all that is called insecure (agutta). Having noted what is secure and insecure, the Storekeeper should repair it. In the cold season, doors and windows should be kept well closed. This is because robes tend to get moldy due to the cold. In the hot season, they should be opened occasionally to let air in. Doing this is called knowing what is secure and insecure.

“Monks, I allow you to appoint as a storehouse (bhaṇḍāgāra) whatever the Saṅgha desires: a monastery (vihāra), a lean-to (aḍḍhayoga), a mansion (pāsāda), an attic (hammiya), or a cave (guha)” (Mahāvagga, 343). In accordance with these words, a storehouse should be appointed and established. In appointing this storehouse, a monastery or a lean-to that is not secluded from monastery-attendants, novices, etc., and is a place where everyone congregates, should be appointed. A remote lodging (paccantasenāsana) should not be appointed. It is not proper for those sitting in a khaṇḍasīmā to go there and appoint this storehouse. Only in the middle of the monastery should it be appointed by kammavācā or by apalokana in the following manner: “Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint the monastery named [so-and-so] as the storehouse,” and so forth.

The three monks, such as the Robe-Receiver (cīvarapaṭiggāhaka), should also know their own duties. Among those three, first, the Robe-Receiver [should receive] all that people offer, such as “in-season robes” (kālacīvara), “out-of-season robes” (akālacīvara), “urgent robes” (acceka-cīvara), “rain-cloths” (vassikasāṭika), “sitting cloths” (nisīdana), “bedspreads” (paccattharaṇa), or “face-towels” (mukhapuñchanacoḷa)...
246:
(Robes) should not be accepted by putting them together in a single heap and mixing them; they must be accepted only after being separated individually. Having done so, they must be handed over to the robe-storer (cīvaranidahaka) with the same explanation. When the robe-storer hands them over to the storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika), he must also explain, "This is a timely robe (kālacīvara) ... [and] ... this is a face-cloth (mukhapuñchanacoḷa)." The storekeeper must also store them by making individual marks in the same manner. Thereafter, when the Saṅgha says, "Bring the timely robe," only the timely robe must be given; ... [and] ... when it is said, "Bring the face-cloth," only that which was specified must be given.

In this way, the Blessed One allowed the robe-receiver (cīvarapaṭiggāhaka), the robe-storer (cīvaranidahaka), the storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika), and the storehouse (bhaṇḍāgāra), not for the sake of accumulation or discontentment, but indeed for the benefit of the Saṅgha. For if the bhikkhus were to take and distribute whatever was brought as it arrived, they would not know what was brought or not brought, what was given or not given, or what was received or not received. They might give whatever was brought at the seats of the elders, or they might take them by cutting them into pieces. If it were so, there would be improper use, and it would not be for the benefit of all. However, by storing the robes in the storehouse, when they become abundant, they will give three robes, or two robes, or one robe to each bhikkhu; then they will know what has been received or not received, and knowing what has not been received, they will intend to favor [those bhikkhus].

Regarding the robe-distributor (cīvarabhājaka): "Bhikkhus, I allow you to appoint a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities as a robe-distributor: one who does not follow the path of favoritism, does not follow the path of hatred, does not follow the path of delusion, does not follow the path of fear, and knows what is distributed and what is not distributed." According to these words, only a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities should be appointed, either by a formal act (kammavācā) or by an act of announcement (apalokanakamma), in this manner: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the bhikkhu named so-and-so as the robe-distributor."

In this distribution of robes, one who gives a valuable robe to bhikkhus who are his friends, even if they are not entitled to it, is said to follow the path of favoritism (chandāgati). One who, out of dislike, does not give a valuable robe to other senior elders even if they are entitled to it, but gives a robe of little value, is said to follow the path of hatred (dosāgati). One who, being confused by delusion, does not know the duties of giving robes, is said to follow the path of delusion (mohāgati). One who, out of fear of foul-mouthed new monks, gives a valuable robe even if they are not entitled to it, is said to follow the path of fear (bhayāgati). One who...
247:
...does not follow [these four biases], but remains impartial like a scale and a standard towards everyone, should be appointed [as the distributor]. That bhikkhu, when distributing the robes, must first select and examine the cloths, saying, "This cloth is coarse, this cloth is fine, this cloth is thick, this cloth is thin, this cloth is used, this cloth is unused, this cloth is this much in length, and this much in width." Having done so, he must determine the value, saying, "This cloth is worth this much, this cloth is worth this much." If everyone can receive a robe worth ten [units] each, that is good. If not, a cloth worth nine or eight [units] should be tied together with other cloths worth one or two [units]. In this way, having prepared portions of equal value, lots (kusa) should be cast. If the distribution of robes to each individual cannot be completed in a single day, ten bhikkhus should be counted at a time, and ten portions of robes should be tied together as one bundle and placed as a single robe-portion. Lots should then be cast for these placed robe-portions. Those ten bhikkhus must then cast lots again to distribute them among themselves.

"Bhikkhus, I allow you to give a half-share to novices (sāmaṇeras)," according to these words, those novices who live independently and do not perform the duties of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, but are only engaged in learning and questioning [scriptures] and perform duties only for their own teachers and preceptors and not for other bhikkhus—to such novices only a half-share should be given. However, those novices who perform the duties of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha both in the morning and in the evening should be given an equal share [with the bhikkhus]. This statement is made only regarding the out-of-season robes (akālacīvara) stored in the storehouse that arise outside the kaṭhina period. As for the timely robes (kālacīvara), they must be given an equal share. Furthermore, regarding the rains-residence robes (vassāvāsika-cīvara) in the collection, they should be taken after performing services for the Saṅgha, such as sweeping and binding [brooms]. This is the duty for all novices in this matter. Regarding the robes in the storehouse, if the novices come and shout, "Venerable sirs, we cook the congee, we cook the rice, we cook the food, we clear the grass and plants, we bring the tooth-sticks, we prepare the bark for dye in a permissible way; what task is there that we have not done?"—then an equal share must be given. It is in reference to those novices who fail in these duties or whose performance of duties is not evident that it was said, "Bhikkhus, I allow you to give a half-share to novices." In the Kurundī commentary, however, it is stated: "If the novices request, saying, 'Venerable sirs, why should we remain without performing the duties of the Saṅgha? We will perform them,' then an equal share should be given."
248:
If a certain bhikkhu, having taken his own share and found a traveling companion, wishes to depart for another region after crossing a river or a wilderness, in accordance with the words, "I allow, O bhikkhus, the giving of his own share to one who is crossing [a wilderness]" (Mahāva. 343), the robes should be brought out from the storehouse, the bell should be struck to assemble the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and the robe-distributor, estimating that "this bhikkhu should receive this much of a share," should give the robe in an equal share by way of a general method. Indeed, it is impossible to give exactly as if weighed by a scale; therefore, whether it be slightly less or more, giving by such an estimated method is well-given. What is deficient should not be given again, and what is in excess should not be taken back. If there are ten bhikkhus and ten cloths, and one is worth twelve units while the others are worth ten each, and if lots are cast with all being valued at ten, the bhikkhu who draws the lot for the cloth worth twelve must give an allowable article of his own equal in value to the excess in that share and then take that extra portion. If all bhikkhus have received five cloths each and there are still cloths remaining, but not enough for each to have one more, those remaining cloths should be cut and distributed.

When cutting, they should be made into pieces sufficient for small circles (aḍḍhamaṇḍala) and the like, or for shoe-bags and the like, and then distributed. At the minimum, it is allowable to make and distribute a piece that is four finger-breadths wide and of a length sufficient for a binding (anuvāta). However, it should not be made useless. If one or two cloths are lacking in a bhikkhu's share, another requisite for a novice should be placed in that share, and after giving that share to a bhikkhu who is satisfied with it, the casting of lots for the remaining bhikkhus should be performed. If, when grouping bhikkhus into tens, one group is not full and has only eight or nine, those eight or nine shares should be given to them with the words, "You take these shares and distribute them among yourselves." Only after giving in this way should the subsequent casting of lots be performed.
