Now, the decision should be understood by virtue of the eight headings (mātikā) taught for the purpose of showing the scope of robe acquisition: "Bhikkhus, there are these eight headings for the arising of robes: giving by boundary, giving by agreement, giving by food-stipend, giving to the Saṅgha, giving to both Saṅghas, giving to the Saṅgha that has spent the Vassa, giving by designation, and giving to an individual" (Mahāva. 379).
249:
Among those (eight headings), one who gives while referring to the boundary in this way, "I give within the boundary," is said to give within the boundary. An object thus given within the boundary should be distributed by all the bhikkhus who have arrived within that boundary. That which is called a boundary (sīmā) is of fifteen kinds: Khaṇḍasīmā, Upacārasīmā, Samānasaṃvāsasīmā, Avippavāsasīmā, Lābhasīmā, Gāmasīmā (village boundary), Nigamasīmā (town boundary), Nagarasīmā (city boundary), Abbhantarasīmā, Udakukkhepasīmā (water boundary), Janapadasīmā (district boundary), Raṭṭhasīmā (province boundary), Rajjasīmā (kingdom boundary), Dīpasīmā (island boundary), and Cakkavāḷasīmā (world-system boundary).

Among those, the Khaṇḍasīmā has already been mentioned in the Sīmākathā. The Upacārasīmā is defined by the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or by the area suitable for an enclosure of an unenclosed monastery. Alternatively, the Upacārasīmā should be understood as the area within two stone-throws of a man of average strength from the regular meeting place of the bhikkhus, or from the dining hall situated at the edge, or from the dwelling where they constantly reside. That Upacārasīmā increases when the dwellings increase and decreases when they decrease. However, in the Mahāpaccari, it is said, "It also increases when the bhikkhus increase." Therefore, if bhikkhus sitting together in a monastery form a continuous line reaching even a hundred yojanas, the area of a hundred yojanas is also the Upacārasīmā, and the gain accrues to all of them. Both the Samānasaṃvāsasīmā and Avippavāsasīmā have also been mentioned already. 

The Lābhasīmā (boundary of gain) is not something prescribed by the Fully Enlightened Buddha, nor established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma. Rather, kings and great ministers, having built a monastery, demarcate an area of a gāvuta, half a yojana, or one yojana all around, and after erecting pillars inscribed with the name, "This is the Lābhasīmā of our monastery," they establish the boundary saying, "Whatever taxes and the like arise within this area, we give all to our monastery." This is called Lābhasīmā. The Gāmasīmā, Nigamasīmā, Nagarasīmā, Abbhantarasīmā, and Udakukkhepasīmā have also been mentioned already.

The Janapadasīmā means that within the Kāsi and Kosala provinces, there are many districts; the boundary of each individual district is the Janapadasīmā. The Raṭṭhasīmā (province boundary) is the boundary of provinces such as Kāsi and Kosala. The Rajjasīmā (kingdom boundary) is the area over which the authority of an individual king extends, such as "the domain of the Coḷa king" or "the domain of the Keraḷa king." The Dīpasīmā (island boundary) refers to the great islands and small islands bounded by the ocean. The Cakkavāḷasīmā is bounded only by the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. Thus, among these boundaries, if one sees the Saṅgha assembled for some legal act in a Khaṇḍasīmā and says, "I give to the Saṅgha in this very boundary," all the bhikkhus who have arrived within that Khaṇḍasīmā should distribute it. That gain accrues only to those bhikkhus, not to those in another inter-boundary space (sīmantarikā) or...
250: The gains do not reach the monks standing in the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā). However, they do reach a monk standing on a tree or a mountain within a partial boundary (khaṇḍa-sīmā), or one who has gone into the middle of the earth. Robes given with the words, "I give to the Saṅgha in this upacāra-sīmā," reach even the monks standing in the khaṇḍa-sīmā and the inter-boundary spaces (sīmantarikā). Robes given with the words, "I give to the Saṅgha in the samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā," do not reach those standing in the khaṇḍa-sīmā and the inter-boundary spaces. Robes given in the avippavāsa-sīmā and the lābha-sīmā reach those who have entered within those boundaries. Robes given in village boundaries (gāma-sīmā), etc., reach even the monks standing in the bound boundaries (baddha-sīmā) within those boundaries. Robes given in the inner boundary (antara-sīmā) and the water-thrown boundary (udakukkhepa-sīmā) reach only those within those boundaries. In the cases of district boundaries (janapada-sīmā), state boundaries (raṭṭha-sīmā), island boundaries (dīpa-sīmā), and world-system boundaries (cakkavāḷa-sīmā), the decision is the same as stated for village boundaries, etc. If a person standing in Jambudīpa says, "I give to the Saṅgha in Tambapaṇṇidīpa," even a single monk coming from Tambapaṇṇidīpa is entitled to take the share for the entire Saṅgha. If a monk of the same category (sabhāga) in that very island takes the share of other monks of the same category, he should not be prevented. Thus should the decision be understood regarding a gift given by one who refers to a specific boundary. If a person does not know how to say "in such-and-such a boundary" but, knowing only the word "boundary" (sīmā), comes to the monastery and says, "I give in the boundary," or "I give to the Saṅgha standing in the boundary," he should be asked, "There are many kinds of boundaries; which boundary do you mean?" If he says, "I do not know such-and-such a boundary; let the Saṅgha standing in the boundary divide and take it," in which boundary should it be divided? It is said that the Elder Mahāsīva said, "It should be divided in the avippavāsa-sīmā." Then other wise ones said to that Elder: "An avippavāsa-sīmā can be as large as three yojanas. If so, monks standing within three yojanas will take the gains. Having stood at three yojanas, they would have to fulfill the duties of a guest (āgantuka-vatta) before entering the monastery. A traveling monk would have to travel three yojanas to ask for lodgings (senāsana). For one practicing under dependence (nissaya), the dependence would lapse upon exceeding three yojanas. A monk undergoing probation (parivāsa) would have to travel three yojanas to see the dawn rise. A nun would have to stand at three yojanas to ask for permission to enter the monastery. All this should be done only according to the extent of the upacāra-sīmā. Therefore, it should be divided only in the upacāra-sīmā." In the phrase "katikāya deti" (gives by agreement), "agreement" (katika) refers to the agreement for equal gains (samānalābha-katika). In that agreement for equal gains, the agreement should be made thus: If the monks assembled in one monastery wish to support another monastery and make the gains equal, they should mention the name of that monastery and state a reason such as, "Such-and-such a monastery is an ancient one," or...
251: ...they desire; they should mention the name of that monastery and state a reason such as, "Such-and-such a monastery is an ancient one," or "it is a place where the Buddha once resided," or "it is a monastery with few gains." Then they should announce three times, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha to make the gains of that monastery equal with this monastery." By this announcement, even one sitting in that monastery is considered as sitting here. In that monastery too, the Saṅgha should do the same. By this announcement, even one sitting here is considered as sitting there. When gains are being divided in one monastery, it is proper to take a share for a monk staying in the other monastery. In this way, many dwellings (āvāsa) can be made to have equal gains along with one monastery. When this is done, a gift given in one dwelling is considered as given in all. "Bhikkhā-paññatti" (designation of alms) refers to the place where one makes known their own donation; in that place, permanent provisions (dhuvakāra) are made for the Saṅgha. Regarding these permanent provisions, if in a certain monastery there is a regular meal provision (pākavaṭṭa) for the Saṅgha belonging to this robe-donor, or if in a certain monastery he makes it his responsibility to always feed the monks at his house, or if he has built a dwelling in a certain place, or if ticket-food (salākabhatta), etc., are established—these are called permanent providers (dhuvakāra). For one who has established an entire monastery, there is nothing more to be said. Therefore, if that donor says, "I give in the place where my permanent provisions are made," or "Give in that place," and if there are permanent provisions in many places, it is considered as given in all those places of donation. If, however, there are more monks in one monastery, those monks should say, "In one place of your permanent provisions there are many monks, and in another, there are few." If he says, "Take according to the number of monks," then it is proper to divide and take accordingly. Among these gift-objects, even small amounts of cloth, medicine, etc., are easily divided. If, however, there is only one bed (mañca) or one chair (pīṭha), the donor should be asked; and if he directs it for a certain monastery, or for a certain lodging within a single monastery, it should be given there. If he says, "Let such-and-such a monk take it," that is also proper. But if he says, "Give in the place of my permanent provisions," and leaves without directing specifically, it is proper for the Saṅgha to decide. It should be decided thus: "Give it to the place where the Senior Elder of the Saṅgha (Saṅghatthera) resides." If the lodgings there are complete, it should be given where they are insufficient. If a monk says, "There are no lodging utensils in my place of residence," it should be given there. Regarding the phrase "gives to the Saṅgha," if one enters a monastery and gives, saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha," the Saṅgha standing in the upacāra-sīmā [should ring] the bell...
252:
(The Sangha Elder residing in the precinct boundary) should strike the bell and announce the time for distribution. Even if a person is within the boundary but has not yet reached (the distribution site), one who takes a share on their behalf should not be prevented. If the monastery is large, and while the cloths are being distributed starting from the elders' seats, senior monks of a lazy nature arrive late, one should not say, 'Venerable sirs, the distribution is now for those with twenty years of seniority; your turn has passed.' The sequence should be paused, and after giving to those elders, the distribution should proceed in order.

Hearing that 'many robes have arisen in such-and-such a monastery,' if monks come even from a monastery a league (yojana) away, the robes should be given starting from the position where each monk arrives. Even if they have not yet arrived, if they have entered the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) and their disciples or others take a share for them, it must be given. If it is said, 'Give to those staying outside the precinct boundary,' it should not be given. However, if they are continuous with the monks entering the precinct boundary and are at the monastery gate or even within the monastery, the boundary is said to be extended by the power of the assembly (parisā); therefore, it should be given. Even after giving to the youngest monk (saṅghanavaka), it must still be given to those who arrive later. In a second round of distribution, however, for those who arrive after the elder's seat has been reached, the first share does not reach them; they should be given from the second share according to their seniority (vassagga).

If there are ten monks in a monastery and ten cloths are offered with the words, 'We give to the Sangha,' they should be distributed individually. If they take them all, saying, 'All these cloths reach us,' and go away, it is said to be both improperly assigned and improperly taken; wherever they go, those items remain the property of the Sangha (saṅghika). However, if one cloth is set aside and assigned to the Sangha Elder with the words, 'This cloth reaches you, venerable sir,' and then they take the rest saying, 'The remaining cloths reach us,' it is allowable. If they bring even a single cloth and say, 'We give to the Sangha,' and take it without distributing, saying, 'It reaches us,' it is both improperly assigned and improperly taken. If they make a mark with a small knife or with turmeric and assign a portion to the Sangha Elder, saying, 'This part reaches you, venerable sir,' and then take the rest saying, 'The remaining portion reaches us,' it is allowable. It is not allowable to make a division using the patterns or folds of the cloth itself. If they pull out a single thread and give it to the elder, saying, 'This part reaches you, venerable sir,' and then take the rest saying, 'The remaining portion reaches us,' it is allowable. Distribution by cutting the cloth into pieces is also certainly allowable.

In a monastery with only a single monk, when robes for the Sangha arise, if that monk takes them saying, 'All these robes reach me,' according to the method mentioned before,
253:
it is a proper taking, but the sequence (ṭhitikā) is not established. If he takes them one by one, saying, 'This robe reaches me,' then the sequence is established. In a case where the sequence is not established, if another monk arrives when another robe arises, it should be cut in the middle and taken by both monks. When the sequence is established, if another robe arises and a junior monk (navakatara) arrives, the sequence moves down. If a senior monk (vuḍḍhatara) arrives, the sequence moves up. If there is no other monk, he should assign it to himself again and take it.

Robes offered by referring to the Sangha in any manner, such as 'We give to the Sangha' or 'We give to the Bhikkhu Sangha,' are not allowable for monks who wear rag-robes (paṃsukūlika). This is because it is said, 'I reject householder robes (gahapaticīvara) and undertake the ascetic practice of rag-robes (paṃsukūlikaṅga),' and not because the robes are unallowable (akappiya). Even if given after the Bhikkhu Sangha makes a formal request, they should not be taken. If a monk gives his own property, that gift is called a 'monk's gift' (bhikkhudattiya) and is allowable, but it is not a rag-robe (paṃsukūla). Even so, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is not broken. If, however, it is said, 'We give to the monks' or 'We give to the elders,' then it is allowable even for those who wear rag-robes. Cloth given with the words, 'We give this cloth to the Sangha; with this, let them make sandal bags, bowl bags, waistbands (āyogapaṭṭa), shoulder straps, and so on,' is also allowable.

If the cloths given for bowl bags and such are numerous and sufficient for a robe, it is allowable to make a robe from that cloth and wear it. However, if the Sangha distributes the cloths remaining after a distribution by cutting them for the purpose of sandal bags and such, it is not allowable to take from that. Only what is managed by the owners is allowable, not the other (what is managed by the Sangha). If it is said, 'We give to the Sangha for the purpose of water-filter (dhammakaraṇa) cloths and so on,' it is allowable for rag-robe-wearing monks to take them; for even rag-robe-wearing monks should desire what are called requisites (parikkhāra). If there is an excess in that cloth, it is allowable to convert it into a robe. If thread is given to the Sangha, it should also be taken by rag-robe-wearing monks. This is the decision regarding robes given by entering the monastery and saying, 'I give these robes to the Sangha.'

If, seeing monks traveling on the road in the precinct outside the monastery, one informs the Sangha Elder or the youngest of the Sangha, saying, 'I give to the Sangha,' then if the assembly is continuous even for a league, it reaches all the monks. However, it does not reach those monks who have not yet reached the assembly within twelve cubits (hattha).

Regarding the phrase 'Giving to the Ubhatosaṅgha' (both Sanghas), even if one says, 'I give to the Ubhatosaṅgha,' or 'I give to the two-fold Sangha,' or 'I give to the two Sanghas,' or 'To the Bhikkhu Sangha and...'
254:
Even if it is said, “I give to the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha,” it is considered as given to both Sanghas (Ubhatosaṅgha). In such a donation, if there are many monks but only one bhikkhunī, half must be given; it means that after making two equal parts, one part must be given. If there are many bhikkhunīs but only one monk, half must be given. When it is said, “I give to both Sanghas and to you, venerable sir,” if there are ten monks and ten bhikkhunīs, twenty-one shares should be made: one share given to the individual, ten to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, and ten to the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha. The person who receives the individual share is also entitled to take from the Sangha's portion according to their seniority (vassa-order). Why? Because they are included in the term “Ubhatosaṅgha.” The same rule applies when it is said, “I give to both Sanghas and to the Cetiya.” However, in this case, there is no share for the Cetiya that comes from the Sangha's portion; it is simply a share equal to that of one individual. If it is said, “I give to both Sanghas, to you, and to the Cetiya,” twenty-two shares should be made: ten for the monks, ten for the bhikkhunīs, one for the individual, and one for the Cetiya. In that case, the individual is entitled to take from the Sangha's portion according to their seniority, but for the Cetiya, there is only one share.

If it is said, “I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to the bhikkhunīs,” it should not be divided in the middle; it should be given by counting the monks and bhikkhunīs. If it is said, “I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, to the bhikkhunīs, and to you,” the individual does not receive a separate share; they receive only one share from their place of entitlement. Why? Because they are included in the term “Bhikkhu-saṅgha.” Even when it is said, “I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, to the bhikkhunīs, to you, and to the Cetiya,” a share for one individual is obtained for the Cetiya, but the individual does not receive a separate share. Therefore, after giving one share to the Cetiya, the remaining shares should be distributed by counting the monks and bhikkhunīs.

Even when it is said, “I give to the monks and to the bhikkhunīs,” it should not be divided in the middle; it should be distributed only by the number of individuals. Even when it is said, “I give to the monks, to the bhikkhunīs, and to you,” or “to the monks, to the bhikkhunīs, and to the Cetiya,” or “to the monks, to the bhikkhunīs, to you, and to the Cetiya,” one share is obtained for the Cetiya, but there is no separate share for the individual; it should be distributed only by counting the monks and bhikkhunīs. Just as the method was led starting with the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, it should also be led starting with the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha.
255:
When it is said, “I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to you,” the individual does not receive a separate share; it should be taken only according to seniority (vassa-order). However, when it is said, “I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to the Cetiya,” a separate share is obtained for the Cetiya. Even when it is said, “I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, to you, and to the Cetiya,” a separate share is obtained only for the Cetiya, not for the individual. Even when it is said, “I give to the monks and to you,” a separate share is not obtained. When it is said, “I give to the monks and to the Cetiya,” a share is obtained for the Cetiya. Even when it is said, “I give to the monks, to you, and to the Cetiya,” a separate share is obtained only for the Cetiya, not for the individual. This should be applied in the same way starting with the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha.

In the past, people gave offerings to both Sanghas with the Buddha at the head. The Blessed One sat in the middle. The monks sat on the right side, and the bhikkhunīs sat on the left side. The Blessed One was the Sangha-Elder (Saṅghatthera) of both Sanghas. At that time, the Blessed One personally used the requisites he received and also gave them to the monks. Nowadays, however, wise people place an image or a Cetiya containing relics and give offerings to both Sanghas with the Buddha at the head. Placing an alms-bowl on a stand in front of the image or the Cetiya and pouring the water of donation, they offer, saying, “We give to the Buddhas.” In that case, they first offer hard and soft food. Or, having brought it to the monastery, they offer alms-food, flowers, scents, etc., saying, “We give this to the Cetiya.” How should one act regarding those offered items? First, flowers, scents, etc., should be placed on the Cetiya. Banners and streamers should be made from the cloths. Lamps should be lit with the oil. As for alms-food, honey, molasses, etc., they should be given to the person—whether a monk or a layman—who regularly cleans and maintains the Cetiya. If there is no regular maintainer, it is proper to set aside the brought food, perform the duties (cleaning), and then consume it. If it is a time close [to the meal deadline], it is also proper to consume it first and perform the duties later. Among flowers, scents, etc., if it is said, “Take this and perform an offering at the Cetiya,” it should be taken and offered even if it is far away. Even if it is said, “Take it to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha,” it should be taken. However, if it is said, “I am wandering for alms; there are monks in the nearby rest-house, they will take it,” and the donor says, “I give it only to you, venerable sir,” then it is proper to consume it. Otherwise, if while someone is carrying it saying, “I will give it to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha,” the time [for the meal] becomes near while on the way, it is proper to take it for oneself and consume it.

Regarding the words, “I give to the Sangha who have completed the Rains Retreat,” if one enters a monastery and gives, saying, “I give these robes to the Sangha who have completed the Rains Retreat,” then however many monks in that residence have completed the first Rains Retreat without breaking it, it should be distributed by them; it does not reach others. Even for those who have gone to another place, if there is someone to receive their share...
256:
Offerings should be made until the conclusion of the Kaṭhina ceremony. Teachers who know the characteristics (lakkhaṇaññū) say: "When the Kaṭhina has not been spread, a robe given in the winter with the words 'I give to the Saṅgha who have completed the Vassa' also reaches the monks who have completed the later (pacchimika) Vassa." However, this matter is not decided in the Commentaries. If, while standing outside the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā), one says, "I give to the Saṅgha who have completed the Vassa," it reaches all the monks who have arrived at that place. Otherwise, if one says, "I give to the Saṅgha who have completed the Vassa in such-and-such a monastery," it reaches only the monks who completed the Vassa in that monastery until the conclusion of the Kaṭhina ceremony. If one speaks thus starting from the first day of summer (the 1st waning day of Phagguna), it reaches all the monks present in that monastery. Why? Because it occurs at the beginning of the [latter] season (piṭṭhisamaya). If it is said during the Vassa itself, "I give to the monks observing the Vassa," those who have broken their Vassa do not receive it; only those still observing the Vassa receive it. However, during the robe-season month (from the 1st waning day of Assayuja to the full moon of Kattika), if it is said, "I give to the monks observing the Vassa," it reaches only those who entered the later (pacchimika) Vassa; it does not reach those who entered the earlier (purimika) Vassa nor those who have broken their Vassa.

From the robe-season month until the last day of winter, if it is said, "We give the rains-residence robe (vassāvāsika)," whether the Kaṭhina has been spread or not, it reaches only the monks who have completed the past Vassa. If it is said starting from the first day of summer, it should be presented to the schedule (mātikā) [by asking]: "Five months have passed since the previous Vassa residence, and the upcoming Vassa residence will be in four months; to which Vassa-resident do you give?" If the donor says, "I give to the monks who have completed the past Vassa," that robe reaches only the monks who resided during that past Vassa; fellow monks (sabhāga-bhikkhus) are also entitled to take the share of monks who have gone elsewhere. If the donor says, "I give the rains-residence robe for the upcoming Vassa," it should be kept and taken on the day of entering the Vassa. Otherwise, if the donor says, "The monastery is not secure, there is danger from thieves, it is not possible to keep it, nor is it possible to carry it around while traveling," and then says, "I give to the monks who have arrived," it should be distributed and taken. If the donor says, "Venerable Sir, I have not yet given the rains-residence robe for the third Vassa from this year; I give that robe now," it reaches the monks who completed the Vassa during that third Vassa. If those monks have gone elsewhere, and another trusted monk takes it, it should be given. If only one monk remains and the rest have passed away, the entire robe reaches that single monk alone. If not even one remains, it becomes the property of the Saṅgha (saṅghika) and should be distributed by the monks present.

## Regarding "Giving by Designation" (Ādissa deti)
In this term "Ādissa deti," a person who gives by referring to and specifying gruel (yāgu), alms-food, edibles, robes, a monastery, or medicine is said to be "giving by designation." In such giving, this is the decision: For the monks [invited] for today...
257:
...or for tomorrow, having invited them for gruel (yāgu), the donor gives gruel to those monks who have entered the house. After giving the gruel, referring to the monks who have finished drinking it, if the donor gives robes saying, "I give these robes to those by whom my gruel was drunk," they reach only those monks who were invited and drank the gruel. However, if monks passing by the front of the house on alms-round duty (bhikkhācāra-vatta) or monks who entered the house received the gruel, or if people took alms-bowls from the sitting hall (āsanasālā) and gave to monks, or if monks were sent by elders, they are not entitled to those robes. If many other monks arrive along with the invited monks, filling the inside and outside of the house, and the donor says, "Whether invited or not, let all the monks to whom I gave gruel receive these clothes," then all are entitled to them. However, monks who received the gruel through the hands of the elders are not entitled. If the donor says, "Let all who drank my gruel receive them," then all are entitled. The same principle applies to alms-food and edibles.

In the case of robes, if there were monks who previously resided for Vassa with that donor and had been given robes before, and that donor, after feeding the monks, says, "I previously gave robes to certain monks; let this robe, or thread, or butter, honey, molasses, etc., be for those same monks," then all of it reaches only those monks. Regarding a monastery, if it is said, "Let this belong to the monk who resides in the vihāra or pariveṇa built by me," it belongs only to that monk. Regarding medicinal requisites, if it is said, "We occasionally give medicines such as butter to the elders; let this belong to those same monks who received them," then it reaches only those monks.

In this term "Giving to an individual" (puggala), the decision is: If one gives either in the recipient's absence, saying, "I give this robe to the monk named so-and-so," or in the recipient's presence, placing it at his feet and saying, "Venerable Sir, I give this to you," it belongs only to that monk. If, however, one says, "I give this to you and your pupils (antevāsika)," it reaches both the elder and the pupils. If there is one who has come to receive instruction or one who is leaving after receiving it, that pupil is also entitled. If it is said, "I give to the monks who are constant companions (nibaddacārika) with you," it reaches all those who perform the duties of a resident pupil and travel about receiving instruction and asking questions. This is the decision on the term "Giving to an individual."

If only a single monk is residing for the Vassa, and people give robes saying, "We give to the Saṅgha," what should be done in that case? "Bhikkhus, I allow..."
258:
According to the words (Mahāvagga, 363), "Until the Kathina is withdrawn, those robes belong only to that monk," if a quorum of monks is obtained and the Kathina has been spread, it is for five months; if the Kathina has not been spread, even if the robes are taken to another place during the one-month robe-season (from the 1st waning day of Assayuja to the full moon day of Kattika), those robes belong only to that monk; no one else has authority over those robes. Whatever robes are given with the words, "We give to the Saṅgha," or "We give intending for the Saṅgha," or "We give to the Saṅgha that has completed the Vassa," or "We give robes for those who have resided for the Vassa," if they enter that monastery without the robes of a deceased monk being distributed, all of that belongs only to that monk. If that monk receives robes given to those who have resided for the Vassa, whether from cloth deposited for the sake of the rains-residence or from what has arisen in that monastery, all is indeed properly received. Herein, this is the defining characteristic: in whatever manner cloth arises for the Saṅgha, it falls to the monk who has spread the Kathina for five months, and to the monk who has not spread the Kathina for the one-month robe-season.

If a certain monk lives alone during a season other than the rainy season, and at that time people give robes saying, "We give to the Saṅgha," that monk should resolve, "These robes are for me." The monk who resolves must know the duty. That monk should ring a bell or announce the time and wait for a while; if monks arrive because of the sound of the bell or the announcement of the time, the robes should be shared with them. While those monks are distributing the robes, if another monk arrives before the lots (kusa) are cast, an equal share must be given; if another monk arrives after the lots are cast, a share need not be given if one does not wish to. For even if there are a thousand monks, as soon as the lot-sticks are cast for a single portion, the robe is considered taken; therefore, a share need not be given if one does not wish to. If they wish to give of their own accord, let them give. This same method applies to sub-shares as well.

Furthermore, if other monks do not arrive because of the sound of the bell or the announcement of the time, he should resolve, "These robes fall to me." When resolved in this way, all the robes belong only to that monk, but the seniority order does not stand. If he takes them one by one, saying, "This is the first portion that falls to me, this is the second portion," then the taking is properly done, and the seniority order stands; for a monk who takes them by having them brought to him in this way, it is also considered resolved. If, whether having rung the bell or not, whether having announced the time or not...
259:
If he takes them thinking, "I alone am here, these robes are mine alone," they are improperly taken. But if he takes them thinking, "There is no other monk here, these robes fall to me," they are properly taken. If, without resolving, he takes those robes and goes toward another monastery intending, "I will distribute them with the monks there," those robes remain the property of the Saṅgha in every place he goes. In this matter, the mere sight by monks is the measure. Therefore, if some monks coming from the opposite direction ask, "Friend, where are you going?" and having heard the matter, say, "Friend, are we not the Saṅgha?" and distribute and take them right there, they are properly taken. If that monk turns off the path and enters a certain monastery, or a refectory, or enters a single house while wandering for alms, and if monks see him there, inquire about the matter, distribute and take them, they are indeed properly taken.

Because of the words (Mahāvagga, 364), "Monks, a share of robes should not be accepted elsewhere than where the Vassa was resided; whoever should accept it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," if a monk who has completed the Vassa in one place accepts a share in another place, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing. Although the offense here is light, nevertheless, those robes taken must be given back at the place where they were taken. If they are lost or worn out, that monk alone must replace them. If he does not give them when told, "Give them," he should be made to act according to the value of the goods in the relinquishing of the burden.

If a monk, thinking, "In this way, many robes will arise for me," resides for the Vassa in two monasteries, he receives only a single person's share. Therefore, if he stays in each monastery for one day each or seven days each, he should be given half of the share that one person receives from each monastery. Only when given in this way is it called giving a single person's share. If a monk residing in one monastery lets the dawn rise in the other monastery every seven days, he should be given the share from the monastery where he stayed more often. Even so, it is called giving only a single person's share. This is said regarding monasteries within the same boundary (sīmā) having various gains and various precincts. But in monasteries with different boundaries, the taking of lodgings is settled. Therefore, a share of robes does not fall to him there; however, all other things such as alms-food, snacks, and medicine fall to any monk who has entered within the boundary in all monasteries.

"Monks, when a monk has passed away, the Saṅgha is the owner of his bowl and robes. However, caregivers of the sick (gilānupaṭṭhāka) are very helpful. I allow, monks, that the Saṅgha..."
260:
"Monks, when a monk passes away, the Saṅgha owns his bowl and robes. However, those who attend to the sick (gilānupaṭṭhāka) are of great service. Monks, I allow the triple robe and bowl to be given to the caregivers. Among those requisites, I allow the light articles and light requisites to be distributed by the Saṅgha present there. As for the heavy articles and heavy requisites, they are not to be given away or distributed, being the property of the Saṅgha of the four quarters, both present and future." In accordance with these words (from the Mahāvagga Pali), when a monk passes away, one may either request permission or perform the following formal act:

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. The monk named so-and-so has passed away. These are his triple robe and bowl. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this triple robe and bowl to the caregivers. This is the motion (ñatti).

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. The monk named so-and-so has passed away. These are his triple robe and bowl. The Saṅgha gives this triple robe and bowl to the caregivers. Whichever venerable one approves of giving this triple robe and bowl to the caregivers, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

"This triple robe and bowl have been given by the Saṅgha to the caregivers. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this."

After announcing the formal act (kammavācā) in this manner and giving the bowl and robes to the caregivers, the remaining light requisites should be distributed and taken by the Saṅgha present.

21. Regarding the share received by the caregivers, this is the decision: If the monk passes away while the entire community of monks (bhikkhu-saṅgha) is attending to him, all are entitled to a share. If he passes away while being attended to by a rotation system where some have finished their turn and others have not yet served, some teachers say, "Since all would have served when their turn arrived, all are entitled to a share." Other teachers say, "Only those who actually performed the nursing receive it; those who have not yet served do not receive it." When a novice (sāmaṇera) passes away, if there are robes, they should be given to the caregivers. If there are no robes, whatever is available should be given. If other requisites exist, they should be valued as a robe-share and given. If a monk and a novice have attended equally, an equal share should be given. However, if only the novice performs the nursing and the monk merely manages the arrangements, the novice should be given the elder's share (the larger portion). If...
261:
If the novice only cooks the gruel with water brought by the monk and merely offers it, while the monk performs the actual nursing, the monk should be given the elder's share. If many monks attend together in harmony, an equal share should be given to all. Among these monks, if one attends exceptionally, a special portion should be made for him.

Even if a person cooks and offers gruel or arranges a bath as a caregiver for only a single day, that person is considered a caregiver. One who does not come near but only sends medicine, rice, etc., is not a caregiver. One who searches for and brings supplies is indeed a caregiver. One person may attend out of a sense of duty, while another attends with the hope of receiving food or gifts. If both desire it at the time of death, it should be given to both. If a person, after attending, goes elsewhere for the patient's business or his own business, saying, "I will return and attend again," it should be given to him as well. If a person, after attending for a long time, gives up the responsibility saying, "I can no longer do it," and leaves, and if the patient passes away on that very day, the caregiver's share should not be given to him. Whether a caregiver is a layperson, a monk, or even a woman, all receive a share. 

If that monk possesses only a bowl and robes and nothing else, everything must be given to the caregivers. Even if that bowl and robes are worth a thousand, they must be given. However, the caregivers do not receive other numerous requisites; those belong only to the Saṅgha. If the remaining articles are many and valuable, but the triple robe is of little value, a portion should be taken from those articles to provide a set of requisites along with the triple robe; all this is obtained only from the Saṅgha's property. However, if the patient, while still alive, relinquished all his requisites and gave them to someone, or if someone took them out of intimacy (vissāsa), they belong only to the one to whom they were given or by whom they were taken. The caregivers receive only according to that person's wish. Requisites kept in a distant place without being given to others also belong only to the Saṅgha in those respective places. If property belongs to two monks and is not yet divided, when one passes away, the other becomes the owner. The same principle applies to property owned by many. When all have passed away, it becomes the property of the Saṅgha. If it is given to co-residents (saddhivihārika) and others without being divided, it is as if it were not given. Only giving after division is a proper gift. That which is given after division belongs only to the co-residents and others even after those [donors] pass away; it does not become the property of the Saṅgha.
262:
If a monk who has completed the Rains Retreat (vassa) departs either before the robes have arisen or after they have arisen but before they are distributed, and if he is mad, deranged, afflicted by pain, or has been expelled, his share (bhāga) must be given if there is a suitable recipient. However, if he disrobes, dies, or confesses to being a novice (sāmaṇera); or if he is one who renounces the training, one who has committed an offense involving defeat (pārajika), a eunuch (paṇḍaka), one living by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka), one who has gone over to a non-Buddhist sect (titthiyapakkantaka), an animal (tiracchānagata), a matricide, a patricide, a killer of an Arahant, a violator of a nun, a schismatic, one who has shed the blood of a Buddha, or if he confesses to being a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka)—in these cases, the Sangha alone is the owner; the share must not be given.

If the Sangha is divided before the robes have arisen for the monks who have completed the Rains Retreat, and they become two groups like the monks of Kosambī, and in that situation, people give libation water (dakkhiṇodaka), incense, and so forth to one side, and give robes to the other side saying, "We give to the Sangha"; or if they give libation water to a certain group and give robes to that same group saying, "We give to the Sangha"—those robes belong to the Sangha alone. They are to be received by both groups. After striking the gong (ghaṇṭi), they should be distributed by both sides together. However, if people give libation water and incense to one side, and give robes to the other side saying, "We give to this group (pakkha)," those robes belong only to that group. In such a donation, the group to whom the libation water was given receives only the libation water. The group to whom the robes were given receives only the robes. In a place where the libation water is the standard, if one group receives the robes because they received the libation water, and the other group receives the robes because they were the ones given the robes, then both groups should join together and distribute them according to seniority (vassa). It is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā: "This is the decision in Parasamudda (the island of Ceylon)." If libation water is given to a certain group and robes are given to that same group saying, "We give to this group," those robes belong only to that group; the other group has no ownership. If the Sangha is divided after the robes have arisen for the monks who have completed the Rains Retreat but before they are distributed, they must be distributed equally among all.

If, while many monks are traveling on a journey, some monks enter a cemetery for the sake of refuse-rag cloth (paṃsukūla) and others depart without waiting, the share must not be given to those who depart without waiting if they do not wish to give it. However, the share must be given to those who wait, even if they do not wish to give it. If people give saying, "Let only those who have come here take it," or if they depart after making a sign saying, "Let those who arrive take it," then for all those who arrive...
263:
...it reaches them. If they depart after abandoning it, whoever takes it is the owner. If some monks enter the cemetery first and some enter later, those who entered first receive the refuse-rag cloth (paṃsukūla), while those who entered later do not. According to the words: "I allow you, monks, not to give a share to those who enter later if they do not wish to" (Mahāvagga 341), a share must not be given to those who enter later if they do not wish to give it. However, if all enter together and some receive it while others do not, according to the words: "I allow you, monks, to give a share to those who enter together even if they do not wish to" (Mahāvagga 341), a share must be given to those who enter together even if they do not wish to give it. If they enter the cemetery after making an agreement outside saying, "We shall all distribute and take whatever refuse-rag cloth is obtained," and some receive it while others do not, according to the words: "I allow you, monks, to give a share to those who enter after making an agreement even if they do not wish to" (Mahāvagga 341), a share must be given to those who enter after making an agreement even if they do not wish to give it. This concludes the discussion on the distribution of robes.

Regarding the distribution of alms-food (piṇḍapāta), there is this decision concerning the Sangha-meal (saṅghabhatta) and others allowed thus: "I allow, monks, a Sangha-meal, a designated meal (uddesabhatta), an invitation (nimantana), a ticket-meal (salākabhatta), a fortnightly meal (pakkhika), an Uposatha meal (uposathika), and a meal on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipadika)" (Cūḷavagga 325).

A Sangha-meal is a meal given to the entire Sangha. Therefore, in a Sangha-meal, there is no such thing as a turn (ṭhitikā). For that very reason, one should not say regarding that Sangha-meal, "We have been eating for ten or twelve days now; now bring monks from elsewhere." Nor is one allowed to say, "We did not receive it on previous days; now give that share of the meal to us." That Sangha-meal reaches whoever happens to arrive.

In the case of designated meals (uddesabhatta) and so forth, this is the method: When a king or a king's great minister sends word saying, "Having designated from the Sangha, bring this many monks," the time should be announced and the turn (ṭhitikā) should be asked. If there is a turn, it should be given starting from that turn. If not, it should be given starting from the seat of the senior elders (thera). The monk who designates the alms should not bypass even those who are alms-food collectors (piṇḍapātika). However, those monks, out of regard for their ascetic practice (dhutaṅga), will bypass it themselves. While the alms are being given in this way, if senior elders of a lazy nature arrive later, one should not say, "Venerable sirs, it is being given to monks of twenty years' standing; your turn has passed." One should suspend the turn, give to those senior elders, and then continue giving according to the turn.
264:
## 
Hearing that 'Many assigned meals (uddesabhatta) have arisen in that monastery,' monks come even from a monastery a yojana away. For those who have arrived, they should be allowed to receive [the turn for the meal] starting from the place where they are standing. Even if they have not yet arrived, if their pupils or resident students who have entered the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) are receiving it, it should indeed be allowed. Some say, 'Let those standing outside the precinct boundary receive it,' but it should not be allowed. If they are continuous (ekābaddha) with those who have entered the precinct boundary and are at their own monastery gate or inside the monastery, it is considered a boundary expanded by the size of the assembly; therefore, it should be allowed. Even after it has been given to the most junior monk (saṅghanavaka), it should still be allowed for senior elders who arrive later. In the second distribution, however, for monks who arrive after the elders have taken their seats, the first turn is no longer available; they should receive from the second turn according to seniority (vassagga).

In a monastery, having designated a single place for assigning meals, an assigned meal (uddesabhatta) announced anywhere within the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) measuring about a gāvuta should be received at that very place for assigning meals. If a person sends word to a monk, saying, 'Tomorrow, please assign and send ten monks from the Saṅgha's turn,' that monk should inform the meal-assigner (bhattuddesaka) of that matter. If he forgets on that day, he should inform him early the next morning. If he forgets and remembers only while entering for alms, as long as he has not yet crossed the precinct boundary, he should be allowed to receive according to the established turn at the refectory (bhojanasālā). Even if he has crossed the precinct boundary, if the monks are continuous (ekābaddha) with those within the precinct boundary, traveling without leaving a gap of twelve cubits from one another, they should be allowed to receive according to the established turn. If the monks are not so continuous and he remembers at some place outside the precinct boundary, he should be allowed to receive by making a new turn at that place. If he remembers at an assembly hall (āsanasalā) inside a village, he should be allowed to receive according to the turn at the assembly hall. Wherever he remembers, it should indeed be allowed; it is not proper not to receive it. This is because that assigned meal cannot be obtained on the second day.

If someone, seeing monks traveling from their own monastery to another monastery, requests an assigned meal (uddesabhatta), as long as they are within the precinct boundary or are continuous (ekābaddha) with the monks within the precinct boundary as previously mentioned, they should be allowed to receive according to the turn at their own monastery. Regarding the assigned meal offered to those standing outside the precinct boundary, [if they say,] 'Venerable Sir, from the Saṅgha...'
265:
## 
When it is said, 'Please assign this many monks,' all monks who have arrived should be allowed to receive. In that case, those standing far away but continuous (ekābaddha) without leaving a gap of twelve cubits should also be understood as having arrived. If they hear [the announcement] upon entering the monastery they are going to, they should receive according to the turn (vāra) of that monastery. If someone, seeing monks at a village gate, on a street, at a crossroads, or inside a house, announces a Saṅgha-assigned meal, the monks who have reached the precinct (upacāra) in those respective places should be allowed to receive.

In this matter, the precinct of a house (gharūpacāra) should be understood by way of these four types: (1) single house—single precinct, (2) single house—multiple precincts, (3) multiple houses—single precinct, and (4) multiple houses—multiple precincts. Among these, a house belonging to a single family with a single use is called a single precinct within the boundary of a winnowing tray's throw (suppapāta). An assigned meal (uddesabhatta) arising in that precinct reaches all monks standing in that single precinct according to the duty of alms-gathering. This is called 'single house—single precinct.' If it is a single house but a wall is raised in the middle to allow two wives to live comfortably with separate entrances, the assigned meal arising in that house does not reach the monk on the other side of the wall; it reaches only the monk sitting in that specific place. This is called 'single house—multiple precincts.' In a house where many monks are invited and seated continuously from inside the house, filling even the neighboring houses, the assigned meal arising there reaches all the monks. Even if it is the residence of different families, if they use it with a single entrance without a wall in the middle, the same rule applies. This is called 'multiple houses—single precinct.' When an assigned meal arises for monks sitting in separate residences, even if the monks can be seen through a hole in the wall, it reaches only the monks sitting in those respective residences. This is called 'multiple houses—multiple precincts.'

If a monk obtains an assigned meal at a village gate, street, or crossroads, and since there is no other monk, he takes it for himself, and on the second day he obtains another at the same place, he should allow any other monk, whether junior or senior, whom he sees to receive it. If there is no one, he should take it for himself and consume it. If, while monks are sitting in an assembly hall (āsanasalā) waiting for the mealtime, someone comes and says, 'Please give a Saṅgha-assigned bowl,' 'Please give an assigned bowl,' 'Please assign from the Saṅgha and give a bowl,' or 'Please give a Saṅgha-owned (saṅghika) bowl,' he should allow it to be received according to the turn and give it. The same rule applies when it is said, 'Please give a Saṅgha-assigned monk,' 'Please assign from the Saṅgha and give a monk,' or 'Please give a Saṅgha-owned monk.'
266:
## 
When requesting the assignment of meals in this manner, it is desired that the assigner of meals (uddesaka) be one who loves virtue, is modest, and is endowed with wisdom. That assigner of meals should inquire three times for the one whose turn it is; if there is no one who knows the turn, it should be taken starting from the seat of the senior elder. If a certain monk says, "I know, the turn is reached at ten years of seniority," he should be asked, "Friend, are there monks with ten years of seniority?" If, upon hearing his words, many monks come saying, "We have ten years, we have ten years," one should not say, "It reaches you, it reaches you," but rather say, "Let all the monks be silent," and arrange them in order. Having arranged them in order, the lay devotee (upāsaka) should be asked, "How many monks do you desire?" If he says, "Venerable sir, I desire this many monks," one should not say, "It reaches you, it reaches you," but should inquire of the youngest monk regarding his seniority (vassa), the season, the part of the day, and the shadow [measured at the time of ordination]. If another senior elder arrives while the shadow is being inquired about, the bowl should be given to that elder. Furthermore, if a senior elder arrives after the shadow has been inquired about and it has been said, "It reaches you," that elder does not receive it. Indeed, whether one is engaged in various talk, sitting, or even sleeping, if the turn is reached, the taking is considered well-taken, and the passing is considered well-passed. For such assigned meals (uddesabhatta) reach only those who have arrived. The state of having arrived there should be determined by the precinct (upacāra) of the hall. The area within the enclosure of the sitting hall (āsanasālā) is called the precinct; the gain reaches the monk who is within that precinct.

Suppose someone has eight bowls brought from the sitting hall to assign meals, fills seven bowls with choice food and one with water, and sends them to the sitting hall. If those who brought the bowls place them in the hands of the monks without saying anything and depart, whatever is received by whom belongs to that person. However, the monk who received the water should be given another assigned meal, setting aside the turn that has passed. Whether that meal be coarse or choice, or even accompanied by a set of three robes, it belongs only to that monk. This is due to that monk's special merit. Since water is not material food (āmisa), he receives another assigned meal. If, however, those who brought the bowls say, "Venerable sirs, please divide and consume all of this," and then depart, all the monks should divide and consume the food and drink the water.

If a monk says, "Assign from the Saṅgha and give to eight great elders, give to the middle-seated monks, give to the junior monks, give to the novices of full years, give to the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya etc., give to my relative monks," he should be told, "Lay follower, though you say this, according to the order of turns, it does not reach them," and the meals should be given only according to the turn.

When junior novices receive assigned meals, if the donors'...
267: ...house has an auspicious ceremony, it should be said, 'Send your teachers and preceptors.' In an assigned meal (uddesabhatta) where the first portion reaches the novices and the subsequent portion reaches the great elders, the novices do not get to go ahead of the great elders saying, 'We received the first portion'; they must go only according to the sequence. When it is said, 'Come here as assigned by the Sangha,' one should take it only according to the turn, saying, 'For me, you will know another time, but the turn proceeds in this way.' Furthermore, if someone says, 'Give the bowl assigned by the Sangha,' and before the bowl is even set down, he takes any monk's bowl, fills it, and brings it, that brought meal must also be taken only by the one whose turn it is. A person was sent saying, 'Bring the bowl assigned by the Sangha,' and he says, 'Venerable sir, give me a bowl; I will bring the invited meal.' If the monks, knowing that he came from the house that gives assigned meals, ask, 'Did you not come from such-and-such a house?' and he says, 'Yes, venerable sir, it is not an invited meal, it is an assigned meal,' then it must be taken by the one whose turn it is. When told, 'Bring a bowl,' if he asks, 'What shall I say to bring it?' and is told, 'Bring it saying whatever you like,' the one who comes is called a 'trusted messenger' (vissaṭṭhadūta). To him, whatever he desires—an assigned bowl, a sequential bowl, or a personal bowl—should be given. If a foolish and incompetent person is sent saying, 'Bring the assigned bowl,' and he does not know what to say and stands silent, he should not be asked, 'To whom have you come?' or 'Whose bowl will you take?' For if asked thus, he might say, according to the nature of the question, 'I have come to you' or 'I will take your bowl.' Then other monks, loathing that monk, would not look at him. Therefore, one should only ask, 'Where are you going? What are you wandering about for?' If he says, 'I have come for the assigned bowl,' the monk whose turn it is should be identified and the bowl given. There is a type called a 'deceptive turn' (kūṭaṭṭhitikā). In the house of a king or a great royal minister, eight very excellent assigned meals are constantly given. Having made those into meals for individual wanderers, the monks consume them separately according to the turn. Some monks, noting their turn, go thinking, 'Now it will reach us tomorrow.' While they have not yet arrived, other guest monks arrive and sit in the sitting hall. At that very moment, the king's men arrive and say, 'Give the bowls filled with excellent food.' The guest monks, not knowing the turn, take them. At that very moment, the monks who know the turn arrive and [ask], 'What are you taking?'
268:
Monks who know the sequence say, "This is excellent alms-food from the city of Rājagaha." If they ask, "From how many years of seniority (vassa) does it start?" and the answer is, "It starts from this many years," then one should forbid others by saying, "Do not take it," and it should be taken only according to the established sequence (ṭhitikā). When the bowl has been taken, for those monks who know the seniority and arrive at the time of giving the bowl, or arrive after the bowl has been given, or arrive when the bowls are brought back filled from Rājagaha, or when the King sends word saying, "Let only the monks come today," and offers alms-food only into the hands of the monks—when they arrive at the time of bringing such offered alms-food, the monks who know the sequence should forbid them, saying, "Do not eat," and ensure it is taken only according to the sequence.

If the King invites those monks, feeds them, and also fills their bowls and offers them, that brought alms-food should be taken only according to the sequence. However, if he says, "Do not let them go empty-handed," and puts only a little into the bowls, that should not be taken as a turn in the sequence. Mahāsumma Thera said, "If they eat and return with empty bowls, the food they ate becomes an obstruction in their throats (gīvā)." But Mahāpaduma Thera said, "In such eating, there is no obstruction in the throat. Monks who do not know the sequence should wait until those who know the sequence arrive. Even so, the food eaten by the monks is well-eaten. However, when the turn for the seniority sequence arrives now, it should not be taken again."

An alms-offering worth a hundred kahāpaṇas, accompanied by a set of triple robes (ticīvara), was received by a monk who had not yet completed a single vassa. It was recorded in the monastery, "Such an alms-offering was received by a monk with no vassa." Sixty years later, when a similar alms-offering arises again, the question is whether it should be taken according to the sequence of one with no vassa or according to the sequence of one with sixty vassa. It is said that it should be taken only according to the sequence of sixty vassa. This is because this monk has grown senior while holding this position in the sequence. If a monk becomes a novice (sāmaṇera) after eating an allocated meal (uddesabhatta), he is entitled to take that meal again when it arrives according to the novice's sequence. This person is known as one with an "interim meal" (antarābhattaka). If a novice who has completed twenty years of age thinks, "I will receive the allocated meal tomorrow," and receives higher ordination (upasampadā) today, his turn in the sequence has passed. If an allocated meal arrives for a monk and his bowl is not empty, he has the bowl given to another person sitting nearby. If they take that bowl with the intention to steal, it becomes an obstruction in the throat (gīvā). However, if that monk himself gives it, saying, "I give my bowl," there is no obstruction in the throat for him. Furthermore, if he has no need for that food and says, "Enough for me, ..."
269:
"I give this alms-food to you; send the bowl and bring it back," if one says this to another, everything brought in that bowl belongs only to the owner of the bowl. If the bowl is taken with the intention to steal, it is a case of theft, but because the food was already given, there is no fault regarding the food.

In a monastery, there are ten monks; nine of them are practitioners of the alms-gathering dhutaṅga (piṇḍapātika), and one is a receiver of allocated meals (sādiyanaka). When it is said, "Give ten bowls of allocated meals," the alms-gathering monks do not wish to take them. If the remaining monk says, "Let all come to me," and takes them, it does not constitute a sequence (ṭhitikā). However, if he takes them after each has been assigned to a monk, the sequence remains valid. Having accepted them in this way and having them brought in ten bowls, he says, "Venerable sirs, please favor me," and gives nine bowls to the alms-gathering monks. This is called "Bhikkhudattiya" (food given by a monk) and is allowable to be taken.

If that lay devotee (upāsaka) requests, "Venerable sirs, please come to my house," and that monk also says to the other monks, "Venerable sirs, please come as my companions," and they go to his house, everything received there belongs only to that monk. The other monks receive only the food given by that monk. Alternatively, if he has them sit in the house, pours the water of donation, and offers rice gruel (yāgu), snacks (khajjaka), etc., saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept whatever the people offer," then because of that monk's words, it is allowable for the other monks to accept. If they fill the bowls of the monks who have finished eating and give them for the journey back, all of it belongs only to that monk, and it is allowable for the others only if given by him.

However, if while still at the monastery, that monk says, "Venerable sirs, please accept my alms-food; it is proper to comply with the words of the people," and they go, then everything they eat and bring back there belongs to them personally. Alternatively, if they go without him saying, "Accept my alms-food," but saying, "It is proper to comply with the words of the people," and there, upon hearing one monk's melodious voice chanting the Anumodanā, or being inspired by the calm demeanor of the elders, the people offer many monastic requisites (parikkhāra), this is called "Akatabhāga" (an undivided portion) arising from faith in the elders. Therefore, it belongs to all the monks.

A person, having requested from the Sangha and taken a bowl according to the sequence, fills it with excellent hard and soft food, brings it back, and offers it, saying, "Venerable sirs, let the entire Sangha enjoy this alms-food." It should be shared and enjoyed by all. As for the owner of the bowl, another allocated meal should be given, setting aside the turn that has passed. If, from the very beginning, the person says, "Give me all the bowls belonging to the Sangha," the bowl of a conscientious (lajjī) monk should be given. After bringing it back, "All..."
270:
If a donor says, “Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha partake,” the food should be distributed and then consumed. If a person brings food in a dish and says, “I offer this food designated for the Saṅgha (saṅghuddesa),” it should not be given out morsel by morsel, but should be given according to the roster, providing enough for one monk’s sustenance. If that person brings the food and remains silent, not knowing what to say, one should not ask, “For whom have you brought this? To whom do you wish to give it?” This is because, following the nature of the question, they might say, “I brought it for you, sirs; I wish to give it to you.” If that happens, other bhikkhus might feel disgusted with that bhikkhu and consider him unworthy of even a glance. However, if they are asked, “Where are you going? What are you wandering about for?” and they reply, “I have come with food designated for the Saṅgha,” then a conscientious (lajjī) bhikkhu whose turn it is should accept it according to the roster. If the food brought is abundant and sufficient for everyone, there is no need for the roster procedure. It should be offered by filling the bowls, starting from the seats of the elders.

If someone says, “Please give the bowl for the food designated for the Saṅgha,” one should not ask, “What will you bring?” but should simply have it accepted according to the normal roster. If milk-rice (pāyāsa) or food rich in flavor is always received, a separate roster should be established for such refined foods. Likewise, a separate roster should be made for rice gruel (yāgu) with its accompaniments, expensive fruits, and refined snacks (khajjaka). For ordinary rice, gruel, fruits, and snacks, only a single roster should be maintained. If someone says, “I will bring ghee,” a single roster is appropriate for all types of ghee; the same applies to all types of oil. However, if they say, “I will bring honey,” a single roster is appropriate for honey; the same applies to molasses, liquorice, and other medicines. If someone offers scents and garlands designated for the Saṅgha, is it allowable for a bhikkhu who observes the alms-food eater’s practice (piṇḍapātika)? It is allowable because only material food (āmisa) is prohibited. However, some say, “It should not be accepted because it is given specifically to the Saṅgha.”

## The Discussion on Designated Food (Uddesabhattakathā) is finished.

If an invited meal is personal (puggalika), the individual monk himself is the master of it. If it is for the Saṅgha (saṅghika), it should be accepted only according to the method mentioned in the section on designated food. However, if the messenger in this case is clever and says, “Venerable sirs, please accept alms,” instead of saying, “Accept the meal for the Bhikkhu-Saṅgha in Rājagaha,” then it is also allowable for those who are alms-food eaters. If the messenger is not clever and says, “Accept the meal,” but the monk who assigns the meals (bhattuddesaka) is clever and does not say “meal” but instead—
271:
—says, “Venerable sirs, please go; please go,” then in this way it is also allowable for the alms-food eaters. However, if he says, “Venerable sirs, the meal reaches you according to the roster,” then it is not allowable (for the alms-food eaters). If a person coming to invite monks enters the assembly hall (āsanatālā) and says, “Please give eight bhikkhus,” or “Please give eight bowls,” then in this case too, it is allowable for the alms-food eaters; and the assigning monk should say, “You go, and you go.” If the person says, “Please give eight bhikkhus, accept the meal,” or “Please give eight bowls, accept the meal,” then it must be accepted according to the roster. If the monk who facilitates the acceptance cuts off the word “meal” and says, “You go, and you go,” it is allowable for the alms-food eaters. If the person says, “Venerable sirs, please give your bowls; please come,” then the monks should go, saying, “Very well, lay devotee (upāsaka).” Even if it is said, “Please come, having been designated from the Saṅgha,” it should be accepted according to the roster.

For someone who comes from the house of an invited meal to get a bowl, the bowl should be given according to the roster, just as mentioned in the section on designated food. If someone does not say, “A bowl according to the Saṅgha’s roster,” but merely says, “Give me one bowl,” and before the bowl is officially accepted, he takes anyone’s bowl, fills it, and brings it back, that bowl belongs only to the owner of the bowl. It should not be accepted according to the roster as in the case of designated food. Here too, if someone comes and stands in silence, one should not ask, “To whom have you come?” or “Whose bowl will you take?” For if asked, they might say, “I have come to you; I will take your bowl,” and because of that, that bhikkhu would be someone to be disgusted by other bhikkhus. However, when it is said, “Where are you going? What are you doing as you wander about?” and the person says, “I have come for the bowl of such-and-such a person,” the bowl should be given by accepting it according to the roster for meals. Even if they say, “Give me a bowl for carrying the meal,” it should be given only according to the roster for meals. If they bring the food and say, “May the whole Saṅgha partake,” it should be distributed and eaten. Even if the turn of the bowl’s owner has passed, that turn should be set aside and another meal should be accepted according to the roster.

If a person brings food in a dish and says, “I give this to the Saṅgha,” it should be distributed by dividing it into morsels, starting from the roster for morsel-meals. If he remains silent, [one should not ask], “For whom have you brought this? For whom...”
272:
One should not ask, "To whom do you wish to give?" However, if asked, "Where are you going? Why are you wandering about?" and one replies, "I have brought food for the Saṅgha; I have brought food for the Elders," then it should be taken and distributed in order, morsel by morsel. If the food brought in this way is abundant and sufficient for the entire Saṅgha, it is called 'abhihaṭabhikkhā' (brought-alms). It is also allowable for monks who go on alms-round. There is no need to keep asking for the order; the bowls should be filled and offered starting from the seats of the Elders.

If a lay devotee sends a message to the Saṅghatthera, or to a monk famous for his mastery of the scriptures and ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), or to the meal-allocator (bhattuddesaka), saying, "Please bring eight monks to receive our food," even if they were sent by relatives or attendants, these three persons do not have the right to ask the donor [for clarification]; the established order (mātikā) is simply applied. Eight monks should be designated from the Saṅgha, and one should go with them, making nine monks in total. Why? Because through these monks, gains arise for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. However, a resident monk who is not well-known for scriptural mastery or ascetic practices has the right to ask the donor. Therefore, that monk should ask, starting with, "Should I take them from the Saṅgha, or shall I come with those I know?" and then act according to what the donors say. If they say, "Bring your disciples or those you know," he is allowed to go with those he desires. If they say, "Send eight monks," they must be sent only from the Saṅgha. If he himself can obtain alms in another village, he should go to that other village. If he cannot, he should enter that same village for alms.

While the invited monks are seated in the assembly hall, if people come saying, "Give us your bowls," the uninvited monks should not give theirs. They should say, "These are the invited monks." Only if they say, "You give [yours] too," is it proper to give. On festival days, people themselves go to the monastery precincts and meditation halls and invite Tipiṭaka-holders and Dhamma-preachers along with a hundred monks. At that time, those monks may go taking those they know. Why? Because people who desire a large number of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha do not go to individual precincts or meditation halls, but rather take as many monks as they can from the place of assembly.
273:
If the Saṅghatthera, or a person famous for scriptural study and ascetic practices, or the meal-allocator, returns to his own place after spending the rainy season elsewhere or after traveling somewhere, and people make offerings to that visiting monk, for the first time, those who know him should take [the food] and go. From the time it becomes a regular occurrence, starting from the second time, it should be taken and gone with according to the Saṅgha's order. If they are newly arrived visitors and go thinking, "I will see my relatives or attendants," and if their relatives and attendants make offerings there, in this case also, it is proper for those who know them to take [the food] and go.

If a monk is one who receives many gains, and his regular residence and the place he visits as a guest are similar—where in all such places people remain having prepared food for the Saṅgha—he should take [the food] and go only according to the Saṅgha's order. This is the distinction regarding invited food (nimantanabhatta). All remaining questions should be understood in the same manner as stated under allocated food (uddesabhatta). In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is stated: "If it is said, 'Give to eight Great Elders,' then only eight Great Elders should be given." This same method applies to middle-ranking monks and so on. If it is said without specification, "Give to eight monks," they should be given according to the Saṅgha's order.

## The Discussion on Invited Food is Finished.

Regarding ticket-food (salākabhatta), according to the words [of the Buddha], "Monks, I allow food to be designated by tying [a name] to a ticket or a strip and piling them up" (Cūḷavagga 326), one should write the letters "The ticket-food of so-and-so" on a ticket made of heartwood, or on a strip made of bamboo splints, fiber, palm leaf, and so on. These should be placed in a basket or a fold of a robe, and after piling all the tickets together and stirring them repeatedly from bottom to top, the meal-allocator, who is endowed with the five qualities, should distribute the tickets starting from the fixed order if there is one, or if not, starting from the seat of the Elder. For those who arrive later, or those who are far away but part of the continuous group, they should be given in the same manner as stated under allocated food (uddesabhatta).

If there are many alms-villages around the monastery but the monks are not many, the tickets may reach them according to the village. One should have them taken by village, saying, "You receive ticket-food in such-and-such village." In taking them this way, even if there are sixty various kinds of ticket-food in each village, all of them are considered taken. If there are two or three other ticket-foods near the village that the monk has reached, they should be given to that monk alone. This is because it is not possible to send another monk for those two or three ticket-foods. This is how it should be understood. In some villages, many ticket-foods are marked and given to seven or eight monks. At the time of offering, four or five meals...
274:
If there are ticket-meals (salākabhatta), those meals must be given to that monk alone. This is because it is not possible to send another monk for the sake of those meals.

If it is noted that there are many ticket-meals in some villages, they should be given to seven or eight monks. When giving them, however, tickets for four or five meals should be tied together and given. If there is another village beyond that village, and in that village only a single ticket-meal is given early in the morning, one of those monks should be urged (to accept it even if unwilling) and given it, saying: "Take that meal early in the morning first, and afterwards take the other meals in the nearer village." If he goes with the mistaken idea that he has already taken the ticket-meals in the nearer village before actually taking them, he should take the ticket-meal in the further village, return to the monastery, take the others, and then go to the nearer village. This is because it is not allowable to take Sangha gains outside the boundary (sīmā). This method is stated in the Kurundī. If there are many monks and the tickets are insufficient by village, they should be taken by street, or by house-row in a street, or by family. In places such as streets where there are many meals, they should be taken by many monks according to the method mentioned for the village. If there are no physical tickets, they should be taken by designation.

The monk who distributes the tickets (salākadāyaka) must know the duties. He should rise early, take his bowl and robes, go to the refectory, sweep the unswept places, and set out drinking and washing water. Noting the time, thinking "By now the monks will have finished their duties," he should strike the bell. When the monks have assembled, he should first have them take the ticket-meals for the village whose turn it is. He should say, "A ticket for such-and-such a turn-village falls to you; go there." If the village is further than a gāvuta and they would be exhausted if they went on that day, he should have them take it today, saying, "Your turn in the village falls tomorrow." If a monk is sent to a turn-village but does not go and requests another ticket, it should not be given. This is because it could lead to the loss of merit for faithful people and the loss of gain for the Sangha. Therefore, on the second or third day as well, another ticket should not be given to him; he should be told, "Go and eat at the place that fell to you." For a monk who does not go for three days, he should be made to take a ticket in a village nearer than the turn-village. If he does not take even that which is given, from then on, it is not proper to give him another ticket, and a firm penalty (daṇḍakamma) must be imposed.
275:
(This) should be done. It should not be decreased from sixty or fifty. After having them take (tickets) for the turn-village, the monastery-guard turn should be taken. He should be told, "The monastery-guard turn falls to you." To the monk whose turn it is to guard the monastery (vihāravārika), two or three tickets for gruel and three or four tickets for meals are given; however, they should not be given as a permanent arrangement. For the donors of gruel and meals might undergo a change of heart (loss of faith), thinking, "Only the monastery guards eat our gruel and meals." Therefore, they should be given from other families.

If they bring and give the portion for the monastery guards, this is good. If not, after taking the turn, the gruel and meals should be fetched for them; to that extent, their tickets are simply an increase in benefit. When their turn comes by seniority (vassagga), they are certainly entitled to take other choice meal-tickets as well. For extra delicacies (uttaribhaṅga) or a meal for one person, tickets should be given by making a separate seniority list. If a monk receives a ticket but does not get that meal on that day, he should be allowed to take it the next day. If he gets only the meal but not the delicacy, even so, he should be allowed to take it again. The same method applies to milk-rice tickets.
