If he gets only the milk but not the meal, he should not be allowed to take it again after receiving the milk. If two or three single-person meals fall to one person, during a time of scarcity when new monks receive them, they should be untangled and taken separately. A monk who does not receive the regular ticket-meal should also be allowed to take it the next day.

If the monastery is small and all monks share common property, the one taking the sugarcane ticket should distribute it to whichever monk is present, and for the Great Elders and others, it is proper to peel it and give it during the day. Having distributed the juice tickets, even after the meal (at night), it should be strained or made into molasses and given to alms-collectors (piṇḍapātika) and others. Tickets should be taken knowing whether guests have arrived or not. In a large monastery, they should be taken by making a seniority list. Whey tickets should also be distributed in a suitable place, or smoked, or cooked, and given to the Elders. In a large monastery, one should proceed exactly as described. Tickets for fruit, cakes, medicine, scents, and flowers should also be taken by separate seniority turns. Although medicine tickets and the like are allowable for alms-collectors (piṇḍapātika), they should not be consented to (sāditabbā) because they are taken by way of tickets. If they give ticket-meals consisting of only the first-alms...
276:
The order of turns must be asked and accepted. If there is no established order, it should be accepted starting from the seats of the senior elders (Mahātheras). If there is a large amount of such food, two or three portions should be given to each monk. If not many, give only one each, and when the sequence is completed, start again from the seats of the senior elders. Furthermore, if there is an interruption in between, the order of turns must be noted. If the food is a regular offering, the monk to whom it falls should be told, "Whether you receive it or not, please accept it tomorrow as well." Some food-tickets (salāka) are not regular, but on the day they are available, one receives as much as desired. If the days of not receiving are more frequent, the monk to whom that ticket falls should be told, without him having received it yet, "Please accept it tomorrow."

A monk who arrives late after the food-tickets have been taken should not be given the tickets that have already passed. A food-ticket can only be obtained by coming and stretching out one's hand from the time the bell is struck. Even if another person comes and stands nearby, if the turn has passed, it has indeed passed. However, if there is someone to accept it on behalf of that monk, he may receive it even if he does not come himself. In a common area (sabhāga-ṭṭhāna), if it is known that "such and such a monk has not yet arrived," it is proper to set aside a ticket, saying, "This is the ticket for that monk." If they make an agreement that "it shall not be given to one who does not come," it is an unrighteous (adhammika) practice. This is because the distributable goods ought to reach a monk who is within the precincts (upacāra). If they make a loud noise saying, "Give it to the one who does not come," a disciplinary act (daṇḍakamma) should be imposed, and they should be told, "Let them come and accept it."

If about five or six food-tickets are lost and the food-allocator (bhattuddesaka) does not remember the names of the donors, if he assigns those lost tickets to a senior elder or to himself and says to the monks, "I have assigned the food-ticket meal in such and such a village for myself; you may consume the food-ticket meal obtained there," it is proper. However, it is not proper to receive that food at the alms-hall (āsanassālā) and consume it there before it has reached the monastery. When it is said, "From today onwards, accept the food-ticket meal for me," it is not proper to accept it at that alms-hall; it must be brought to the monastery and then accepted. If it is said, "From tomorrow onwards," the food-allocator should be informed, "From tomorrow onwards, such and such a family will offer a food-ticket meal; please remember this at the time of receiving the food-tickets." When food-ticket meals have been suspended during a famine and are resumed when food is plentiful, if they see a certain monk and say, "From today onwards, please accept our food-ticket meal,"
277:
...it should not be accepted inside the village but should be brought to the monastery and then accepted. For this food-ticket meal (salāka-bhatta) is not like an assigned meal (uddesa-bhatta); it is offered specifically with reference to the monastery. Therefore, it is not proper to accept it outside the precincts (upacāra-sīmā) of the monastery. However, if it is said, "Accept it from tomorrow onwards," it should indeed be accepted at the monastery.

If a traveling monk wishes to go to a certain direction and another monk has obtained a food-ticket for a village in that direction whose turn it is, it is proper for him to take that ticket and go after saying to the other monk, "You accept the ticket that falls to me." That remaining monk should accept the ticket of the traveling monk before the latter has crossed the boundary of the precincts (upacāra-sīmā). If people establish a food-ticket meal at an abandoned monastery, saying, "Let them consume it after looking after the Bodhi tree, the cetiya, etc.," and if monks living in common areas (sabhāga-ṭṭhāna) go there early, perform their duties (vatta), and consume that food, it is proper. If those monks, after assigning their portions for the next day, have left, and a visiting monk (āgantuka bhikkhu) stays in the abandoned monastery, performs the duties early, strikes the bell, assigns the food-ticket meal to himself, and goes to the alms-hall (āsanassālā), he alone is the master of that food. If a certain monk, while other monks are still performing their duties, merely sweeps the ground two or three times, strikes the bell, and goes saying, "The food-ticket meal in the front village falls to me," he does not deserve that food because it was taken by theft. It belongs only to the monks who come later after performing their duties and assigning the portions.

If a village is very far away and the monks do not wish to go there regularly, and the people say, "We are being excluded from merit," the monks in common areas who are in a monastery near that village should be told, "On the days these monks do not come, you may consume it." However, the food-tickets should be assigned daily. In doing so, they are not considered assigned merely by striking the bell or merely by shaking the basket. The basket should be taken and the tickets poured out onto a low stool (pīṭhaka). The basket should not be held by its rim. For if there is a snake or a scorpion in that basket, it could cause suffering. Therefore, it should be held from the bottom, with the basket facing away, and the tickets should be poured out with the thought, "Even if there is a snake, let it flee from here." After pouring out the tickets in this manner, they should be accepted according to the village's turn, following the method previously mentioned.
278:
Furthermore, having assigned one ticket to the Great Elder and thinking, "The remaining tickets fall to me," and having performed the duties and paid homage to the Cetiya, when asked by the monks standing in the reflection-pavilion (vitakkamaḷaka), "Friends, have the tickets been assigned?" one should say, "Yes, venerable sirs, please take the ticket-food in whichever village you go to." If said in this way, even if they are assigned, they are well-assigned.

If monks go to another monastery to listen to the Dhamma throughout the night, and they go without taking tickets, saying, "We will not take the gift there, but will return after wandering for alms in our own alms-resort village," it is allowable if they come to eat the ticket-food that has fallen to the Great Elder in the monastery. At that time, the Great Elder also thinks, "What shall I do here?" and goes with them. When those monks reach the alms-resort village without eating at the monastery they visited, and they say, "Venerable sirs, please give us the bowls; we will bring the ticket-gruel and so on," the bowls should not be given. If asked, "Venerable sirs, why do you not give them?" one should say, "Food established for a monastery belongs to the monks residing in that monastery; we resided in another monastery." However, if they say, "Venerable sirs, please give them; we do not give to protect the monastery, we give to you; please take our alms-food," then it is allowable.

## The discussion on ticket-food is finished.

Regarding fortnightly food (pakkhikabhatta) and so on: food given by those striving for merit on the marked fortnights—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, the fifth, and the eighth—for the purpose of reminding them to observe the Uposatha, is called pakkhikabhatta. That food has the same status as ticket-food and should be taken and eaten. If both ticket-food and fortnightly food are abundant and reach all monks without distinction, both types of food should be taken separately. If the Saṅgha of monks is large, one should have them take the fortnightly food and then take the ticket-food according to its turn; or have them take the ticket-food and then take the fortnightly food according to its turn. Those monks who do not receive it will wander for alms. If both types of food are abundant but the monks are few, ticket-food is available daily; therefore, setting that aside, one should give only the fortnightly food, saying, "Friends, eat the fortnightly food." If they give excellent fortnightly food, a separate turn should be established. One should not take fortnightly food today, saying, "Tomorrow is the fortnight." However, if the lay donors say, "Tomorrow there will be coarse food in our house; please designate the fortnightly food today itself," then it is allowable.
279:
Uposathikaṃ (Uposatha food) refers to the donation of the very food that one eats oneself after undertaking the Uposatha factors on the Uposatha day of every half-month. Pāṭipadikaṃ (food for the first day of the fortnight) refers to the donation given on the first day of the fortnight, reflecting: "On the Uposatha day, many faithful and devoted people make offerings to the monks, but on the first day, the monks are weary; a gift given on the first day is like a gift given in times of famine and is of great fruit; or a gift given on the second day to those whose virtue is purified by the Uposatha act is of great fruit." Both of these also have the same status as ticket-food. Thus, all these seven types of food are not allowable for those who are alms-round eaters (piṇḍapātika); they indeed cause the breaking of the dhutanga.

Other types of food are also mentioned in the Cīvarakkhandhaka, given after Visākhā requested the boons: āgantukabhatta (food for incoming monks), gamikabhatta (food for outgoing monks), gilānabhatta (food for the sick), and gilānupaṭṭhākabhatta (food for those attending the sick)—these four types of food appear in the Pali. Therein, food given to incoming guests is called āgantukabhatta. The same method applies to the remaining types. If, in this context, both the āgantukabhatta and the incoming monks are numerous, every monk should take one each. If the food is insufficient, it should be taken according to the turn. If one incoming monk arrives first, takes all the āgantukabhatta for himself, and sits down, it all belongs to him. Incoming monks who arrive later should consume the food given by him. He, too, should take one for himself and give the rest. This is generosity (noble conduct). However, if he arrives first but sits silently without taking for himself, it should be taken in order along with those who arrive later. If incoming monks arrive constantly, it should be consumed only on the day of arrival. If they arrive occasionally, it may be consumed for two or three days. In the Mahāpaccari, however, it is said: "It is allowable to consume it for seven days." If a resident monk returns after going somewhere, he too may consume āgantukabhatta. If that food is designated for the monastery, it should be taken at the monastery. If the monastery is far and it is designated at the rest-house (āsanasālā), it should be taken at the rest-house. If the lay donors say, "If there are no incoming monks, let the resident monks also eat," then it is allowable; if they do not say so, it is not allowable.

The same explanation applies to gamikabhatta (food for outgoing monks). This is the distinction: an incoming monk receives only āgantukabhatta, but an outgoing monk receives both āgantukabhatta and gamikabhatta. A resident monk who wishes to depart also becomes an outgoing monk (gamika).
280:
One receives a traveler's meal (gamikabhatta). However, unlike the guest meal (āgantukabhatta) which may be received for two, three, or seven days, this traveler's meal cannot be received for such a long period. If, after having eaten the meal with the intention 'I will depart,' one does not depart on that day due to some reason, it is permissible to consume that meal again on the following day because the effort to depart still exists. For a monk who has eaten with the intention 'I will depart,' if robbers block the path, or if there is a flood or rain, or if the caravan does not depart, he should consume it while maintaining the effort to go. It is stated in the Mahāpaccari commentary: 'A monk who considers these dangers is permitted to consume it for two or three days.' However, one should not consume it by making a false pretext, saying 'I will depart, I will depart.'

As for the meal for the sick (gilānabhatta), if it is sufficient for all the sick, it should be given to all. If it is not sufficient, it should be taken by establishing a rotation system. If one sick person is not severely ill and can go into the village, while another cannot, the one who cannot go is called 'seriously ill' (mahāgilāna), and the meal for the sick should be given to him. If there are two seriously ill persons, and one is famous and receives many gains and abundant food, while the other is helpless and receives little, having to enter the village for alms, the meal for the sick should be given to that less fortunate sick person. There is no limit to the number of days for the sick-person's meal; as long as the illness is not cured, if one cannot sustain oneself without consuming suitable food, it may be consumed for that duration. However, if at some point one consumes mixed congee or mixed rice intended for the healthy and the illness does not flare up, from that time onwards, it should no longer be consumed.

The meal for the sick-attendant (gilānupaṭṭhākabhatta) also, if sufficient for all, should be given to all. If not sufficient, it should be taken by establishing a rotation system. This sick-attendant's meal, if there are two sick persons, should be given to the one attending the seriously ill; if there are two seriously ill persons, it should be given to the one attending the helpless sick person. If a certain family offers both the sick-person's meal and the sick-attendant's meal, and a certain sick person receives the sick-person's meal there, his attendant should also take his meal from that same house. There is also no limit to the number of days for the sick-attendant's meal; as long as the sick person receives it, his attendant also receives it. If these four types of meals are offered with the words, 'Let the guests, travelers, the sick, and the sick-attendants take my alms-food,' then it is also permissible for monks who live by alms-gathering (piṇḍapātika). However, if they are offered with the words, 'I establish a regular supply of food for the four types of persons such as guests; let them take my food,' then it is not permissible for the alms-gathering monks.

## There are also three other types of meals: dhurabhatta, kuṭibhatta, and vārakabhatta. Among these three, dhurabhatta refers to a regular meal (niccabhatta). This dhurabhatta is of two kinds: that belonging to the Saṅgha (saṅghika) and that belonging to an individual (puggalika). Among these two, the meal established with the words, 'I offer dhurabhatta to the Saṅgha,' follows the same rule as the meal distributed by tickets (salākabhatta).
281:
A meal offered with the words, 'Take my regularly offered alms-food,' is also permissible for alms-gathering monks. In the case of a meal-duty offered to an individual, if it is said, 'I offer you a regular meal-duty,' it is not permissible if he is an alms-gathering monk. But if it is said, 'Take my regularly offered alms-food,' it is permissible and should be accepted. If, after a few days have passed, the donor says, 'Take the regular meal-duty,' it is permissible because it was properly accepted at the beginning.

What is called kuṭibhatta (dwelling-duty meal) is a meal established after building and offering a dwelling to the Saṅgha, with the words, 'Let the monks residing in our dwelling take only our food.' This meal is just like the ticket-food (salākabhatta); it should be accepted and consumed. However, if it is said, 'Let the monks residing in our dwelling take our alms-food,' then it is also permissible for alms-gathering monks. But if a meal is offered out of devotion to a specific individual, after building a dwelling for him, with the words, 'I offer this to you, Venerable Sir,' that meal belongs to that individual alone. If that person goes elsewhere, his disciples may consume it.

What is called vārakabhatta (meal by rotation) is a meal offered during a time of famine, starting from a house with a regular duty, with the words, 'We will support the monks by rotation.' If this meal is offered using the word 'alms-food' (bhikkhā), it is permissible for alms-gathering monks. But if it is called 'vārakabhatta,' it follows the rule of ticket-food (salākabhatta). If they send rice and so on, saying, 'Let the novices cook and offer it,' it is permissible for alms-gathering monks. Thus, these three types of meals mentioned and the four types starting with guest-meals (āgantukabhatta) make seven; together with the Saṅgha-meals (saṅghabhatta) and others, there are fourteen types of meals.

In the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), four other types of meals are also mentioned: vihārabhatta, aṭṭhakabhatta, catukkabhatta, and guḷhakabhatta. Among these, what is called vihārabhatta is a meal that arises at the monastery; it is included within the Saṅgha-meal (saṅghabhatta). This vihārabhatta was accepted at places like Tissamahāvihāra and Cittalapabbata by Arahants who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidāpatta) in such a way that alms-gathering monks could also consume it; therefore, in such places, it is permissible for alms-gathering monks. Meals offered with the words, 'We offer to eight monks' or 'We offer to four monks,' are called aṭṭhakabhatta and catukkabhatta respectively. These are also permissible for alms-gathering monks because they are offered using the word 'alms-food' (bhikkhā). A meal consisting of very delicious cakes prepared with great effort, placed in an alms-bowl and covered before being offered, is called guḷhakabhatta. These three types of meals follow the same rule as ticket-food (salākabhatta). There is also another type called guḷhakabhatta. In this Dispensation, some people, after organizing a grand Dhamma-hearing ceremony and a monastery-offering ceremony, say, 'We are unable to offer to the entire Saṅgha; let two or three hundred monks take our alms-food.' They give molasses-balls (guḷhaka) to indicate the number of monks. This meal is also permissible for alms-gathering monks.

## The section on the distribution of alms-food is finished.
282:
The distribution of medicinal requisites for the sick (gilānapaccayabhājanīya) should be understood as follows (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā, 325, Pakkhikabhattādikathā): Regarding medicinal requisites such as ghee, kings and their great ministers first send a hundred or a thousand jars of ghee to the monastery. Having struck the bell, the jars brought should be filled and offered, starting from the seats of the elders; it is also allowable for alms-collecting monks. If great elders of a lazy nature arrive late, one should not say, "Venerable sirs, we are giving to monks of twenty years' standing; your turn has passed." Instead, one should set aside the order of the elders, give to those great elders, and then offer according to the sequence. If monks from a monastery a league (yojana) away arrive after hearing that "much ghee has been received at that monastery," it should be offered to all who have arrived, starting from where they are standing. Even if they have not yet reached the assembly, if the disciples or others of the monks who have entered within the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) receive it, it is indeed well-offered. If it is said, "Give to those standing outside the precinct boundary," it should not be given. However, if they are continuous with the monks who have entered the precinct boundary and are at the monastery gate or within the monastery itself, the boundary is said to be expanded by the force of the assembly; therefore, it should be given. Even while giving to the youngest of the Saṅgha, it should indeed be given to monks who arrive later. In the second portion, however, senior monks who arrive after the elders' seats have been occupied do not obtain the first portion; it should be given from the second portion according to seniority (vassagga). If the offering is made at an unspecified place within the monastery after entering the precinct boundary, all of it must be distributed only at the place of assembly.

In a monastery where there are ten monks and ten jars of ghee are given, they should be distributed at the rate of one jar each. If there is only one jar of ghee, the ten monks should divide and take it. If they take it saying, "It comes to us just as it stands," it is a bad taking (duggahita); that ghee remains the property of the Saṅgha wherever it goes. However, having tilted the jar and put a little ghee into a bowl, saying, "This portion reaches the great elder, the remainder reaches us," and then pouring that back into the jar, they may take as much as they desire and go; this is allowable. If the ghee is frozen, having made a mark and saying, "The part beyond this mark reaches the great elder, the remainder reaches us," even if taken thus, it is a good taking (suggahita). Even if the number of monks and jars of ghee are less or more than the stated measure, they should be distributed by this same method. If there is only one monk and one jar, it is allowable to strike the bell and take it, saying, "This jar reaches me." It is also allowable to make it reach him little by little, saying, "This portion is the first portion and reaches me; this is the second portion." This is the method.
283:
The same method applies to fresh butter and so on. However, in the case of clear sesame oil and the like where a mark cannot remain, it should be ladled out and distributed. Ginger, pepper, and other medicines, as well as all other Samana-requisites such as remaining alms-bowls and bowls, should be well-noted and distributed according to the aforementioned method. This concludes the discussion on the distribution of medicinal requisites for the sick (gilānapaccayabhājanီyakathā).

## Now, the decision regarding the acceptance of lodgings (senāsanaggāha) should be understood

This so-called acceptance of lodgings is of two kinds: during the ordinary season (utukāla) and during the Rains-residence (vassāvāsa). Among these, to speak first of the ordinary season, some visiting monks (āgantuka) arrive before the meal (morning); some arrive after the meal, during the first watch, the middle watch, or the last watch of the night. At whatever time those monks arrive, the resident monks should be made to rise and the lodgings should be given to them at that very time; there is no such thing as an improper time. However, the monk who assigns the lodgings (senāsanapaññāpaka) must be wise; he should keep one or two couch-spaces ready. If one or two elders arrive at an improper time during the night, they should be addressed thus: "Venerable sirs, if we make everyone rise starting from the beginning, all the monks will be as if moving with their baggage (ubbhāṇḍika); please stay in our place of residence."

If many monks arrive, however, the residents should be made to rise and lodgings given in order. If there is enough for one precinct (pariveṇa) each, one precinct should be given to each. All the fire-halls, long halls, circular pavilions, etc., within that precinct also belong to the monk who receives that precinct. If it is not sufficient in this way, they should be given according to mansions (pāsāda); if not sufficient by mansions, by rooms (ovaraka); if not sufficient by rooms, by beds (seyya); if not sufficient by beds, by couch-spaces (mañcaṭṭhāna); if not sufficient by couch-spaces, they should be given according to the space of a single stool (pīṭhaka). A monk should not be made to take only enough space to stand. This is because such a place is not called a lodging (senāsana).

If even stool-spaces are not sufficient, a single couch-space or a single stool-space should be given to three persons, saying, "Venerable sirs, please rest by turns." This is because one cannot stay in the open air (ajjhokāsa) all night during the cold season. After the senior elder has rested for the first watch and come out, he should tell the second elder, "Friend, enter here and rest." If the senior elder is one who is fond of sleep (niddāgaruka) and does not know the time, the second elder should clear his throat, knock on the door, and say, "Venerable sir, the time has come; the cold is oppressive." He (the senior) must come out and give the turn; he is not allowed not to give it. The second elder also, for the duration of the middle watch...
284:
After the second elder has rested peacefully, he should give the place to the other person in the same manner as previously mentioned. If he is one who oversleeps, he should be awakened in the manner stated. In this way, within one night, a single bed-place should be given in turns to three monks. In Jambudīpa, however, some monks, considering that "a lodging, whether a bed-place or a stool-place, may be suitable for some and unsuitable for others," take up a lodging daily, whether visitors are present or not. This is called the taking of lodgings during the season (utu-kāla).

Regarding the rains retreat (vassa), there are the duties of a visitor (āgantuka-vatta) and the duties of a resident (āvāsika-vatta). A visiting monk who wishes to leave his own place and stay elsewhere should not go there only on the day the retreat begins. This is because the place of residence there might be cramped, or alms-gathering might not be successful, and thus he would not live comfortably; therefore, he should enter that monastery about a month in advance, thinking, "The rains retreat will begin in about a month." While staying there for about a month, if he is one who seeks instruction (uddesa), he should observe the success of instruction; if he is a meditator (kammaṭṭhāna), he should observe the suitability for meditation; if he is one who seeks requisites (paccaya), he should observe the gain of requisites, and only then should he stay comfortably during the retreat. Also, when going there from his own place, he should not disturb the alms-resort village. He should not say to the people there, "Depending on you, I do not receive food-by-tickets, gruel, snacks, or rains-retreat robes; this item is for the cetiya, this is for the Uposatha hall, these are the key and the needle; you yourselves take back your monastery." Instead, he should look after the lodging, put away the wooden and earthenware utensils, fulfill the duties of a traveler (gamika-vatta), and then depart.

When going in this way, he should not go through the village gate showing himself off by having young monks carry his bowl and robe-bundles, or carry the oil-tube and walking stick, or hold an umbrella over him; he should go only by a concealed forest path. If there is no forest path, he should not go by trampling through bushes and thickets; rather, he should fulfill the duties of a traveler, cut off thoughts (of gain), and go according to the duties of traveling with a pure mind. If there is a path only through the village gate, and people, seeing him traveling with a retinue, run to him saying, "He is like our elder," and ask, "Venerable sir, where are you going taking all your requisites?" and if one of them says, "This is the time for the rains retreat; monks go to places where alms-food is easily obtained throughout the retreat and where robes are provided," then...
285:
If, upon hearing his words, those people say, "Venerable sir, in this village too, people eat and dress; do not go elsewhere," and after calling and consulting with friends and colleagues, they establish regular duties in the monastery, such as food-by-tickets and rains-retreat robes, and request, "Venerable sir, please stay only here," then it is proper for all the monks to accept. All such giving is both allowable and blameless. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is stated: "When asked 'Where are you going?', one should say 'To such and such a place'; when asked 'Why are you going there?', the reason should be told." Both of these are blameless because of the purity of mind. This is called the duty of a visitor (āgantuka-vatta).

This is the duty of a resident monk (āvāsika-vatta). Indeed, resident monks should look after the monastery beforehand; they should carry out repairs of broken or dilapidated parts and apply plaster; they should look after the night-quarters, day-quarters, toilets, urinals, the meditation house, the monastery, and the paths—all these must be tended to. Plastering the cetiya, oiling the railings of the terrace, and cleaning the beds and stools—all this should be done with the intention: "May monks who wish to spend the rains retreat come and live comfortably while engaging in instruction, inquiry, and meditation." Monks who have performed these preparatory tasks (parikamma) should inquire about the rains-retreat robes (vassāvāsika) starting from the fifth day of the waxing moon of Āsāḷha. Where should they inquire? They should inquire from those donors from whom they normally receive. It is not proper to inquire from those who have never given before. Why should they inquire? Because sometimes people give, but sometimes they do not give due to being troubled by famine and so forth; in that case, if the rains-retreat robes are taken without inquiring from those who will not give, it becomes an obstacle to gain (lābhantarāya) for the monks who take them; therefore, they should be taken only after inquiring.

When inquiring, one should say, "The time for receiving your rains-retreat robes is near." If they say, "Venerable sir, this year we are troubled by famine and so forth, we are unable to give," or "We will give less than what we gave before," or "Now cotton is easy to obtain, we will give more than what we gave before," then having noted that, the monks staying in that lodging should accept the rains-retreat robes in a manner consistent with that. If the people say, "Let the monk who receives our rains-retreat robes provide drinking water for the three months, look after the monastery path, look after the cetiya courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard, and pour water on the Bodhi-tree," then this should be told to the monk who receives it. If a village is at a distance of one or two leagues from the monastery, and the families there...
286:
Apart from the wealth deposited with the grove-keepers and others, if they offer rains-residence robes (vassāvāsika) at the Pahāra region, one should ask those donors or perform duties in their monastery and then accept the rains-residence robe. However, if a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika) resides in their monastery and they, upon seeing the arriving rag-robe wearer, say, 'We give the rains-residence robe to you,' that rag-robe wearer must inform the Saṅgha. If those donors do not wish to give to the Saṅgha but say, 'We give only to you,' a fellow monk (sabhāga) should be told, 'Perform the duties and accept it.' However, this rains-residence robe is not allowable for a rag-robe wearer. Thus, the lay donors who give out of faith should be consulted.

Regarding the property arising in that monastery, the lay-attendants (kappiyakārakas) should be consulted. How should they be consulted? 'Friends, will there be cloth for the Saṅgha to cover themselves?' If they say, 'Venerable sirs, there will be; we will offer a nine-cubit cloth to each; please accept the rains-residence robe,' then it should be accepted. Even if they say, 'There is no cloth, but there are materials like rice; please accept them, venerable sirs,' it is proper to accept even when there are allowable materials (kappiyavatthu) like rice. The reason is that whatever allowable item comes from materials like gold or silver given to lay-attendants with the instruction 'Use this for allowable items,' all of that is permitted for use. In this case, property given specifically for the purpose of alms-food or for medicine for the sick: if monks wish to use it for robes, they must announce it to the Saṅgha for its welfare and then use it. Property given specifically for the purpose of lodgings is heavy property (garubhaṇḍa). For property given specifically for robes or for the four requisites, there is no need for a formal announcement (apalokana) for monks who wish to use it for robes. Those who perform the act of announcement should do so individually, not on behalf of the Saṅgha. Announcement regarding gold, silver, or raw grain is not allowable; it is only allowable regarding allowable items (kappiyabhaṇḍa) such as robes, rice, and so on. That announcement should be made thus: 'Now food is abundant and alms are easy to get, but monks are struggling for robes; it is pleasing to use this portion of rice to make robes for the monks,' or 'Medicine for the sick is easy to get, or there are no sick; it is pleasing to use this portion of rice to make robes for the monks.'

When the robe-requisite has been considered and the time for distributing lodgings is announced and the Saṅgha has assembled, a lodging-assigner (senāsanaggāhaka) should be appointed. It is said that the Saṅgha should appoint two. When appointed thus, a junior will let a senior accept, and a senior will let a junior accept. In large monasteries like the Mahāvihāra, three or four people should be appointed. In the Kurundī Commentary, it says 'eight or even sixteen people...'
287:
"...it is proper to appoint.' The appointment of these is valid either by formal act (kammavācā) or by announcement (apalokana). Those appointed monks should inspect the lodgings (senāsana). The cetiya-house, bodhi-house, assembly hall, cleaning shed, wood shed, latrine, brick hall, carpenter's hall, gatehouse, water-pot stand, path (long hall), and pond (hall) are not lodgings. A vihāra (dwelling with two roof-slopes), aḍḍhayoga (dwelling with one roof-slope), pāsāda (mansion), hammiya (long mansion), cave, pavilion, foot of a tree, and bamboo grove are called lodgings. These dwellings should be assigned.

The monk assigning the lodgings, in accordance with the words starting with 'I allow you, monks, first to count the monks, then to count the beds, and then to assign according to the number of beds' (Cūḷavagga 318), should first count the monks in the monastery and then count the bed-spaces. Thereafter, each bed-space should be assigned to each monk. If bed-spaces are in excess, they should be assigned by monastery. If monasteries are also in excess, they should be assigned by precinct (pariveṇa). If there is an excess even in precincts, another portion should be given again. For when monks are very few, two or three precincts should be given to a single monk. If another monk arrives after a second portion has been taken, that portion should be given to him even if one does not wish to. If the one who has taken it gives either the second portion or the first portion of his own will, it is allowable.

Because of the words 'Monks, a lodging should not be assigned to one standing outside the boundary; if one should assign it, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)' (Cūḷavagga 318), it should not be assigned to one standing outside the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā). Within the precinct boundary, however, it is obtainable even for one standing at a distance.

Because of the words 'Monks, I allow you to give a suitable bed to a sick monk' (Cūḷavagga 316), for one who is sick with cough, asthma, fistula, diarrhea, etc., and needs spittoons or waste pots, or one who has leprosy and might soil the lodging, a lodging at one end among the lower mansions or leaf-huts should be given. If the lodging is not damaged while he resides there, even an excellent bed should be given to him. It is also proper to give a suitable lodging to a monk undergoing medical treatments such as drinking oil, purgation, or nasal treatment.
288:
Any monk who consumes any kind of medicine is considered a sick person (gilāna). For such a monk, a suitable lodging (senāsana) should be given after due consideration.

Because of the word: “Monks, one person should not block (take) two (lodgings); for one who blocks them, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa)” (Cūḷavagga 319), two lodgings should not be taken by one person. If one does take them, the previous taking is nullified by the subsequent taking. Indeed, taking nullifies taking, taking nullifies attachment (ālaya), attachment nullifies taking, and attachment nullifies attachment.

How is this so? In this Dispensation, a certain person takes a lodging in one monastery on the day of entering the rains (vassūpanāyika), then goes to a nearby monastery and takes one there as well; for that monk, the previous taking is nullified by this subsequent taking. Another person makes a mere attachment, thinking, “I will stay here,” then goes to a nearby monastery and takes a lodging there; for that monk, the previous attachment is nullified by this very taking. One person, having either taken a lodging or made an attachment thinking, “I will stay here,” goes to a nearby monastery and makes an attachment thinking, “Now I will stay only here”; thus, for that monk, taking is nullified by attachment, or attachment is nullified by attachment. In all cases, it remains with the subsequent taking or the subsequent attachment. As for a monk who takes a lodging in one monastery and leaves thinking, “I will stay in another monastery,” his taking of the lodging is nullified when he crosses the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā). However, if he goes thinking, “If it is comfortable there, I will stay; if not, I will return,” and returns after realizing it is not comfortable, it is allowable.

The distributor of lodgings, having had the monk take the lodging, should then have him take the rains-residence cloth (vassāvāsika). At the time of taking, if there are two types of robe-requisites—communal (saṅghika) and gifts of faith (saddhādeyya)—the monks should take whichever they wish to take first, and after that is established, the other should be distributed in order. “If, because monks are few, when lodgings are being taken by compound (pariveṇa), one compound receives many gains, such as ten or twelve robes, those gains should be divided and placed in other monasteries that have no gains, and other monks should be made to take them,” said Elder Mahāsumatthera. Elder Mahāpadumatthera, however, said, “No... (this should not be done).”
289:
It should be done in this way (only in their own monastery). The reason is that people give requisites for the purpose of maintaining their own monastery. Therefore, other monks should enter (receive) in that monastery.

If, in this matter, a Great Elder (Mahatthera) objects, saying, “Friends, do not take them in this way; follow the instruction of the Blessed One. For the Blessed One said, ‘Monks, I allow you to take by compound (pariveṇa)’” (Cūḷavagga 318), one should not abide by that Great Elder’s objection, but should explain, “Venerable Sir, the monks are many and the requisites are few; it is proper to provide support,” and then they should indeed be taken. The authorized (sammata) monk who is distributing should go to the Great Elder and say, “Venerable Sir, a lodging has reached you; please accept the requisites.” If he asks, “Friend, do the requisites of such-and-such a family and such-and-such a lodging reach me?” one should reply, “Venerable Sir, they reach you; please take them.” If he says, “Friend, I take them,” they are considered taken. Elder Mahāsumatthera said, “If, when told ‘Venerable Sir, they are taken by you,’ he says ‘They have been taken by me,’ or when told ‘Venerable Sir, will you take them?’ he says ‘I will take them,’ they are considered not yet taken.” Elder Mahāpadumatthera, however, said, “Whether it be past, future, or present speech, the mere arising of mindfulness and the mere act of making an attachment is the standard here; therefore, they are indeed considered taken.”

A monk who wears rag-robes (paṃsukūlika) may also take a lodging and renounce the requisites. This monk should not be sent to another monastery; it is proper to let another monk take the requisites while staying in the fire-hall (aggisālā), the long hall (dīghasālā), or at the foot of a tree within that same compound. The rag-robe monk will look after the lodging thinking, “I will stay here,” and the other will think, “I will take the requisites.” Through these two reasons, the lodging will be better maintained. In the Mahāpaccariya, it is said: “When a rag-robe monk takes a lodging for staying, the monk who assigns the lodging should ask, ‘Venerable Sir, there are requisites in this lodging; what should be done with them?’ That rag-robe monk should say, ‘Let another take them below.’ If he stays without saying anything, and at the end of the rains they offer a robe by placing it at his feet, it is allowable. If they say, ‘We offer the rains-residence cloth (vassāvāsika),’ it reaches the monks who spent the rains in that lodging.”

For those to whom people offer only the requisites without a lodging, it is proper to take those requisites in a lodging where the rains were not spent. People build a stupa (thūpa) and have the rains-residence cloth taken. A stupa...
290:
## 
A cetiya is not a lodging (senāsana); one should accept the rainy season robe (vassāvāsika) by tying it to a tree or a pavilion near that cetiya. The monk who so accepts it must look after the cetiya. The same method applies to the Bodhi tree, the Bodhi-tree house (bodhighara), the assembly hall (āsanaghara), the sweeping area, the wooden platform, the latrine (vaccakuṭi), the gateway, the water-house, the water-pot stand, and the tooth-wood stand. A dining hall, however, is indeed a lodging; therefore, it is proper to accept that dining hall by designating it for one or for many. All of this is stated in detail in the Mahāpaccariya Commentary.

The monk authorized to assign lodgings should accept them from the time of dawn on the first day of the lunar month until the next dawn (before the dawn breaks). This is the period for accepting lodgings. If, after a lodging has been accepted early in the morning, another monk who wanders about with many thoughts arrives and requests a lodging, he should be told, "Venerable sir, the lodging has been taken, the Saṅgha has entered the rains, the monastery is delightful; please stay wherever you wish, such as at the foot of a tree."

On the day of the second entry into the rainy season (pacchimavassūpanāyika), if a person brings a cloth of ten cubits and offers it as a rainy season robe when the time is announced and the Saṅgha has assembled, it should be given to the visiting monk if he is the senior elder of the Saṅgha (saṅghatthera). If he is a junior monk, the authorized monk should say to the senior elder of the Saṅgha, "Venerable sir, if you wish, please relinquish the first portion and take this cloth." It should not be given to a senior elder who does not relinquish it. If he takes it after relinquishing the rainy season robe previously accepted, it should be given. By this same method, starting from the second elder, after exchanging in sequence, it should be given to the visitor at the appropriate place. If the monks who entered the first retreat received two, three, four, or five cloths, they should be made to relinquish them by this same method until it is equal to the visitor's portion. When the visitor has received an equal portion, the remaining part should be given to the senior elder. When there are material gains, it is proper to make an agreement to accept them by turn.

If there is a famine and the monks who have entered the rains in both the first and second retreats are weary for lack of alms-food and say, "Friends, all of us living in this monastery are weary; it would be good if we divide into two groups. Let those monks who have relatives or places of invitation stay there and return at the time of Pavāraṇā to receive their own rainy season robes." Among them, those who stay there and return at the time of Pavāraṇā should be given the rainy season robes after informing the others. For even if they desire them, those who broke the retreat are not the owners of the rainy season robes, and the resident monks have no right to refuse giving them. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is stated that an agreement should be made: "For all of us in this monastery..."
291:
"...rice gruel and meals are not sufficient; stay in a suitable place and then return; you will receive the rainy-season robes that come to you." If one person objects to that agreement, it is well-objected. If no one objects, the agreement is well-made. Later, the robes should be given to those monks who stayed elsewhere and returned, after informing the others; at the time of informing, no objection can be made.

It is also stated: "If, among the monks who have entered the retreat, some do not receive rainy-season robes, and the monks make an agreement: 'It is pleasing to us to give the rainy-season robes to these monks who have broken their retreat (chinnavassa), as well as the rainy-season robes that are about to arise, to these monks,' when such an agreement is made, it is just like having already received the robes; whatever robes arise should be given only to those monks." A monk who prepares drinking water for the three months, looks after the monastery paths, the shrine terrace (cetiyangaṇa), and the Bodhi terrace (bodhiyangaṇa), and waters the Bodhi tree, still receives the rainy-season robe even if he leaves or disrobes (vibbhamati). This is because he has performed the duties like a hired laborer. However, as for the saṅghika robe accepted after informing the Saṅgha, he receives it even if he disrobes during the retreat. But some say that if it was accepted based on the requisites (paccaya), he does not receive it.

If a monk who has completed the retreat and is about to leave for another direction takes some allowable item (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) from the resident monk and says, "My rainy-season robe has arrived at such-and-such a family; please take it," and then disrobes at his destination, that rainy-season robe becomes saṅghika. However, if he leaves after having the laypeople acknowledge it in his presence, he receives it. If it is said, "We offer this rainy-season robe to the monk who resided in our dwelling," it belongs only to the monk who was assigned that dwelling. If, out of a desire to please the owner of the dwelling, children and others bring many cloths and say, "We offer these to our dwelling," only one cloth should be given to the monk who spent the retreat in that dwelling, and the rest become saṅghika. They should be accepted according to the turn for rainy-season robes; if there is no turn, they should be accepted starting from the senior monk's place. The same rule applies when many cloths are brought and offered with the words "We offer to the dwelling" due to faith inspired by the monk who spent the retreat in that dwelling. However, if they place it at his feet and say, "We offer to this monk," it belongs only to him.

In a donor's house, there are two rainy-season robes; the first turn was assigned to a novice (sāmaṇera), and the second to the senior monk's place. That donor sends one ten-cubit cloth and one eight-cubit cloth, saying, "Give these to the monks who are entitled to rainy-season robes." After selecting, the superior one is given to the novice, and the inferior one is given to the senior monk's place.
292:
...should be given. However, if the donor invites both (the novice and the senior monk) to the house, feeds them, and places the gift at their feet himself, then whatever is given to whom belongs to that person. Hereafter is the method found in the Mahāpaccariya. In a certain house, a rainy-season robe (vassāvāsika) is due to a young novice. If the donor asks, "Who receives our rainy-season robe?" one should not say "The novice," but say "You will know at the time of donation," and on the day of donation, a senior monk (mahatthera) should be sent to collect it. If the person entitled to the rainy-season robe disrobes or passes away, and the people ask, "Who receives our rainy-season robe?" they should be told the truth. If they say, "We give it to you, venerable sirs," then it belongs to those monks. If they give it to the Saṅgha or to a group (gaṇa), it belongs to the Saṅgha or the group. If the monks who have completed the rains-retreat are strictly rag-robe wearers (paṃsukūlika), the donated rainy-season robe should be used for monastery furnishings or made into pillows and so on.

## This is the Discussion on the Taking of Lodgings
## by Virtue of the Day of Entering the Rains-Retreat.

Besides this, one should also know the taking of lodgings during the seasons (winter and summer) called 'antarāmuttaka'. There are three types of taking lodgings according to the day: purimaka, pacchimaka, and antarāmuttaka. For it has been said: "Monks, there are these three takings of lodgings: the early (purimaka), the late (pacchimaka), and the interim (antarāmuttaka). The early one should be taken on the day after the full moon of Āsāḷha. The late one should be taken one month after the full moon of Āsāḷha. The interim one should be taken on the day after the Pavāraṇā ceremony for the sake of future residence during the rains." (from the Mahāvagga).

Among these three takings of lodgings, the two known as purimaka and pacchimaka are permanent takings. The antarāmuttaka, however, was permitted by the Blessed One for the purpose of cleaning and repairing the lodgings. This is because in a certain monastery, there may be lodgings where gains are abundant; the donors of the lodgings respectfully attend to the monk who has entered the rains-retreat with the four requisites, and upon his departure after the invitation (pavāraṇā), they donate many monastic requisites. Senior monks (mahattheras) come from afar, and on the day of entering the rains-retreat...
293:
...taking those gains, they live comfortably, and after the rains retreat, they take the gains and depart. The resident monks think, "We do not receive the gains that arise in this monastery; only the visiting senior monks always receive them. Those very monks will come and maintain this monastery," and thus they do not even look at it even when it is falling into ruin. For the sake of maintaining that lodging, the Blessed One said: "The interval-released (antarāmuttaka) lodging is to be taken on the day after the Pavāraṇā ceremony for the sake of future residence during the rains."

The monk who causes that lodging to be taken should say to the Sangha Elder, "Venerable sir, please take the interval-released lodging." If he takes it, it should be given. If not, by this same method, it should be given to whoever accepts it, starting from the next senior monk down to even a novice. That person must maintain that lodging for eight months; if there is any breakage or crack in the roof, walls, or floor, all of it must be repaired. It is allowable to spend the day in teaching or questioning and stay there at night; it is also allowable to stay in the precinct at night and spend the day there; it is also allowable to stay there both day and night. Senior monks who arrive during the seasons should not be refused. However, when the day for entering the rains arrives, if the Sangha Elder says, "Give this lodging to me," he does not get it. One should not give it, saying, "Venerable sir, this interval-released lodging has been taken and maintained by a certain monk"; it is taken only by the monk who maintained it for eight months. However, in a lodging where they give requisites twice a year, every six months, that lodging should not be taken as an interval-released one. Or where they give three times a year, every four months, or four times a year, every three months, that lodging should not be taken as an interval-released one. This is because that lodging will receive maintenance through those very requisites. But in a monastery where they give many requisites only once a year, this lodging should be taken as an interval-released one.

Based on the words: "Monks, I allow you to give a monastery that is not yet built or a new construction (navakamma) that is unfinished; having looked at the work in small monasteries, I allow you to give new construction for five or six years; having looked at the work in aḍḍhayoga houses, for seven or eight years; having looked at the work in large monasteries or mansions (pāsāda), for ten or twelve years," a lodging that is not yet built or is unfinished should be assigned to a monk either by announcement (apalokana) or by a formal act (kammavācā)...
294:
For the purpose of residing while performing new construction (*navakamma*), [lodgings] should be given according to the aforementioned time limit. A monk performing new construction (*navakammika*) obtains that dwelling during the rains retreat (*vassa*); during the seasons (*utukāla*—summer and winter), he cannot be barred. A monk who has received [permission for] new construction should not perform the work himself by holding an adze, axe, chisel, etc.; he should only supervise to know whether the work is completed or not. If that dwelling is old and decaying, he should inform the donor of the dwelling or someone born of that donor’s lineage, saying, 'Your dwelling is perishing; look after this dwelling.' If that person is unable, the monks should urge relatives or lay supporters (*upaṭṭhākas*) to repair it. If they also are unable, it should be repaired with Saṅgha property (*saṅghika*). If such Saṅgha property is also unavailable, one dwelling should be sacrificed and the remaining dwellings should be repaired. It is also permissible to sacrifice many [dwellings] to maintain one dwelling.

During times of famine, when monks depart, all dwellings tend to perish. Therefore, monks who consume the gruel, rice, robes, etc., obtained from sacrificing one, two, or three dwellings, must repair the remaining dwellings.

In the *Kurundī* Commentary, however, it is stated: 'If Saṅgha property is unavailable, a monk should be told—I will give you a space for a couch; take it and repair it. If he desires more than that, it should be repaired even by giving him a third or a half. If only the pillars remain in this dwelling and he does not wish to repair it because there is too much work to be done, it should be given to him by saying—repair it by making it your own private property (*puggalika*). Even by giving it in this way, it should be repaired with the thought that the Saṅgha will obtain a place to store requisites and a place for junior monks to reside. A dwelling repaired in this way is private property while that person is alive; when he dies, it becomes Saṅgha property. If he wishes to give it to his co-residents (*saddhivihārikas*), the work should be inspected and it should be repaired by making a third or a half of it private property. Only by doing so does he have the right to give it to his co-residents. If there is no one to repair it in this way, it should be repaired by the method of sacrificing one dwelling, and so forth.' This other statement is also mentioned in that same *Kurundī*.

Two monks take Saṅgha land, clear it, and build a Saṅgha dwelling; whoever took that land first is the owner (*sāmī*). Even if both build a private dwelling, that same person is the owner. If one builds a Saṅgha dwelling and the other builds a private dwelling, if there are many other places to build dwellings, the one building the private dwelling should not be barred. However, in another such suitable place...
295:
If there is no such suitable place, that monk should be barred, and only those building a Saṅgha dwelling should build it. The expenditure (*vayakamma*) incurred by that monk there must be reimbursed.

If there are shade-giving trees or fruit-bearing trees at the completed dwelling or at the site for building a dwelling, they should be removed after informing the Saṅgha. If those trees are private property (*puggalika*), the owners should be asked. If they do not give permission, they should be asked up to three times, and [the trees] should be removed after saying, 'We will give the value of the trees.'

If a monk builds a private dwelling on Saṅgha land with building materials he himself brought, without taking even a single creeper belonging to the Saṅgha, half belongs to the Saṅgha and half is private property. If it is a multi-storey building (*pāsāda*), the lower floor is Saṅgha property and the upper floor is private property. If he desires the lower floor, the lower floor is his property. If he desires both the lower and upper floors, he receives half of both places. If he builds two dwellings, one is Saṅgha property and one is private property. If he builds with materials taken from a Saṅgha dwelling, he receives a third. If he builds a foundation (*caya*) or a portico (*pamukha*) outside the wall in an undeveloped area, half belongs to the Saṅgha and half to that individual. If he fills a large uneven area and builds a dwelling where there was no site for a dwelling, the Saṅgha has no authority (ownership) over that dwelling.

If a monk takes rafters (*gopānasi*), etc., from a Saṅgha dwelling and installs them in another Saṅgha dwelling, they are well-installed. Those who wish to install them in a private dwelling must either pay the price or restore them to their original state. For a monk who takes beds, chairs, etc., from an abandoned dwelling with theftuous intent, the offense should be determined according to the value of the property from the moment he moves it. For one who takes them saying, 'I will return them when there is a resident again,' and uses them as Saṅgha property, if they are destroyed, they are well-destroyed; if they are worn out, they are well-worn out. If they remain undamaged, they should be returned to their original state. For one who uses them as private property, if they are destroyed or worn out, he is liable for restitution (*gīvā*). If doors, windows, etc., from that dwelling are installed in either a Saṅgha dwelling or a private dwelling, they must be returned. If any Saṅgha dwelling decays, it is permissible to take the beds, chairs, etc., therein to another place for the sake of security. Therefore, for one who takes them elsewhere and uses them as Saṅgha property, if they are destroyed, they are well-destroyed; if they are worn out, they are well-worn out. If they remain undamaged, they should be returned to their original state when that dwelling is repaired. For one who uses them as private property, if they are destroyed or worn out, he is liable for restitution; they must be given back when that dwelling is repaired. This is the Discussion on the Acceptance of Lodgings (*Senāsanaggāhakathā*).
296:
In particular, this is the discussion concerning the four requisites (Catupaccayadhāraṇakathā). (Cūḷavagga Aṭṭhakathā, 325, Pakkhikabhattādikathā). A monk appointed by the Saṅgha as the distributor of minor items (appamattakavissajjaka), when asked by a monk making a robe, "Give me a needle," should give two needles: one long and one short. There is no need to ask, "This is undistributed Saṅgha property." To one desiring black pepper, black pepper should be given; to one wishing to set out on a difficult journey, a pair of sandals; to one needing a waistband, a waistband; to a monk who comes saying, "My shoulder strap is worn out," a shoulder strap; to a monk needing a water filter, a water filter; to one needing a dhammakaraṇa (water strainer), a dhammakaraṇa. If there is no strainer-cloth, the dhammakaraṇa should be given together with a cloth. To a monk requesting, "I will attach an outer border (āgantukapatta)," enough for the kusi (longitudinal seams) and aḍḍhakusi (latitudinal seams) should be given. To a monk who comes saying, "The maṇḍala (circular panels) are not enough," enough for one maṇḍala should be given, or enough for two half-maṇḍalas. To a monk requesting two large maṇḍalas, they should not be given. To one needing an anuvāta-paribhaṇḍa (border and binding), enough for the border of one robe should be given. To a sick monk needing ghee, butter, etc., one measure (nāḷi) of medicine should be prepared, and one-third of that medicine should be given. Having given in this way for three days, when the measure is full, from the fourth day onwards, it should be given only after informing the Saṅgha. For a lump of molasses (guḷapiṇḍa) also, one-third should be given per day. Having given the lump of molasses over three days in this manner, thereafter it should be given after informing the Saṅgha. Monks appointed by the Saṅgha such as the gruel-distributor (yāgubhajaka) may give a half-portion to those who come to the distribution place without informing [the Saṅgha]. However, those not appointed must inform the Saṅgha before giving.

When Saṅgha property is being given by an appointed monk or by monastery attendants (ārāmika) etc. commissioned by him, or when laypeople's property is being given by the owner or by one commissioned by the owner, if someone takes it by referring to a non-existent person, saying "Give a portion for another person," he must return the item (bhaṇḍādeyya). If one takes what is being given by someone other than the appointee, owner, or commissioned person [in this way], he must be made to pay the value of the item (bhaṇḍaggha). If, while an unappointed or uncommissioned person is giving, one takes by saying "Give another portion also" or by falsely counting the years [of seniority], he must be made to pay the value of the item. If one takes in this way while an appointee or commissioned person is giving, the item must be returned. If the owner himself says "Give to this person" or gives it himself, it is considered "well-given" (sudinna). This is the essence of the decisions found in all the Commentaries.
297:
For a monk who has entered for alms, it is proper to take a portion of cooked rice only while standing within the precinct (upacāra). However, if the donors say, "Venerable sirs, please accept portions for the monks standing outside the precinct as well; they will consume it upon returning to the monastery," then it is proper to take portions for the monks who are within the village when such a request is made.

A wise person, having observed and reflected upon the Pāḷi and the Commentaries,
Should thus distribute the Saṅgha's requisites without negligence.

## Thus, in the Pāḷimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha, in every respect,
## the Discussion on the Decision for the Distribution of the Four Requisites is concluded.

## 29. Kathinatthāravinicchayakathā

In this Kathinatthāravinicchayakathā, which monks are entitled to spread the Kathina, and which are not? In terms of number, at the minimum, five monks are entitled; upwards, even a hundred thousand are entitled. If there are fewer than five, they are not entitled. In terms of the rains retreat (vassa), those who entered the first rains retreat (purimikā vassa) and performed the invitation (pavāraṇā) at the first pavāraṇā are entitled. Those who broke their vassa or those who entered the later rains retreat (pacchimikā vassa) are not entitled. It is stated in the Mahāpaccari that "Monks who completed the vassa in another monastery are also not entitled." All those who serve as quorum-fillers (gaṇapūraka) for the monks who entered the first rains retreat do not receive the benefits (ānisaṃsa); the benefits belong only to the others (those who entered the first vassa at that monastery). If there are four, three, two, or even one monk who entered the first rains retreat, the Kathina should be spread by making other (vassa-broken) monks the quorum-fillers. If there are four monks who entered the first rains retreat and one novice who has completed the vassa, and if that novice receives higher ordination during the later vassa period, he becomes a quorum-filler and also receives the benefits. The same method applies if there are three monks and two novices, two monks and three novices, or one monk and four novices. If the monks who entered the first rains retreat are not skilled in spreading the Kathina, they should search for and invite Elders who are reciters of the Khandhakas (Khandhakabhāṇaka) and skilled in the spreading. Those Elders, having recited the formal act (kammavācā) and spread the Kathina, will depart after accepting and consuming the gift (dāna); however, the benefits belong only to the others (the monks who resided there for the vassa).
298:
By whom is the Kathina offered appropriately? It is appropriate if offered by a deva, a human, or any of the five fellow-dhamma practitioners. The Kathina donor has duties to perform. If that donor, not knowing the duties, asks, "Venerable sir, how should the Kathina be offered?" he should be told: "It is appropriate to offer a cloth sufficient for one of the three robes at the time of sunrise, saying, 'We offer this Kathina robe.' It is also appropriate to offer as many needles, as much thread, and as much dye as needed for the preliminary work of that Kathina, as well as congee and rice for as many monks as are performing the preliminary work."

The monk spreading the Kathina must also know the duties when spreading a Kathina obtained in accordance with the Dhamma. A cloth that is starched, just as it was brought from a weaver's house, is not appropriate; a dirty cloth is also not appropriate. Therefore, upon receiving the Kathina cloth, it should be well washed, and after preparing the sewing materials such as needles, it should be sewn on that very day together with many monks. After the sewing is finished, it should be dyed, marked with the kappa-bindu, and then the Kathina should be spread. If, before that cloth is spread, another Kathina cloth is brought, or many other Kathina accessory cloths are offered, the Kathina should be spread with the cloth of the person who offers many accessories. The other (initial) donor should be persuaded and informed in such and such a manner.

By whom is the Kathina spread? It is spread by the monk to whom the Saṅgha gives the Kathina robe. To whom does the Saṅgha give it? It is given to the monk whose robes are worn out. If many have worn-out robes, it should be given to the elder. Among the elders, it should be given to the one who has many assistants and is able to make and spread the robe on that very day. If the elder is unable but a junior monk is able, it should be given to him. Nevertheless, the Saṅgha should show favor to the Mahāthera; therefore, it should be said, "Venerable sir, please accept it; we will make it and offer it to you."

Among the three robes, it should be given for whichever one is worn out. For one who normally wears a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭī), it should be given to be double-layered. Even if that monk's single-layered robe is thick and the Kathina cloth is thin, it should be given as a double-layered one to be suitable. It is appropriate to give a double-layered one even to one who says, "If I do not get it, I will wear only a single-layered one." However, it should not be given to one who is naturally greedy. That monk also should not accept it with the intention, "After spreading the Kathina, I will later unpick it and make two robes." For the one to whom it is given—

"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This Kathina cloth has arisen for the Saṅgha. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should give this Kathina cloth to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the Kathina. This is the motion (ñatti)."
299:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This Kathina cloth has arisen for the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha gives this Kathina cloth to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the Kathina. Whichever venerable one approves of giving this Kathina cloth to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the Kathina, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

This Kathina cloth has been given by the Saṅgha to the monk named so-and-so for the purpose of spreading the Kathina. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this matter."

In this way, it should be given with the second kammavācā.

When the Kathina is thus given, if that Kathina cloth has already had its preliminary work finished, that is good. If the preliminary work is not yet finished, one must not remain without doing it, thinking "I am an elder" or "I am learned." All monks must assemble and complete the washing, sewing, and dyeing. Indeed, this Kathina duty is a duty praised by the Buddhas. In the past, the Blessed One Padumuttara also performed the Kathina duty. It is said that his chief disciple, the Elder Sujāta, received the Kathina. The Teacher performed that Kathina while sitting together with six million eight hundred thousand monks.

The monk who takes the completed Kathina and spreads it, if he wishes to spread the Kathina with the saṅghāṭī (double-layered robe), he should relinquish the old robe, determine the new saṅghāṭī, and speak the words: "I spread the Kathina with this saṅghāṭī." If he wishes to spread the Kathina with the uttarāsaṅga (upper robe), he should relinquish the old robe, determine the new uttarāsaṅga, and speak the words: "I spread the Kathina with this uttarāsaṅga." If he wishes to spread the Kathina with the antaravāsaka (inner robe), he should relinquish the old robe, determine the new antaravāsaka, and speak the words: "I spread the Kathina with this antaravāsaka."

That monk who has spread the Kathina should approach the Saṅgha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage with joined palms, and say: "Venerable sirs, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the Kathina is in accordance with the Dhamma; please rejoice." Those...
300:
The monks who are expressing appreciation (anumodanā), having arranged their upper robes over one shoulder and raising their joined palms in salutation, should say to that monk [who spread the Kathina]: "Friend, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the Kathina is righteous; we appreciate it." That monk who spread the Kathina, having approached many monks, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder and raising his joined palms in salutation, should say: "Venerable Sirs, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the Kathina is righteous; please appreciate it." Those monks who express appreciation, having arranged their upper robes over one shoulder and raising their joined palms in salutation, should say to that monk: "Friend, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the Kathina is righteous; we appreciate it." That monk who spread the Kathina, having approached a single monk, arranging his upper robe over one shoulder and raising his joined palms in salutation, should say: "Friend, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the Kathina is righteous; please appreciate it." That monk who expresses appreciation, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and raising his joined palms in salutation, should say to that monk: "Friend, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the Kathina is righteous; I appreciate it." In this way, the Kathina is spread for all monks. For this was said in the Parivāra: "The Kathina is spread for two persons: the one who spreads it and the one who appreciates it" (Pari. 403). Again, it was said: "The Saṅgha does not spread the Kathina, the group (gaṇa) does not spread the Kathina; only an individual spreads the Kathina. Because of the appreciation of the Saṅgha, the appreciation of the group, and the spreading by the individual, the Kathina is considered spread for the Saṅgha, spread for the group, and spread for the individual" (Pari. 414).

When the Kathina has been thus spread, if donors bring accessories and benefits (offerings) along with the Kathina robe and say, "We give these only to the one who received our Kathina robe," the Bhikkhu-saṅgha has no authority over them. However, if they give them without such distinction and depart, the Bhikkhu-saṅgha has authority. Therefore, if the remaining robes of the monk who spread the Kathina are worn out and weak, the Saṅgha, after asking for leave, should give those cloths for the sake of that monk; however, the formal act (kammavācā) needs to be recited only once. Among the remaining Kathina accessories and offerings, durable cloths should be given according to the order of the rainy-season residence (vassāvāsika); if there is no such order, they should be given starting from the senior elders. Heavy items (garubhaṇḍa) should not be distributed. If there are many monasteries within a single boundary (sīmā), all monks should be assembled and the Kathina should be spread in only one place; it is not proper to spread it separately.
301:
"Monks, for you who have spread the kathina robe, five benefits will be allowable: wandering without having asked for permission (anāmantacāra), wandering without taking the complete set of robes (asamādānacāra), a group meal (gaṇabhojana), keeping as many robes as one likes (yāvadatthacīvara), and whatever robe-cloth arises there [for the Saṅgha] will be theirs." In accordance with these words (from the Mahāvagga), monks who have spread the kathina robe obtain the five benefits beginning with anāmantacāra.

Among those five, anāmantacāra means wandering without informing [another monk] as long as the kathina is not withdrawn; it means there is no offense according to the Cāritta training rule. Asamādānacāra means wandering without taking the [full set of] robes, which means separation from the robe (cīvaravippavāsa). Gaṇabhojana means the absence of offense according to the Gaṇabhojana training rule. Yāvadatthacīvara means that as many robes as desired may be kept without being formally determined (adhiṭṭhāna) or assigned (vikappanā). "Whatever robe-cloth arises there" means the robe of a deceased monk within the kathina boundary, or robes offered specifically to the Saṅgha, or robes obtained from communal property; it means that communal robe-cloth arising in any manner will belong to those monks.

## Thus, in the Palimuttaka Vinayavinicchaya Saṅgaha,
## The Discussion on the Determination of Spreading the Kathina is finished.

## 30. Discussion on the Determination of Heavy Articles (Garubhaṇḍa)

Regarding heavy articles (garubhaṇḍa): "Monks, there are these five non-disposable things (aviṣṣajjiya) that should not be disposed of by the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual. Even if disposed of, they are not [legally] disposed of. Whoever should dispose of them, there is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya)." In this manner (from the Cūḷavagga), the five types of heavy articles are shown as: a monastery (ārāma), a monastery site (ārāmavatthu), a dwelling (vihāra), a dwelling site (vihāravatthu), a couch (mañca), a chair (pīṭha), a mattress (bhisi), a pillow (bimbohana), a metal pot (lohakumbhī), a metal jar (lohabhāṇaka), a metal water-pot (lohavāraka), a metal basin (lohakāṭaha), an adze (vāsī), an axe (pharasu), a hatchet (kuṭhārī), a hoe (kudāla), a chisel (nikhādana), creepers (valli), bamboo (veḷu), muñja grass, pabbaja grass, grass, clay, wooden articles, and clay articles.

Among those heavy articles, a monastery (ārāma) means either a flower garden or a fruit garden. A monastery site (ārāmavatthu) means the area demarcated for the purpose of those monasteries, or the original ground of those monasteries when they have fallen into ruin.
302:
A dwelling (vihāra) refers to any residence such as a multi-storied building. A dwelling site (vihāravatthu) is the place where that dwelling stands. A couch (mañca) is any one of these four types: masāraka, bundikābaddha, kuḷīrapādaka, or āhaccapādaka. A chair (pīṭha) is any one of the four types of chairs similar to the masāraka, etc. A mattress (bhisi) is any one of the five types of mattresses, such as those stuffed with wool. A pillow (bimbohana) is any one of those made from tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, or poṭakī-cotton.

A metal pot (lohakumbhī) is a pot made of iron, copper, or any kind of metal. The same method applies to metal jars (lohabhāṇaka) and so on. Here, bhāṇaka refers to a large water jar that holds a lot of water. Vāraka is a small water pot (ghata). Kaṭāha is a metal basin. Regarding the adze (vāsī) and so on, and creepers (valli) and so on, there is nothing difficult to understand.

The term "five" is spoken by way of groups; however, by way of individual items, there are twenty-five kinds of these heavy articles. Thus it has been said:

"Two groups contain two items each, the third contains four,
The fourth has nine parts, and the fifth has eight divisions.
Thus, by these five groups, the Lord endowed with the five-fold pure vision,
Declared the heavy articles to be of twenty-five kinds."

Regarding these heavy articles, this is the legal determination: All these heavy articles are called "non-disposable" (aviṣṣajjiya) in the Senāsanakkhandhaka, and shown as "non-divisible" (avebhaṅgiya) in the Kīṭāgiri case. However, in the Parivāra, it is stated: "The Great Sage spoke of five non-disposable and non-divisible heavy articles; the wise have considered that there is no offense for one who disposes or uses them [in a certain way]."

Therefore, the intention here should be understood as follows: they are non-disposable and non-divisible by way of absolute alienation (mūlacchēda), but there is no offense for one who disposes or uses them by way of exchange (parivattana).

In that exchange, to speak in order: these five kinds of heavy articles should not be specifically used to obtain robes, alms-food, or medicine. However, it is allowable to exchange permanent property for permanent property, and heavy articles for heavy articles. Regarding permanent property, it is not allowable for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha to manage, accept, or receive permanent property such as fields, farm lands, tanks, or canals. They are allowable only as kappiya property when managed by lay attendants (kappiya-kāraka).
