It is allowable to exchange these four: a monastery for a monastery, a monastery site, a dwelling, or a dwelling site.

The method of exchange is as follows: If the Saṅgha's coconut grove is in a distant place and lay attendants consume much of it, and even for the fruits that are not consumed, only a small amount can be brought back after paying for cartage. Another grove belonging to village laypeople is in a place near the monastery. Those laypeople approach the Saṅgha and request to exchange their grove for that [distant] grove. After performing a formal consultation (apalokana) to see if the Saṅgha is pleased, it should be accepted. If the monks' thousand trees...
303:
It is not allowable for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to manage, receive, or accept permanent property of this nature (such as rice fields, farms, tanks, canals, etc.). Only property managed by lay-stewards (kappiyakārakas) is allowable. However, it is allowable to exchange these four: a park (ārāma) for a park, a park-site (ārāmavatthu), a monastery (vihāra), or a monastery-site (vihāravatthu).

In such an exchange, this is the method of exchange: If the Saṅgha's coconut grove is far away and the lay-stewards consume much of it, and even for the remaining fruit, only a small amount is received after paying for cart-hire to transport it; and if there are villagers living not far from that grove who have a grove near the monastery, and those people approach the Saṅgha and ask to exchange their grove for the Saṅgha's grove, the Saṅgha should accept it after performing a formal announcement (apalokana), asking, "Does this please the Saṅgha?"

Even if the bhikkhus' trees number one thousand and the laypeople's trees are only five hundred, one should not say, "Your grove is small." Although this grove is small, it actually yields more income than the other. Even if it yields an equal amount, it should be accepted because it can be used whenever desired. If the laypeople's trees are more numerous, one should say, "Are your trees not more numerous?" If they say, "May our merit increase; we donate it to the Saṅgha," it should be accepted after informing them.

If the bhikkhus' trees are bearing fruit and the laypeople's trees are not yet bearing fruit, it should still be accepted with the thought, "They will bear fruit before long." If the laypeople's trees are bearing fruit and the bhikkhus' trees are not, one should say, "Are your trees not bearing fruit?" If they say, "Please take them, Bhante; it will be for our merit," it should be accepted after informing them. In this way, a park is to be exchanged for a park. Following this same method, a park may be exchanged for a park-site, a monastery, or a monastery-site; and a park-site, whether large or small, may be exchanged for a park, a park-site, a monastery, or a monastery-site.

How is a monastery to be exchanged for a monastery? If the Saṅgha owns a house inside a village and laypeople own a mansion (pāsāda) in the middle of a monastery, and both are equal in value, if the laypeople ask to exchange that mansion for the house, it is allowable to accept. If the bhikkhus' house is more valuable, even if they say, "Our house is more valuable," if the laypeople say, "Although it is more valuable, it is unsuitable for those who have gone forth; it is not possible for monks to live in the middle of a village; only this mansion is suitable, please take it," then it should be accepted.

If the laypeople's mansion is more valuable, one should say, "Is your house not more valuable?" If they say, "May it be for our merit, Bhante; please take it," it should be accepted. In this way, a monastery is to be exchanged for a monastery. Following this same method, a monastery may be exchanged for a monastery-site, a park, or a park-site; and a monastery-site, whether of high or low value, may be exchanged for a monastery, a monastery-site, a park, or a park-site. Thus, the exchange of permanent property should be understood.

Regarding the exchange of heavy items (garubhaṇḍa), whether a bed (mañca) or a chair (pīṭha) is large or small, even one with legs only four finger-breadths high made by village children playing with sand-houses...
304:
...it is not possible for those who have gone forth to live there in the middle of the village; only this mansion is suitable, please take it," if they say so, it is allowable to accept. If the laypeople's mansion is very valuable, one should say, "Is your house not very valuable?" If they say, "Let it be, Bhante; it will be for our merit; please take it," then it is allowable to accept. In this way, a monastery is to be exchanged for a monastery. By this same method, a monastery-site, a park, or a park-site may be exchanged for a monastery; and a monastery-site, whether of high or low value, may be exchanged for a monastery, a monastery-site, a park, or a park-site. Thus, the exchange of permanent property for permanent property should be understood.

In the exchange of heavy items (garubhaṇḍa) for heavy items, whether a bed or a chair is large or small, even a bed with legs only four finger-breadths high made by village children playing with sand-houses becomes garubhaṇḍa from the moment it is given to the Saṅgha. If kings, royal ministers, and others donate a hundred beds or a thousand beds at once, all allowable beds should be accepted. After accepting them, they should be given out with the instruction, "Use them as communal property of the Saṅgha according to seniority"; they should not be given as personal property. It is also allowable to set out surplus beds in storehouses and the like to place bowls and robes upon them.

A bed given outside the boundary (sīmā) with the words "We give to the Saṅgha" should be placed in the dwelling of the Saṅgha Elder. If there are many beds there and there is no need for a bed, it should be given to whatever dwelling has a need, with the instruction, "Use it as communal property of the Saṅgha." If one valuable bed worth a hundred or a thousand is exchanged for a hundred other beds, it should be taken in exchange. Not only a bed for a bed, but it is also allowable to exchange parks, park-sites, monasteries, monastery-sites, chairs, bolsters (bhisi), and pillows (bimbohana). This method also applies to chairs, bolsters, and pillows. Among these items, unallowable (akappiya) ones should not be used; allowable ones should be used as communal property of the Saṅgha. One may exchange an unallowable valuable item or an allowable item to obtain the aforementioned objects. There is no such thing as a bolster or pillow that does not fall under the category of garubhaṇḍa.

Bronze pots (lohakumbhī), bronze jars (lohabhāṇaka), and bronze cauldrons (lohakataha)—these three, whether large or small, even those holding only a handful of water, are indeed garubhaṇḍa. As for bronze water-pitchers (lohavāraka) made of any kind of metal such as black iron, copper, brass, or bronze, those used in the island of Sihala for taking water to wash the feet should be distributed. A 'pāda' measure is equal to five nāḷis by the Magadhan nāḷi measure.
305:
It holds water; a pot that can hold more than that is *garubhaṇḍa* (heavy property). These are the bronze vessels that appear first in the Pāḷi. Although not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi, items such as pitchers, spittoons, ladles, spoons, scoops, basins, plates, small cups, caskets, braziers, and smoke-ladles for extracting smoke—whether small or large—are all *garubhaṇḍa* only. Alms-bowls, iron bowls, and copper bowls are *bhājanīya* (distributable) items. Various vessels made of bronze or *vaṭṭaloha* (circular metal/alloy) are allowable for use as *saṅghika* (communal) property or as items for lay use, but they are not allowable for *puggalika* (personal) use. It is stated in the *Mahāpaccariya* that even if bronze vessels and the like are given to the Saṅgha, it is not allowable to carry them away; they should be used only in the manner of lay utensils.

Aside from various vessels, other allowable metal items such as collyrium pots, collyrium rods, ear-picks, needles, styluses, small needles, small chisels, keys, locks, walking staffs, perforating tools, nail cutters, forks, iron hammers, iron pots, iron balls, iron lumps, iron discs, and other unfinished metal items are *bhājanīya* (distributable) property. However, smoking pipes, ploughshares, lamp-stands, lamp-dishes, hanging lamps, figures of women, men, or animals, or other items to be attached to walls, roofs, or door-leaves—down to even an iron nail—all such metal items are *garubhaṇḍa* only. Even if one obtains them personally, they should not be carried away and used as personal property; they are allowable only as *saṅghika* property or as lay utensils. The same principle applies to lead items. Plates, small cups, etc., made of milk-colored white stone (marble) are also *garubhaṇḍa* only.

A small water pot or an oil tube that can hold more than the amount of water used for washing the feet is *garubhaṇḍa*. Vessels made of gold, silver, rubies, or crystal are not allowable even in the form of lay utensils, let alone for use as *saṅghika* or *puggalika* property. However, in the use of dwellings (*senāsana*), everything is allowable, whether it is an object that may be touched (*āmāsa*) or may not be touched (*anāmāsa*).

Among adzes (*vāsi*) and the like, an adze that cannot perform any major work other than cutting tooth-sticks or sugarcane is *bhājanīya* property. An adze larger than that, made in any form, is *garubhaṇḍa* only. As for axes (*pharasu*), even a small axe used by physicians for bloodletting is *garubhaṇḍa* only. Regarding the large knife (*kuṭhāri*), the decision is the same as for the axe. A large knife made in the form of a weapon is an untouchable (*anāmāsa*) object. A hoe (*kudāla*), even if it is only four inches in size, is *garubhaṇḍa* only. A chisel (*nikhādana*), whether it has a four-sided face, or is shaped like the bow of a boat, or is curved, or is straight...
306:
Ultimately, even a small chisel for boring a broom handle is *garubhaṇḍa* if it is fitted with a handle. If the small chisel for boring a broom handle has no handle and is just the blade, and can be carried by putting it in a bag, that small chisel is *bhājanīya* property. The chisel-head is also included as a part of the chisel. If people who have donated adzes and the like to a monastery come and request, "Venerable sirs, our houses have burned down or have been plundered by thieves; please lend us the tools for a while, we will replace them later," they should be given. If they bring them back, they should not be refused; if they do not bring them back, they should not be asked for.

All iron tools such as anvils, hammers, tongs, and scales belonging to blacksmiths, carpenters, turners, reed-workers, lapidaries, and bowl-repairers are *garubhaṇḍa* from the time they are given to the Saṅgha. The same principle applies to the tools of tin-cutters, goldsmiths, and leather-workers. However, there is this distinction: among the tools of a tin-cutter, the small knife for cutting tin; among the tools of a goldsmith, the small knife for cutting gold; and among the tools of a leather-worker, the small knife for cutting prepared leather—these are *bhājanīya* property. Among the tools of barbers and tailors, excluding large scissors, large tongs, and large tweezers, all are *bhājanīya* property; the large scissors and the like are *garubhaṇḍa*.

Among creepers and the like, any creeper such as rattan that is half a forearm's length (about one span and four finger-breadths) in size, whether it was donated to the Saṅgha or grew there and was protected and tended by the Saṅgha, is *garubhaṇḍa*. If such creepers remain after the work of the Saṅgha or the work of a stūpa is completed, it is allowable to use them even for personal matters. A creeper that is not tended is not *garubhaṇḍa*. Ropes or cables made of thread, hemp, bark fiber, coconut fiber (coir), or leather—whether single-stranded or double-stranded—made by twisting bark fiber or coconut fiber, are *garubhaṇḍa* from the time they are given to the Saṅgha. Thread, hemp, bark fiber, and coconut fiber that are donated without being twisted are *bhājanīya* property. If the people who donated these ropes and cables take them for their own needs, they should not be stopped.

Ultimately, even a piece of bamboo only eight inches long and as thick as a stylus, whether donated to the Saṅgha or grown there and tended by the Saṅgha, is *garubhaṇḍa*. That bamboo, too, if it remains after the work of the Saṅgha or the stūpa is completed, is allowable to be given for personal matters. However, an oil tube for washing feet, a walking staff, a shoe-pull, an umbrella handle, and umbrella ribs—these items here are *bhājanīya* property. People whose houses have burned...
307:
People whose houses are on fire should not be prevented if they take [bamboo] and leave. One who takes bamboo protected by the Saṅgha should take it by performing an act of increase (phātikamma) with permanent property of equal or greater value. At the very least, it should be taken by performing an act of increase even with a creeper equal to the value of that bamboo. One who takes it without performing an act of increase should use it only in that same place. When leaving for another place, it should be left in the Saṅgha monastery before going. If taken away unintentionally, it should be sent back. One who has gone to another region should leave it in the Saṅgha monastery where they have arrived.

Grass refers to all remaining types of grass except for Muñja and Pabbaja grass. In places where there is no grass, they cover [roofs] with leaves; therefore, leaves are also included under the category of grass. Thus, among these, whether it be a handful of grass such as Muñja, or a single leaf such as a palm leaf, whether it is offered to the Saṅgha, or grows in that monastery, or is grass grown from a Saṅgha grass-field outside the monastery grounds, if it is protected by the Saṅgha, it is heavy property (garubhaṇḍa). Even such grass and leaves, after being used for Saṅgha duties or Cetiya duties, the remainder is allowable to be given for personal use. People whose houses are on fire should not be prevented if they take them and leave. A blank palm leaf (rittapotthaka) of eight finger-breadths in length is also heavy property.

Earth may be natural earth, or earth of five colors, or lime, or any substance such as resin, wood-oil, or lac, whether it is brought from a rare place and offered, or it originates in that Saṅgha land; if it is protected and is at least the size of a ripe palmyra fruit, it is heavy property. Even such earth, after being used for Saṅgha duties or Cetiya duties, the remainder is allowable to be given for personal use. However, asafoetida (hiṅgu), vermilion (hiṅgulaka), yellow orpiment (haritāla), red arsenic (manosilā), and collyrium (añjana) are distributable property (bhājanīya).

Regarding wooden property, it is stated in the Kurundī: "Any wooden object, even as small as a needle-case of eight finger-breadths in length and the thickness of a stylus, whether it is offered to the Saṅgha in a place where wood is scarce, or originates there, or is protected by the Saṅgha, this is heavy property." In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, all varieties such as wood, bamboo, skin, and stone are included under wooden property, and the decision on wooden property is stated starting from the long chair (āsandika). The method therein is: among these chairs—a long chair (āsandika), a chair with a backrest (sattanga), a state chair (bhaddapīṭha), a small chair (pīṭhikā), a one-legged chair, a chair with legs like the stem of a wood-apple, a wooden plank, a wicker-work seat (koccha), or a straw-seated chair—whether small or large, if offered to the Saṅgha, it is heavy property. Here, chairs made of banana leaves and the like are also included under the straw-seated chair. A wicker-work seat (koccha) surrounded by figures of wild beasts, embroidered with jewels, or covered with tiger skin is also heavy property. A curved plank, a long plank, a robe-washing plank,
308:
A curved board (or kneading board) used in washing robes, a robe-beating mallet, a mallet for driving a peg when cutting a tooth-stick or a mallet for striking a stone gong, a wooden water-trough used for pouring drinking water, a wooden trough for dye, a vessel for catching squeezed liquid, a casket with or without legs made of wood, ivory, or bamboo, a flower basket (or a small basket), a basket larger than the size held by the base, a water trough, a water jar, a ladle, a spoon, a drinking bowl, a drinking conch—if any of these objects are given to the Saṅgha, they are heavy property (garubhaṇḍa). However, a conch-shell cup is distributable (bhājanīya); likewise, a wooden water-bottle is distributable.

A circular stand used for washing or rubbing feet, whether made of wood, cloth, leaves, etc., is all heavy property. A bowl-stand, a bowl-lid, a palm-leaf fan, a winnowing fan, a flower basket, a basket, a broom with a handle, a handful of broom-grass—among these objects, whether small or large, anything made of bamboo, leaves, skin, etc., is heavy property. Any building component of a house such as pillars, beams, stairs, or planks, whether made of wood or stone, a mat, a floor covering, or allowable skin—all these, if given to the Saṅgha, are heavy property and are allowable to be spread on the ground. Sheepskin, being similar to a bed-cover, is also heavy property. Allowable skins, however, are distributable. In the Kurundī Commentary, it is said: "All skins the size of a rabbit are heavy property."

A mortar, a pestle, a winnowing basket (or sieve), a grindstone, a small grindstone, a stone trough, a stone jar, weaving tools, a shuttle, a bellows, etc.—all tools of weavers and the like, all agricultural tools, and all vehicles with wheels are heavy property. The legs of a bed (mañca), the frame of a bed, the legs of a chair, the frame of a chair, the handles of adzes, axes, etc.—among these, only unfinished or partially carved works are distributable; once carved and smoothed, they become heavy property. The handle of an allowed hatchet, an umbrella handle, a palm leaf, a walking stick, sandals, a water strainer (dhammakaraka) with its stand and cord, a gourd not larger than a foot-washing stand, a raw clay pot (or a pot made of fruit), a gourd-pot, a gourd-lid, a lacquered peg—all these are distributable property (bhājanīya); if larger than that, they are heavy property. Ivory or any horn that is uncarved and in its natural state is distributable. Regarding bed-legs and the like made from such ivory, the decision is the same as mentioned before. Even if carved and finished, a casket for asafoetida, a wooden pin (or waist-knob), a collyrium box, a collyrium stick, and a water-wiping cloth—all these are only distributable.

Among clay property, all utensils for human use and enjoyment such as pots, stands, and potter's vessels, bowl-shards for repairing bowls, shards for holding embers, incense burners, lamp-stands...
309:
Lamp stands, bricks, roofing tiles, and pinnacles are heavy items (garubhaṇḍa) from the time they are offered to the Saṅgha. However, small items (bhājanīyabhaṇḍa) here include ladles, bowls, cups, bronze vessels, and water pots of a size not exceeding a foot-washing basin. Just as a water pot is included in the category of small items among earthenware, so too does a water pot belong to the category of small items among bronze ware; this is the sequential decision in this matter.

## Thus in the Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha:

## The Discussion on the Decision regarding Heavy Items is finished.

## 31. Discussion on the Decision regarding Accusations and so forth

Regarding the decision on accusations and so forth, who is entitled to accuse and who is not? Firstly, no one is entitled to accuse by taking the words of a weak accuser (dubbalacodaka). A weak accuser is one who, while many monks are sitting in conversation, speaks about a case of defeat (pārājika) without specifying any particular person. Another person, having heard that, goes to that monk and says, 'It is said that you said such and such about me.' That monk replies, 'I do not know of such an occurrence; I only spoke without specifying anyone during the course of the conversation. If I had known of your misfortune, I would not have said even this much.' This person is called a weak accuser. No one is entitled to accuse that monk by taking his conversation. However, without taking such words, a monk endowed with virtue may accuse either a monk or a nun; and a nun endowed with virtue may accuse only a nun—so says the Elder Mahāpaduma. The Elder Mahāsumma, however, says, 'All five co-religionists are entitled to accuse.' The Elder Godatta says, 'It is not that no one is entitled; they are indeed entitled,' and he cites this Sutta: 'Having heard from a monk, he accuses; having heard from a nun... having heard from the disciples of other sects, he accuses.' In the views of all three Elders, the decision must be made only upon the admission of the accused.

This accusation is of three types: accusation based on what is seen (diṭṭhacodanā), accusation based on what is heard (sutacodanā), and accusation based on suspicion (parisaṅkitacodanā). There are also four other types: accusation of failure in virtue (sīlavipatticodanā), accusation of failure in conduct (ācāravipatticodanā), accusation of failure in view (diṭṭhivipatticodanā), and accusation of failure in livelihood (ājīvavipatticodanā). Among them, accusation of failure in virtue is to be understood by way of the two classes of grave offenses.
310:
Accusation of failure in conduct (ācāravipatticodanā) is to be understood by way of the remaining five classes of offenses. Accusation of failure in view (diṭṭhivipatticodanā) is to be understood by way of wrong view and extremist view. Accusation of failure in livelihood (ājīvavipatticodanā) is to be understood by way of the six training rules prescribed on account of livelihood.

There are also four other types of accusation: pointing out the ground (vatthusandassanā), pointing out the offense (āpattisandassanā), refusal of communion (saṃvāsapaṭikkhepa), and refusal of proper duties (sāmīcipaṭikkhepa). Among these four, 'pointing out the ground' is an accusation that proceeds thus: "You have indulged in sexual intercourse, you have taken what was not given, you have killed a human being, you have spoken what is not true (regarding superhuman states)." 'Pointing out the offense' is an accusation that proceeds in this manner: "You have fallen into a Pārājika offense of sexual intercourse." 'Refusal of communion' is an accusation that proceeds thus: "There is no longer Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, or legal act of the Saṅgha together with you." 'Refusal of proper duties' is the non-performance of major and minor duties such as paying homage, rising from one's seat, saluting with joined palms, and fanning. This refusal of proper duties is to be understood when one performs homage and so forth in sequence but omits it for one person while performing it for the rest. By this much, it is called an accusation. However, merely asking only the person one desires for gruel, rice, food, and so forth (and not asking others) does not constitute an accusation.

In another way, in the Pātimokkhaṭṭhapana-kkhandhaka, starting with "Monks, there is one unrighteous suspension of the Pātimokkha and one righteous suspension," up to ten unrighteous suspensions and ten righteous suspensions, and so forth, one hundred and ten accusations are taught—fifty-five unrighteous and fifty-five righteous. For one who accuses based on what is seen (diṭṭha), there are 110; for one who accuses based on what is heard (suta), there are 110; for one who accuses based on suspicion (parisaṅkā), there are 110; making a total of 330. When these 330 are multiplied by three—accusing by body (kāya), by speech (vācā), and by both body and speech—they become 990. When these 990 are further divided into accusing by oneself and causing another to accuse, they become 1,980 (two thousand less twenty). Furthermore, it should be understood that there are many thousands of accusations by way of being grounded (samūlika) or groundless (amūlika) in the divisions of 'seen' and so forth.

Among these various types of accusations mentioned, when a case (vatthu) arises in the midst of the Saṅgha by way of any one of these accusations, the accused (cuditaka) and the accuser (codaka) should be asked: "Will you be satisfied with our decision?" If
311:
If the accuser and the accused say, "Will you decide our case according to the Vinaya?", the Saṅgha should accept that legal issue (adhikaraṇa). If, however, they say, "Venerable sirs, please decide first; if we can endure it, we will accept (the decision)," they should be dismissed after delaying them by saying, "First, go and worship the shrine," and so on. When they have been exhausted for a long time, their followers have departed, their faction is broken, and they request again, the legal issue should be decided only when they are free from pride, after having rejected them up to three times.

In deciding, if the assembly is full of shameless ones (alajjī), the legal issue should be decided by the committee method (ubbāhikā). If the assembly is full of fools (bāla), one should say, "Search for Vinaya experts who are compatible with you," and after having them search for Vinaya experts, the legal issue should be settled according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher's Instruction (satthusāsana).

In that context, "Dhamma" means the true facts. "Vinaya" means the accusation (codanā) and the reminding (sāraṇā). "Teacher's Instruction" means the perfection of the motion (ñatti-sampadā) and the perfection of the proclamation (anussāvana-sampadā). Therefore, when the accuser presents the facts, the accused should be asked, "Is this matter present in you, or not?" After investigating the facts in this way, having him accused and reminded with the true facts, the legal issue should be settled through the perfection of the motion and the perfection of the proclamation.

Among those accusers and accused, if a shameless monk (alajjī) accuses a conscientious monk (lajjī), and that shameless one is foolish and incompetent, he should not be given the method; he should only be asked, "On what grounds do you accuse him?" Then he will certainly say, "Venerable sir, what is this? On what grounds should I accuse him?" One should dismiss him, saying, "You do not know anything; it is not proper for a fool like you to accuse another," and he should not be given a cross-examination. If, however, that shameless one is wise and competent, and is able to overwhelm and complete the case by what is seen or heard, he should be allowed to cross-examine, but the act (kamma) should be performed only according to the confession of the conscientious one.

If a conscientious monk accuses a shameless one, and that conscientious monk is foolish and incompetent and unable to conduct a cross-examination, he should be given the method: "Do you accuse him of a lapse in virtue (sīla-vipatti) or a lapse in conduct (ācāra-vipatti), etc.?" One might ask, "Why is the method given only to this conscientious monk and not to the other? Is it not improper for Vinaya experts to follow a wrong course (agati)?" It is indeed improper. However, doing this is not following a wrong course; it is called "favoring the Dhamma" (dhammānuggaha). For the training rule was laid down for the purpose of restraining the shameless and supporting the conscientious. Among those two, if the shameless one receives the method, he will come to overwhelm (the other)...
312:
When a conscientious monk (lajjī) receives the method, he will speak based on the sequence of what was seen or heard; therefore, favoring him with the Dhamma is appropriate. If that conscientious monk is wise and competent, he speaks firmly; but if the shameless monk (alajjī) does not give a confession, saying, "This case does not exist, that case does not exist," the decision should be made only with the confession of that shameless one.

To clarify this point, this story should be known: It is said that the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, after teaching Vinaya to monks beneath the Lohapāsāda, rose in the evening. At the time of his rising, two rival monks started a dispute. One did not give a confession. Then, when only a little of the first watch of the night remained, an impure view (suspicion) arose in the Elder regarding that person: "This accuser speaks firmly, but this accused does not confess; yet many facts are relevant; surely this act must have been committed." Then, tapping the footstool with the handle of his fan to give a signal, he said, "Friends, I am not fit to decide; have it decided by another Vinaya expert." When asked "Why, venerable sir?", the Elder told him the reason. A burning sensation arose in the body of the accused person. Then, that monk prostrated to the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, for the decision, there should only be a suitable Vinaya expert like you, and the accuser should also be like this," and after putting on white garments and apologizing, "I have troubled you for a long time," he departed.

In this way, if a shameless monk accused by a conscientious monk does not give a confession even though many facts have arisen, he should not be called "pure," nor should he be called "impure"; he is called "the living dead" (jīvamataka) and "raw and rotten" (āmakပူတိက). If another such case arises for him, it should not be decided; he shall be destroyed in that same way. If a shameless monk accuses another shameless monk, he should be told, "Friend, what can be said to this monk based on your words?" After saying the same to the other, they should be dismissed, saying, "Both of you, live together sharing the same communal life and use of requisites." A decision should not be made for the sake of their virtue; however, for the sake of requisites like bowls, robes, and dwellings, a decision should be made if suitable witnesses are obtained.

Then, if a conscientious monk accuses another conscientious monk and their dispute is over a trifle, they should be made to understand and, after having them confess the fault, saying, "Do not do this again"...
313:
They should be dismissed. However, in this matter, if the monk who is accused has committed a mistake suddenly, but has not been known as one who is shameless (alajjī) from the beginning, and while he remains without giving an admission in order to protect his own faction, many people stand up and say, "We believe him, we believe him," then by their testimony, let that monk be purified once or twice. However, if he does not remain in that position from the time of the mistake, the judgment should not be given.

One who decides on a case of taking what is not given (adinnādāna) should carefully note the twenty-five types of theft (avahāra). Among those decisions, a skilled expert in the Vinaya (Vinayadhara) should not judge the case that has arisen hastily, but should examine five factors. Referring to these five factors, the ancient teachers said:

"Having weighed these five factors—the object, the time, the place, the value, and fifthly, the usage—the wise Vinayadhara should render a judgment."

Among those five, 'object' (vatthu) refers to the stolen goods. Even if the monk who took it says, "I have stolen such and such an object," one should not immediately charge him with an offense, but should investigate whether that object is "with an owner (sasāmika) or without an owner (asāmika)." Even if it has an owner, one should investigate whether the owners have attachment (ālaya) or are without attachment. If it was taken while the owners still had attachment, the object should be valued and the offense should be assigned. If it was taken at a time when they were without attachment, the offense of Pārājika should not be assigned. However, if the owners of the goods ask for them back, they should be given. This is the proper conduct (sāmīci) in this matter.

To clarify this meaning, there is this story: During the time of King Bhātiya, for the purpose of worshipping the Mahācetiya, a monk from the southern region entered the courtyard of the stupa with a seven-cubit yellowish-red robe (paṇḍukāsāva) placed on his shoulder. At that very moment, the King also arrived to worship the stupa. Then, as the people were being cleared away, a great crowd pressed in. That monk, being pressed by the crowd, did not notice the robe falling from his shoulder and left. After leaving, not seeing the robe, he thought, "Who could find a robe in such a crowd? It is no longer mine," and having abandoned his claim (dhuranikkhepa), he went away. Then another monk, coming later, saw that robe and took it with the intention to steal (theyyacitta). Later, feeling remorse, the thought arose, "I am no longer a monk; I will return to the lay life." Then he thought, "I will ask the Vinayadharas and find out."
314:
At that time, the Elder Cūḷasumana, who was a bearer of the entire scriptures (Sabbapariyattidhara) and the chief teacher of Vinaya, resided in the Mahāvihāra. That monk approached the Elder, paid homage, and having asked for permission, inquired about his doubt. The Elder, knowing that the monk had taken the robe after the crowd had dispersed, thought, "There is still an opportunity here," and said, "If you can bring the monk who is the owner of the robe, it will be possible to provide a support for you." When the monk asked, "Venerable sir, how shall I find him?", the Elder said, "Go to various places and look." That monk looked in the five great monasteries but did not find him.

Then the Elder asked him, "From which direction do many monks come?" He replied, "From the southern direction, venerable sir." "If that is so, measure the length and width of the robe and keep it; then, search through the succession of monasteries in the southern direction and bring that owner monk," the Elder commanded. The monk did as the Elder said, found the monk, and brought him to the Elder. The Elder asked, "Is this robe yours?" "Yes, venerable sir," he replied. "Where did it fall for you?" The monk explained everything.

The Elder, having heard about the abandonment of claim (dhuranikkhepa) made by that monk, asked the other monk who had taken it, "Where did you see and take this?" He also reported everything. Then the Elder said to him, "If you had taken it with a pure heart, there would be no offense for you. But because you took it with the intention to steal, you have committed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Confess that dukkaṭa offense and become one without offense. Then, making this robe your own property, give it to this very monk." That monk felt as if he had been sprinkled with ambrosia and attained great relief. In this way, the facts of a case (vatthu) should be examined.

'Time' (kāla) refers to the time of the theft. For that same object may be of little value at one time and of great value at another. Therefore, the offense should be determined by the value that the object has at the very time it was stolen. In this way, the time should be examined.

'Place' (desa) refers to the place of the theft. For that same object should be valued according to the price it has in the very place where it was stolen. This is because an object may be of little value in the place where it is produced, but of great value elsewhere.

To clarify this meaning, there is this story: It is said that on an island in the middle of the ocean, a monk found a well-shaped coconut shell, and having placed it on a lathe, he made a delightful water cup resembling a mother-of-pearl bowl. He left it right there and went to Cetiyagiri...
315:
(That monk) went away. Another monk went to Antarasamudda and, while residing in that monastery, saw that coconut shell bowl. Taking it with the intention to steal, he came to Cetiyagiri. While that monk was drinking rice gruel at Cetiyagiri, the monk who owned the bowl saw it and asked, "Where did you get this?" "I brought it from Antarasamudda," he replied. The owner monk, saying, "This is not yours; you have stolen it," dragged him into the midst of the Saṅgha. Being unable to reach a decision there at Cetiyagiri, they went to the Mahāvihāra. There, they beat the drum and held an assembly near the Mahācetiya to begin the adjudication. The Vinaya-expert elders declared that it constituted a theft.

In that assembly, there was an elder named Ābhidhammika Godatta Thera who was skilled in the Vinaya. That elder asked, "Where did this monk steal this bowl?" "He stole it at Antarasamudda," they replied. "What is the value of that bowl in that place?" he asked. "It has no value at all, because in that place, people split the coconut, eat the meat, and discard the shell; it is only useful as firewood," they replied. "What is the value of the handiwork performed on this bowl by this monk?" he asked. "It is worth one māsaka or less than one māsaka," they replied. He then asked, "Is there any Pāḷi text where the Fully Enlightened One has prescribed a Pārājika offense for the value of one māsaka or less than one māsaka?" When he asked this, a simultaneous cry of "Sādhu! Sādhu! Well said! Well decided!" arose. At that time, King Bhātiya, who had come out of the city to worship the Cetiya, heard that sound and asked, "What is this?" After hearing the whole matter in sequence, he had a drum beaten throughout the city and proclaimed: "As long as I am alive, the legal cases (adhikaraṇa) of monks, nuns, and laypeople decided by Ābhidhammika Godatta Thera are very well decided. I shall place under royal authority anyone who does not abide by his decision." In this way, the region (desa) should be considered.

Value (aggha) refers to the price of the goods. The value of a new item tends to decrease later. For example, a newly washed alms-bowl may be worth eight or ten coins, but later, due to being broken, having a hole, or being struck by a bolt-knot (damaged), it becomes of little value. Therefore, an item should not always be valued at its original price. In this way, the value (aggha) should be considered.

Usage (paribhoga) refers to the use of the goods. Through use, the value of items such as an adze (vāsi) also decreases. Therefore, it should be investigated thus: If someone steals an adze worth one pāda belonging to another, the owner of the adze should be asked, "For how much did you buy this adze?" If he says, "For one pāda, venerable sir," then one must further ask, "Did you just keep it after buying, or did you use it?" If he says, "For one day, I..."
316:
...cut a tooth-stick, or bark for dyeing, or firewood for firing an alms-bowl, or if I sharpened it by rubbing," then it should be known that its former original value has decreased. As with an adze, so too with a collyrium pot, a collyrium rod, or a key; even by just rubbing and washing them once with straw, husk, or brick powder, the value decreases. By cutting a tin alms-bowl stand into a makara-tooth pattern, or by merely polishing it; by wearing a water-cloth once, or by merely placing it on the shoulder or head for the purpose of use; by winnowing rice and such, or by removing one or two grains from it, or even by just picking out and discarding a single pebble; by pouring ghee, oil, etc., from one vessel to another, or even by just picking out and discarding a fly or an ant from that oil; by piercing a lump of molasses with a fingernail and taking just a tiny bit to know its sweetness—in all these cases, the value decreases. Therefore, if any object worth one pāda has been reduced to less than a pāda by the owner's own use in the manner described, the monk who steals that item should not be made subject to a Pārājika offense. In this way, the value should be examined.

Thus, a wise Vinaya expert should weigh these five points and establish whether there is an offense or no offense, and whether it is a heavy or light offense, in its proper place. Therefore, the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariya) said:

There is no other training rule equal to this one; it is interspersed with many methods and contains deep judicial decisions.

Therefore, when a case arises, a monk who is an expert in the Vinaya should make a decision here for the sake of upholding the Vinaya.

Having thoroughly delved into the Pāḷi and the Commentary along with their intentions, a decision should be made with heedful mindfulness.

One should never strive with the intent to see an offense; one should set the mind only to look for the absence of an offense.

Even upon seeing an offense, one should not speak immediately, but should reflect repeatedly, consult with the wise, and only then pronounce that offense.
317:
In this Dispensation, worldlings (puthujjanas), by following the whims of their fickle minds, tend to fall away from the virtues of monkhood—namely, morality—even regarding allowable objects. Therefore, a wise monk should clearly perceive another's requisites as a venomous snake or as fire, and should not handle or touch them. (This is the instruction in that regard.)

A monk who wishes to judge the reporting of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma)—states such as jhāna, path, and fruit that are superior to the ten wholesome courses of action of humans—should investigate and clear these six points: (1) What did you attain? (2) How did you attain it? (3) When did you attain it? (4) Where did you attain it? (5) Which of your defilements have been abandoned? (6) Which states have you acquired? If any monk reports the attainment of a superhuman state, one should not yet offer honor based merely on those words, but to investigate these six points, one should ask: "What did you attain? Was it jhāna or one of the liberations (vimokkha), etc.?" For the state one has attained is clear to oneself.

If he says, "I have attained such-and-such a state," then one should further ask, "How did you attain it?" (Meaning) Which of the marks, such as impermanence (aniccalakkhaṇa), did you take as the lead to attain it? Or, among the thirty-eight objects of meditation, or among the states of the grounds of insight (vipassanābhūmi) such as materiality and mentality (rūpa-nāma), internal and external (ajjhatta-bahiddha), etc., through which gateway of entry did you apply your mind? For one's own method of application is clear to oneself.

If he says, "This is my method of application, and thus I attained it," then one should further ask, "When did you attain it?" Was it in the morning, or at midday, or at some other time? For the time of one's own attainment is clear to all monks.

If he says, "I attained it at such-and-such a time," then one should further ask, "Where did you attain it?" Was it in a place used for the day, or in a place used for the night, or in some other location? For the location of one's own attainment is clear to all monks.

If he says, "I attained it in such-and-such a location," then one should further ask, "Which of your defilements have been abandoned?" Was it the defilements abandoned by the first path (Sotāpattimagga), or those abandoned by the higher paths such as the second path? For the defilements abandoned by the path one has attained are clear to all monks.

If he says, "Such-and-such defilements have been abandoned," then one should further ask, "Which states have you acquired?" Did you acquire the path of Stream-entry, or one of the paths such as Once-returning (Sakadāgāmimagga), etc.? For the state one has attained is clear to all monks...
318:
...is clear. If he says, "I have acquired these named states," even with this much, his words should not yet be believed. For monks who are very learned and skilled in learning and questioning are able to clear and answer these six points. However, this monk's path of arrival (practice) should be investigated. If the path of arrival is not pure, one should reject the claim, saying, "By this practice, the supramundane state (lokuttaradhamma) cannot be attained." But if his path of arrival is pure, and it is known that for a long time he has been diligent in the three trainings (sikkhā), devoted to wakefulness, unattached to the four requisites, and dwells with a mind like a palm in the sky, then that monk's declaration matches his practice. It is like what was said: "Just as the water of the Ganges matches and meets the water of the Yamuna, even so, the practice leading to Nibbāna well-expounded by the Blessed One for his disciples matches both Nibbāna and the practice." However, even with this much (purity of practice), honor should not yet be offered. Why? Because even some worldlings may have a practice similar to that of an Arahant (khīṇāsava). Therefore, that monk should be frightened (tested) by various means. An Arahant has no fear, trembling, or horripilation even if a thunderbolt falls on his head, but for a worldling, it can happen even with a small thing.

In this regard, there are these stories: It is said that Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya Thera, being unable to discern whether a certain Piṇḍapātika Thera was an Arahant, gave a sign to a young monk. That young monk dived into the water at the mouth of the Kalyāṇī River where the Thera was bathing and grabbed his leg. The Piṇḍapātika Thera, thinking it was a "crocodile," shouted loudly. At that time, they knew him to be a "worldling."

During the time of King Candamukha Tissa, however, an Arahant Elder who was the Sangha Elder at the Mahāvihāra stayed only in the monastery because of weak eyesight. The king, thinking "I will investigate the Elder," approached quietly when the monks had gone for alms and grabbed his leg like a snake. The Elder remained motionless like a stone pillar and asked, "Who is there?" When the king replied, "Venerable sir, I am King Tissa," the Elder said, "King Tissa, you smell very fragrant." Thus, for an Arahant, there is no such thing as fear.

However, some worldlings are also very brave and have no fear. Such a person should be investigated with an attractive object. King Vasabha, also wishing to investigate an Elder, invited him to sit in the palace and placed jujube pulp before him...
319:
(King Vasabha) sat kneading a ripe plum. At that time, the saliva of the Mahāthera flowed, and thus the elder's state as a worldling (puthujjana) became manifest. Indeed, for an Arahant, craving for taste (rasataṇhā) has been thoroughly abandoned; there is no attachment even to divine tastes. Therefore, by investigating with such means, if fear, trembling, or craving for taste arises in that person, he should be dismissed with the words, "You are not an Arahant." However, if he remains fearless, untrembling, and undaunted, sitting like a lion, and if no attachment arises even for divine objects, it should be understood that this monk is one who is accomplished in answering regarding the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) he possesses, and is worthy of the offerings sent by kings, royal ministers, and others from all around. Thus should the decision regarding the declaration of superhuman states be determined.

A Vinaya expert (Vinayadhara) who desires proficiency in all Vinaya decisions should know the fourfold Vinaya.

In ancient times, the Great Elders who were reciters of the Dhamma (Dhammasaṅgāhaka) and possessed great psychic power, extracted and revealed the fourfold Vinaya.

What are the four types of Vinaya? They are Sutta, Suttānuloma, Ācariyavāda, and Attanomati. Referring to these four, it was said: "O Great King, (decisions are made) by way of the direct text (āhaccapada), the essence (rasa), the lineage of teachers (ācariyavaṃsa), and the intention (adhippāya)." Here, 'āhaccapada' means Sutta (the Pali text). 'Rasa' means Suttānuloma. 'Ācariyavaṃsa' means Ācariyavāda. 'Adhippāya' means Attanomati.

Among these four, Sutta refers to the Pali text in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka.

Suttānuloma refers to the four Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa) taught by the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught those four Great Authorities as follows:

"Monks, if a matter has not been directly rejected by me, saying 'This is not allowable,' if it conforms with what is not allowable and contradicts what is allowable, then that matter is not allowable for you. Monks, if a matter has not been directly rejected by me, saying 'This is not allowable,' if it conforms with what is allowable and contradicts what is not allowable, then that matter is allowable for you. Monks, if a matter has not been directly permitted by me, saying 'This is allowable,' if it conforms with what is not allowable and contradicts what is allowable, then that matter is not allowable for you. Monks, if a matter has not been directly permitted by me, saying 'This is allowable,' if it conforms with what is allowable and contradicts what is not allowable, then that matter is allowable for you."
320:
Ācariyavāda refers to the lineage of the Commentaries (Atthakathā) established by the five hundred Arahants who performed the communal recitation (Saṅgāyanā) of the Dhamma; it is distinct from the Pali text and consists of pure decisions. Attanomati refers to the statement of a point that becomes clear through one's own subsequent knowledge (anubuddhi) and method of reasoning (nayaggāha) by means of inference, setting aside the Sutta, Suttānuloma, and Ācariyavāda. Furthermore, all the Theravāda (views of the elders) found in the Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya Commentaries are also called Attanomati. One who speaks by taking such Attanomati should not speak with firm attachment; rather, having reflected on the reason, one should speak by comparing the Pali with the meaning, and the meaning with the Pali. Attanomati should be measured against Ācariyavāda. If it fits and agrees with Ācariyavāda, it should be accepted. If it does not fit or agree, it should not be accepted. This Attanomati is the weakest of all. Ācariyavāda is stronger and superior to Attanomati.

Ācariyavāda should also be measured against Suttānuloma. Only if it fits and agrees with Suttānuloma should it be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted. Suttānuloma is stronger and superior to Ācariyavāda. Suttānuloma should also be measured against Sutta. Only if it fits and agrees with Sutta should it be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted. Sutta alone is stronger and superior to Suttānuloma. Indeed, the Sutta (Pali text) is unalterable; it is like the Saṅgha that performed the communal recitation, and it is like the time when the Buddhas were still present.

Therefore, when two monks discuss, if the proponent of one's own school (Sakavādī) speaks by taking the Sutta, and the proponent of another school (Paravādī) speaks by taking Suttānuloma, they should not criticize or blame each other, but should measure Suttānuloma against the Sutta. If it fits and agrees, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted, and one should stand by the Sutta alone. If this Sakavādī speaks by taking the Sutta, and the other speaks by taking Ācariyavāda, they also should not criticize or blame each other, but should measure Ācariyavāda against the Sutta. If it fits and agrees, it should be accepted. An Ācariyavāda that does not fit or agree is blameworthy and should not be accepted; one should stand by the Sutta alone. If this Sakavādī speaks by taking the Sutta, and the other speaks by taking Attanomati, they also should not criticize or blame each other, but should measure Attanomati against the Sutta. If it fits and agrees, it should be accepted; if not, it should not be accepted, and one should stand by the Sutta alone.
321:
If a person holding a certain view speaks based on the Great Authority (Suttānuloma), and another speaks based on the Pāli (Sutta), that Pāli should be compared with the Great Authority. If it fits and conforms, and is evident as being included in the Pāli established in the Three Councils, it should be accepted. If it is not evident, does not fit, and does not conform—whether it be an external Sutta (bāhirakasutta), a verse (siloka), or a censurable Sutta (gārayhasutta) brought from one of the Suttas of the Mahāsaṅghikas such as the Guḷhavessantara, Guḷhavinaya, or Cūḷavedalla—it should not be accepted; one should stand by the Great Authority alone.

If this person speaks based on the Great Authority, and another speaks based on the Commentary (Ācariyavāda), that Commentary should be compared with the Great Authority. If it fits and conforms, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted; one should stand by the Great Authority alone.

If this person speaks based on the Great Authority, and another speaks based on their own opinion (Attanomati), that opinion should be compared with the Great Authority. If it fits and conforms, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted; one should stand by the Great Authority alone.

If this person speaks based on the Commentary, and another speaks based on the Pāli, that Pāli should be compared with the Commentary. If it fits and conforms, it should be accepted. Any other censurable Pāli (that does not fit) should not be accepted; one should stand by the Commentary alone.

If this person speaks based on the Commentary, and another speaks based on the Great Authority, that Great Authority should be compared with the Commentary. Only that which fits and conforms should be accepted; anything else should not be accepted; one should stand by the Commentary alone.

If this person speaks based on the Commentary, and another speaks based on their own opinion, that opinion should be compared with the Commentary. If it fits and conforms, it should be accepted. If not, it should not be accepted; one should stand by the Commentary alone.

Furthermore, if this person speaks based on their own opinion, and another speaks based on the Pāli, that Pāli should be compared with their own opinion. If it fits and conforms, it should be accepted. Any other censurable Pāli should not be accepted; one should stand by their own opinion alone.

If this person speaks based on their own opinion, and another speaks based on the Great Authority, that Great Authority should be compared with their own opinion. Only that which fits and conforms should be accepted; anything else should not be accepted; one should stand by their own opinion alone.

If this person speaks based on their own opinion, and another speaks based on the Commentary, that Commentary should be compared with their own opinion. If it fits and conforms, it should be accepted. Any other censurable Commentary view should not be accepted,
322:
one should stand by one's own opinion alone; one should make one's own grasp firm. In all instances, one should not reject or disparage (the views of others).

If this person speaks taking it as 'allowable' (kappiya), and another says 'not allowable' (akappiya), it should be compared with the Pāli and the Great Authority. If it is allowable, one should stand by what is allowable. If it is not allowable, one should stand by what is not allowable. If this person shows many reasons and decisions from the Pāli to prove its allowability, and the other finds no reason, one should stand by what is allowable. If the other person shows many reasons and decisions from the Pāli to prove its non-allowability, this person should not stand firmly by their own view; having accepted it saying 'Very well', they should stand by what is not allowable. If there is a semblance of reason on both sides, it is better to reject it; one should stand by what is not allowable. For when it comes to the Vinaya, in investigating what is allowable and not allowable, one should prohibit (the doubtful), act firmly, cut off the flow (of desire), and stand by the side of gravity (garuka).

If this person speaks taking it as 'not allowable', and another says 'allowable', it should be compared with the Pāli and the Great Authority. If it is allowable, one should stand by what is allowable; if not allowable, one should stand by what is not allowable. If this person shows many reasons for non-allowability through Pāli decisions, and the other finds no reason, one should stand by what is not allowable. If the other person shows many reasons for allowability through Pāli decisions, and this person finds no reason, one should stand by what is allowable. If there is a semblance of reason on both sides, one should not abandon one's own grasp. Just as the decision was stated regarding 'allowable and not allowable' and 'not allowable and allowable', so too should the decision be understood regarding 'no offense and offense', 'offense and no offense', 'light offense and grave offense', and 'grave offense and light offense'. Here, there is only a difference in name; there is no difference in the method of interpretation (yojanānaya). Therefore, it is not elaborated further.

When such decisions regarding allowability and non-allowability arise, one should stand by the view of the one who obtains superior reasons among the Pāli, the Great Authority, the Commentary, and one's own opinion. If one does not obtain a decisive reason in any way, the Pāli should not be abandoned; one should stand by the Pāli alone. Thus, one who desires skill in all Vinaya decisions should know these four types of Vinaya.

Even after knowing these four types of Vinaya, a person who is a Master of Discipline (Vinayadhara) must be endowed with three characteristics. The three characteristics of a Master of Discipline are desired.
323: What are the three? (1) For that Vinayadhara (expert in Vinaya), the Vinaya Pali is well-learned, well-rehearsed, and well-determined both in terms of the text (sutta) and the phrasing (anubyañjana). This is the first characteristic. (2) Furthermore, he is firmly established in the Vinaya and is unshakeable (asanhīra) by others. This is the second characteristic. (3) Furthermore, for that Vinayadhara, the lineage of teachers (ācariyaparamparā) is well-mastered, well-reflected upon, and well-retained. This is the third characteristic. In this context, 'Sutta' refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. 'Tadassa svāgataṃ hoti' means it is well-learned. 'Suppavatti' means it is well-rehearsed, fluent, or mastered by heart. 'Suvinicchitaṃ suttato anubyañjanato' means it is well-determined through the Pali text, through questioning, and through the Commentary, having been mastered by cutting off all doubts. 'Vinaye kho pana ṭhito hoti' means being established in the Vinaya by way of conscientiousness (lajjī-bhāva). For even a learned person, if he is shameless (alajjī), he may, out of regard for gain, misrepresent the Pali text, presenting what is not Dhamma as Dhamma and what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, thereby causing great harm to the Teacher’s Dispensation and even causing schisms and rifts in the Saṅgha. However, a conscientious person (lajjī) is scrupulous and desirous of training; even for the sake of his life, he does not misrepresent the Pali text but presents the Dhamma as Dhamma and the Vinaya as Vinaya, thus showing great respect for the Teacher’s Dispensation. Indeed, for this reason, the great elders of old proclaimed three times: 'In the future, the conscientious will protect the Dispensation; the conscientious will protect it; the conscientious will protect it.' Thus, one who is conscientious, without abandoning or transgressing the Vinaya, remains well-established in the Vinaya through his conscientiousness. 'Asanhīra' means: a 'shakeable' person (sanhīra) is one who, when questioned on the Pali or the Commentary, from the beginning or the end, or according to the sequence of words, becomes agitated and wavers, unable to remain firm; he accepts whatever others say, abandoning his own doctrine and adopting the doctrine of others. But one who, when questioned on the Pali or the Commentary, from above or below, or according to the sequence of words, does not agitate or waver, but answers like one picking up individual hairs with a pair of tweezers, saying, 'Thus we say; thus our teachers say'—in such a person, the Pali and the determination of the Pali remain without exhaustion or depletion, like lion’s fat (sīhavasā) placed in a golden vessel. Such a person is called 'unshakeable' (asanhīra). 'Ācariyaparamparā kho panassa suggahitā hoti' means the lineage of elders and the lineage of the clan is well-mastered by that Vinayadhara. 'Sumanasikatā' means well-reflected upon, so that it becomes clear like a lit lamp as soon as it is brought to mind. 'Sūpadhāritā' means well-retained by way of the connection between preceding and following words, by way of meaning, and by way of reason.
324: 'Upadhāritā' means being one who has well-retained [the teachings] through the connection of preceding and following words, through the meaning, and through the reasons. He is one who speaks according to the pure view of the teachers, having abandoned his own personal opinion. He presents [the lineage] thus: 'My teacher learned from such-and-such a teacher, and that teacher learned from such-and-such,' thus tracing the entire lineage of teachers, the component of the Theravāda Pali, back to the Elder Upāli who learned it in the presence of the Fully Enlightened Buddha. Tracing it from the Fully Enlightened Buddha: the Elder Upāli learned it in the presence of the Fully Enlightened Buddha; the Elder Dāsaka from his preceptor, the Elder Upāli; the Elder Soṇa from his preceptor, the Elder Dāsaka; the Elder Sigjava from his preceptor, the Elder Soṇa; and the Elder Moggaliputtatissa from his preceptors, the Elder Sigjava and the Elder Caṇḍavajji. In this way, he presents the entire lineage of teachers, the component of the Theravāda Pali, down to his own teacher. A lineage of teachers learned in this way is said to be 'well-mastered.' If one is unable to master the entire lineage, one must certainly learn from at least two or three generations of teachers. At the very least, one should know how the teacher and the teacher’s teacher explain the Pali and the determination (vinicchaya). When a Vinayadhara endowed with these three characteristics enters a Saṅgha meeting to settle a case, and when the incident (vatthu) has been presented and the accuser (codaka) and the accused (cuditaka) have spoken what needs to be said, he should not decide hastily but should examine six points. What are the six? The incident (vatthu) must be examined, the matrix (mātikā) must be examined, the word-for-word analysis (padabhājanīya) must be examined, the triad definitions (tikapariccheda) must be examined, the intermediate offenses (antarāpatti) must be examined, and the exemptions (anāpatti) must be examined. Examining the incident (vatthu), the Vinayadhara sees a certain offense such as: 'One should come covered with grass or leaves; one should not come naked; if one comes [naked], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).' That Vinayadhara, having cited that Sutta Pali, will settle that legal issue. Examining the matrix (mātikā), he sees one of the five classes of offenses, such as: 'In deliberate lying, there is an offense involving expiation (pācittiya).' That Vinayadhara, having cited that Sutta Pali, will settle that legal issue. Examining the word-for-word analysis (padabhājanīya), he sees: 'If one practices sexual intercourse with a corpse that is not yet decomposed or destroyed, there is an offense of defeat (pārājika). If one practices sexual intercourse with a corpse that is mostly decomposed...'
325:
In the Padabhājanīya (word-by-word commentary), he sees one of the seven classes of offenses in such a way as: "He indulges in sexual intercourse, there is an offense of thullaccaya (grave offense)," and so on (similar in meaning to Pārājika Pāḷi 59). That Vinaya expert, having brought the text from the Padabhājanīya, shall settle that legal issue (adhikaraṇa).

Even when looking at the Tika (triad) section, the Vinaya expert sees a triad saṅghādisesa, a triad pācittiya, a triad dukkaṭa, or any other offense in the Tika section. That Vinaya expert, having brought the text from that Tika section, shall settle that legal issue.

Even when looking at an intermediate offense (antarāpatti), the Vinaya expert sees such an intermediate offense in various training rules as: "He lifts a firebrand, there is an offense of dukkaṭa" (Pācittiya 355). That Vinaya expert, having brought that text, shall settle that legal issue.

Even when looking at non-offenses (anāpatti), the Vinaya expert sees the non-offenses specified in various training rules as: "There is no offense for a monk who does not consent, who has no intention to steal, no intention to kill, no intention to speak [falsely], no intention to release [semen], or who is unintentional, unmindful, or unaware" (slightly different in Pārājika 72, 136, 180, 225, 263). That Vinaya expert, having brought that text, shall settle that legal issue.

If a monk who is skilled in the fourfold Vinaya and endowed with the three characteristics settles a legal issue after looking into these six points, his decision is irreversible, as if the Buddha himself had sat and decided. If a monk who has committed a transgression of a training rule approaches such a monk skilled in decision-making and asks about his own remorse (kukkucca), that Vinaya expert should reflect well. If there is no offense, he should say, "There is no offense." If there is an offense, and it is a desanāgāminī (confessable), he should say, "It is desanāgāminī." If it is vuṭṭhānagāminī (requiring rehabilitation), he should say, "It is vuṭṭhānagāminī." But if a shadow of pārājika appears to that Vinaya expert, he should not yet say, "It is a pārājika offense." Why? Because the transgression of sexual intercourse and the transgression of claiming superhuman states are gross; however, the transgressions of taking what is not given and human-killing are subtle and involve a quickness of mind. One falls into them subtly and guards against them subtly. Therefore, especially when asked about remorse concerning such a matter, he should not say, "It is an offense," but if that Vinaya expert's teacher is living, he should send that monk, saying, "Go and ask our teacher." If...
326:
If that monk returns and says, "Your teacher, having looked into it according to the texts and methods, told me, 'You are one with a curable offense (satekiccha),'" then that Vinaya expert should say to him, "Very well, do as the teacher says." But if he has no teacher, but has a senior fellow student (saddhiṃ uggahitathera), he should be sent to him, saying, "There is a senior fellow student of ours who is a leader of the group; go and ask him." If that elder also decides, "He is one with a curable offense," he should say, "Very well, do as he says." If he has no senior fellow student, but has a wise pupil (antevāsika paṇḍita), he should be sent to him, saying, "Go and ask such-and-such a young monk." If that young monk also decides, "He is one with a curable offense," he should say, "Very well, do as he says." If even to the young monk only a shadow of pārājika appears, that Vinaya expert should still not say, "You are a pārājika." For the arising of a Buddha is rare, and even rarer than that are the going forth (pabbajjā) and the higher ordination (upasampadā). Instead, he should be told: "Having swept a secluded place, sitting in a place for the day's rest, and having purified your virtues, first contemplate the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra)."

If that monk's virtue is healthy and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) connects, the formations (saṅkhāra) become clear and manifest, and the mind becomes one-pointed as if reaching access or absorption concentration (upacāra-appanā). He might not even know that the whole day has passed. When he comes to attend after the day has passed, he should be asked, "How is the occurrence of your mind?" When the occurrence of the mind is reported, he should be told, "The purpose of the monkhood is the purity of mind; be diligent and perform the recluse's duties (samaṇadhamma)."

But if someone's virtue is broken, the meditation subject does not connect for him. His mind trembles like an elephant goaded by a pike; it is burned by the fire of remorse. Like one sitting on a hot stone, he rises at that very moment. When that monk comes, he should be asked, "How is the occurrence of your mind?" When the occurrence of the mind is reported, he should be told, "There is no such thing as a secret place in the world for one who does an evil deed. First of all, when doing evil, one knows it oneself. Then, his guardian deities, recluses and brahmins who know the minds of others, and other deities know. Now, you yourself must seek your own safety." When a monk who has thus committed a transgression comes and reports it himself, one should act accordingly.

## Now, for the sake of knowing the success and failure of that very accusation (codanā) with its various divisions mentioned before, the decision should be understood by way of the beginning, middle, end, and so forth.
327: It should be known. As follows: What is the beginning of an accusation, what is the middle, and what is the end? In an accusation, asking for permission in this way, "I wish to speak to you, may the venerable one grant me the opportunity," is the beginning. Accusing by entering into the facts and deciding through reminding is the middle. Settlement by establishing whether it is an offense or not an offense is the end. How many roots, how many grounds, and how many bases are there for an accusation? There are two roots for an accusation: with a root or without a root. There are three grounds: seen, heard, and suspected. There are five bases: "I will speak at the right time, not at the wrong time; I will speak what is true, not what is false; I will speak gently, not harshly; I will speak what is beneficial, not what is unbeneficial; I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with an angry heart." Furthermore, in this accusation, the person who accuses should be established in the fifteen factors taught in the Upālipañcaka, such as "Am I of pure bodily conduct?" and so on. The accused (cuditaka) should be established in two things: truthfulness and non-anger. The investigator (anuvijjaka) should question the accuser: "Friend, for what reason do you accuse this monk? Do you accuse him because of a failure in virtue (sīlavipatti), a failure in conduct (ācāravipatti), or a failure in view (diṭṭhivipatti)?" If that accuser says, "I accuse him because of a failure in virtue, or a failure in conduct, or a failure in view," he should be asked: "Friend, do you know what is a failure in virtue, do you know what is a failure in conduct, do you know what is a failure in view?" If he says, "Friend, I know failure in virtue, failure in conduct, and failure in view," he should be asked: "Friend, what is failure in virtue, what is failure in conduct, and what is failure in view?" If he says, "The four Pārājikas and the thirteen Saṅghādisesas are called failure in virtue. Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkaṭa, and Dubbhāsita are called failure in conduct. Wrong view and extremist view are called failure in view," then he should be asked: "Friend, do you accuse this monk because of what was seen, or heard, or suspected?"
328:
"I accuse," (if he says so). If that accuser says, "I accuse based on what was seen, or heard, or suspected," then that accuser should be spoken to thus: "Friend, when you accuse this monk based on what was seen, what did you see, how did you see it, when did you see it, and where did you see it? Did you see him committing a Pārājika offense? Did you see him committing a Saṅghādisesa offense? Did you see him committing a Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkaṭa, or Dubbhāsita offense? Where was this monk, where were you, what were you doing, and what was this monk doing?" (he should be questioned).

If that accuser says, "Friend, I do not accuse this monk based on what was seen, but rather I accuse him based on what was heard," then that accuser should be spoken to thus: "Friend, when you accuse this monk based on what was heard, what did you hear, how did you hear it, when did you hear it, and where did you hear it? Did you hear that he committed a Pārājika offense? Did you hear that he committed a Saṅghādisesa offense? Did you hear that he committed a Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkaṭa, or Dubbhāsita offense? Did you hear it from a monk, from a nun, from a female trainee, from a novice, from a female novice, from a layman, from a laywoman, from kings, from royal ministers, from sectarians, or from disciples of sectarians?" (he should be questioned).

If that accuser says, "Friend, I do not accuse this monk based on what was heard, but rather I accuse him based on suspicion," then that accuser should be spoken to thus: "Friend, when you accuse this monk based on suspicion, what do you suspect, how do you suspect, when do you suspect, and where do you suspect? Do you suspect that he committed a Pārājika offense? Do you suspect that he committed a Saṅghādisesa, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkaṭa, or Dubbhāsita offense? Did you suspect after hearing the words of a monk, after hearing the words of a nun ...pe... after hearing the words of disciples of sectarians?" (he should be questioned).

What is seen agrees with what is seen; what is seen corresponds with what is seen.
One does not reach (an offense) based on what is seen; it is suspected with an unpurified suspicion.
Based on that person's acknowledgement, the Uposatha should be performed with him.

What is heard agrees with what is heard; what is heard corresponds with what is heard.
One does not reach (an offense) based on what is heard; it is suspected with an unpurified suspicion.
Based on that person's acknowledgement, the Uposatha should be performed with him.
329:
What is sensed (such as being alone with a woman, etc.) matches the accuser's word 'sensed'; what is sensed should be compared with what is sensed. Based on what is sensed, one does not reach [guilt]; that person who is not trusted to be pure should be allowed to perform the Uposatha with [the group] based on their confession. Among shameful (lajjī) persons, a decision is made by confession (promise); among shameless (alajjī) persons, it is not so. A shameless person might speak much; therefore, one should make them act according to a confession consistent with proper conduct.

Furthermore, in this matter, a monk who is to decide a legal issue (adhikaraṇa)—like a warrior entering a battlefield—when approaching the Saṅgha, should approach with a humble mind, like a foot-wiping cloth. He should be skilled in seating and sitting. Without pushing against senior elders and without blocking new monks from their seats, he should sit in a suitable seat. He should not speak various kinds of useless talk; he should not speak 'animal talk' (tiracchānakathā). He himself should either speak Dhamma or invite another to speak Dhamma; noble silence (ariya-tuṇhībhāva) should not be looked down upon.

An interrogator (anuvijjaka) authorized by the Saṅgha who wishes to investigate should not ask about the [accuser's or accused's] preceptor (upajjhāya), teacher (ācariya), co-resident (saddhivihārika), pupil (antevāsika), fellow preceptor-student, or fellow teacher-student. He should not ask about their caste, name, clan, the scriptures they have learned, specific lineage, or birthplace. Why is that? Because love or hatred might arise toward that person. If there is love or hatred, one might follow the path of favoritism (chandāgati), malice (dosāgati), delusion (mohāgati), or fear (bayāgati).

The person authorized by the Saṅgha who wishes to investigate should respect the Saṅgha, not the individual. He should respect the True Dhamma (Saddhamma), not material gains (āmisa). He should focus on the meaning, not on following the wishes of the assembly. He should investigate at the right time, not at the wrong time. He should investigate with facts, not with falsehoods. He should investigate with gentle words, not with harsh words. He should investigate with beneficial words, not with useless words. He should investigate with a mind of loving-kindness, not with an inner state of anger. He should not whisper in someone's ear, should not look askance, should not wink, should not frown, should not lift his head [haughtily], should not make hand gestures, and should not show his fists or arms.
330:
He should be skilled in seating and sitting. Looking only a yoke's length ahead, weighing the meaning, he should sit in his own seat. He should not rise from his seat, should not diminish the decision, should not follow a wrong path, and should not speak while waving his arms. He should be one who does not decide hastily, who does not act impulsively. He should be one who is not harsh and whose speech is patient. He should have a mind of loving-kindness, looking after the welfare [of others]. He should be compassionate, seeking the benefit [of others]. He should not speak frivolous talk but should speak measured words. He should not follow the wishes of those who hold grudges and should be without argumentative speech.

He should investigate and reflect upon himself, others, the accuser (codaka), the accused (cuditaka), the unrighteous accuser, the unrighteous accused, the righteous accuser, and the righteous accused. Without omitting what has been said and without revealing what has not been said, he should learn well the words and phrases that have been presented before him, question the other person, and make them act according to their confession. He should gladden the dull, comfort the fearful, restrain the fierce, and make clear the intent of the impure. With uprightness and gentleness, he should not follow the path of favoritism, malice, delusion, or fear. He should have an impartial mind (majjhatta) toward both the Dhamma and the individuals. An interrogator (anuvijjaka) who investigates in this way is one who carries out the Teacher's instruction and is dear, pleasing, respected, and esteemed by his wise fellow practitioners.

## Thus ends the Discussion on the Decision regarding Accusations and so forth in the Pālimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha.

## 32. Garukāpatti-vuṭṭhāna-vinicchaya-kathā

Rehabilitation from grave offenses (garukāpatti-vuṭṭhāna) means rising from (purifying) a grave offense through Vinaya procedures such as probation (parivāsa) and mānatta. In that context, there are three types of probation: paṭicchanna-parivāsa (probation for concealed offenses), suddhanta-parivāsa (complete-cleansing probation), and samodhāna-parivāsa (combined probation). Among these three, paṭicchanna-parivāsa is first given in accordance with the offense that was concealed. For some monks, there is an offense concealed for one day; for some, an offense concealed for two days; for some, there is one offense; for some, there are two, three, or more offenses. Therefore, regarding paṭicchanna-parivāsa...
331:
The one giving (Parivāsa) must first know the state of concealment. This so-called offense (āpatti) is concealed by ten factors.
