In this regard, this is the Mātikā (Matrix): There is an offense and there is the perception of an offense; one is in good standing (pakatatta) and there is the perception of being in good standing; one is without obstacles (anantarāyika) and there is the perception of being without obstacles; one is capable (pahu) and there is the perception of being capable; there is the desire to conceal and there is concealment.

In that Mātikā, 'there is an offense and there is the perception of an offense' means: whatever offense he has committed, that offense must be a real offense, and that monk must also have the perception that he has committed an offense. If he conceals it knowing this, it is called concealed. If he has the perception that it is not an offense, it is called not concealed. However, if he conceals what is not an offense, whether with the perception of it being an offense or not, it remains not concealed. If he conceals a light (lahuka) offense as heavy (garuka), or a heavy offense as light, he stands on the side of the shameless (alajjī), yet the offense is called not concealed. If he confesses a heavy offense thinking it is light, it is neither called confessed nor concealed. If he conceals a heavy offense knowing it is heavy, it is called concealed. Even if he does not know whether it is heavy or light, if he conceals it with the thought 'I will conceal the offense,' it is indeed concealed.

'Pakatatta' refers to one who has not been subjected to the three types of Ukkhepaniya-kamma (act of suspension). If such a person conceals with the perception of being in good standing, it is called concealed. If he conceals with the perception of not being in good standing, thinking 'A legal act has been performed against me by the Saṅgha,' it is called not concealed. For one who is not in good standing (one under a legal act), whether he conceals with the perception of being in good standing or not, it remains not concealed. It is also said:

'He falls into a heavy offense with a remainder,
He conceals it due to lack of respect;
He is not a bhikkhunī, nor would he touch the fault (of concealment),
This question is considered by the wise.'

This question is spoken in reference to a suspended monk (ukkhittaka).

'Anantarāyika' refers to one who has not even one of the ten obstacles. If such a person conceals with the perception of being without obstacles, it is called concealed. If that person, being of a fearful nature, conceals in the dark with the perception of having obstacles due to fear of non-humans or wild beasts, it remains not concealed. For a monk living in a mountain monastery...
332:
...who must cross a canyon or a river to inform [another], and while there are dangers such as fierce wild animals or non-humans on the way, or pythons lying on the path, or the river is full—if he conceals with the perception of having obstacles while such obstacles exist, it is called not concealed. As long as a monk with obstacles conceals with the perception of having obstacles, it remains not concealed.

'Pahu' (Capable) means he is able to go to a monk and inform him. If such a person conceals with the perception of being capable, it is called concealed. If he has a small boil in his mouth, or suffers from jaw-ache, or a toothache, or has received very little food, and because of such reasons he is truly unable to speak or go, yet he has the perception 'I am not capable'—this is called one who is capable but perceives himself as incapable. Even if he conceals, it is called not concealed. For a monk who is incapable of speaking or going, whether he conceals with the perception of being capable or incapable, it remains not concealed.

'Desiring to conceal and concealing'—this phrase has a clear meaning. However, if after deciding 'I will conceal,' whether before or after the meal, or in the first watch of the night, etc., he overcomes the state of shame and informs [another] before dawn, he is called one who desires to conceal but does not conceal. For a monk living in a place where there are no other monks, who, after committing an offense, waits for the arrival of a compatible (sabhāga) monk or is traveling to a compatible monk, even if half a month or a month passes, he is called one who does not desire to conceal but conceals. This monk is also [considered] not concealed. A monk who, as soon as he commits an offense, goes quickly like a man who has stepped on fire to a place where there is a compatible monk and reveals it, is called one who does not desire to conceal and does not conceal. However, if he sees a compatible monk but does not inform him out of shame, thinking 'This is my preceptor (upajjhāya) or teacher (ācariya),' the offense is indeed concealed. For in this case, being a preceptor or such is not the criterion; only being a non-hostile compatible monk is the criterion. Therefore, one should inform a non-hostile compatible monk. If a monk is incompatible (visabhāga) and has the desire to broadcast [the offense] upon hearing it, one should not inform even a preceptor of such a nature.

In informing thus, whether the offense was committed before or after the meal, by day or by night, it should be informed as long as dawn has not yet risen.
333:
At dawn, the offense becomes concealed, and because of that concealment, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It is not proper to reveal one's offense in the presence of a monk who has committed a similar (sabhāga) Saṅghādisesa offense. If one does reveal it, the offense is indeed revealed, but one is not released from the dukkaṭa offense. Therefore, it should be revealed in the presence of a pure monk. The monk who reveals it should say, "I reveal an offense in your presence," or "I inform you," or "I make it known," or "Know that I have fallen into an offense." Or he may say, "I reveal a heavy offense (garuka-āpatti)," and so on. In all these ways, the offense is considered unconcealed; thus it is stated in the Kurundī. However, if he says, "I reveal a light offense (lahuka-āpatti)," and so on, it remains concealed. Whether he informs about the basis (vatthu), the offense (āpatti), or both, it is considered informed in all three ways.

Thus, having examined these ten reasons, one who grants the probation for concealment (paṭicchanna-parivāsa) must first know the fact of concealment. Then, having noted the days of concealment and the offenses, if it has been concealed for one day, he should have the monk request it as follows: "Venerable Sir, I have intentionally committed an offense of emission of semen and concealed it for one day." Then, having recited the kammavācā according to the method found in the Khandhaka, the parivāsa should be granted. If it has been concealed for two or three days, etc., it should be formulated according to the number of days up to fourteen days: "concealed for two days, concealed for three days, concealed for four days, concealed for five days... [pe]... concealed for fourteen days." If concealed for fifteen days, it should be formulated as "concealed for a fortnight (pakkha)." Beyond that, up to the twenty-ninth day, it should be stated as "concealed for more than a fortnight." Beyond that, it should be formulated as "concealed for one month, concealed for more than one month, concealed for two months, concealed for more than two months, three months... [pe]... concealed for more than eleven months." When a year is complete, "concealed for one year," and beyond that, "more than one year, two years," up to "sixty years, concealed for more than sixty years," or even longer periods should be formulated.

If there are two, three, or more offenses, just as it was said "one offense," one should say "two offenses, three offenses." Beyond that, whether it be a hundred or a thousand, it is proper to say "many (sambahulā)." Even for offenses with various bases: "Venerable Sir, I [have committed] many..."
334:
"Venerable Sir, I have committed Saṅghādisesa offenses: one emission of semen, one bodily contact, one lewd words, one serving one's own lust, one matchmaking, concealed for one day." Thus, it should be formulated by way of counting the number. Or, "Venerable Sir, I have committed many Saṅghādisesa offenses of various bases, concealed for one day." Thus, it should be formulated by way of mentioning the bases. Or, "Venerable Sir, I have committed many Saṅghādisesa offenses, concealed for one day." Thus, it should be formulated by way of the name alone. In that regard, the name is of two kinds: common to its own class (sajāti-sādhāraṇa) and common to all (sabba-sādhāraṇa). Here, "Saṅghādisesa" is common to its own class. "Offense" (āpatti) is common to all. Therefore, it is also proper to perform it by way of the name common to all, such as: "I have committed many offenses, concealed for one day." Indeed, this disciplinary act (vinaya-kamma) of parivāsa and so on may be performed by way of the basis (vatthu), the class (gotta), the name (nāma), or the offense (āpatti).

In this context, "emission of semen" (sukka-vissaṭṭhi) is both the basis and the class. "Saṅghādisesa" is both the name and the offense. Here, by the words "emission of semen, bodily contact," etc., and by the words "offenses of various bases," both the basis and the class are included. By the word "Saṅghādisesa" and by the word "offenses," both the name and the offense are included. Therefore, the kammavācā should be performed by way of any of these. However, in this work, we will demonstrate the formulation of the kammavācā in all instances by way of the commonality of all offenses and by the method of "many" (sambahula). For even if one who has committed a single offense performs the disciplinary act saying "many," he emerges [from the offense], because there is no "many" without the "one." But if one who has committed many offenses performs it saying "I have committed one," he does not emerge. Therefore, we will formulate it only by the method of "many." For example, if it is an offense concealed for one day, the one granting the parivāsa [should have the monk say]: "Venerable Sir, I have committed many offenses, concealed for one day. Venerable Sir, I request the Saṅgha for a one-day parivāsa for those many offenses concealed for one day. Venerable Sir, I have committed many offenses, concealed for one day. For the second time, Venerable Sir, I request the Saṅgha for a one-day parivāsa for those many offenses concealed for one day. Venerable Sir, I have committed many offenses..."
335:
"...for (offenses) concealed for one day, Venerable Sir, for the third time, I request from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for many offenses concealed for one day." Having had him request thus three times:

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This monk named [so-and-so] has committed many offenses concealed for one day. He requests from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give a one-day probation to the monk named [so-and-so] for the many offenses concealed for one day. This is the motion.

Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This monk named [so-and-so] has committed many offenses concealed for one day. He requests from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha is giving a one-day probation to the monk named [so-and-so] for the many offenses concealed for one day. Whichever venerable one approves of giving a one-day probation to the monk named [so-and-so] for the many offenses concealed for one day, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

A second time I speak this matter... [pe]... A third time I speak this matter... [pe]...

The Saṅgha has given a one-day probation to the monk named [so-and-so] for the many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this matter."

Thus, taking the name of each monk who has committed an offense, the kammavācā should be performed.

At the end of the kammavācā, that monk, while still within the māḷaka boundary, should undertake the duty, saying, "I undertake the probation, I undertake the duty." Having undertaken it, he should inform the Saṅgha right there. When informing:

"Venerable Sirs, I have committed many offenses concealed for one day. I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. To me, the Saṅgha [gave] for many offenses..."
336:
"...gave a one-day probation for offenses concealed for one day. I am undergoing that probation. Venerable Sirs, I inform you. Let the Saṅgha recognize me as one who informs." Thus it should be announced. Taking this meaning, it is permissible to announce it in any language.

After announcing (Cullavagga Commentary 102), if he wishes to lay it down, he should lay it down saying, "I lay down the probation, I lay down the duty." Here, the probation is considered laid down even with one phrase. However, with two phrases, it is well laid down. The same method applies to undertaking. From the time it is laid down, he remains in the status of a monk of regular standing (pakatatta). When monks come out from the māḷaka, it is permissible to lay it down in the presence of even a single monk. A monk who remembers after leaving the māḷaka should lay it down in the presence of a monk traveling with him. If that traveling monk has also departed, he should inform and lay it down before another monk who was not yet informed at the māḷaka. The monk informing should say at the end, "Let the venerable one recognize me as one who informs." If informing two monks, "Let the venerable ones recognize..."; if informing three, "Let the venerable ones recognize..."

If it is a monastery with few monks where compatible (sabhāga) monks reside, he should determine the night within the monastery itself without laying down the duty. If it is not possible to keep it pure (due to many monks), he should lay down the duty by the aforementioned method. At dawn, together with one monk, he should go beyond two stone-throws from the enclosure of a monastery with an enclosure, or from the area corresponding to an enclosure for a monastery without one. Leaving the main road, he should sit in a place concealed by a thicket or a fence. Before dawn rises, he should undertake the duty and inform by the aforementioned method. When informing, if the other monk is junior, he should say "Friend" (Āvuso). If senior, he should say "Venerable Sir" (Bhante). If any other monk comes to that place for some business, if the monk undergoing the duty sees him or hears his voice, he must inform him. For one who does not inform, there is both a break in the nights and a breach of duty. However, if he descends into the precinct (upacāra) of twelve cubits and passes by without knowing, there is a break in the nights, but no breach of duty. When the dawn has risen, the duty should be laid down. If that monk has departed for some business, he should inform and lay it down before whichever other monk he sees first. Even upon returning to the monastery, he should inform and lay it down before the monk he sees first. This is the procedure (parihāra) for a monk who has laid down the duty.
337:
If an offense has been concealed for a certain number of days, one should undergo probation (parivāsa) for that many days, or even more than that for the purpose of dispelling remorse (kukkucca). Then, approaching the Saṅgha and undertaking the duties (vatta), one should request the penance (mānatta). For when the duties are undertaken, having laid down the duties and completed the probation, he is one worthy of the penance. However, for a monk who has not laid down the duties, there is no need for a second undertaking. He becomes worthy of the penance simply by the passing of the days of concealment; therefore, the penance should indeed be given to him.

The Saṅgha giving that penance [should have him request it thus]: "Venerable sirs, I have fallen into many offenses concealed for one day. I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gave me a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. Venerable sirs, having completed the probation, I request from the Saṅgha a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day. Venerable sirs... [as before]... having completed the probation, for the second time, venerable sirs, I request from the Saṅgha a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day. Venerable sirs... [as before]... having completed the probation, for the third time, venerable sirs, I request from the Saṅgha a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day."

Having had him request thus three times [the motion should be made]: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so has fallen into many offenses concealed for one day. He requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gave to the monk named so-and-so a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. Having completed the probation, he requests from the Saṅgha a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day. If it seems proper to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give a six-night penance to the monk named so-and-so for those many offenses concealed for one day. This is the motion. Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so has fallen into many offenses concealed for one day. He..."
338:
"...requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gave to the monk named so-and-so a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. Having completed the probation, he requests from the Saṅgha a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gives a six-night penance to the monk named so-and-so for those many offenses concealed for one day. Whichever venerable one approves of giving the six-night penance to the monk named so-and-so for those many offenses concealed for one day, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak. For the second time I speak this matter... [as before]... For the third time I speak this matter... [as before]... The Saṅgha has given a six-night penance to the monk named so-and-so for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I bear this in mind."

In this way, the formal act (kammavācā) should be performed. At the conclusion of the formal act, that monk, within that very same precinct (māḷaka-sīmā), should undertake the duties, saying: "I undertake the penance; I undertake the duties." Having undertaken them, he should inform the Saṅgha in that very same place. The one informing should say: "Venerable sirs, I have fallen into many offenses concealed for one day. I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gave me a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. Having completed the probation, I requested from the Saṅgha a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gave me a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day. I am now undergoing the penance. Venerable sirs, I make it known; let the Saṅgha bear in mind that I am making it known."

Having taken this meaning, it is indeed proper to inform the Saṅgha with whatever words [are appropriate].
339:
After informing, if he wishes to lay down the duty, he should do so in the midst of the Saṅgha, saying, "I lay down the penance, I lay down the duty." When the monks have left the māḷaka, it is permissible to lay it down in the presence of even a single monk. A monk who remembers after leaving the māḷaka should lay it down in the presence of a monk traveling with him. If that companion has also departed, he should inform and lay it down before another monk who was not informed at the māḷaka. The one informing should say at the end, "May the venerable one recognize me [as having laid down the duty]." If informing two monks, he should say, "May the venerable ones recognize me," and if informing three, "May the venerable ones recognize me."

From the time of laying down the duty, he remains in the status of a pakatatta (a monk in good standing). If it is a monastery with few monks where sabhāga monks (monks of the same status) reside, the nights should be counted within the monastery itself without laying down the duty. If he cannot purify the offenses there, he should lay down the duty as described, and at dawn, go with four or five monks beyond the fence of a fenced monastery, or—if the monastery is unfenced—beyond a distance of two stone-throws from the monastery's proper area. He should move away from the main road and sit in a place concealed by bushes or a fence. Before dawn, he should undertake the duty and inform as described. If any other monk comes to that place for some business, if this monk sees him or hears his voice, he must inform him. Failure to inform results in both the loss of the night (ratticcheda) and a breach of duty (vattabheda). If he goes beyond the twelve-cubit precinct without knowing, there is only a loss of the night, not a breach of duty.

From the time of informing, he may leave one monk and the rest may go if they have business. At dawn, he should lay down the duty in the presence of that monk. If that monk also leaves before dawn for some business, he should inform and lay down the duty before the first monk he sees, whether leaving the monastery or arriving as a guest. Because this monk stayed after informing the group and noting the presence of monks, he does not incur the fault of practicing in a deficient group (ūne gaṇe carana) or being in diaspora (vippavāsa). If he sees no one, he should go to the monastery and lay it down before the first monk he sees. This is the procedure for a monk who has laid down the duty.

Having practiced the six-night penance without interruption in this manner, where there is a Saṅgha of twenty monks, that monk should be rehabilitated (abbhāna). Those rehabilitating him...
340:
First, he should be made fit for rehabilitation (abbhāna). The reason is that this monk who wishes for rehabilitation has laid down his duties (vatta) and stands in the status of a regular monk (pakatatta). It is not proper to perform rehabilitation for a regular monk. Therefore, he should be made to undertake the duties. Only after undertaking the duties does he become fit for rehabilitation. That monk, having undertaken the duties and having informed [the Saṅgha], should request rehabilitation. For a monk who has not laid down his duties, there is no need to undertake the duties again. He becomes fit for rehabilitation simply by the passing of the six nights. Therefore, that monk should be rehabilitated. And when rehabilitating—

“Venerable sirs, I have fallen into many offenses concealed for one day. I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation (parivāsa) for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gave me a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. Having completed the probation, I requested from the Saṅgha a six-night penance (mānatta) for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gave me a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day. Venerable sirs, having practiced the penance, I request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha. Venerable sirs ...pe... having practiced the penance, for the second time, venerable sirs, I request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha. Venerable sirs ...pe... having practiced the penance, for the third time, venerable sirs, I request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha.”

Having made him request thus three times—

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. This monk named [so-and-so] fell into many offenses concealed for one day. He requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gave the monk named [so-and-so] a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. Having completed the probation, he requested from the Saṅgha a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day. The Saṅgha gave the monk named [so-and-so] a six-night penance for those many offenses concealed for one day. Having practiced the penance, he is requesting rehabilitation from the Saṅgha. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha rehabilitate the monk named [so-and-so]. This is the motion (ñatti).

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. This monk named [so-and-so] fell into many offenses concealed for one day. That monk...”
341:
...requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation for those many offenses concealed for one day. Thus, first, the concealed probation (paṭicchanna-parivāsa), the giving of penance (mānatta), and the rehabilitation (abbhāna) for an offense concealed for one day should be understood. In this same way, for offenses concealed for two days and so forth, the appropriate formal act should be performed.

If it is an unconcealed offense (appaṭicchanna āpatti), without giving probation, only penance is given, and after practicing the penance, he should be rehabilitated. How? When giving penance, first—

He requests a six-day mānatta for many unconcealed offenses. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should grant a six-day mānatta for many unconcealed offenses to the monk named so-and-so. This is the motion.

## The Discussion on Paṭicchanna-parivāsa is Finished.

There remain two other types of probation: Suddhanta-parivāsa and Samodhāna-parivāsa. Among these, Suddhanta-parivāsa is of two kinds: Cūḷasuddhanta and Mahāsuddhanta. Both kinds of Suddhanta-parivāsa are granted to one who does not know, cannot remember, or is doubtful about the exact limit of the nights, whether in their entirety or in part. As for the limit of the offenses, whether he knows “I have committed this many offenses” or not, that knowledge or lack thereof is not the deciding factor. Between these two, when a monk is asked—either in forward order (anuloma) starting from his ordination, or in reverse order (paṭiloma) starting from the day he reported the offenses—“Do you know your state of purity on such and such a day, fortnight, month, or year?” if he says, “Yes, Venerable Sir, I know; I have been pure for this much time,” the Suddhanta-parivāsa granted to that monk is called Cūḷasuddhanta.

A person undergoing probation after taking that Cūḷasuddhanta should exclude the period for which he knows his purity and undergo probation for the remaining one month or two months. If, after reflecting “I was impure for about a month” and taking it, he remembers another month while undergoing probation, he must undergo probation for that remembered month as well; there is no need for a further formal granting of probation. If, after reflecting “I was impure for about two months” and taking it, he decides while undergoing probation “I was impure for only about one month,” he need only undergo probation for one month; there is no need for a further formal granting of probation. This Suddhanta-parivāsa...
348:
This Suddhantaparivāsa (cleansing probation) goes up and also goes down. This is the characteristic of that Suddhantaparivāsa. However, in the case of rising (vuṭṭhāna) from other offenses besides Suddhantaparivāsa, this is the characteristic: If a monk performs the disciplinary act for an unconcealed offense thinking it is 'concealed', he rises from that offense. If a monk performs the disciplinary act for a concealed offense thinking it is 'unconcealed', he does not rise from it. For a monk who performs it for a recently concealed offense thinking it is 'long-concealed', he also rises from the offense. For a monk who performs it for a long-concealed offense thinking it is 'recently concealed', he does not rise from the offense. For a monk who, having committed a single offense, performs it thinking 'many offenses', he rises from the offense, because there are no 'many offenses' excluding the one. For a monk who, having committed many offenses, performs it thinking 'I committed one', he does not rise from the offenses.

When a monk, even after being questioned in the forward and backward order as mentioned, does not know the limit of nights, cannot remember, or is in doubt, the Suddhantaparivāsa given to him is called Mahāsuddhanta (Great Cleansing Probation). Having taken that Mahāsuddhanta, he must undergo the probation by counting the nights from the day he took it back to the day of his higher ordination (upasampadā). This Mahāsuddhanta does not go up, but it does go down. Therefore, if the monk undergoing probation makes a determination regarding the limit of nights, thinking 'It has been a month or a year since I committed the offense', he must undergo probation for a month or a year.

The characteristic of requesting and granting probation in this Suddhantaparivāsa should be understood thus: That bhikkhu should approach the Saṅgha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage to the feet of the senior bhikkhus, sit on his heels, and with palms joined, he should say this:

'Venerable sirs, I have committed many saṅghādisesa offenses. I do not know the limit of the offenses, I do not know the limit of the nights. I do not remember the limit of the offenses, I do not remember the limit of the nights. I am in doubt about the limit of the offenses, I am in doubt about the limit of the nights. Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha for Suddhantaparivāsa for those offenses.'

He should request a second time. He should request a third time.

A competent and capable bhikkhu should inform the Saṅgha (with a motion):

## The Discussion on Suddhantaparivāsa is Finished.
353: Samodhānaparivāsa (combined probation) is of three kinds: Odhānasamodhāna, Agghasamodhāna, and Missakasamodhāna. Among these three (according to Cūḷavagga Commentary 102), Odhānasamodhāna refers to the probation granted to a monk who, while undergoing penance, commits an intervening offense (antarāpatti) and conceals it; it involves discarding the days already spent and combining the later offense with the original offense's starting period. The decision in this matter is as follows: If a monk, while undergoing probation for a concealed offense, or while being liable to Mānatta, or while practicing Mānatta, or while being liable to Abbhāna, without having laid down the duties (anikkhittavatta), commits another offense and conceals it for a number of nights equal to or less than the original offense, then by means of Mūlāyapaṭikassana (throwing back to the beginning), all the days spent in probation and the days spent in Mānatta are discarded and made as if they were not days; then the later offense is combined with the original offense and probation must be granted. In granting it, if the original offense was concealed for a fortnight (15 days) and the intervening offense was concealed for less than a fortnight, he must undergo probation for a fortnight again. Or if the intervening offense was also concealed for a fortnight, he must undergo probation for a fortnight. In this manner, even if the original offense was concealed for sixty years, the decision should be understood. Even if he has lived through sixty years of probation and is liable to Mānatta, if he conceals an intervening offense for even a single day, he becomes liable to undergo sixty years of probation again. Thus, when Mūlāyapaṭikassana is performed for an offense committed while practicing Mānatta or while liable to Mānatta, all the days of practicing Mānatta and the days of living through probation are considered discarded. However, if a monk who has laid down the duties (nikkhittavatta) commits an offense, he is not liable to Mūlāyapaṭikassana. Why? Because he did not commit it while undergoing probation, but committed it while in the status of a Pakatatta (normal monk). Therefore, he must practice Mānatta separately for that offense. If it was concealed, he must also undergo probation. "If the intervening offense was concealed for a longer period than the original offense, what should be done there?" When asked, the Elder Mahāsumma said, "This person is incurable (atekiccha); 'incurable' means he should be made to reveal the offense and be dismissed." But the Elder Mahāpaduma said, "Why is he called incurable? Is this Samuccayakkhandhaka not like the time when the Buddhas were present? Whether an offense is concealed or not, or concealed for an equal, lesser, or greater period, the only standard here is the ability of the Vinayadhara (expert in discipline) to formulate the Kammavācā. Therefore, whichever..."
354:
If an offense is concealed for a longer period (than the original offense), that offense is made the basis, and other offenses belonging to the same category as that original offense are combined, and probation is given. This is called Odhānasamodhāna (Added Combination).

When giving that probation, the monk is first thrown back to the beginning, and then probation is given. If a certain monk, while undergoing probation for offenses concealed for a fortnight, commits further offenses concealed for five days without having given up his duties in the meantime, that monk should approach the Saṅgha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the senior monks, sit on his haunches, and with joined palms, speak thus:

'Venerable sirs, I have committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. I requested the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave me a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While I was undergoing probation, I committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha to throw me back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days.'

He should request a second time. He should request a third time.

A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha with a motion:

'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He requested the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While he was undergoing probation, he committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He requests the Saṅgha to throw him back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should throw the monk named so-and-so back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. This is the motion.

Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He requested the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for those many offenses...'
355:
...for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave him a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While he was undergoing probation, he committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He requests the Saṅgha to throw him back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha throws the monk named so-and-so back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. Whichever venerable one approves of throwing the monk named so-and-so back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

A second time I speak this matter... [etc.] ... A third time I speak this matter... [etc.] ...

The monk named so-and-so has been thrown back to the beginning by the Saṅgha for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I understand this.

In this way, throwing back to the beginning should be done.

In this way also, Samodhānaparivāsa (combined probation) should be given. That monk, having approached the Saṅgha... [etc.] ... should speak thus:

'Venerable sirs, I have committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. I requested the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave me a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While I was undergoing probation, I committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. I requested the Saṅgha to throw me back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha has thrown me back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha for combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days together with the previous offenses.'

He should request a second time. He should request a third time.

A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha with a motion:

'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He [requested] the Saṅgha...'
356:
That monk requests a fortnight's probation for many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gives that monk of such-and-such a name a fortnight's probation for many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While undergoing that probation, he commits many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He requests the Saṅgha for a pulling back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassana) for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha pulls that monk of such-and-such a name back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He then requests the Saṅgha for a combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa) for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should give that monk of such-and-such a name a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. This is the motion (ñatti).

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This monk of such-and-such a name committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He requested the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave that monk of such-and-such a name a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While undergoing that probation, he committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He requested the Saṅgha for a pulling back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha pulled that monk of such-and-such a name back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He is now requesting the Saṅgha for a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. The Saṅgha gives that monk of such-and-such a name a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. Whichever venerable one approves of giving a combined probation to this monk of such-and-such a name for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

“For the second time, I speak this matter... For the third time, I speak this matter...

“The Saṅgha has given a combined probation to that monk of such-and-such a name for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses.
357:
The Saṅgha approves of giving the combined probation; therefore, it is silent. Thus I record this.

In this way, the combined probation is given.

At the end of the formal act (kammavācā), all matters such as undertaking the duties (vatta-samādāna) are exactly as previously stated. However, the monk who is informing (ārocanā) should say:

“Venerable sir, I committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. I requested the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave me a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While undergoing that probation, I committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. I requested the Saṅgha for a pulling back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha pulled me back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. I requested the Saṅgha for a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. The Saṅgha gave me a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. I am undergoing that probation. Venerable sir, I inform [the Saṅgha of this]. Let the Saṅgha record me as one who informs.”

In this way, it should be informed.

When one wishes to give penance (mānatta) to a monk who has completed the probation:

“Venerable sir, I committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. I requested the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave me a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While undergoing that probation, I committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. I requested the Saṅgha for a pulling back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha pulled me back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. I requested the Saṅgha for a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. The Saṅgha [gave] me...
358:
"...gave me a combined probation for the many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. Venerable sirs, I, having completed that probation, request from the Saṅgha a six-night penance for the many offenses."

Having had him request thus three times—

"Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. This monk named [so-and-so] committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He requested from the Saṅgha a fortnightly probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave him a fortnightly probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While he was undergoing that probation, he committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He requested from the Saṅgha to be sent back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha sent that monk named [so-and-so] back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He then requested from the Saṅgha a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. The Saṅgha gave that monk named [so-and-so] a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combining them with the previous offenses. That monk, having completed the probation, is now requesting from the Saṅgha a six-night penance for the many offenses. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant a six-night penance to the monk named [so-and-so] for the many offenses. This is the motion.

"Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. This monk named [so-and-so] committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He requested from the Saṅgha a fortnightly probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave him a fortnightly probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While he was undergoing that probation, he committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He requested from the Saṅgha to be sent back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha sent that monk named [so-and-so] back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He then requested from the Saṅgha..."
359:
(The monk) requests a combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa) for many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses. The Saṅgha grants the combined probation for many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses, to the monk named so-and-so. That monk, having completed the probation, requests from the Saṅgha a six-day penance (mānatta) for many offenses. The Saṅgha grants the six-day penance for many offenses to the monk named so-and-so. If the granting of the six-day penance for many offenses to the monk named so-and-so is pleasing to the venerable ones, let them be silent. If it is not pleasing, let them speak.

"For the second time I speak this matter... For the third time I speak this matter."

"The Saṅgha has granted the six-day penance for many intervening offenses to the monk named so-and-so. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this." This is how the kammavācā should be performed.

At the end of the kammavācā, everything such as the undertaking of mānatta is exactly as previously described. However, the monk who is announcing (that he is undergoing mānatta) should say:

"Venerable sirs, I committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight (pakkha). I requested from the Saṅgha a fortnight's probation (pakkha-parivāsa) for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha granted me a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While I was undergoing that probation, I committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. I requested from the Saṅgha a throwing back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassana) for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha threw me back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. I requested from the Saṅgha a combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa) for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses. The Saṅgha granted me a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses. Having completed that probation, I requested from the Saṅgha a six-day penance (mānatta) for many offenses. The Saṅgha granted me a six-day penance for many offenses."
360:
"(The Saṅgha) has granted (the penance). I, venerable sirs, am practicing the penance. I inform (the Saṅgha of this). May the Saṅgha recognize me as one who is informing." This is how it should be announced.

When rehabilitating (abbhāna) a monk who has completed the penance:

"Venerable sirs, I committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. I requested from the Saṅgha a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha granted me a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While I was undergoing that probation, I committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. I requested from the Saṅgha a throwing back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha threw me back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. I requested from the Saṅgha a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses. The Saṅgha granted me a combined probation for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses. Having completed that probation, I requested from the Saṅgha a six-day penance for many offenses. The Saṅgha granted me a six-day penance for many offenses. Venerable sirs, having completed the penance, I request rehabilitation from the Saṅgha." Thus, he should be made to request three times.

"Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He requested from the Saṅgha a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha granted a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight to the monk named so-and-so. While he was undergoing that probation, he committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He requested from the Saṅgha a throwing back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. The Saṅgha threw the monk named so-and-so back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses concealed for five days. He..."
361:
"(He) asked the Saṅgha for a combined probation (samodhānaparivāsa) for many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses; the Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a combined probation for many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses; that monk, having lived through the probation, asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for many offenses; the Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a six-day mānatta for many offenses; that monk, having practiced the mānatta, asks the Saṅgha for rehabilitation (abbhāna); if it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha rehabilitate the monk named so-and-so. This is the motion (ñatti).

"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight; he asked the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for many offenses concealed for a fortnight; the Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a fortnight's probation for many offenses concealed for a fortnight; while he was living through the probation, he committed many intervening offenses concealed for five days; he asked the Saṅgha to be pulled back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassana) for many intervening offenses concealed for five days; the Saṅgha pulled back the monk named so-and-so to the beginning for many intervening offenses concealed for five days; he asked the Saṅgha for a combined probation for many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses; the Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a combined probation for many intervening offenses concealed for five days, combined with the former offenses; he, having lived through the probation, asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for many offenses; the Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a six-day mānatta for many offenses; that monk, having practiced the mānatta, asks the Saṅgha for rehabilitation; the Saṅgha rehabilitates the monk named so-and-so. Whichever venerable one approves of the rehabilitation of the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

"A second time I speak this matter ... A third time I speak this matter."

"The monk named so-and-so has been rehabilitated by the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent; thus I record this act." Thus should the formal act (kammavācā) be performed.
362:
If a monk worthy of mānatta, or one undergoing mānatta, or one worthy of rehabilitation, while not having laid down his duties, commits an intervening offense and conceals it, then, in the manner already stated, having noted the number of days of the former offenses and the intervening offenses, he should be pulled back to the beginning by a formal act (kammavācā) appropriate for those offenses, given probation, and after he has lived through the probation, he should be given mānatta, and after practicing mānatta, he should be rehabilitated.

If, however, a monk living through probation for a concealed offense commits an intervening offense and does not conceal it, he should only be pulled back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassana); there is no further need to give probation again. However, because the days already lived through in probation are nullified by being pulled back to the beginning, he must live through the probation again starting from the very beginning. After he has lived through the probation, he should be given mānatta by combining the original offenses and the intervening offenses, and after practicing mānatta, he should be rehabilitated.

How so? One who performs the pulling back to the beginning, if the original offense was one concealed for a fortnight, should first be made to request three times:

"Venerable sirs, I committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. I asked the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha gave me a fortnight's probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While I was living through that probation, I committed many intervening offenses which were not concealed. Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha to be pulled back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses which were not concealed."

## "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. "Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named [so-and-so] committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha agrees to the sending back to the beginning of the monk named [so-and-so] for those many intervening offenses that were not concealed; therefore, it is silent. Thus I record this." — This is how the formal act (kammavācā) should be performed.

The monk who has been sent back to the beginning in this way must undergo probation again from the start. And while undergoing probation:

"Venerable Sirs, I committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. I requested the Saṅgha for a fortnightly probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. The Saṅgha granted me the fortnightly probation for those many offenses concealed for a fortnight. While undergoing probation, I committed many intervening offenses that were not concealed. I requested the Saṅgha for a sending back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses that were not concealed. The Saṅgha sent me back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses that were not concealed. I am undergoing probation; I inform [you], Venerable Sirs. Let the Saṅgha record me as one who is informing." — Thus should the announcement (ārocanā) be made.
364:
## On granting Mānatta to a monk who has completed probation –

"Venerable Sirs, I committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. I requested the Saṅgha for a fortnightly probation (pakkha-parivāsa) for those many offenses. Having had him request three times –

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named [so-and-so] committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He requested the Saṅgha for a pakkha-parivāsa for those offenses. If it seems timely to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant the six-day penance for those concealed offenses and unconcealed offenses to the monk named [so-and-so]. This is the motion (ñatti).

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named [so-and-so] committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He requested the Saṅgha for a pakkha-parivāsa for those offenses. ## In the case of rehabilitation (abbhāna) for a monk who has completed the penance:

"Venerable sirs, I committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. I requested the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation (pakkha-parivāsa) for those offenses. Venerable sirs, having completed the penance, I request the Saṅgha for rehabilitation (abbhāna)."

Having made him request thus three times:

"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named [so-and-so] committed many offenses concealed for a fortnight. He requested the Saṅgha for a fortnight's probation for those offenses. The Saṅgha granted the fortnight's probation to the monk named [so-and-so] for those offenses. While he was undergoing probation, he again committed many intervening offenses that were not concealed. He requested the Saṅgha for a throwing back to the beginning for those intervening offenses. The Saṅgha performed the throwing back to the beginning for that monk for those intervening offenses. Having completed the probation, he requested the Saṅgha for the six-day penance for those concealed and unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha [granted] the six-day penance to the monk named [so-and-so] for those offenses..."
367:
The Saṅgha has given the mānatta; that monk who has finished the mānatta requests the Saṅgha for abbhāna (rehabilitation). If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should rehabilitate the monk named so-and-so. This is the motion (ñatti).

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so committed many offenses concealed for half a month. He requested the Saṅgha for a probation (parivāsa) of half a month for those many offenses concealed for half a month. The Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a probation of half a month for those many offenses concealed for half a month. While undergoing probation, he committed many intervening offenses (antarāpatti) that were not concealed. He requested the Saṅgha to be thrown back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassana) for those many intervening offenses that were not concealed. The Saṅgha threw that monk back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses that were not concealed. That monk, having completed the probation, requested the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed. The Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a six-day mānatta for those many offenses, both concealed and unconcealed. That monk, having finished the mānatta, requests the Saṅgha for abbhāna. The Saṅgha rehabilitates the monk named so-and-so. If the rehabilitation of the monk named so-and-so is pleasing to any venerable one, let him be silent. If it is not pleasing, he should speak.

For the second time I speak this matter... (pe)... For the third time I speak this matter... (pe)...

The monk named so-and-so has been rehabilitated by the Saṅgha. It is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this.” — Thus the kammavācā should be performed.

In this manner, if one commits an intervening offense and does not conceal it during the time when one is fit for mānatta, or while undergoing mānatta, or when one is fit for abbhāna, one should only be thrown back to the beginning, and after combining the original offense and the intervening offense, mānatta should be given, and after the mānatta is finished, abbhāna should be performed. However, in this context, where it says “I, while undergoing probation,” one should say “I, having completed probation and being fit for mānatta,” or “I, while undergoing mānatta,” or “I, having finished mānatta and being fit for abbhāna.”
368:
If, while undergoing mānatta for an unconcealed offense, one commits an intervening offense and does not conceal it, that monk should be thrown back to the beginning, given mānatta again for the intervening offense, and after the mānatta is finished, he should be rehabilitated. How? One who performs the throwing back to the beginning should first [make the monk say]:

“Venerable sir, I have committed many unconcealed offenses. I requested the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave me a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. While undergoing mānatta, I committed many intervening offenses that were not concealed. Venerable sir, I request the Saṅgha to be thrown back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses that were not concealed.” Having made him request thus three times:

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so committed many unconcealed offenses. He requested the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. While undergoing mānatta, he committed many intervening offenses that were not concealed. He requests the Saṅgha to be thrown back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses that were not concealed. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should throw the monk named so-and-so back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses that were not concealed. This is the motion (ñatti).

Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so committed many unconcealed offenses. He requested the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave the monk named so-and-so a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. While undergoing mānatta, he committed many intervening offenses that were not concealed. He requests the Saṅgha to be thrown back to the beginning for those many intervening offenses that were not concealed. The Saṅgha [throws] the monk named so-and-so [back to the beginning] for those many intervening...
369:
... throws back to the beginning for many unconcealed offenses. Whichever venerable one approves of the throwing back to the beginning of monk so-and-so for many unconcealed intervening offenses, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

For the second time I speak this matter ... For the third time I speak this matter ...

The Saṅgha has thrown back monk so-and-so to the beginning for many unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this act. In this way, the kammavācā should be performed.

After being thrown back to the beginning in this way, the one who is to be given mānatta should say:

“Venerable sirs, I committed many unconcealed offenses. I asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave me a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. While I was undergoing that mānatta, I committed many unconcealed intervening offenses. I asked the Saṅgha to be thrown back to the beginning for those many unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha threw me back to the beginning for those many unconcealed intervening offenses. Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed intervening offenses.” Having made him request thus three times—

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk so-and-so committed many unconcealed offenses. He asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave monk so-and-so a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. While he was undergoing that mānatta, he committed many unconcealed intervening offenses. He asked the Saṅgha to be thrown back to the beginning for those many unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha [threw back] that monk for many intervening offenses...”
370:
... throws back to the beginning for unconcealed intervening offenses. He asks the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for many unconcealed intervening offenses. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give a six-day mānatta to monk so-and-so for many unconcealed intervening offenses. This is the motion (ñatti).

“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk so-and-so committed many unconcealed offenses. He asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave monk so-and-so a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. While he was undergoing that mānatta, he committed many unconcealed intervening offenses. He asks the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha gives a six-day mānatta to monk so-and-so for those unconcealed intervening offenses. Whichever venerable one approves of giving a six-day mānatta to monk so-and-so for those unconcealed intervening offenses, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

For the second time I speak this matter. For the third time I speak this matter.

The Saṅgha has given a six-day mānatta to monk so-and-so for those unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this matter.” In this way, the kammavācā should be performed.

At the conclusion of the kammavācā, the undertaking of mānatta and so forth are exactly as previously stated. However, the one making the announcement (ārocanā) should say:

“Venerable sirs, I committed many unconcealed offenses. I asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave me a six-day mānatta for those many unconcealed offenses. I...”
371:
“While I was undergoing mānatta, I committed several intervening offenses which were not concealed. I asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha threw me back to the beginning for those unconcealed intervening offenses. I then asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha gave me a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses. I am now undergoing mānatta. Venerable sirs, I inform you (of my undergoing mānatta). May the Saṅgha recognize me as one who informs.” This is how it should be informed.

And for the one who rehabilitates a monk who has completed mānatta:

“Venerable sirs, I committed several unconcealed offenses. I asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those several unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave me a six-day mānatta for those several unconcealed offenses. While I was undergoing mānatta, I committed several intervening offenses which were not concealed. I asked the Saṅgha to be thrown back to the beginning for those several offenses. The Saṅgha threw me back to the beginning for those unconcealed intervening offenses. I then asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha gave me a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses. Venerable sirs, having completed the mānatta, I ask the Saṅgha for rehabilitation.” After having him ask three times:

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. This monk named so-and-so committed several unconcealed offenses. He asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those several unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave a six-day mānatta for those several unconcealed offenses to the monk named so-and-so. While undergoing mānatta, he committed several intervening offenses which were not concealed.
372:
He asked the Saṅgha to be thrown back to the beginning for those unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha threw him back to the beginning for those unconcealed intervening offenses. He asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha gave a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses to the monk named so-and-so. Having completed the mānatta, he now asks the Saṅgha for rehabilitation. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha rehabilitate the monk named so-and-so. This is the motion.

“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. This monk named so-and-so committed several unconcealed offenses. He asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those several unconcealed offenses. The Saṅgha gave a six-day mānatta for those several unconcealed offenses to the monk named so-and-so. While undergoing mānatta, he committed several intervening offenses which were not concealed. He asked the Saṅgha to be thrown back to the beginning for those unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha threw him back to the beginning for those unconcealed intervening offenses. He asked the Saṅgha for a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses. The Saṅgha gave a six-day mānatta for those unconcealed intervening offenses to the monk named so-and-so. Having completed the mānatta, he now asks the Saṅgha for rehabilitation. The Saṅgha rehabilitates the monk named so-and-so. Whichever venerable one approves of the rehabilitation of the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent. Whichever one does not approve, let him speak.

For the second time, I speak this matter... (etc.)... For the third time, I speak this matter... (etc.)...

The monk named so-and-so has been rehabilitated by the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this.” After performing the formal act (kammavācā) in this way, he should be rehabilitated.

Even at the time when one is worthy of rehabilitation, if one commits an intervening offense and does not conceal it, the throwing back to the beginning, the giving of mānatta, and the rehabilitation should be understood in this same manner.
373:
In this context, however, one should not say "one who is practicing mānatta," but specifically "one who has practiced mānatta and is worthy of abbhāna."

## The Discussion on Odhānasamodhāna-parivāsa is Finished.

What is called Agghasamodhāna is this: among many offenses, when one, two, three, or many offenses have been concealed longer than all others, a probation is given for the remaining offenses that were concealed for a shorter duration, by combining them with the value of those [longer-concealed] offenses. This is called Agghasamodhāna. If for a monk, one hundred offenses are concealed for ten days, and another hundred offenses are also concealed for ten days, and doing so ten times, a thousand offenses are concealed for a hundred days; what should that monk do? He should combine them all and undergo probation for ten days. In this way, by undergoing ten days once, the hundred days are also undergone. This meaning is also stated (in the Parivāra):

"Having concealed a thousand offenses for a hundred nights,
By undergoing ten nights,
The monk undergoing probation shall be released from the offenses."

This is called Agghasamodhāna.

The characteristic of informing and granting that Agghasamodhāna should be understood thus: If for a monk, one offense is concealed for one day, one offense for two days, one offense for three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine days, and one offense is concealed for ten days, that monk should approach the Sangha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder... and should speak thus:

"Venerable sirs, I have committed many saṅghādisesa offenses. Many offenses were concealed for one day, many offenses for two days... many offenses for ten days. Venerable sirs, I request from the Sangha an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days."

He should request a second time. He should request a third time.
374:
A competent and capable monk should inform the Sangha:

"Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so has committed many saṅghādisesa offenses. Many offenses were concealed for one day... many offenses for ten days. He requests from the Sangha an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. If it is suitable for the Sangha, let the Sangha grant to the monk named so-and-so an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. This is the motion.

Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so has committed many saṅghādisesa offenses. Many offenses were concealed for one day... many offenses for ten days. He requests from the Sangha an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. The Sangha grants to the monk named so-and-so an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. Whichever venerable one approves of the granting of the agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days, to the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

A second time I speak this matter... A third time I speak this matter...

The agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days, has been granted by the Sangha to the monk named so-and-so. The Sangha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this act."

In this way, the kammavācā should be performed.

At the conclusion of the kammavācā, everything such as the undertaking of duties is exactly as previously mentioned. However, the monk who is informing [the Sangha]:
375:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed many saṅghādisesa offenses. I concealed many offenses for one day... many offenses for ten days. I requested from the Sangha an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. The Sangha granted me an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. Venerable sirs, I am undergoing probation. I am informing [the Sangha]. May the Sangha recognize me as one who is informing."

Thus it should be informed.

When one wishes to give mānatta to a monk who has completed probation:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed many saṅghādisesa offenses. I concealed many offenses for one day... many offenses for ten days. I requested from the Sangha an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. The Sangha granted me an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. Venerable sirs, having completed probation, I request from the Sangha the six-night mānatta to be practiced for those offenses."

Having made him request three times:

"Venerable sirs, may the Sangha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so has committed many saṅghādisesa offenses. He concealed many offenses for one day... many offenses for ten days. He requested from the Sangha an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. The Sangha granted to this monk named so-and-so an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses, combining them with the value of those offenses which were concealed for ten days. Having completed probation, this monk is requesting from the Sangha the six-night mānatta to be practiced for those offenses. If to the Sangha..."
376:
"If the time is right for the Saṅgha, it would be good if the Saṅgha were to grant the six-day mānatta for those offenses to the bhikkhu named [so-and-so]. This is the motion (ñatti).

Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This bhikkhu named [so-and-so] has committed several Saṅghādisesa offenses. Several offenses were concealed for one day... [p]... several offenses were concealed for ten days. That bhikkhu requested from the Saṅgha an agghasamodhānaparivāsa for those offenses concealed for ten days, based on the value of those offenses. The Saṅgha granted the agghasamodhānaparivāsa for those offenses concealed for ten days to the bhikkhu named [so-and-so]. That bhikkhu, having completed the parivāsa, is requesting from the Saṅgha the six-day mānatta for those offenses. The Saṅgha is granting the six-day mānatta for those offenses to the bhikkhu named [so-and-so]. Whichever venerable one approves of granting the six-day mānatta for those offenses to the bhikkhu named [so-and-so], let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, let him speak.

For the second time I speak this matter... [p]... For the third time I speak this matter... [p]...

The six-day mānatta for those offenses has been granted by the Saṅgha to the bhikkhu named [so-and-so]. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this (kammavācā)."

Thus the formal act (kammavācā) should be performed.

At the end of the kammavācā, the undertaking of mānatta and so forth are just as previously stated. However, the informing bhikkhu should say:
"Venerable Sirs, I committed several Saṅghādisesa offenses. Several offenses were concealed for one day... [p]... several offenses were concealed for ten days. I requested from the Saṅgha an agghasamodhānaparivāsa for those offenses concealed for ten days, based on the value of those offenses. The Saṅgha granted me the agghasamodhānaparivāsa for those offenses concealed for ten days. Having completed the parivāsa, I requested from the Saṅgha the six-day mānatta for those offenses."
377:
"The Saṅgha granted me the six-day mānatta for those offenses. I am practicing the mānatta. Venerable Sirs, I inform [the Saṅgha]. May the Saṅgha recognize me as one who informs."

The bhikkhu who has completed the mānatta should be rehabilitated (abbhāna). The bhikkhu who wishes to be rehabilitated should say:
"Venerable Sirs, I committed several Saṅghādisesa offenses. Several offenses were concealed for one day... [p]... several offenses were concealed for ten days. I requested from the Saṅgha an agghasamodhānaparivāsa for those offenses concealed for ten days, based on the value of those offenses. The Saṅgha granted me the agghasamodhānaparivāsa for those offenses concealed for ten days. Having completed the parivāsa, I requested from the Saṅgha the six-day mānatta for those offenses. The Saṅgha granted me the six-day mānatta for those offenses. Venerable Sirs, having completed the mānatta, I request rehabilitation (abbhāna) from the Saṅgha."
Having made him request three times:

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This bhikkhu named [so-and-so] committed several Saṅghādisesa offenses. Several offenses were concealed for one day... [p]... several offenses were concealed for ten days. That bhikkhu requested from the Saṅgha an agghasamodhānaparivāsa for those offenses concealed for ten days, based on the value of those offenses. The Saṅgha granted the agghasamodhānaparivāsa for those offenses concealed for ten days to the bhikkhu named [so-and-so]. If the time is right for the Saṅgha, it would be good if the Saṅgha were to rehabilitate the bhikkhu named [so-and-so]. This is the motion.

Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This bhikkhu named [so-and-so] committed several Saṅghādisesa offenses. Several..."
378:
... (Abridged) ... There were many offenses concealed for one day ... (Abridged) ... many offenses concealed for ten days. That monk requested the Saṅgha for an agghasamodhāna-parivāsa (combined probation according to the value of the duration) for those offenses concealed for ten days. The Saṅgha granted the agghasamodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses to the monk named so-and-so. After having completed the probation, that monk requested the Saṅgha for the six-day mānatta (penance). The Saṅgha granted the six-day mānatta to that monk. After having practiced the mānatta, that monk requested the Saṅgha for abbhāna (rehabilitation). The Saṅgha performs the abbhāna for that monk. Whosoever of the venerable ones agrees to the rehabilitation of the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent. Whosoever does not agree, let him speak.

"For the second time I speak this matter... (Abridged)... For the third time I speak this matter... (Abridged)."

"The Saṅgha has rehabilitated the monk named so-and-so; the Saṅgha agrees, therefore it is silent; thus I record this." In this manner, by performing the kammavācā (formal act), the rehabilitation should be carried out.
