## The Discussion on Agghasamodhāna-parivāsa is Finished.

What is called missakasamodhāna (mixed combination) is a type of probation granted by combining offenses involving various grounds (vatthu). In this regard, the method is as follows:

"Venerable Sir, I have committed many Saṅghādisesa offenses: one instance of sukka-vissaṭṭhi (emission of semen), one of kāyasaṃsagga (bodily contact), one of duṭṭhullavācā (lewd words), one of attakāma (serving oneself), one of sañcaritta (acting as a go-between), one of kuṭikāra (building a hut), one of vihārakāra (building a vihara), one of duṭṭhadosa (maliciously accusing), one of aññabhāgiya (using a different ground for accusation), one of saṅghabhedaka (causing a schism), one of saṅghabhedānuvattaka (following a schismatic), one of dubbaca (being difficult to speak to), and one of kuladūsaka (corrupting families). Venerable Sir, I request the Saṅgha for a samodhāna-parivāsa for those offenses." Having made him request thus three times, the probation should be granted with the appropriate kammavācā.

In this case also, whether saying "I have committed Saṅghādisesa offenses involving various grounds" or "I have committed Saṅghādisesa offenses," according to the method previously mentioned...
379:
Since it is proper to perform the formal act by combining them according to the ground (vatthu), the clan (gotta), the name, or the offense, we shall not show the kammavācā separately here in this missakasamodhāna. Because emergence (vuṭṭhāna) from offenses involving various grounds is possible through the same kammavācā previously shown as common to all offenses, that kammavācā alone is sufficient here.

## The Discussion on Missakasamodhāna-parivāsa is Finished.

If a monk disrobes or becomes a novice while undergoing probation, the probation is not valid for the disrobed monk or the novice. If he is ordained again, the previous granting of probation remains valid for him. The probation that was given is well-given; the probation that was lived is well-lived; he should continue to live the remaining probation. If one who is liable to mānatta disrobes or becomes a novice while practicing mānatta, or if one who is liable to abbhāna does so, and if he is ordained again, the previous granting of probation remains valid for him. The probation that was given is well-given; the probation that was lived is well-lived; the mānatta that was given is well-given; the mānatta that was practiced is well-practiced; that monk should be rehabilitated (abbhāna).

If a monk becomes insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain while undergoing probation, the probation is not valid for the insane, the mentally deranged, or the one afflicted by pain. If he becomes sane, not mentally deranged, and not afflicted by pain again, the previous granting of probation remains valid. The probation that was given is well-given; the probation that was lived is well-lived; he should continue to live the remaining probation. The same method applies to those liable to mānatta and so forth.

If a monk is suspended (ukkhittaka) while undergoing probation, the probation is not valid for the suspended one. If he is reinstated (osāreti) again, the previous granting of probation remains valid for him. The probation that was given is well-given; the probation that was lived is well-lived; he should continue to live the remaining probation. The same method applies to those liable to mānatta and so forth.

If the female sex appears in a monk, the preceptor he took while a man remains his preceptor, and the ordination he received remains his ordination. A new preceptor should not be taken, and a new ordination should not be received. The number of years (vassa) since his ordination as a monk remains the same. The number of years of the monk should not be recounted anew from the time of the change of sex. Since it is now inappropriate for that person to live among monks, he should go to a nunnery and live with the bhikkhunīs. Among the offenses that are desanāgāmin (to be confessed) and vuṭṭhānagāmin (requiring rehabilitation), those offenses common to bhikkhunīs should be dealt with by performing the Vinaya acts performed by bhikkhunīs in the presence of those bhikkhunīs. There are offenses such as sukka-vissaṭṭhi which are not common to bhikkhunīs; he is no longer guilty of those offenses. When the sex changes, those offenses are considered as already emerged from (vuṭṭhita). Even if the original male form appears again, he remains not guilty of those uncommon offenses. The same method applies when the male sex appears in a bhikkhunī. Thus it is said: "At that time... there is no offense." That statement was made. At that time, the female sex appeared in a certain monk.
380:
Regarding the counting of years (vassa), one should not start counting anew from the time of this gender change. Now, it is inappropriate for that person who has changed gender to live among monks; therefore, they must go to the bhikkhunī quarters and live with the bhikkhunīs. For offenses that are common to both monks and bhikkhunīs, whether they are desanāgāminī or vuṭṭhānagāminī, the disciplinary acts must be performed only in the presence of bhikkhunīs. Regarding offenses that are specific to monks and not shared with bhikkhunīs, such as sukkhavissaṭṭhi (emission of semen) and others, one is no longer guilty of those offenses. When the gender changes, those offenses are considered as having been cleared (vuṭṭhita). Even if one becomes a natural man again, one remains free from those offenses. The same method applies when a male gender appears in a bhikkhunī. It has been said:

“At that time, the female gender appeared in a certain monk. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. [The Buddha said:] ‘Bhikkhus, I allow that same preceptor, that same ordination, and those same years to be joined with the bhikkhunīs. For those offenses that are common to both monks and bhikkhunīs, I allow them to be cleared in the presence of the bhikkhunīs. For those offenses that are specific to monks and not shared with bhikkhunīs, there is no offense.’”

“At that time, the male gender appeared in a certain bhikkhunī. They reported this matter to the Blessed One. [The Buddha said:] ‘Bhikkhus, I allow that same preceptor, that same ordination, and those same years to be joined with the bhikkhus. For those offenses that are common to both bhikkhunīs and monks, I allow them to be cleared in the presence of the bhikkhus. For those offenses that are specific to bhikkhunīs and not shared with monks, there is no offense.’”

In this matter, the Pāḷimuttakavinicchaya is as follows: Between these two genders, the male gender is superior, and the female gender is inferior. Therefore, the male gender disappears due to strong unwholesome kamma, and the female gender is established due to weak wholesome kamma. When the female gender disappears, it disappears due to weak unwholesome kamma, and the male gender is established due to strong wholesome kamma. Thus, both genders disappear due to unwholesome kamma and are regained due to wholesome kamma.
381:
In the event of such a disappearance or appearance of gender, if two monks are reciting together or discussing the Dhamma and sleep in the same building, and while they are asleep, female organs appear in one monk, both monks incur an offense of sleeping together (sahaseyya). When that monk who has changed gender wakes up and sees their transformation, becoming distressed and unhappy, if they inform the other monk during the night, that monk should console them, saying: “Let it be, do not worry; this fault is merely the fault of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). The Fully Enlightened One has provided an opening. Whether one is a monk or a bhikkhunī, the Dhamma is not closed, and the path to heaven and Nibbāna is not barred.”

After consoling them, he should say: “It is proper for you to go to a bhikkhunī quarters. Do you have any bhikkhunīs whom you know?” If that bhikkhunī who has changed gender has acquaintances, she should say “I have,” and if not, “I have not.” Then she should say to that fellow monk: “Please support me; now, first take me to the bhikkhunī quarters.” That monk should take that person and go to the presence of bhikkhunīs known to her or to himself. When going, he must not go alone but should go with four or five monks, carrying torches and walking sticks, and making arrangements to be free from the offense of making an appointment, saying “We are going to such and such a place.” If the monastery is in a distant place outside the village, there is no offense for the offenses of entering another village, crossing to the other side of a river, staying overnight away from the monastery, or being separated from the group during the journey.

Upon arriving at the bhikkhunī quarters, those bhikkhunīs should be asked: “Do you know a monk named so-and-so?” If they reply, “Yes, venerable sir,” he should say: “Female organs have appeared in that monk; now, please provide support to this person.” If those bhikkhunīs say, “Very well, venerable sir, now we too shall recite and listen to the Dhamma; please proceed, venerable sirs,” and provide support, and if those bhikkhunīs are conscientious (lajjī) ones who are pleasing and supportive, one should not leave them to go elsewhere after causing them dissatisfaction. If one does go, one is not exempt from the offenses of entering another village, crossing to the other side of a river, staying overnight away, or being separated from the group.

However, if they are conscientious but do not provide support, one is allowed to go elsewhere. Even if they are shameless (alajjī) but provide support, one is allowed to leave them and go elsewhere. If they are both conscientious and supportive but are not relatives, and there are other related bhikkhunīs in a nearby village who would look after her, it is said that it is also proper to go to them. Having gone there, if she was still practicing under dependence (nissaya) while a monk, she must take dependence under a suitable bhikkhunī. If the Mātikā or the Vinaya has been learned and well-mastered, there is no reason to learn them again. If she was one who had a following even while a monk, then in the presence of that same person...
382:
One who has been ordained as a monk remains well-ordained [in the new status]; dependence (nissaya) should be taken from another monk. Disciples who previously lived depending on that person should also take dependence from another. A novice (sāmaṇera) who has completed his years should also take a preceptor (upajjhāya) from another monk. If there are the triple robe (ticīvara) and the bowl (patta) which were determined (adhiṭṭhita) during his life as a monk, that determination is lost; they must be determined again. The bodice (saṅkaccika) and the bathing cloth (udakasāṭika) should also be taken. If there is an extra robe or an extra bowl that was kept after performing a formal act of Vinaya (vinaya-kamma), all those formal acts are lost; they must be performed again. The acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa) of oil, honey, molasses, and so on, which were accepted, is also lost. If the gender changes on the seventh day from the time of acceptance, it is allowable for seven days after being accepted again. If property belonging to another monk was accepted during the time as a monk, that acceptance is not lost. If communal property belonging to both parties is kept without being divided, the monk who has not changed gender shall look after it. If it has been divided and is the property of that person alone, that acceptance is lost. This matter is stated in the Parivāra: 

“If one personally takes and stores oil, honey, molasses, and ghee, and consumes them within seven days when there is a reason, there is an offense; this question has been considered by the wise.” (Pari. 480). 

This statement is made with reference to the change of gender. What is called ‘acceptance’ is lost due to change of gender, death, renouncing the training, returning to the lower life, giving to one who is not ordained, abandoning without regard, and taking by force. Therefore, even if a single piece of yellow myrobalan (harītakī) has been accepted and kept, all of that person's acceptance is lost. If any property of that person is kept in the monks' monastery, whether accepted or not accepted, that person alone is the owner of all of it; it should be taken after having it brought. If there are fixed lodgings (senāsana) or trees planted by oneself in that monastery which are that person's property, they may be given to whomever one wishes. Among the thirteen authorizations (sammuti), all authorizations obtained during the life as a monk are extinguished; the previous taking of vassa-residence is extinguished. If the gender changes after the later vassa-residence has been taken, and the Saṅgha of monks wishes to give the gains that have arisen to that person, they should be given after informing the Saṅgha.

If the gender changes while one is undergoing probation (parivāsa) for a concealed offense shared with bhikkhunīs, only the fortnightly penance (pakkha-mānatta) should be given again. If while practicing mānatta...
383:
...the gender changes, only the fortnightly penance (pakkha-mānatta) should be given again. If the gender changes for a monk who has completed the penance (mānatta), the bhikkhunīs should perform the act of rehabilitation (abbhāna). If, when the result of unwholesome karma is exhausted, the gender changes again during the time of practicing pakkha-mānatta, only the six-day penance (mānatta) should be given. If the gender changes after the pakkha-mānatta has been completed, the monks should perform the act of rehabilitation (abbhāna).

In the case of a bhikkhunī’s change of gender as well, the entire decision should be understood in the same manner as already stated. However, this is the distinction: if an offense of acting as a go-between (sañcaritta) committed while being a bhikkhunī is concealed, there is no granting of probation (parivāsa); only the six-day penance (mānatta) should be given. If the gender changes while practicing pakkha-mānatta, there is no benefit from that pakkha-mānatta; only the six-day penance (mānatta) should be given. If the gender changes for a woman who has completed the penance (mānatta), the monks should rehabilitate (abbheti) her without giving the penance again. If the gender changes again before the monks have given the penance, the bhikkhunīs should give only the pakkha-mānatta. If the gender changes again while practicing the six-day penance, only the pakkha-mānatta should be given. When a change of gender occurs for a monk who has completed the penance, the bhikkhunīs should perform the act of rehabilitation (abbhāna). For a woman who remains in the status of a bhikkhunī after the gender has changed again, the offenses that were previously settled remain well-settled.

## From here on, we shall show the duties of those on probation (pārivāsika) and others:

A monk undergoing probation (parivāsa) should not ordain others as a preceptor (upajjhāya); however, it is allowable to ordain others after setting aside the duties (vatta). Even as a teacher (ācariya), he should not recite the formal act (kammavācā); if no one else is present, it is allowable to recite it after setting aside the duties. Dependence (nissaya) should not be given to incoming monks (āgantuka). Those who have already taken dependence in the normal way should be told: “I am performing a formal act of Vinaya (vinaya-kamma); take dependence from such-and-such an Elder; do not perform duties for me; do not ask my permission to enter the village.” If they still perform them even after being told this, there is no offense for those performing them from the time they were forbidden. Another novice (sāmaṇera) should not be accepted; a novice who has already been accepted by giving him a preceptor should be told: “I am performing a formal act of Vinaya; do not perform duties for me; do not ask my permission to enter the village.” If they still perform them even after being told this, there is no offense for those performing them from the time they were forbidden. The authorization to exhort bhikkhunīs (bhikkhunovādaka-sammuti) should not be accepted; even if authorized, bhikkhunīs should not be exhorted. Therefore, he should say to the Saṅgha of monks: “Venerable sirs, I am performing a formal act of Vinaya...”
384:
“Please know the exhorter of the bhikkhunīs.” Thus should it be requested. Or, the burden should be entrusted to a capable bhikkhu for the purpose of exhorting the bhikkhunīs. To the bhikkhunīs who have arrived, it should be said: “Go to the presence of the Saṅgha; the Saṅgha will know who is to be your exhorter,” or it should be said: “I am performing a Vinaya act; go to the presence of such-and-such a bhikkhu; he will give you the exhortation.”

Whatever offense for which probation (parivāsa) has been given by the Saṅgha, that offense must not be committed again. Neither should another offense of a similar nature nor one that is worse than that be committed. The legal act of the Saṅgha (Saṅghakamma) must not be criticized; the bhikkhus who perform the act must not be criticized. The Uposatha of a monk of regular standing (pakatatta) must not be suspended, nor should his Pavāraṇā be suspended. The formal warning (savacanīya) must not be performed for the sake of obstruction or for the sake of summoning. Indeed, one who performs it for the sake of obstruction does so thus: “I perform a formal warning against the venerable one regarding this matter; do not depart from this monastery to another until this legal issue is settled.” One who performs it for the sake of summoning does so thus: “I perform a formal warning against you; come, let us go into the presence of the Vinaya experts together.” Both of these must not be done.

One must not assume a position of seniority in the monastery. One must not be a reciter of the Pātimokkha or an inviter for a Dhamma talk. One must not exercise authority even by way of a single formal appointment (sammuti) among the thirteen formal appointments. One must not cause a monk of regular standing to ask for permission, saying, “May the venerable one grant me leave; I wish to speak about that matter.” One must not accuse another regarding a matter or an offense. One must not remind another, saying, “This is your fault.” One must not cause a quarrel by inciting bhikkhus against one another. Even if one is a senior elder of the Saṅgha, one must not walk or sit in front of a monk of regular standing. Leaving a distance of twelve cubits, one must walk and sit alone. The lowest seat, the lowest bed, and the lowest lodging of the Saṅgha should be given to that bhikkhu.

Among those three, the 'lowest seat' refers to the lowest seat of the Saṅgha in places such as the refectory; that should be given to him, and he should sit there. The 'lowest bed' refers to the last of the beds, the most inferior couch or bench. This bhikkhu on probation does not have the right to take a bed in the place he reaches according to his seniority. After all the bhikkhus have selected and taken theirs, the remaining inferior bed, filled with monkey dung and bound with cane or creepers, should be given to him. Just as with the bed, the lodging where he stays is also not allowed to be taken according to his seniority. After all the bhikkhus have selected and taken theirs, the remaining dusty floor...
385:
...a leaf-hut filled with bat dung and mouse dung should be given to that bhikkhu. If all the monks of regular standing are forest-dwellers or open-air dwellers and do not enter a roofed dwelling, then among all these abandoned dwellings, he may obtain whichever he desires.

On the day of entering the rains (vassūpanāyika), he is entitled to take the requisites by staying at the end of the line according to seniority; however, he is not entitled to take a rains-residence (senāsana). One who wishes to take a permanent rains-residence must lay down his duties and take it. In a place where one is invited by relatives, when invited saying, “Please bring this many bhikkhus and come,” he must not approach the families by acting as the leader or the follower of the bhikkhus, having arranged it thus: “Venerable sirs, such-and-such a family invites the bhikkhus; come, let us go there.” However, it is proper to speak in a roundabout way according to the Vinaya (vinayapariyāya) thus: “Venerable sirs, people in such-and-such a village desire the arrival of bhikkhus; it would be good if you would favor them.”

One must not undertake the forest-dweller’s practice (āraññika dhutaṅga) out of shame of having to announce one's status to every bhikkhu who arrives. Even for one who has undertaken it normally, he must take a companion bhikkhu and cause the dawn to rise in the forest; he must not stay alone. Similarly, one must not undertake the alms-food eater’s practice (piṇḍapātika dhutaṅga) out of shame of sitting at the end of the seats in places like the refectory. For one who normally practices the alms-food eater’s practice, there is no prohibition; however, he must not have alms-food brought for that reason, thinking, “Let them not know about me.” Having had the alms-food brought, it is proper to eat while staying only in the monastery. One must not have alms-food brought for the reason: “I will count the nights; if I, while going for alms, see a bhikkhu and fail to announce my status, there would be an interruption of the nights (ratticcheda).” Also, with the intention “Let not even a single bhikkhu know about me,” he is not allowed to have novices cook and serve him in the monastery; he must certainly enter the village for alms. However, for a sick bhikkhu, or one occupied with new construction or the duties of teachers and preceptors, it is proper to stay only in the monastery.

If hundreds of bhikkhus are wandering in the village and it is not possible to announce to them, it is proper to go to a small village monastery and stay in a suitable place. For it has been said: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu on probation must announce his status when he arrives as a guest, he must announce it to a guest bhikkhu, he must announce it on the Uposatha day, he must announce it on the Pavāraṇā day; if he is sick, he must announce it even by a messenger.”
386: As stated, a monk on probation acting as a visitor who goes to any monastery must inform the monks there. If he sees all the monks staying in one place, he must inform them while they are in that one place. If they are staying separately under trees and so on, he must go to those various places and inform them. For a monk who, knowing this, does not inform them out of a desire not to inform, there is a break of the night (ratticcheda) and a dukkaṭa offense for the breach of duty (vattabheda). If, however, he searches but does not see some monks, there is only a break of the night; there is no dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty.  A visiting monk, whether one or many, who arrives at the monastery where the monk on probation resides, must also be informed in the same manner as mentioned. In this case, the break of the night and the breach of duty should also be understood in the same manner as mentioned. If visiting monks pass through the middle of the monastery, whether after resting for a moment or without resting, they must also be informed. If they go without the monk on probation knowing, and he finds out only after they have gone, he must follow them and inform them. For a monk who is unable to catch up or to make them hear, there is only a break of the night; there is no dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty. For those who do not enter the monastery but pass through the precinct (upacāra-sīmā), if this monk on probation hears the sound of their umbrellas, the sound of coughing, or the sound of sneezing and knows they are visitors, he must go and inform them. Even a monk who finds out after they have gone must follow and inform them. For one who is unable to catch up, there is only a break of the night; there is no dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty. Even if a visiting monk comes at night and leaves during the same night, he causes a break of the night for the monk on probation. However, because it was unknown, there is no dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty. If one performs the rehabilitation (abbhāna) without knowing of a break, it is as if it were not performed—so it is stated in the Kurundī Commentary. Therefore, one should perform it by taking more nights than the required number. This is the certain practice (apaṇṇakapaṭipadā).  If one sees a monk traveling by boat on a river or the like, or standing on the opposite bank, or traveling through the air, or standing at a distance such as at the foot of a mountain or in a forest, and if there is the recognition that 'this is a monk,' one must inform him by going by boat, or by shouting loudly, or by following quickly. For a monk who does not inform, there is both a break of the night and a dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty. If, despite making an effort, he is unable to catch up or to make him hear, there is only a break of the night; there is no dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty. However, the Elder Saṅghasenābhaya speaks in terms of range and non-range (visaya/avisaya): 'It is said that for one who does not inform within range, there is both a break of the night and a dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty; but outside of range, neither exists.' The Elder Karavīkatissa said: 'The recognition that "this is a recluse" is the only standard. Even if it is outside of range, there is only no dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty, but the break of the night certainly occurs.'
387: On Uposatha days, visiting monks often come, saying, 'We will arrive in time for the Uposatha.' Even monks traveling by psychic power (iddhi), upon knowing it is the Uposatha day, descend from the sky and perform the Uposatha. Therefore, for the purpose of clearing the status with visiting monks, one must inform them even on Uposatha days. The same method applies to the Pavāraṇā day. A sick monk who is unable to go himself must send another monk to inform; it is not proper to send an unordained person (anupasampanna).  A monk on probation (pārivāsika) must not go from a monastery with monks, or a place that is not a monastery, to a monastery or a place that is not a monastery where there are no monks or where there are monks of separate communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka), without a regular monk (pakatatta) or without a danger. This is because one must not stay in a place where there is not even a single regular monk. The nights spent in such a place are not countable for the probation. However, if there are the ten kinds of dangers, even if the nights are not countable, one must go in order to be free from danger. Therefore, it was said, 'except in case of danger.' It is not proper to perform Vinaya acts together with monks of separate communion; even if one does not inform them, there is no break of the night, as it is similar to a monastery without monks. Therefore, it was said, 'or a monastery with monks of separate communion.'  A monk on probation must not stay under the same roof (ekacchanna) with a regular monk, whether in a monastery or a place that is not a monastery. In this context, 'monastery' (āvāsa) means a dwelling place (senāsana) made for living. 'Non-monastery' (anāvāsa) means a cetiya house, a bodhi-tree house, a sweeping-shed, a wood-shed, a water-pot stand, a latrine, a gate-house, and so on. 'In any of these places, in a space under one roof defined by the drip-line of the eaves, a suspended monk (ukkhittaka) is not allowed to stay; however, a monk on probation is not allowed to stay only in a residence (āvāsa)'—so it is stated in the Mahāpaccariya. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated without distinction: 'It is forbidden by the drip-line of the eaves (udakapāta).' In the Kurundī, however, it is stated: 'In these many places covered by the five kinds of roofing, a monk on probation and a suspended monk are forbidden from staying with a regular monk within the drip-line of the eaves.' Therefore, even if the precincts (upacāra) are different, it is not proper if they are under the same roof. If, in this case, a regular monk ordained that very day enters and lies down first, and a monk on probation of sixty years seniority enters later and lies down knowingly, there is both a break of the night and a dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty. If he lies down without knowing, there is only a break of the night; there is no dukkaṭa offense for breach of duty. If, while that probationer monk is sleeping, later...
388:
If a regular monk (pakatatta) has entered and is already asleep, and later a monk undergoing probation (parivāsa) enters and sleeps, if that monk undergoing probation knows, there is a break in the night (ratticcheda) and an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) due to the breach of duty (vattabheda). If he does not know, there is only a break in the night, and no offense of wrongdoing for the breach of duty.

A monk undergoing probation, even if he sees a regular monk ordained on that very day, must rise from his seat. Having risen, he must not turn away thinking, "This person has made me rise while I was sitting comfortably." He must invite the regular monk to the seat, saying, "Teacher, this is a seat; please sit here." Thus, he must indeed invite the regular monk with a seat. However, a junior monk should not go to a senior monk undergoing probation with the intention, "I will cause trouble for the Great Elder." A monk undergoing probation must not sit on the same seat with a regular monk; if the regular monk sits on a low seat, he must not sit on a high seat; if the regular monk sits on the ground, he must not sit on a seat. However, it is permissible to sit if a distance of twelve cubits (hattha) is maintained. A monk undergoing probation must not walk on the same walking path (caṅkama) with a regular monk; if the regular monk is walking on a low path, he must not walk on a high path; if the regular monk is walking on the ground, he must not walk on a path. In this regard, if [the regular monk] is walking on ground that is not demarcated, it is not permissible [for the probationer] to walk even on a low path that has been demarcated, spread with sand, and fitted with railings; what then need be said about a path constructed with bricks and surrounded by a fence? However, if it is surrounded by a wall, or equipped with a gatehouse, or well-concealed in mountain clefts, forests, or thickets, it is permissible to walk on such a path. Even in an unconcealed place, it is permissible to walk if a distance of twelve cubits is maintained.

A monk undergoing probation must not stay under the same roof, whether in a monastery or a non-monastery, with a monk undergoing probation who is senior to him, or with a monk liable to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), a monk liable to penance (mānattāraha), a monk undergoing penance (mānattacārika), or a monk liable to rehabilitation (abbhānāraha). In this regard, if a senior monk undergoing probation is already asleep and a junior one enters and sleeps while knowing, for that junior one, there is a break in the night and an offense of wrongdoing due to the breach of duty. For the senior one, there is only a break in the night, and no offense of wrongdoing for the breach of duty. If they sleep without knowing, there is no breach of duty for both, but there is a break in the night. If a junior monk undergoing probation is already asleep and a senior one enters and sleeps later, if the junior one knows, his night is broken and there is an offense of wrongdoing due to the breach of duty. For the senior one, there is only a break in the night, and no breach of duty. If they do not know, there is no breach of duty for both, but there is a break in the night. If they sleep at the same time, neither before nor after, for the senior one there is only a break in the night, while for the junior one there is both a break in the night and a breach of duty—so it is stated in the Kurundī commentary. Another...
389:
Among two monks undergoing probation of equal seniority, if one is already asleep and the other sleeps later while knowing, for the one who sleeps later, the night is broken and there is an offense of wrongdoing due to the breach of duty. For the one who was already asleep, there is only a break in the night, not a breach of duty. If the one who sleeps later also does not know, there is no breach of duty for both, but there is a break in the night. If both sleep at the same time, neither before nor after, for both there is only a break in the night, not a breach of duty.

If two monks undergoing probation were to live together, they might become aware of each other's transgressions and, becoming disrespectful or remorseful, might commit that same offense or one even worse, or they might disrobe. Therefore, their sleeping together is prohibited in every way. In this context, those such as one liable to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha) should be understood as standing in the position of monks undergoing probation. Therefore, a monk undergoing probation must not sit on the same seat with one liable to be sent back to the beginning, one liable to penance, one undergoing penance, or one liable to rehabilitation. He must not sit on a high seat while they are sitting on a low seat; he must not sit on a seat while they are sitting on the ground. He must not walk on the same walking path; he must not walk on a high path while they are walking on a low path; he must not walk on a path while they are walking on the ground.

"Monks, a monk undergoing probation should not consent to a regular monk's salutation, rising to greet him, salutation with joined palms, proper homage, bringing a seat, bringing a bed, providing water for washing the feet, providing a footstool, providing a foot-towel, receiving the bowl and robes, or rubbing the back during a bath. Whoever should consent to these, there is an offense of wrongdoing"—according to this word, except for a monk undergoing probation who is junior to himself, if he consents to the salutation and so on of others, including even those liable to be sent back to the beginning and so on, there is an offense of wrongdoing. Even if he consents to the service of his co-residents (saddhivihārika), it is still an offense of wrongdoing. Therefore, those disciples should be told: "I am performing a Vinaya procedure; do not perform duties for me; do not ask my permission to enter the village." If sons of good family who have ordained out of faith say, "Venerable sirs, please perform your Vinaya procedure," and continue to perform duties and ask permission to enter the village, from the time they were forbidden, there is no offense.

"Monks, I allow monks undergoing probation to perform for one another, according to seniority, salutation, rising to greet, salutation with joined palms, proper homage, bringing a seat, bringing a bed, providing water for washing the feet, providing a footstool, providing a foot-towel, receiving the bowl and robes, and [rubbing the back] during a bath..."
390:
According to the word "piṭṭhiparikamma," among monks undergoing probation (parivāsa), a senior monk is permitted to accept the salutation and so forth from a junior monk.

According to the word, "Monks, I allow five things for monks undergoing probation to be done according to seniority: Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, the rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭika), relinquishing (oṇojana), and meals (bhatta)," these five, such as Uposatha, should be performed according to seniority together with monks of regular standing (pakatatta). Therefore, when the Pātimokkha is being recited, one should sit within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa). In the Mahāpaccariya, however, it is stated: "One should sit without staying in the regular order, leaving the order but without leaving the hatthapāsa."

When performing the Pārisuddhi-uposatha, one should sit at the place of the most junior of the Saṅgha, and while sitting right there, perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha according to one's own seniority. In Pavāraṇā also, one should sit at the place of the most junior of the Saṅgha, and while sitting right there, perform the invitation (pavāretabbaṃ) according to one's own order. One should also take the rainy-season robe distributed by the Saṅgha by striking the bell when it reaches one's turn.

Oṇojana means relinquishing. If a monk on probation receives two or three portions of designated meals (uddesabhatta) and so forth, and has an expectation of receiving another private meal, he should accept those meals in order and then relinquish them, saying: "Venerable sirs, please take these for those below; today I have an expectation of a meal, I will take it only tomorrow." If he relinquishes in this way, he is entitled to receive those meals on subsequent days. It is stated in the Kurundī: "On the next day, it should be given to that monk before everyone else." If he neither takes them nor relinquishes them, he will not receive them the next day. This oṇojana is allowed specifically for a monk on probation. Why? Because for that monk sitting at the most junior place of the Saṅgha, gruel, snacks, and so forth in the refectory may or may not reach him; therefore, this is allowed specifically to support him, so that "that monk may not be exhausted by seeking alms-food."

"Meal" (bhatta) refers to the Catussāla meal of the Saṅgha in the monastery, which is taken by all arriving monks according to seniority. Although he receives that meal according to seniority, he is not permitted to walk or stand in the regular order. Therefore, he should step out of the order, stand within the hatthapāsa, and take it by stretching out his hand, just as a hawk swoops down and takes its prey. He is not permitted to have temple attendants (ārāmika) or novices (sāmaṇera) bring it for him. If they bring it of their own accord, it is permissible. The same method applies to the King's Mahāpeḷa meal. In the case of the Catussāla meal, if he wishes to relinquish it, he should say regarding the meal taken for himself: "Today I have a meal, I will take it only tomorrow." In the Mahāpaccariya, it is stated that he receives two portions the next day. Designated meals (uddesabhatta) and so forth should also be taken only by stepping out of the order. In a place where they are offered while sitting, he should sit as the senior-most of the novices or as the junior-most of the Saṅgha. This is the duty of one on probation (pārivāsika-vatta). It should be understood that this same duty applies to those deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), those deserving penance (mānattāraha), those undergoing penance (mānatta-cārika), and those deserving rehabilitation (abbhānāraha). Specifically, in the duty of a monk undergoing penance, there is the distinction: "He must announce it daily." Regarding the interruption of nights (ratticcheda), because of the word: "Upāli, there are three causes for the interruption of nights for a monk on probation: living together (sahavāsa), living apart (vippavāsa), and non-announcement (anārocanā)"...
391:
Regarding the meal set aside for oneself, one should say: "Today I have a meal, I will take it only tomorrow." It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya Commentary: "On the next day, he receives two portions of the meal." Designated meals (uddesabhatta) and so forth should also be taken only by stepping out of the regular order. In a place where they serve while sitting, if he is a novice, he should sit as the senior-most; if he is a monk, he should sit as the junior-most of the Saṅgha. This is the duty of one on probation (pārivāsika-vatta).

It should be understood that this same duty is the duty to be practiced by those deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), those deserving penance (mānattāraha), those undergoing penance (mānatta-cārika), and those deserving rehabilitation (abbhānāraha). However, in the duty of a monk undergoing penance, there is the special requirement: "He must announce it daily." Regarding the interruption of nights (ratticcheda), it is stated: "Upāli, there are three causes for the interruption of nights for a monk on probation: living together (sahavāsa), living apart (vippavāsa), and non-announcement (anārocanā)." Thus, the interruption of nights for a monk on probation occurs due to any one of these three causes: living together, which is described as "living under one roof with a monk of regular standing" and so forth; living alone; and non-announcement to visiting monks and others.

For a monk undergoing penance, however, it is stated: "Upāli, there are four causes for the interruption of nights for a monk undergoing penance: living together, living apart, non-announcement, and practicing in an incomplete group (ūne gaṇe caraṇa)." Thus, the interruption of nights occurs due to any one of these four causes. Here, "group" (gaṇa) means four monks or more than four. Therefore, even if he lives with three monks, the interruption of nights certainly occurs.

## Thus ends the discussion on the decision regarding rehabilitation from grave offenses
## in the Pālimuttakavinayavinicchayasaṅgaha.
## 33. Kammākamma-vinicchaya-kathā

In this decision regarding valid and invalid formal acts (kammākamma), there are four types of formal acts: the act of announcement (apalokana-kamma), the act with a motion (ñatti-kamma), the act with a motion and one proclamation (ñattidutiya-kamma), and the act with a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma). By how many factors do these four acts fail? They fail by five factors: due to the object (vatthu), the motion (ñatti), the proclamation (anussāvana/kammavācā), the boundary (sīmā), or the assembly (parisā).
392:
How do legal acts fail because of the object (vatthu)? He performs an act in the absence of the person that should be performed in their presence; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs an act without interrogation that should be performed after interrogation; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs an act without an acknowledgement that should be performed after an acknowledgement; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He gives a verdict of past insanity (amūጹhavinaya) to one who is entitled to a verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya); that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs an act of specific depravity (tassapāpiyasika-kamma) for one who is entitled to a verdict of past insanity; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs an act of censure (tajjanġya-kamma) for one who is entitled to an act of specific depravity; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs an act of subordination (niyassa-kamma) for one who is entitled to an act of censure; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs an act of banishment (pabbājanġya-kamma) for one who is entitled to an act of subordination; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs an act of reconciliation (paṭisāraṇġya-kamma) for one who is entitled to an act of banishment; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs an act of suspension (ukkhepanġya-kamma) for one who is entitled to an act of reconciliation; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He gives probation (parivāsa) to one who is entitled to an act of suspension; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs the act of sending back to the beginning (mũlāyapaṭikassanā) for one who is entitled to probation; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He gives penance (mānatta) to one who is entitled to being sent back to the beginning; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He rehabilitates (abbhāna) one who is entitled to penance; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He ordains (upasampadā) one who is entitled to rehabilitation; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs the Uposatha on a day that is not an Uposatha day; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He performs the Pavāraṇā on a day that is not a Pavāraṇā day; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. He ordains a eunuch (paṇḍaka); he ordains one who lives by stealth (theyyasaṃvāsaka), one who has gone over to another sect (titthiyapakkantaka), an animal (tiracchānagata), a matricide, a patricide, a killer of an Arahant, a violator of a nun, a schismatic, one who has shed the blood of a Buddha, a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka), or a person under twenty years of age; that act is an unlawful act with a defective object. In this way, legal acts fail because of the object.

How do legal acts fail because of the motion (ñatti)? Legal acts fail because of the motion in five ways: he does not mention the object, he does not mention the Saṃgha, he does not mention the person, he does not mention the motion, or he places the motion last. In these five ways, legal acts fail because of the motion.

How do legal acts fail because of the proclamation (anussāvana)? Legal acts fail because of the proclamation in five ways: he does not mention the object, he does not mention the Saṃgha, he does not mention the person, he omits parts of the proclamation, or he recites it at the wrong time. In these five ways, legal acts fail because of the proclamation.

How do legal acts fail because of the boundary (sġmā)? Legal acts fail because of the boundary in eleven ways: he designates a boundary that is too small, he designates a boundary that is too large, he designates a boundary with broken marks, he designates a boundary with shadow marks, he designates a boundary without marks...
393:
...he designates a boundary; he designates a boundary while standing outside the boundary; he designates a boundary in a river; he designates a boundary in the sea; he designates a boundary in a natural lake; he overlaps a boundary with another boundary; he encompasses a boundary with another boundary. In these eleven ways, legal acts fail because of the boundary.

How do legal acts fail because of the assembly (parisa)? Legal acts fail because of the assembly in twelve ways: in an act to be performed by a group of four (catuvagga), as many bhikkhus as are entitled to the act do not come, the consent of those entitled to give consent is not brought, and those present protest. In an act to be performed by a group of four, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to the act come, but the consent of those entitled to give consent is not brought, and those present protest. In an act to be performed by a group of four, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to the act come, and the consent of those entitled to give consent is brought, but those present protest.

In an act to be performed by a group of five... [etc.] ...in an act to be performed by a group of ten... [etc.] ...in an act to be performed by a group of twenty (vġsativagga), as many bhikkhus as are entitled to the act do not come, the consent of those entitled to give consent is not brought, and those present protest. In an act to be performed by a group of twenty, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to the act come, but the consent of those entitled to give consent is not brought, and those present protest. In an act to be performed by a group of twenty, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to the act come, and the consent of those entitled to give consent is brought, but those present protest. In these twelve ways, legal acts fail because of the assembly.

In an act to be performed by a group of four, four bhikkhus who are in good standing (pakatatta) are entitled to the act; the remaining bhikkhus in good standing are entitled to give consent. The person for whom the Saṃgha performs the act is neither entitled to the act nor entitled to give consent; rather, he is the one against whom the act is performed (kammāraha). In an act to be performed by a group of five, five bhikkhus who are in good standing are entitled to the act; the remaining bhikkhus in good standing are entitled to give consent. The person for whom the Saṃgha performs the act is neither entitled to the act nor entitled to give consent; rather, he is the one against whom the act is performed. In an act to be performed by a group of ten, ten bhikkhus who are in good standing are entitled to the act; the remaining bhikkhus in good standing are entitled to give consent. The person for whom the Saṃgha performs the act is neither entitled to the act nor entitled to give consent; rather, he is the one against whom the act is performed. In an act to be performed by a group of twenty, twenty bhikkhus who are in good standing are entitled to the act...
394:
The remaining pakatatta (monks of pure virtue) are entitled to give their consent (chanda). When the Saṅgha performs a legal act (kamma) against a person, that monk is neither one to whom the act has been applied (kammapatta) nor one entitled to give consent; rather, he is truly one who is the object of the act (kammaraha).

To how many instances does an act of announcement (apalokanakamma) apply? To how many instances do a motion act (ñattikamma), a motion-and-second act (ñattidutiyakamma), and a motion-and-fourth act (ñatticatutthakamma) apply? An act of announcement applies to five instances. A motion act applies to nine instances. A motion-and-second act applies to seven instances. A motion-and-fourth act applies to seven instances.

To which five instances does an act of announcement apply? (1) Rehabilitation (osāraṇa), (2) expulsion (nissāraṇa), (3) the act of shaving the head (bhaṇḍukamma), (4) the imposition of the Brahma-punishment (brahmadaṇḍa), and (5) acts characterized by the nature of the act itself, such as abhivandiya and others, which is the fifth. An act of announcement applies to these five instances.

To which nine instances does a motion act apply? (1) Rehabilitation, (2) expulsion, (3) Uposatha, (4) Pavāraṇā, (5) authorization (sammuti), (6) giving (dāna), (7) acceptance of an offense (paṭiggahaṇa), (8) postponement of Pavāraṇā (paccukkaḍḎhana), and (9) motion-proclamations (ñattikammavācā) characterized by the nature of the act itself, which is the ninth. A motion act applies to these nine instances.

To which seven instances does a motion-and-second act apply? (1) Rehabilitation, (2) expulsion, (3) authorization, (4) giving, (5) removal (uddharaṇa), (6) declaration (desana), and (7) motion-proclamations characterized by the nature of the act itself, which is the seventh. A motion-and-second act applies to these seven instances.

To which seven instances does a motion-and-fourth act apply? (1) Rehabilitation, (2) expulsion, (3) authorization, (4) giving, (5) censure (niggaha), (6) admonition (samanubhāsana), and (7) acts such as the higher ordination act (upasampadakamma) characterized by the nature of the act itself, which is the seventh. A motion-and-fourth act applies to these seven instances. This is the method according to the Pāḷi text.

## Herein is the discussion regarding the decision from the beginning (Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā 482)

What is called an act of announcement (apalokanakamma) is an act performed by clearing the Saṅgha residing within the boundary (sīmā), bringing the consent of those entitled to give consent, and announcing it three times with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha. What is called a motion act (ñattikamma) is an act performed by the same aforementioned method, with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha, by a single motion (ñatti). What is called a motion-and-second act (ñattidutiyakamma) is an act performed by the same aforementioned method, with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha, by a single motion and a single proclamation (anussāvanā), thus making the proclamation the second part. What is called a motion-and-fourth act (ñatticatutthakamma) is an act performed by the same aforementioned method, with the approval of the harmonious Saṅgha, by a single motion and three proclamations, thus making the proclamations the fourth part.
395:
Among those four types of acts, an act of announcement should be performed only by announcing; it should not be performed by means of a motion act. A motion act should also be performed only by establishing a single motion; it should not be performed by means of an act of announcement. As for a motion-and-second act, there are instances where it is performed by announcing and instances where it is not.

Between those two—what should and should not be performed—these six acts: (1) authorizing a boundary (sīmāsammuti), (2) abolishing a boundary (sīmāsamūhana), (3) giving the kaṭhina robe (kaṭhinadāna), (4) removing the kaṭhina (kaṭhinuddhāra), (5) designating a site for a hut (kuṭivatthudesanā), and (6) designating a site for a monastery (vihāravatthudesanā), are heavy acts (garukakamma). Therefore, they are not allowed to be performed merely by announcing; they must be performed only by reciting the motion-and-second proclamation (ñattidutiyakammavācā). The remaining thirteen authorizations, such as the authorization of the assigner of lodgings (senāsanaggāhaka) and the authorization for giving robes of the deceased (matakacīvaradāna), are light acts (lahukakamma). Therefore, they are allowed to be performed even by announcing; however, they should certainly not be performed by means of a motion act or a motion-and-fourth act. "If performed by means of a motion-and-fourth act, it becomes much firmer; therefore, it should be done so," some teachers say. If done in this way, there is a confusion of acts (kammasaṅkara); therefore, it is rejected as something that should not be done.

If there is a deficiency in letters, or a deficiency in words, or a word that is poorly pronounced, it is allowable to say it repeatedly to purify it. Such repeated recitation is called making a non-failing act firm; even a failing act becomes a non-failing act and remains valid. A motion-and-fourth act must be performed only by reciting one motion and three proclamations; it should not be performed by means of an act of announcement and so forth.

In the statement, "One performs an act that should be done in the presence [of the parties] in their absence; it is an unlawful act with a flawed basis (vatthuvipanna)," there are acts to be done in the presence and acts to be done in the absence. Among those two types of acts, what is called an act to be done in the absence consists of eight kinds: (1) higher ordination by a messenger (dūtenūpasampadā), (2) turning the bowl upside down (pattanikkujjana), (3) turning the bowl upright (pattukkujjana), (4) the authorization of insanity for an insane monk (ummattakasammuti), (5) the authorization of training for families in training (sekhasammuti), (6) the imposition of the Brahma-punishment on the monk Channa, (7) the act of public proclamation (pakāsanīyakamma) against Devadatta, and (8) the act of non-salutation (avandiyakamma) to be performed by the community of nuns against a monk who shows uninspiring behavior. Even if these eight kinds of acts are performed in the absence, they are well-performed and non-failing (akuppa). All remaining acts, however, must be performed only in the presence. They must be performed only by bringing these four types of "presence-discipline" (sammukhāvinaya): presence of the Saṅgha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the person. Acts performed in this way are well-performed. If not performed in this way, because they are done without this basis known as "presence-discipline," those acts are called acts with a flawed basis. Therefore, it is said, "One performs an act that should be done in the presence in their absence; it is an unlawful act with a flawed basis." In acts such as those to be performed after questioning, the act of questioning itself is called the basis (vatthu); because they are performed excluding that basis, the state of those acts having a flawed basis should also be understood. Indeed, whether it be a person who is not yet twenty years old, or a person who has previously committed a pārājika offense...
396:
For one who confers ordination on any of the eleven types of unfit persons (abhabba-puggala), it is an unrighteous act (adhamma-kamma) due to a failure of the object (vatthu-vipatti). This is the decision regarding the failure of a formal act by way of the object.

Regarding failure by way of the motion (ñatti-vipatti), 'not referring to the object' means that when performing the act of ordination (upasampadā-kamma) and so forth for a person, one does not refer to that person or mention their name. For example, when one should say, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, this Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination (upasampadā-pekkha) of the Venerable Buddharakkhita," one says instead, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, he is the candidate for ordination of the Venerable Buddharakkhita." In this way, it is called not referring to the object.

'Not referring to the Saṅgha' means not mentioning the name of the Saṅgha. When one should say, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, this Dhammarakkhita...", one says instead, "Venerable Sirs, this Dhammarakkhita..." In this way, it is called not referring to the Saṅgha.

'Not referring to the person' means not referring to the person who is the preceptor (upajjhāya) of the candidate, or not mentioning his name. When one should say, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, this Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination of the Venerable Buddharakkhita," one says instead, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, this Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination." In this way, it is called not referring to the person.

'Not referring to the motion' (ñatti) means omitting the motion entirely. In a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (ñatti-dutiya-kamma), one omits the motion and performs the proclamation (anussāvana) twice using only the kammavācā. In a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation (ñatti-catuttha-kamma), one omits the motion and performs the proclamation four times using only the kammavācā. In this way, it is called not referring to the motion.

Alternatively, 'placing the motion afterwards' means performing the proclamation with the kammavācā first, and then saying, "This is the motion," followed by, "The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent; thus I record it." In this way, one places the motion afterwards. Thus, by these five ways, formal acts fail because of the motion.

Regarding failure by way of the proclamation (anussāvana-vipatti), the object and other factors should be understood according to the method already mentioned. Their non-reference occurs in this way: in the first proclamation, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs," or in the second and third proclamations, "A second time I speak this matter... a third time I speak this matter. Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs," when one should say, "This Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination of the Venerable Buddharakkhita," but instead says, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, [the candidate] of the Venerable Buddharakkhita," such a person is said to not refer to the object.
397:
When one should say, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, this person is Dhammarakkhita," but says, "Let [them] hear me, Venerable Sirs, this person is Dhammarakkhita" (omitting the word 'Saṅgho'), such a person is said to not refer to the Saṅgha. When one should say, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, this Dhammarakkhita is the [pupil] of the Venerable Buddharakkhita," but says, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sirs, this Dhammarakkhita is the candidate for ordination" (omitting the preceptor's name), such a person is said to not refer to the person.

'Deficiency in the proclamation' (sāvana-hāpana) means not performing the proclamation with the kammavācā at all; in a ñatti-dutiya-kamma, one only states the motion twice, and in a ñatti-catuttha-kamma, one only states the motion four times. In this way, one causes a deficiency in the proclamation. Also, in a ñatti-dutiya-kamma, if one states the motion once and while reciting the kammavācā once, one either omits a syllable or mispronounces a word, this also constitutes a deficiency in the proclamation. In a ñatti-catuttha-kamma, if one states the motion once and performs the proclamation with the kammavācā only once or twice, or omits a syllable or a word, or mispronounces them, it should be understood that one causes a deficiency in the proclamation.

Regarding the term 'mispronounces' (durutta), the decision is as follows: one who says one syllable when another should be said is said to mispronounce. Therefore, a monk who performs the kammavācā should well observe these ten divisions of articulation (byañjana-buddhi):

"Sithila, dhanita, dīgha, rassa,
garuka, lahuka, niggahita,
sambandha, vavatthita, and vimutta—
these are the ten divisions of articulation."

Among these ten: 'Sithila' (unaspirated) refers to the first and third consonants in the five groups (vagga). 'Dhanita' (aspirated) refers to the second and fourth consonants in those same groups. 'Dīgha' (long) refers to sounds like 'ā' which are pronounced for a long duration. 'Rassa' (short) refers to sounds like 'a' which are pronounced for half the duration of a long sound. 'Garuka' (heavy) refers to long vowels, or sounds pronounced before a conjunct consonant (saṃyoga), such as in "āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassa yassa nakkhamati." 'Lahuka' (light) refers to short vowels, or sounds pronounced without a following conjunct consonant, such as in "āyasmato buddharakkhitattherassa yassa na khamati." 'Niggahita' (nasalized) refers to the sound produced by pressing the vocal organs without releasing them, making a nasal sound with a closed mouth. 'Sambandha' (connected) refers to reciting by connecting with the following word, such as "tuṇhissā" or "tuṇhassā." 'Vavatthita' (distinct) refers to reciting by cutting off the connection with the following word, such as "tuṇhī assā" or "tuṇha assā." 'Vimutta' (released) refers to the sound produced without pressing the vocal organs, releasing them with an open mouth and without a nasal sound.
398:
Among those letters, in the place where 'Suṇātu me' should be said, changing the letter 'ta' to 'tha' and saying 'Suṇāthu me' is called making a sithila (unaspirated) letter into a dhanita (aspirated) one. Similarly, in the place where 'Pattakallaṃ esā ñattī' should be said, saying 'Patthakallaṃ esā ñatthī' etc., is also the same. In the place where 'Bhante saṅgho' should be said, changing the letters 'bha' and 'gha' to 'ba' and 'ga' and saying 'Bante saṅgo' is called making dhanita letters into sithila ones. In the place where 'Suṇātu me' should be said with an open mouth (vimutta), saying 'Suṇāntu me', or in the place where 'Esā ñattī' should be said, saying 'Esaṃ ñattī' without opening the mouth (opening only slightly) so that the niggahita sound is included, is called making a vimutta letter into a niggahita one. In the place where 'Pattakallaṃ' should be said with the mouth not open so that the niggahita sound is included, saying 'Pattakallā' with an open mouth without the niggahita sound is called making a niggahita letter into a vimutta one. Thus, these four types of letters—dhanita for sithila, sithila for dhanita, niggahita for vimutta, and vimutta for niggahita—ruin the legal act (kamma) within the kammavācā. One who speaks thus is said to be saying another letter instead of the intended one, and is said to be reciting poorly.

However, among the remaining six types of letters such as dīgha (long) and rassa (short), one should perform the kammavācā without destroying the traditional lineage by reciting the respective letters according to their proper places: dīgha where it is dīgha, and rassa where it is rassa. If, instead of doing so, one says rassa where dīgha should be said, or dīgha where rassa should be said; or similarly, lahu (light) where garu (heavy) should be said, or garu where lahu should be said; or if one says it separately where it should be connected (sambandha), or connected where it should be separated (vavatthita); even if said in this way, the kammavācā is not invalidated. These six types of letters do not ruin the legal act. Although the Elders who are masters of the Suttas say, 'The letter "da" becomes "ta", "ta" becomes "da", "ca" becomes "ja", "ja" becomes "ca", "ya" becomes "ka", and "ka" becomes "ya". Therefore, when "da" etc. should be said, saying "ta" etc. is not contradictory,' this statement is not appropriate when it comes to kammavācā. Therefore, a Vinaya-holder should not change "da" to "ta"... (etc.) nor "ka" to "ya". One should perform the kammavācā by checking the grammar as it exists in the Pāḷi text and avoiding the aforementioned faults through the ten-fold byañjana-nirutti (articulation of consonants). Otherwise, it is called a deficiency in the proclamation (sāvana).

Proclaiming at the wrong time means performing the anussāvana (proclamation) first without establishing the ñatti (motion) in a place or time where the proclamation should not be made (where there is no opportunity), and then establishing the ñatti afterwards. Thus, through these five ways, the legal acts fail because of the anussāvana.
399:
In the failure regarding the sīmā (boundary), a 'too small boundary' refers to a boundary that cannot accommodate 21 monks. In the Kurundī Commentary, it is stated, 'A boundary in which 21 monks are unable to sit.' Therefore, such a boundary, even if consecrated, is like an unconsecrated one and is just like village land. A legal act performed in that boundary fails. This same principle applies to the remaining boundaries.

Among these, a 'too large boundary' is one that is consecrated exceeding three yojanas, even by the breadth of a hair's tip. A 'broken-sign boundary' (khaṇḍanimittā) refers to a boundary where the marks are not connected. One should proclaim the mark in the east, then successively in the south, west, and north, and then again proclaim the first-mentioned mark in the east to establish it. Only then is it an 'unbroken-sign boundary' (akhaṇḍanimittā). If one brings them in order and proclaims the mark in the north but stops right there, it is a 'broken-sign boundary'.

Another type of 'broken-sign boundary' is one consecrated by making a single mark in between things that do not qualify as marks, such as a tree with bark and heartwood, a stump, a mound of earth, a mound of sand, or something else. A 'shadow-sign boundary' (chāyānimittā) is one consecrated by making any shadow, such as the shadow of a mountain, a mark. An 'unmarked boundary' (animittā) is one consecrated without proclaiming any marks at all. 'Consecrating a boundary while standing outside' means proclaiming the marks and then consecrating while standing outside of those marks.

Consecrating a boundary in a river, ocean, or natural lake means consecrating in those rivers, etc. Even if consecrated in that way, because of the word, 'Bhikkhus, all rivers are not boundaries, all oceans are not boundaries, all natural lakes are not boundaries,' it is indeed unconsecrated. 'Mixing a boundary with another boundary' means mixing one's own boundary with another's. 'Overlapping a boundary with another boundary' means overlapping one's own boundary with another's. The full details of how mixing and overlapping occur have already been stated in the Sīmākathā.

Thus, these eleven types of boundaries are not [valid] boundaries; they are just like village land. A legal act performed while sitting in those boundaries fails. Therefore, it is said, 'Through these eleven ways, the legal acts fail because of the boundary'.

In the failure of a legal act due to the assembly (parisa), there is nothing that is not clear. Regarding what should be said about the characteristics of one who has reached the legal act (kammappatta) and the characteristics of one who is eligible to give consent (chandāraha), it has already been stated later in the manner beginning with, 'Four monks who are pakaṭatta (in good standing) have reached the legal act.' In that statement, 'four monks who are pakaṭatta have reached the legal act' means that in a legal act to be performed by a group of four, the four monks are pakaṭatta, not suspended (anukkhittaka)...
400:
Four monks who have not been expelled and are pure in virtue are those who have reached the act (kamma-pattā). These monks are worthy of the act, suitable for it, and are the masters of the act. Without them, that act cannot be performed, nor can their consent (chanda) or purity (pārisuddhi) be taken. As for the remaining monks, even if there are as many as a thousand, if they belong to the same communion and are all entitled to give consent, whether they come after giving their consent and purity or not, the act remains valid. If the Saṅgha is performing an act such as probation (parivāsa) for a certain monk, that monk is neither one who has reached the act nor one entitled to give consent. However, because the Saṅgha performs the act based on that person as the subject, he is said to be 'worthy of the act' (kammāraha). The same principle applies to other acts.

The act of announcement (apalokana-kamma) applies to five cases. They are: reinstatement (osāraṇa), expulsion (nissāraṇa), shaving of the head (bhaṇḍukamma), the Brahma-punishment (brahmadaṇḍa), and the characteristic of the act (kammalakkhaṇa) as the fifth. Here, saying 'reinstatement and expulsion' is for the sake of smooth phrasing. In reality, expulsion comes first and reinstatement follows. In this context, the punishment and destruction of the novice Kaṇṭaka should be understood as expulsion. Therefore, at present, if a novice speaks dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, or points out what is unallowable as allowable, or is one of wrong view, or is possessed of a fixed wrong view (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi), that novice should be restrained up to three times and made to give up that view. If he does not give it up, the Saṅgha should be assembled and told, 'Give it up.' If he still does not give it up, a competent monk should perform the act of announcement and expel him. The act should be performed thus:

'Venerable Sirs, I ask the Saṅgha. This novice named so-and-so is a speaker of dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and is one of wrong view. While other novices receive the privilege of sharing a cell with monks for two or three nights, for the sake of his not receiving that privilege, does the Saṅgha approve of his expulsion?' Thus he asks a second time. A third time also, 'Venerable Sirs, I ask the Saṅgha. This novice named so-and-so... (as above)... does the Saṅgha approve?' Then he should be expelled, saying, 'Hey, outsider, go away, perish!'

If that novice later comes to apologize, saying, 'Venerable Sir, I did this out of foolishness, ignorance, and misfortune. I beg the Saṅgha's forgiveness,' he should be made to request it up to three times and then reinstated by the act of announcement itself. He should be reinstated thus: A competent monk in the midst of the Saṅgha, with the Saṅgha's permission, should make this announcement:
401:
'Venerable Sirs, I ask the Saṅgha. This novice named so-and-so was a speaker of dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and was one of wrong view. He was expelled so that he would not receive the privilege of sharing a cell with monks for two or three nights, which other novices receive. Now, he is calm, humble in conduct, has entered upon the state of shame, is established in moral shame and dread, has completed his punishment, and confesses his fault. Does the Saṅgha approve of granting this novice the harmony of physical association as before?' Thus it should be said three times. In this way, reinstatement (osāraṇa) and expulsion (nissāraṇa) are accomplished through the act of announcement. Shaving of the head (bhaṇḍukamma) should be understood as stated in the Discussion on the Decision for Ordination (Pabbajjāvinicchayakathā).

The Brahma-punishment (brahmadaṇḍa) was not prescribed for the Elder Channa alone. If any other monk is also harsh-spoken and lives harassing, reviling, and disparaging monks with abusive words, the Brahma-punishment should also be given to him. It should be given thus: A competent monk in the midst of the Saṅgha, with the Saṅgha's permission, should make this announcement:

'Venerable Sirs, this monk named so-and-so is harsh-spoken; he lives harassing, reviling, and disparaging monks with abusive words. Let that monk say whatever he wishes. This monk named so-and-so should not be spoken to, admonished, or instructed by the monks. Venerable Sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: Does the Saṅgha approve of giving the Brahma-punishment to the monk named so-and-so?' He asks a second time... a third time... 'Does the Saṅgha approve of giving the Brahma-punishment to the monk named so-and-so?' Thus the Brahma-punishment is given.

If that monk later conducts himself properly and apologizes, the Brahma-punishment should be settled. It should be settled thus: A competent monk should make this announcement in the midst of the Saṅgha:

'Venerable Sirs, the Saṅgha of monks gave the Brahma-punishment to the monk named so-and-so. That monk is now calm, humble in conduct, has reached the state of shame, and is established in moral shame and dread. Having reflected, he stands in future restraint. Venerable Sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: Does the Saṅgha approve of the settling of the Brahma-punishment for that monk?' Having said this up to three times, the Brahma-punishment should be settled by the act of announcement itself.
402:
The Blessed One spoke the words "Kammalakkhaṇaññeva pañcamaṃ" (the act-characteristic itself is the fifth) in the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka.

At that time, the Chabbaggiya monks, intending that the bhikkhunīs should truly fall in love with them, poured muddy water over them. They exposed their bodies and showed them to the bhikkhunīs; they exposed their thighs and showed them to the bhikkhunīs; they exposed their genitals and showed them to the bhikkhunīs. They addressed the bhikkhunīs with abusive language. Intending that the bhikkhunīs should truly fall in love with them, they sought to associate with them (Cūḷavagga, 411).

Regarding these incidents, the Buddha prescribed a dukkaṭa offense for those monks and said, "Monks, I authorize you to carry out a daṇḍakamma (punishment) against that monk." When doubt arose as to "What kind of daṇḍakamma should be carried out?", He authorized the avandiya-kamma (the act of making one not to be saluted) thus: "Monks, that monk should be made avandiya (one who is not to be saluted) by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha."

That kammalakkhaṇa (act-characteristic) itself is the fifth ground for this apalokanakamma (act of announcement). For that avandiya-kamma, the act itself is the identifying characteristic (lakkhaṇa). Characteristics such as osāraṇā (rehabilitation) and the like do not exist. Therefore, it is called "kammalakkhaṇa."

I shall describe the procedure for performing that avandiya-kamma in detail, along with its revocation. With the consent of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha assembled at the nunnery, a competent bhikkhunī should inform the Saṅgha and ask: "Venerable ladies, this venerable one named so-and-so shows unpleasant behavior to the bhikkhunīs. Do you agree to perform the avandiya-kamma against this venerable one?" She should ask and inform the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha a second time and a third time in the same manner. Having informed them three times, the avandiya-kamma should be performed by means of apalokanakamma.

From then on, that monk should not be saluted by the bhikkhunīs. If, while not being saluted, that monk establishes shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) and conducts himself well, he should ask for forgiveness from the bhikkhunīs. The monk seeking forgiveness should not go to the nunnery but, at his own monastery, approach the Saṅgha, a group, or a single monk. Sitting in a crouching position with joined palms raised, he should ask for forgiveness, saying: "Venerable sirs, having reflected with wisdom, I shall stand in restraint in the future. I will not show unpleasant behavior again. May the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha forgive me."

That Saṅgha or group should send a monk, or a single monk should go by himself, and say to the bhikkhunīs: "This monk, having reflected with wisdom, in the future..."
403:
"...standing in restraint, this monk has confessed his fault and has been forgiven by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. May the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha make this monk vandiya (worthy of salutation)." Thus it should be said. That monk should then be made vandiya. The procedure for doing so is as follows: With the consent of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha assembled at the nunnery, a competent bhikkhunī should inform the Saṅgha: "Venerable ladies, the venerable one named so-and-so was made avandiya by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha because he showed unpleasant behavior to the bhikkhunīs. That monk, having entered into a state of shame and having reflected, now stands in restraint. He has confessed his fault and has been forgiven by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. Do you agree to make that venerable one vandiya?" She should ask and inform the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha three times. Only by such an apalokanakamma is he made vandiya.

In this matter, the Pāḷimuttaka (extra-canonical) decision on kammalakkhaṇa is as follows: Although this kammalakkhaṇa was prescribed based on the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, it is also applicable to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. The apalokanakamma performed by the Bhikkhu Saṅgha during the distribution of meal-tickets (salākabhatta), in the Uposatha hall, and so on, is also kammalakkhaṇa.

For those whose robes have been stolen, lost, or burnt, it is proper to assemble the Saṅgha and, after a competent monk has informed them three times, give them robes by performing an apalokanakamma. However, a monk appointed as the distributor of minor items (appamattakavissajjaka) may give items such as needles, which are mentioned in the Paccayabhājanီya commentary, to a monk sewing robes without making a formal announcement. In giving such items, that monk alone has authority. If he wishes to give more than that, he must give it after making an announcement. This is because the Saṅgha is the owner when giving beyond that limit. Regarding medicine for the sick, he may give it himself according to the measures stated in that Paccayabhājanīya; if he wishes to give more, he must give it after making an announcement.

For a monk who is weak, disabled, unable to go for alms, or severely ill, if one wishes to give a nāḷi (measure) of rice or half a nāḷi daily, or five or ten nāḷis of rice on a single day from the produce of large monasteries, it should be given only after performing an apalokanakamma. It is also proper to give from the monastery's income for the debt-impediment (iṇapali-bodha) of a virtuous monk, to provide permanent lodgings to a learned monk who carries the burden of the Saṅgha, and to provide food and wages to lay attendants (kappiyakāraka) and others who perform duties for the Saṅgha, all by means of apalokanakamma.
404:
It is allowable to maintain a communal (Saṅghika) monastery with the income (accrued funds) donated through the four requisites.
