However, to cut off criticism such as 'This monk is managing things as if he were the owner,' one should maintain it only after asking the Saṅgha, either at the ticket-office shed etc., or at an interim meeting of the Saṅgha. Even from income specifically donated for robes and alms-food, one should maintain the monastery after asking; if one does so without asking, it is still allowable. However, to cut off criticism that might arise, such as 'How bold this monk is to maintain the monastery from items intended for robes and alms-food,' one should maintain it only after performing the act of announcement (apolokana-kamma).

A monk who wishes to build a new umbrella (chatta), a stone railing (vedikā), a Bodhi-tree house (bodhighara), or a pavilion (āsanaghara) at a Cetiya, or one who wishes to repair what is dilapidated or perform plasterwork, etc., it is allowable to do so by encouraging people. If there is no one to do it, it should be done from the specific fund (upanikkhepa) of the Cetiya. If that fund is also absent, it should be done from the monastery income after performing the act of announcement. It is also allowable to perform Cetiya duties with Saṅghika property after asking. It is not allowable to perform Saṅghika duties with property belonging to the Cetiya, even after asking. However, it is allowable to take it temporarily and repay it to its original state. Monks performing plasterwork etc. at a Cetiya, if they do not receive even enough for sustenance from alms-round or from the Saṅgha, it is allowable to take just enough for sustenance from the Cetiya's property and perform the Cetiya duties. It is not allowable to prepare a Saṅgha meal with fish, meat, etc., saying 'We are performing Cetiya duties.'

If fruit trees planted within the monastery grounds are taken possession of by the Saṅgha, they receive care. If the fruits of those trees are shared and consumed after striking a bell, no act of announcement (apolokana-kamma) needs to be performed regarding those trees. However, for trees not yet taken possession of, an act of announcement must be performed. It is allowable to perform that act of announcement at the ticket-office shed, the gruel shed, the dining hall, or at interim meetings; at the Uposatha hall, it is certainly allowable. This is because the consent and purity (chanda-pārisuddhi) of monks who cannot attend are brought to that Uposatha hall, making that act very pure. It should be done in this way: a wise monk, with the agreement of the Saṅgha, should announce as follows:

'Venerable Sirs, within this monastery and within the boundary (sīmā), there are roots, bark, leaves, sprouts, flowers, fruits, and edibles, etc., belonging to the Saṅgha. I ask the Saṅgha: is it agreeable to the Saṅgha that all these may be consumed as desired by monks who have arrived or will arrive?' Thus he should ask three times.
405:
An act performed by four or five monks is well-performed. In a monastery where two or three people reside, an act performed by them sitting together is also just like one performed by the Saṅgha. In a monastery where there is only one monk, the agreement (katikavatta) made by that monk while sitting after performing the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa-pubbakicca) on the Uposatha day is also just like one performed by the Saṅgha.

In making an agreement, it is allowable to do so by the turn of the fruit (phalavāra), or by defining a period such as four months, six months, or a whole year, or without defining a period. If a period is defined, one should consume according to the definition and then make the agreement again. If no period is defined, it is allowable for as long as the trees stand. If other trees are planted from the seeds of those trees, that same agreement applies to those trees as well.

If they are planted in another monastery, the Saṅgha in that monastery where they are planted is the owner. For trees planted later in the former monastery using seeds brought from another monastery, another agreement should be made; once the agreement is made, they stand as private property (puggalika), and it is allowable to consume the fruits etc. as desired. However, if in this monastery they enclose various areas, making enclosures (pariveṇa) and caring for them, they stand as the private property of those monks; others do not get to consume them. Those monks, however, should consume them after giving a tenth part to the Saṅgha. For a monk who protects a tree in the middle of the monastery by surrounding it with branches, the same method applies.

When a respected monk goes to a monastery with an old agreement, they bring large and small fruits, saying 'The Elder has arrived.' If a learned monk who bore the entire Pariyatti (scriptures) had lived there previously, one should consume without hesitation (kukkucca), thinking 'Surely a long-standing agreement must have been made here.' Large and small fruits in the monastery are also allowable for those who observe the alms-food eater's practice; it does not break the dhutaṅga. Novices (sāmaṇeras) give many fruits to their teachers and preceptors; if other monks complain because they do not receive any, that complaining is merely complaining. If there is a famine, and sixty people depend on a single jackfruit tree for their livelihood, at such a time, the fruit should be divided and eaten for the sake of supporting everyone. Such eating is proper conduct (sāmīci).

As long as the agreement (katikavatta) has not lapsed, what is eaten by those monks is well-eaten. When does an agreement lapse? When the unified Saṅgha assembles and announces, 'From today onwards, divide and eat,' then it lapses. In a monastery with only one monk, even if that monk makes the announcement, the previous agreement...
406:
The former agreement is indeed settled. If, after the agreement is settled, the novices (sāmaṇeras) do not drop fruits from the trees, nor pick them up from the ground to offer to the monks, but wander about kicking the fallen fruits with their feet, then a phātikamma (increase/benefit) should be made for those novices, ranging from a tenth share to a half share of the fruits. Surely, desiring to obtain the increase, they will bring and give them. When times of plenty return, and the kappiyakārakas (attendants) come to look after the trees by fencing them with branches and so on, the phātikamma should not be made for the novices; the fruits should be distributed and consumed.

If people from nearby villages come and ask, "Give us a coconut, give us a mango, give us a breadfruit," for the sake of the sick or pregnant women, saying "There are various fruits in the monastery," should they be given or not? They should be given. If not given, they become displeased. A monk who wishes to give should assemble the Saṅgha, inform them up to three times, and give only after performing an apalokana-kamma (act of announcement), or after establishing an agreement. It should be done like this: A competent monk, with the consent of the Saṅgha, should announce:

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. People from nearby villages come and ask for various fruits for the sick and others. Is it pleasing to the Saṅgha of monks that there be no prohibition for those taking two coconuts, two palm fruits, two jackfruits, five mangoes, or five bananas, and no prohibition for those taking fruits from such-and-such a tree?"

This should be said three times. From then on, those who ask in the name of the sick and others should not be told "Take them," but the rule should be explained: "A prohibition has been removed for those taking coconuts and so on in such a quantity, and for those taking fruits from such-and-such a tree." One should not go around looking and say, "This mango tree has sweet fruit; take from here."

At the time of fruit distribution, a monk appointed to distribute fruits should give a half-share (from the monks' portion) to those who arrive. If he is not appointed, he should give after informing the Saṅgha. If a traveler whose provisions are exhausted, a caravan leader, or some other official comes and asks, it should be given only after informing the Saṅgha. If they take and eat by force, they should not be prevented. For if angry, they might cut down the trees or cause other harm. To one who comes to a private cell (pariveṇa) and asks in the name of a sick person, it should be said: "We planted these for the sake of shade and so on; if there are any fruits, you know [what to do]." If the trees are laden with fruit, they might bind thorns and take them in turn. One should give without expectation of return. One who takes by force should not be prevented. The reason for this has been stated before. If it is a fruit orchard belonging to the Saṅgha but it lacks care, and if someone tends it based on duty (vatta), it remains the property of the Saṅgha. However, to a competent monk, [the Saṅgha says] "Good man, tend to this orchard and give [the produce]"...
407:
"We planted these for the sake of shade and so on; if there are any fruits, you know as well as we do," should be said. If the trees are laden with fruit, they might bind thorns and take them in turn. One should give without expectation of return. One who takes by force should not be prevented. The reason for not preventing them has been stated before.

If there is a fruit orchard belonging to the Saṅgha but it lacks care, and if someone tends it based on duty (vatta), it remains the property of the Saṅgha. Furthermore, if the Saṅgha entrusts a competent monk, saying, "Good man, tend to this orchard and give [the produce]," and that monk tends it based on duty, it still remains the property of the Saṅgha. However, for one who expects an increase (phātikamma), the phātikamma should be made with a third or a half share. If he is unwilling, saying "This work is heavy," then it should be said, "Make it all as if it were your own property, and tend it after giving a tenth share as the base portion." However, because it is garubhaṇḍa (heavy property), it should not be given by way of total alienation (mūlacchijja). If that monk, while eating and giving the tenth share, tends to it by building an unbuilt dwelling or maintaining a built one, and then hands over the orchard to his dependents, those dependents must also give the tenth share to the Saṅgha.

When the monks themselves are able to tend it, it should not be given to [outside] monks to tend. They should not be stopped when it is time for fruiting, but only at the time they are about to start tending. It should be said, "You have consumed much; do not tend it now, the Saṅgha of monks will tend it themselves." If there is no one tending based on duty, nor by phātikamma, and the Saṅgha is unable to tend it, and a single monk tends it without asking and increases the phātikamma with expectation, it should be given only after increasing the phātikamma through an apalokana-kamma. Thus, all this is of the nature of a legal act (kammalakkhaṇa). The apalokana-kamma applies to these five instances.

## Regarding the distinctions of the stations of Nattikamma (Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā 495-496):

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This person named so-and-so is the candidate for ordination of the venerable so-and-so. He has been instructed by me. If it is the right time for the Saṅgha, let so-and-so come. He should be told, 'Come.'" This introduction of a candidate for ordination is called Osāraṇā.
408:
“Venerable sirs, may you listen to me. This monk named so-and-so is a Dhamma-speaker. He knows neither the Sutta nor the Suttavibhaṅga. Without noting the meaning, he rejects the meaning by following the mere shadow of the letter. If it is suitable for the venerable ones, having removed the monk named so-and-so, let the remaining monks settle this legal issue.” This removal of a Dhamma-speaker monk in an ubbāhika decision is called nissāraṇā.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth-day Uposatha. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha.” A motion set forth by the power of the Uposatha act in this way is called uposatha.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Pavāraṇā.” A motion set forth by the power of the Pavāraṇā act in this way is called pavāraṇā.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so is the candidate for higher ordination of the venerable one named so-and-so. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I shall instruct the monk named so-and-so,” or “If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the monk named so-and-so instruct the monk named so-and-so,” or “If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I shall question the monk named so-and-so regarding the obstructive factors,” or “If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the monk named so-and-so question the monk named so-and-so regarding the obstructive factors,” or “If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I shall question the monk named so-and-so regarding the Vinaya,” or “If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the monk named so-and-so question the monk named so-and-so regarding the Vinaya,” or “If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I shall answer when questioned regarding the Vinaya by the monk named so-and-so,” or “If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the monk named so-and-so answer when questioned regarding the Vinaya by the monk named so-and-so.” A motion set forth to authorize oneself or another in this way is called sammuti.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. This robe of the monk named so-and-so is to be forfeited and has been forfeited to the Saṅgha. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe to the monk named so-and-so.”
409:
“If it is suitable for the venerable ones, let the venerable ones give this robe to the monk named so-and-so.” The giving of forfeited robes, bowls, and so on in this way is called dāna.

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. This monk named so-and-so remembers, reveals, makes manifest, and confesses an offense. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I shall accept the offense of the monk named so-and-so,” or “If it is suitable for the venerable ones, I shall accept the offense of the monk named so-and-so.” The monk accepting the offense should ask, “Do you see [the offense]?” [The other] should answer, “Yes, I see it.” [The first] should say, “Restrain yourself in the future.” This acceptance of an offense is called paṭiggaha.

“Venerable resident monks, may you listen to me. If it is suitable for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha, recite the Pātimokkha, and perform the Pavāraṇā in the coming dark fortnight.”

Monks, if those monks are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of idle talk, and makers of legal issues in the Saṅgha, and they live together at that time, a wise and competent resident monk should inform the resident monks:

“Venerable resident monks, may you listen to me. If it is suitable for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha, recite the Pātimokkha, and perform the Pavāraṇā in the coming bright fortnight.” This drawing back of the Pavāraṇā performed in this way is called paccukkaḍḍhanā.

All monks should assemble together. Having assembled, a wise and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:

“Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me. While we have been living in strife, in quarrel, and in dispute, many practices unbecoming of a recluse have been committed and many unbecoming words have been spoken. If we were to deal with one another regarding these offenses, that legal issue might lead to harshness, to violence, and to schism. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha...”
410: "The Saṅgha should settle this legal issue by the settlement of covering with grass (tiṇavatthāraka), excluding grave offenses (thullaccaya) and those connected with the laity." In this way, when performing the settlement of covering with grass, the motion (ñatti) which is the very first and all-inclusive is called the characteristic of the act (kammalakkhaṇa). Likewise, the two motions performed individually for each group thereafter, as well as the aforementioned varieties of inclusion (osāraṇa), exclusion (nissāraṇa), and so forth, are also merely characteristics of the act; thus, the ninth motion-act (ñattikamma) reaches these nine instances. Regarding the varieties of the motion-and-second-proclamation act (ñattidutiyakamma), however, the exclusion (nissāraṇa) mentioned in the Khandhaka by way of turning over the bowl (pattanikkujjana) for the Licchavī Vaddha, and the inclusion (osāraṇa) mentioned in the Khandhaka by way of turning the bowl upright (pattukkujjana) for that same person, should be understood. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, the bowl should be turned over for a lay follower who is possessed of eight factors. (What are the eight?) He strives for the monks' non-gain, he strives for the monks' harm, he strives for the monks' non-residence, he reviles and abuses monks, he causes dissension among monks, he speaks in dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks in dispraise of the Dhamma, he speaks in dispraise of the Saṅgha. Monks, I allow the turning over of the bowl for a lay follower possessed of these eight factors. And thus, monks, should it be turned over. A wise and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha: 'Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The Licchavī Vaddha is defaming the venerable Dabba Mallaputta with a groundless charge of a breach of morality. If it seems right to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should turn over the bowl of the Licchavī Vaddha, making him one with whom there is no communion with the Saṅgha. This is the motion. Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The Licchavī Vaddha is defaming the venerable Dabba Mallaputta with a groundless charge of a breach of morality. The Saṅgha turns over the bowl of the Licchavī Vaddha and makes him one with whom there is no communion with the Saṅgha. Whichever venerable one approves of the turning over of the bowl of the Licchavī Vaddha...'"
411:
"...and making him one with whom there is no communion with the Saṅgha, let him be silent. Whichever venerable one does not approve, he should speak. The bowl of the Licchavī Vaddha has been turned over by the Saṅgha; he is one with whom there is no communion with the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this act."

Monks, the bowl should be turned upright for a lay follower who is possessed of eight factors: (1) he does not strive for the monks' non-gain, (2) he does not strive for the monks' harm... (8) he does not speak in dispraise of the Saṅgha. Monks, I allow the turning upright of the bowl for a lay follower possessed of these eight factors.

And thus, monks, should it be turned upright. Monks, that Licchavī Vaddha should approach the Saṅgha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the monks, sit on his heels, join his palms in salutation, and should speak thus:

"Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha turned over my bowl; I am one with whom there is no communion with the Saṅgha. Venerable sirs, I am behaving properly, I am lowering my pride, I am practicing for release from the fault, I ask the Saṅgha for the turning upright of the bowl."

A second time he should ask. A third time he should ask.

A wise and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:

"Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The bowl of the Licchavī Vaddha was turned over by the Saṅgha; he was made one with whom there is no communion with the Saṅgha. That Licchavī Vaddha is behaving properly, he is lowering his pride, he is practicing for release from the fault, and he asks the Saṅgha for the turning upright of the bowl. If it seems right to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should turn the bowl of the Licchavī Vaddha upright and make him one with whom there is communion with the Saṅgha. This is the motion.

Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. The bowl of the Licchavī Vaddha was turned over by the Saṅgha; he was made one with whom there is no communion with the Saṅgha. That Licchavī Vaddha is behaving properly, he is lowering his pride, he is practicing for release from the fault, and he asks the Saṅgha for the turning upright of the bowl. The Saṅgha turns the bowl of the Licchavī Vaddha upright and makes him one with whom there is communion with the Saṅgha. Whichever venerable one approves of the turning upright of the bowl of the Licchavī Vaddha..."
412:
If a venerable one approves of the act of non-association with the Saṅgha, he should remain silent. If he does not approve, he should speak.

"The Saṅgha has turned over the bowl for the Licchavi prince Vaḍḍha; non-association with the Saṅgha has been established. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this act."

In this act of turning over the bowl (according to Cūḷavagga Commentary 265), it is permissible to perform the act of pattanikkujjana (turning over the bowl) against a donor who is endowed with even one of the eight factors. It is permissible to turn over the bowl either within the boundary (sīmā) or by going outside the boundary to places such as a river. When the bowl has been turned over in this way, no gift should be accepted from that donor's house. Other monasteries should also be informed, "Do not accept alms-food at the house of such-and-such a donor."

However, at the time of turning the bowl upright (pattaukkujjana), the donor must be made to apologize up to three times. After having him move away from the forearm's length (hatthapāsa), the bowl should be turned upright by an act consisting of a motion and one resolution (ñattidutiya-kamma).

Designation (sammuti) should be understood by way of these designations: the designation of a boundary (sīmā), the designation of not being parted from the three robes (ticīvara-avippavāsa), the designation of a rug (santhata), and the designations of a meal-allocator, a lodging-assigner, a storekeeper, a robe-receiver, a robe-distributor, a congee-distributor, a snack-distributor, a fruit-distributor, a disposer of minor items, an undergarment-receiver, a bowl-receiver, a monastery-attendant-director, and a novice-director. Giving (dāna) should be understood by way of giving Kathina robes and giving the robes of a deceased monk. Removal (uddhāra) should be understood by way of the removal of Kathina. Instruction (desanā) should be understood by way of the instruction on hut sites and monastery sites. Regarding the settlement as if covering with grass (tiṇavatthāraka-samatha), excluding the three motions—one motion that covers all offenses and one motion for each side—two ñattidutiya-kammavācā are recited, one for each side. The legal mark of the act should be understood by way of those motions. Thus, the ñattidutiya-kamma applies to these seven areas.

Regarding the different areas of the act consisting of a motion and three resolutions (ñatticatuttha-kamma), expulsion (nissāraṇā) should be understood by way of the seven acts such as the act of censure (tajjaniya-kamma), and reinstatement (osāraṇā) should be understood by way of the settling of those same acts. Designation (sammuti) should be understood by way of the designation of the exhorter of nuns. Giving (dāna) should be understood by way of giving probation (parivāsa) and giving penance (mānatta). Restraint (niggaha) should be understood by way of the act of sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassana). Exhortation (samanubhāsana) should be understood by way of these eleven exhortations: the follower of an expelled monk, the eight types requiring three warnings, Ariṭṭha, and Caṇḍakāḷီ. The legal mark of the act should be understood by way of the act of ordination (upasampadā) and the act of rehabilitation (abbhāna). Thus, the ñatticatuttha-kamma applies to these...
413:
...seven areas. In this way, the acts (kamma), the failure of acts (kammavipatti), the definition of the Saṅgha who performs those acts, and the different applications of acts free from failure should be understood.

414:
## 34. Pakiṇṇakavinicchayakathā
Now, the discussion concerning miscellaneous decisions should be understood. Regarding the statement, "Except for [certain] occasions, there is a pācittiya offense for a group meal (gaṇabhojana)," gaṇabhojana arises in two ways: through request (viññatti) or through invitation (nimantana). How does it arise through request? If four monks, while standing or sitting together, see a lay devotee (upāsaka) and request, "Give food to the four of us," or seeing him individually, request, "Give to me, give to me," whether requesting together or separately, and whether they go together or separately, and whether they eat together or separately after receiving the food—if they receive it together, it is a gaṇabhojana; there is an offense for all of them. In this matter, the act of receiving (paṭiggahaṇa) alone is the standard. Thus, it arises through request.

How does it arise through invitation? Approaching four monks, one invites them with any synonym or in another language, mentioning the names of the five types of meals, saying, "Venerable sirs, I invite you with rice; please receive my rice, desire it, look at it, accept it, or welcome it." Monks thus invited together, if they go together, receive together, and eat together today or tomorrow according to the specified time, it is a gaṇabhojana; there is an offense for all. If monks invited together go together or separately, receive together, and eat together or separately, there is still an offense. If monks invited together go together or separately, receive separately, and eat together or separately, there is no offense. Whether one goes to four precincts or to a monastery and is invited separately, or even while standing in one place, one is invited by the son and another by the father—thus being invited separately—whether they go together or separately, and eat together or separately, if they receive together, it is a gaṇabhojana; there is an offense for all. Thus, it arises through invitation.

Therefore, if someone sent to invite for a Sangha meal (saṅghabhatta) comes to the monastery and, instead of saying, "Venerable sir, please receive almsfood (bhikkha) at our house tomorrow," says, "Please receive rice (bhatta)," or "Please receive Sangha-rice," or "May the Sangha receive rice," the meal-assigner (bhattuddesaka) should be a wise person.
415:
Monks who accept invitations should be freed from the fault of gaṇabhojana, and monks who observe the alms-collector's practice (piṇḍapātika dhutanga) should be freed from the breaking of that practice. How are they to be freed? First, it should be said, "Lay devotees, it is not possible tomorrow." If they ask, "Venerable sir, what about the day after tomorrow?" it should be said, "It is still not possible the day after tomorrow." In this way, after delaying even for half a month, one should ask again, "What did you say?" If he says again, "Please receive the Sangha meal," then one should create a diversion by saying, "Layman, first make this flower allowable (kappiya), make this grass allowable," and then ask again, "What did you say?" If he says the same thing again, it should be said, "Friend, you will not get the alms-collecting monks or the elder senior monks; you will only get novices." If he says, "Venerable sir, did they not feed the venerable ones in such and such villages? Why do I not get them?" it should be said, "Those villagers know how to invite; you do not know how to invite." If he asks, "Venerable sir, how did they invite?" it should be said, "They said, 'Venerable sirs, please receive our almsfood (bhikkha).'" If that donor also says the same, it is allowable.

If he says again, "Please receive rice (bhatta)," it should be said, "Friend, now you will not get many monks; friend, you will only get three." If he says, "Venerable sir, did they not feed the entire Sangha of monks in such and such villages? Why do I not get them?" it should be said, "You do not know how to invite." If he asks, "Venerable sir, how did they invite?" it should be said, "They said, 'Venerable sirs, please receive our almsfood (bhikkha).'" If that donor also says the same, "Please receive almsfood," it is allowable. If he says again, "Only rice (bhatta)," then it should be said, "Go away, we have no need for your rice; this [layman's house] is our regular place for collecting alms; we will wander for alms here." When that donor says, "Venerable sirs, please wander," and returns, people ask, "O layman, did you get the monks?" What is the use of such asking? The words spoken here are many. The elders have said, "We will wander for alms tomorrow"; now do not be negligent. On the second day, after performing the duties at the shrine (cetiya-vatta), the Sangha Elder should say to the monks standing there, "Friends, there is a Sangha meal in the nearby village, but an unwise man has gone back; come, let us wander for alms in the nearby village." The monks should follow the words of the elder; they should not be difficult to speak to (dubbaca). They should wander for alms without just standing at the village gate. When those people take the bowls, make them sit, and feed them, they should eat.

If they place the food in the meal-hall and, wandering in the streets, announce, "Venerable sirs, please receive the food in the meal-hall," it is not allowable. But if they say, "Taking the food, go to various places and receive the food,"
416:
First, having brought [the alms] to the monastery and placed them in a suitable location, they give them to whichever monks arrive; such alms are called abhihaṭa-bhikkhā, and it is allowable to eat them. If, however, they prepare an offering at the refectory and send word to various precincts (pariveṇa) saying, 'Please receive alms at the refectory,' it is allowable. When people see monks wandering for alms, sweep the sitting hall, seat them there, and feed them, they should not be refused. When people see monks who, having failed to obtain alms in the village, are departing from the village, and say, 'Venerable sirs, please receive alms,' they should be refused; one should not turn back. If they say, 'Venerable sirs, please turn back and receive alms,' it is allowable to turn back because of the word 'turn back.' If they say, 'Venerable sirs, please turn back; food has been prepared at the house, food has been prepared in the village,' it is allowable to turn back because food at a house or in a village is usually intended for someone or other. If they speak by connecting the words, 'Turn back and receive alms,' it is not allowable to turn back. The same method applies when they see monks departing from the sitting hall to wander for alms and say, 'Venerable sirs, please sit down and receive alms.'

According to the words 'aññatra samayā' (except on [certain] occasions), there is no offense on any of these seven occasions: the time of illness (gilāna-samaya), the time of robe-giving (cīvara-dāna-samaya), the time of robe-making (cīvara-kāra-samaya), the time of traveling (addhāna-gamana-samaya), the time of embarking on a boat (nāvābhiruhana-samaya), the time of a great assembly (mahā-samaya), and the time of a meal for ascetics (samaṇabhatta-samaya). Therefore, when the flesh is visible from outside the thick skin, or at the very least, the soles of the feet are cracked, and even the mere touch of sand or gravel causes pain, and one is unable to wander for alms within the village—in such a state of illness, one should eat, regarding it as the time of illness; one should not make a pretense of illness.

The 'time of robe-giving' means the last month of the rainy season (the month of Tazaungmon) if the kaṭhina has not been spread; if the kaṭhina has been spread, it is five months. During this period, one should eat, regarding it as the 'time of robe-giving.' When the robe is being made, one should eat, regarding it as the 'time of robe-making.' When, having obtained cloth and thread, they make a robe, this is called the 'time of robe-making'; there is no separate 'time of robe-making' [other than this]. Therefore, a monk who performs any task that should be done for that robe [may eat]; in the Mahāpaccarī, it is said, 'even if he is one who only performs needlework.' That monk should eat, regarding it as the 'time of robe-making.' In the Kurundī, however, it is stated in detail: 'One who prepares the robe, cuts it, sets the basting threads, sets the outer layer, sews the seams, joins the outer layer, the border...'
417:
...cutting, joining, or setting [the cloth]; and in those robe-tasks, sewing the seams, twisting the thread, sharpening the small knife, or turning the small knife—all such persons are called 'robe-makers' (cīvara-kāraka). If a monk sits nearby and preaches a Jātaka or the Dhammapada, he is not called a robe-maker. Excepting that preaching monk, there is no offense in a group meal (gaṇabhojana) for the remaining monks who are making the robe.

At the time of traveling, even a monk who wishes to travel at least half a yojana may eat, having resolved, 'I will travel half a yojana.' A monk who is currently traveling may eat. A monk who has arrived after traveling may eat for one day.

At the time of embarking on a boat, one may eat, having resolved, 'I will embark on a boat.' A monk who has embarked may eat until he disembarks, even after reaching his desired destination. A monk who has disembarked may eat for one day.

The 'great assembly' (mahā-samaya) refers to a time when two or three monks can subsist by wandering for alms, but when at least a fourth monk arrives, they cannot subsist. This is called a great assembly. When a hundred or a thousand monks assemble, there is no need to even mention [the insufficiency]. Therefore, at such a time, one should eat, having resolved in mind, 'This is a great assembly.'

The 'time of a meal for ascetics' (samaṇabhatta-samaya) is when someone who has attained the status of an ascetic gives a meal. Therefore, in a meal given by any one of the five classes of co-religionists or by any one of the titthiyas, one should eat, having resolved, 'This is the time of a meal for ascetics.' Since it is stated in the Vinaya Pali: 'There is no offense during the [specified] times; two or three eating together; gathering and eating together after wandering for alms; constant meals, ticket-food, fortnightly meals, Uposatha meals, and meals on the first day of the fortnight—excepting the five [types of] meals, there is no offense in all [these] cases,' there is no offense for those monks even if they accept an unallowable invitation (akappiya-nimantana) and eat together as two or three.

Regarding that group meal, the decision should be known by way of the five types of 'fourth persons': the uninvited fourth (animantita-catuttha), the alms-collector fourth (piṇḍပါတika-catuttha), the novice fourth (sāmaṇera-catuttha), the bowl-sender fourth (pattacatuttha), and the sick fourth (gilāna-catuttha). How? Here, a lay devotee invites four monks, saying, 'Please receive a meal.' Among them, three go, but one does not go. The lay devotee asks, 'Venerable sir, where is the one elder?' When told, 'Lay devotee, he did not come,' that lay devotee invites another monk who has just arrived at that moment, saying, 'Come, venerable sir,' and having brought him into the house, offers the meal to all four.
418:
He gives the alms-food; there is no offense for any of the monks. Why? Because the monk who completes the group (gaṇapūraka) was not invited. Only three monks were invited there and they accepted the alms-food; the group is not completed by those three, and the one who completes the group was not invited, therefore the group is broken. This is the case of the 'uninvited fourth' regarding the meal.

In the case of the 'alms-collector (piṇḍapātika) as the fourth', at the time of invitation, one monk is an alms-collector; he does not accept the invitation. However, at the time of going, when it is said, 'Come, Bhante,' even though he does not wish to come because he did not accept the invitation, they take him along saying, 'Come, you will receive alms-food.' That alms-collector monk breaks the group; therefore, there is no offense for any of them.

In the case of the 'novice (sāmaṇera) as the fourth', they are invited together with a novice; that novice also breaks the group.

In the case of the 'bowl as the fourth', one monk does not come himself but sends only his bowl; even in this way, the group is broken, and therefore there is no offense for any of them.

In the case of the 'sick monk (gilāna) as the fourth', they are invited together with a sick monk; in that case, there is no offense only for the sick monk, but for the other three, the group is completed. The group is not broken by a sick monk; therefore, there is an offense for those three monks. However, in the Mahāpaccariya, it is stated generally without distinction: 'The one who obtains the allowance (samaya) is himself exempt; for the others, because he is the fourth who completes the group, he causes them to incur an offense.' Therefore, the groups of four should also be understood by way of those who obtain the allowance at the time of robe-giving (cīvaradāna-samaya) and so on.

If, among the four monks who have gone after accepting an invitation, one wise monk says, 'I will protect your group; accept the invitation,' and at the end of consuming the gruel and snacks, when they take their bowls for the main meal, he does not give his bowl but remains seated saying, 'Feed these monks first and let them go; I will follow after performing the appreciation (anumodanā).' When those monks have eaten and left, the lay devotee says, 'Bhante, please give me the bowl,' and taking the bowl, he offers the meal; if the monk eats and then goes after performing the appreciation, there is no offense for any of them. The reason is that in the case of a group meal (gaṇabhojana), there is no deviation (visanketa) except by way of the five kinds of soft food; even if invited with cooked rice but they accept another kind of grain (kummāsa), they incur an offense. Furthermore, those foods were not taken by them together at the same time. However, with gruel and such, there is deviation; those were taken by them together at the same time. In this way, one wise monk can cause other monks to be free from offense. 'Niccabhatta' refers to a meal that is permanently established; if it is said, 'Please accept the regular meal (niccabhatta),' it is allowable for many to accept it together. The same method applies to ticket-food (salākabhatta) and so on.
419:
It is stated: 'In the case of an out-of-turn meal (parambarabhojana), except on the proper occasion (samaya), there is an offense of confession (pācittiya).' An out-of-turn meal arises only because of an invitation. If a monk is invited with the words, 'Please accept a meal with any one of the five kinds of soft food,' and setting aside that meal, he eats another of the five kinds of soft food, this meal is called an 'out-of-turn meal' for that monk. For a monk eating in this way, a pācittiya offense is declared for times other than the occasion of sickness (gilāna-samaya), the time of robe-giving (cīvaradāna-samaya), and the time of robe-making (cīvarakāra-samaya). Therefore, one should eat only according to the order of invitation, not out of order.

According to the statement, 'Monks, I allow you to eat an out-of-turn meal after making an assignment (vikappanā),' it is allowable to eat the first-invited meal after assigning it to another monk. This assignment (vikappanā) is allowable whether in the presence or in the absence [of the other]. If seeing [the other] in person, one should eat after saying, 'I assign my expectation of a meal to you,' or 'I give it to you.' If not seeing [the other] in person, one should eat after mentioning the name of any one of the five classes of co-religionists (sahadhammika) and saying, 'I assign my expectation of a meal to such-and-such a person,' or 'I give it to you.' It is allowable to put the meals from two or three invitations into a single bowl, mix them, and eat them as one. For it is stated: 'There is no offense if one eats two or three invitations together.' If many households invite and seat the monks in one place, and they bring and pour rice and curries from here and there so that it becomes mixed as one, here too there is no offense.

However, if the original invited meal is at the bottom and the subsequent invited meals are on top, there is an offense for the monk who eats starting from the top. But if he puts his hand into the bowl, takes out even one morsel from the first-invited meal and eats it, from that time onwards, there is no offense regardless of how he eats. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya: 'If they pour milk or broth into that meal so that the meal drenched with milk etc. becomes of a single taste, there is no offense for the monk who eats starting from the edge.' In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated: 'If others pour milk-rice or broth-rice into the meal of a monk who is seated having received milk-rice or broth-rice, there is no offense for the monk who drinks the milk or broth; the monk who eats should first put a piece of meat or a lump of rice from what was first received into his mouth, and then it is allowable to eat starting from the edge. The same method applies to ghee-rice-milk (sappipāyāsa).'
420:
A great lay devotee invites a monk. When the monk arrives at that devotee's house, the devotee himself, as well as his son, wife, brothers, sisters, and others, bring their respective portions and place them in the bowl. It is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā: "For a monk who eats food received later without first eating the food offered by the lay devotee first, there is an offense." However, in the Kurundī commentary, it is stated: "It is allowable." In the Mahāpaccari, it is stated: "If they cook separately and bring offerings from their own cooked portions, then for a monk who eats the food brought later before the food brought first among those offerings, there is a Pācittiya offense. However, if there is only one cooking for everyone, it does not constitute paramparabhojana (consecutive meals)." 

If the great lay devotee invites and has the monk sit, and another person takes the bowl, it should not be given. If asked, "Venerable sir, why do you not give it?", one should say, "Lay devotee, have you not invited me?" If the devotee says, "Let it be, venerable sir, please eat whatever is received," then it is allowable to eat. It is stated in the Kurundī text: "It is also allowable to eat food brought and offered by another person after asking [permission]." 

When a monk is leaving after giving a blessing (anumodanā), if everyone invites him, wishing to hear the Dhamma, saying, "Venerable sir, please come tomorrow as well," then it is allowable to come the next day and eat whatever is received. Why? Because he was invited by everyone. If a monk, while wandering for alms, receives food and then another lay devotee invites him and has him sit in his house, but that devotee's food is not yet ready; if that monk eats the food he received from his alms-round, there is an offense. While sitting without eating, if asked, "Venerable sir, why do you not eat?", and he says, "Because I was invited by you," and then the devotee says, "Venerable sir, please eat whatever is received," then it is allowable to eat. 

For a monk invited by the entire village acting as one, there is no offense regardless of where he eats in that village. The same rule applies to a group (pūga). It is stated: "There is no offense if a monk invited by the entire village eats anywhere in that village; if a monk invited by a group eats anywhere among that group; if, while being invited, he says, 'I will take alms'; and in the case of regular meals (niccabhatta), ticket-food (salākabhatta), fortnightly meals (pakkhika), Uposatha meals (uposathika), and meals on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipadika), excluding the five kinds of meals, there is no offense in all [these] cases." 

Among those, regarding the phrase "while being invited, he says, 'I will take alms'": if a monk, being invited with "Please accept food," says, "I have no need for your food, I will take alms," it means there is no offense. In this matter, Mahāpaduma Thera said: "A monk speaking thus is able to make it a non-invitation regarding this training rule; however, permission has already been given for eating. Therefore, he is not exempt from gaṇabhojana (group meals) nor from cāritta (itinerary among families)."
421:
Mahāpaduma Thera stated: "Because permission has been given for the purpose of eating, he is not exempt from gaṇabhojana nor from cāritta." Mahāsuma Thera, however, stated: "By whatever means one is able to make it a non-invitation, by that means it becomes neither gaṇabhojana nor cāritta." 

In that context, cāritta refers to: "Should any monk, being invited and being provided with a meal, not having informed a monk who is present, go on an itinerary among families (visiting houses) either before the meal or after the meal, except at the proper time, it is a Pācittiya. Herein, the proper time is the time of robe-giving, the time of robe-making. This is the proper time." This refers to the Cāritta-sikkhāpada as it appears [in the Vinaya]. 

By this training rule, a monk who is invited with one of the five kinds of meals through an improper invitation (akappiya-nimantana) such as "Accept the meal," and while having that invited meal, without informing a present monk with words such as "I am going to the house of such-and-such a lay devotee" or "I am going on an itinerary," whether he has eaten that meal or not, if he enters other family houses besides the one where he was invited within the morning period (before noon), it is stated as a Pācittiya offense for that monk, except for the two kinds of "times" (seasons) with the stated characteristics. Therefore, if while being invited with an improper invitation, he says, "I will take alms," there is no offense by this training rule either. 

Regarding the phrase "without informing a monk who is present (santa)": to what extent is one "present" (santa) and to what extent is one "absent" (asanta)? While staying within the monastery, at the place where the intention to visit families arises, from that point onwards, a monk who is seen either at one's side or directly in front, and who can be informed with a normal voice, is called a "present" (santa) monk. There is no duty to search here and there to inform. One who must be searched for in such a way is indeed "absent" (asanta). Furthermore, if one sees a monk within the precincts of the monastery and goes with the thought "I will inform him," then the monk whom he sees must be informed. If he does not see anyone, he is considered to have entered without informing a present monk. The same method applies to entering a village at the wrong time (after noon).
422:
If many monks enter a village for some business, all must ask permission from one another, saying, "I ask permission to enter the village at an improper time." If the business is not completed in that village and they go to another village, even if it be a hundred villages, there is no need to ask permission again. However, if they have finished their effort and are returning to the monastery, but wish to enter another village on the way, they must ask permission again. If, after finishing a meal at a layperson's house or a rest house, a monk wishes to wander for alms of oil or ghee, and if there is a monk nearby, he should ask permission before going. If there is no monk, he should go thinking, "There is no monk to ask." If he sees a monk after descending to the street, there is no need to ask; he may wander without asking. If there is a road through the middle of a village, and while traveling on it, the thought arises, "I will wander for alms of oil, etc.," he should ask permission if a monk is nearby. But for a monk wandering for alms without leaving the road, there is no need to ask. If a lion or tiger comes, or a rainstorm arises, or any other danger occurs, in such emergencies, it is allowable to enter the village from outside without asking permission.

According to the words, "Monks, a refuse-heap robe (paṃsukūla) should not be taken from a body that is not broken; whoever should take it, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa)," one should not take a refuse-heap robe from a fresh, moist body; if one takes it, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing. Dangers may also befall that monk. However, it is allowable to take it from a broken body.

To what extent is it considered "broken"? It is called broken even if it is slightly torn by the beak or fangs of crows, hawks, dogs, jackals, etc. If only the outer skin is grazed due to a fall but the thick skin is not torn, it is called "unbroken"; it is "broken" only when the thick skin is torn. If there are boils, leprosy, pustules, or wounds that were present while alive, this body is also called "broken." From the third day onwards, a body that has reached the state of a corpse through swelling, etc., is also considered broken. Even if it is entirely unbroken, it is allowable to have cemetery keepers or other people take it. If no one else is available, one should take it after making a wound with a small knife or something else. If it is a female body, one should establish mindfulness, perceive her as a recluse (samaṇa-saññā), and take it after making a wound on the head or the back of the hands or feet.
423:
How should a monk whose robes have been snatched away by thieves conduct himself? "Monks, I allow a monk whose robes have been snatched away or whose robes are lost to ask for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative. At the first residence he reaches, if there is a monastery robe, an upper cover, a floor covering, or a mattress cover belonging to the Saṅgha, he is allowed to take and wear it, thinking, 'I will return it when I obtain a robe.' If there is no monastery robe, upper cover, floor covering, or mattress cover belonging to the Saṅgha, he should come covered with grass or leaves; he should not come naked. If he should come so, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa)." According to these words, he should conduct himself in the manner stated here.

The sequential explanation here is as follows: If, upon seeing thieves, junior monks run away taking their bowls and robes, and the thieves take only the inner and outer robes worn by the senior monks and leave, the senior monks should not yet ask for robes, nor should they break off branches and leaves. If the junior monks run away abandoning all their bundles, and the thieves take the clothes worn by the senior monks as well as the bundles of robes abandoned by the junior monks, the junior monks, upon returning, should not yet give their own inner and outer robes to the senior monks. This is because those junior monks, not being those whose robes were snatched, do not have permission to break branches and leaves for themselves, but they do have permission to do so for the sake of those whose robes were snatched. Only those whose robes were snatched have the right to break branches and leaves for themselves and for others. Therefore, the senior monks should break branches and leaves, bind them with fibers, etc., and give them to the junior monks; or the junior monks should break and bind branches and leaves for the senior monks and, after giving them into their hands or without giving them, wear them themselves and then give their own inner and outer robes to the senior monks. By doing so, there is no pācittiya offense for destroying vegetation (bhūtagāma), nor is there a dukkhaṭa offense for wearing those leaves.

If there are cloths of washermen on the way, or if they see other people with many such clothes, they should ask for a robe. Clothes given by people who, seeing the monks wearing leaves because their robes were snatched, are inspired with faith—whether those clothes have fringes or not, whether they are of various colors like blue, etc., whether they are allowable or unallowable—all are allowable to be worn and used because the monks are in the position of those whose robes have been snatched.
424:
This has also been stated in the Parivāra: 'One may go wherever one wishes wearing a garment that has not been marked with a kappabindu nor dyed with dye; there is no offense for that monk. This Dhamma was taught by the Sugata; this problem has been considered by those skilled in the Vinaya.' (Pari. 481).

This problem is stated with reference to a monk whose robes have been stolen by robbers. Furthermore, if they encounter sectarians (titthiyas) and they offer garments made of kusa grass, bark, or wooden planks, it is allowable to wear them without adopting their views; even when wearing them, their views must not be adopted.

At the first residence reached, one is allowed to take whatever is available among the communal robes and so forth, even without asking, to wear or dress in. In taking them, however, it should be done with the intention: 'When I obtain [robes], I will return them; I will replace them,' and not with the intention of permanent possession. After obtaining [robes] from relatives, attendants, or anyone else, they should be made into regular [monastic robes]. When arriving at another place, they should be placed in a communal residence for communal use. If that garment wears out or is destroyed through use alone, there is no fault. If one does not obtain any of the aforementioned items, from lay clothing to skins, one should come covered with grass or leaves.

'Monks, one should not have imaginative drawings made of female figures or male figures. For whoever has them made, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa).' (Cūḷava. 299). According to this word, it is not allowable for a monk to make or have made a female or male figure. Not only female and male figures, but it is also not allowable for a monk to personally make or say 'make' even an animal figure, down to the figure of an earthworm. One is not even allowed to say, 'Lay follower, make a gatekeeper figure.' However, one is allowed to have others make figures of inspiring subjects such as those from the Jātaka stories, the Unrivaled Almsgiving (Asadisa-dāna), and so forth, or subjects connected with disillusionment (nibbida). One is allowed to personally perform floral work (mālā-kamma) and so forth.

'Monks, a monk who has not finished his meal should not be made to rise. For whoever makes him rise, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa).' (Cūḷava. 316). According to this word, whether in a village, or
425:
in a monastery, or in a forest, or in any place whatsoever, a monk who is eating should not be made to rise before the meal is finished. A monk who arrives later in a village should take his almsfood and leave. If people or monks say, 'Please enter,' it should be said, 'If I enter, the monks will rise.' Only when it is said, 'Venerable sir, please come, there is a seat,' should one enter. If no one says anything, one should go to the assembly hall and stand in a suitable place without going too close. Only when permission is given and it is said, 'Please enter,' should one enter. However, if there is a monk sitting without eating in the seat that falls to that [newly arrived] monk, it is allowable to make him rise. Regarding gruel, snacks, and so forth, as long as another person has not yet arrived after one has drunk or eaten something, it is not allowable to make even a monk who is sitting empty-handed rise. This is because that monk is one who has not yet finished his meal.

If, however, one makes him rise even by transgressing the offense, and both the one who makes him rise and the monk who is eating are pavārita (have finished their meal), the [eating monk] should be told, 'Go, fetch water.' This is the only instance where one may command a monk who is senior to oneself. If that monk does not even bring water, then after properly swallowing the mouthfuls of food, the seat should be given to the senior. This has also been stated: 'If one makes him rise, and he is a pavārita monk, he should be told, "Go, fetch water." If it is obtained in this way, that is good. If it is not obtained, then after properly swallowing the mouthfuls of food, the seat should be given to the senior. Monks, I do not say that the seat of a more senior monk should be withheld by any means. For whoever withholds it, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa).' (Cūḷava. 316).

'Monks, I allow a junior monk who is teaching to sit on an equal seat or a higher seat out of respect for the Dhamma. I allow a senior monk who is being taught to sit on an equal seat or a lower seat out of respect for the Dhamma.' (Cūḷava. 320). According to this word, it is allowable for a junior monk to sit on a higher seat when teaching, and for a senior monk to sit on a lower seat when being taught.
426:
“O monks, I allow sitting together with a monk who is within three years [of seniority].” According to this word, it is allowable to sit together in one place with a monk who is within three years of seniority. “Within three years” (*tivassantara*) refers to one who is either older or younger by two years. As for those who are older or younger by one year, or those of equal seniority, there is no need to even mention it (it is certainly allowed); all these are permitted to sit in pairs on a single couch (*mañca*) or a chair (*pīṭha*). For it was said: “O monks, I allow a couch for a group of two, a chair for a group of two.”

Regarding a place that can accommodate three people, whether it is a portable or non-portable place, it is also allowable to sit on such a wooden plank even with an unordained person. For it was said: “O monks, I allow a long seat (*dīghāsana*) as the minimum that can accommodate three.” However, according to the word: “O monks, I allow sitting on a long seat with those who do not share the same seat, except for a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*), a woman, or a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*),” it is not allowable to sit even on a long seat together with a *paṇḍaka* and so on.

One who nurses the sick should respectfully nurse them, reflecting repeatedly on this instruction of the Blessed One: “O monks, you have no mother, you have no father, who might nurse you. If you, monks, do not nurse one another, then who will nurse you? O monks, he who would nurse me, should nurse the sick.”

If it is the preceptor (*upajjhāya*), the preceptor should be nursed for life; his recovery from illness should be awaited. If it is the teacher (*ācariya*), the teacher should be nursed for life; his recovery should be awaited. If it is a co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*), the co-resident pupil should be nursed for life; his recovery should be awaited. If it is a pupil under tutelage (*antevāsika*), the pupil under tutelage should be nursed for life; his recovery should be awaited. If it is a fellow preceptor (*samānupajjhāyaka*), the fellow preceptor should be nursed for life; his recovery should be awaited. If it is a fellow teacher (*samānācariyaka*), the fellow teacher should be nursed for life; his recovery should be awaited. If there is no preceptor, teacher, co-resident pupil, or pupil under tutelage...
427:
...or fellow preceptor, or fellow teacher, then the Saṅgha must nurse him. If they do not nurse him, there is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*). According to this word (Mahāvagga, 365), if those such as the preceptor are not present in that monastery for that sick monk, and he is a visiting monk traveling alone, he is the responsibility of the Saṅgha. Therefore, the Saṅgha must nurse him. If they do not nurse him, the entire Saṅgha incurs an offense. However, when nursing is arranged by turns, the offense is incurred only by the one who does not nurse during his own turn. Even the Elder of the Saṅgha (*Saṅghatthera*) is not exempt from the nursing turn. If the entire Saṅgha assigns the responsibility to one person, or if a monk endowed with dutifulness says, “I alone will nurse him,” and nurses him, the Saṅgha is released from the offense.

As for the sick monk:
“O monks, a sick person endowed with five qualities is difficult to nurse (*dūpaṭṭho*). He does what is unsuitable (*asappāyakārī*); he does not know moderation in what is suitable; he does not take medicine; he does not disclose the illness as it really is to the nurse who desires his welfare—he does not say ‘the illness is increasing’ when it is increasing, or ‘the illness is decreasing’ when it is decreasing, or ‘the illness is stable’ when it is stable; and he is of a nature that cannot endure arisen bodily feelings that are painful, acute, sharp, severe, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening.” (Mahāvagga, 366). Avoiding these five unsuitable qualities from afar—

“O monks, a sick person endowed with five qualities is easy to nurse (*sūpaṭṭho*). He does what is suitable; he knows moderation in what is suitable; he takes medicine; he discloses the illness as it really is to the nurse who desires his welfare—he says ‘the illness is increasing’ when it is increasing, or ‘the illness is decreasing’ when it is decreasing, or ‘the illness is stable’ when it is stable; and he is of a nature that can endure arisen bodily feelings that are painful, acute, sharp, severe, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening.” (Mahāvagga, 366). As spoken, one should be a sick person endowed with these five qualities.
428:
Regarding the nursing attendant— "Monks, a nursing attendant endowed with five qualities is not fit to look after the sick. He is not capable of preparing medicine; he does not know what is suitable and unsuitable, bringing what is unsuitable and removing what is suitable; he attends to the sick for the sake of material gain and not with a mind of loving-kindness; he is repulsed by removing feces, urine, saliva, or vomit; and he is not capable of instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the sick from time to time with Dhamma talk." One should avoid these five unsuitable qualities from afar.

"Monks, a nursing attendant endowed with five qualities is fit to look after the sick. He is capable of preparing medicine; he knows what is suitable and unsuitable, removing what is unsuitable and bringing what is suitable; he attends to the sick with a mind of loving-kindness and not for the sake of material gain; he is not repulsed by removing feces, urine, saliva, or vomit; and he is capable of instructing, urging, rousing, and gladdening the sick from time to time with Dhamma talk." One should be endowed with these five qualities.

When giving a Dhamma talk, one should not praise the virtue of death to a sick monk in this way: "You are virtuous, one who has performed merit. Why do you fear death? For one who is virtuous, heaven is separated only by death, is it not?" If, upon hearing such praise, the monk makes an effort such as cutting off food and dies prematurely even when one javana-process of life remained, the attendant is guilty of killing. A wise monk should only give advice in this manner: "The attainment of the Path and Fruit is not a wonder for one who is virtuous. Therefore, without clinging to the monastery and such things, establish mindfulness on the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, and the body, and remain diligent in reflection." Even if the virtue of death is praised, if the sick monk does not make any effort because of that praise and his...
429:
...naturally according to his lifespan or the continuity of his life-process, the monk who praised it should not be held liable for an offense.

Because of the word, "Monks, one should not cast oneself down from life; whoever should cast himself down, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," a sick monk should not kill himself by any means, even by the minimum of cutting off food. If a sick monk, while medicine and attendants are available, cuts off food because he wishes to die, it is a dukkaṭa offense. However, if a monk has a grave illness that has persisted for a long time, and the monks attending him are exhausted and repulsed, wearying of it and thinking, "When shall we be free from this sick person?"—if that sick monk reflects, "This body does not last even when cared for, and the attending monks are exhausted," and cuts off food or does not use medicine, it is allowable. If a monk reflects, "This disease is severe, the life-formations do not last, and my attainment of the extraordinary Dhamma appears as if it were already in my hand," and cuts off food, it is indeed allowable. Even for one who is not sick, if spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arises and he cuts off food for the sake of meditation, thinking, "Searching for food is a distraction; I will only devote myself to the meditation subject," it is allowable. If one cuts off food after proclaiming the attainment of extraordinary Dhamma, it is not allowable. However, it is allowable to speak of it to fellow modest monks.

Because of the word, "Monks, one should not sit on a seat without having investigated it; whoever should sit, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," one should not sit on a seat without investigating and reflecting on it. What kind of seat should be investigated, and what kind should not? A seat that is purely bare without any covering, or a seat that is spread in the very sight of monks who have arrived and are standing, may be sat upon without reflection; it is allowable. It is also allowable to sit on a seat that people have pressed with their own hands and offered, saying, "Venerable sir, please sit here." If those who arrived and sat first later move upwards or downwards, there is no need for reflection. If a seat is covered with a thin cloth such that the floor can be seen, there is no need for reflection. However, if a seat has been spread beforehand with rugs, carpets, and so on, one should sit only after touching it with the hand and noticing whether there are creatures beneath. In the Mahāpaccari, however, it is stated: "Even if spread with a thick cloth, if no fold or wrinkle is apparent, it need not be investigated."
430:
## 
“Bhikkhus, a stone should not be rolled for play. Whoever should roll one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).” Because of this statement, a stone should not be rolled with the intention of jesting. Not only a stone, but it is also not allowable to roll or throw any other piece of wood or piece of brick, whether by hand or by machine. If, for the sake of a stupa (cetiya) and so forth, one rolls, throws, or lifts stones and such while laughing, it is allowable as it is a “time of work” (kammasamaya). Also, when performing other such new construction work, or when washing robes, it is allowable to lift and throw a tree or a washing-stick. In times such as when offering food, it is allowable to drive away crows or dogs by throwing a piece of wood or a potsherd.

“Bhikkhus, a forest fire should not be set. Whoever should set one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).” Because of this statement, one should not set fire in a forest. However, if one sets a fire with the thought, “Let whatever being is in this interval die,” then according to the cases of Pārājika, Ānantariya, Thullaccaya, and Pācittiya, there occur the Pārājika and other such offenses, as well as a mass of unwholesome merit. For one who sets a fire with the thought, “Let the green grass, forest, and so forth burn,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). For one who sets a fire with the thought, “Let the grass seeds, which are the materials for dabba-grass, be destroyed,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It is stated in the Saṅkhepa-aṭṭhakathā that “even if one sets fire with the intention of play, it is a dukkaṭa.” For one who sets a fire with the thought, “Let anything, whether wet or dry, with life-faculties or without life-faculties, burn,” the offenses of Pārājika, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, and Dukkaṭa should be understood according to the nature of the object.

However, the Blessed One has allowed the giving of a counter-fire and the making of a perimeter. Therefore, in the forest, seeing a fire approaching that was set by forest workers or that arose spontaneously, it is allowable to give a counter-fire to that fire with the thought, “Let the grass-roofed huts not be destroyed.” This is so that the approaching fire, meeting with the counter-fire, will be extinguished due to the lack of fuel. In the statement “it is also allowable to make a perimeter,” it means clearing the ground or digging a trench around the grass-roofed huts. Only then will the approaching fire be extinguished, having no fuel. All of this is allowable for one to do oneself if no layperson or novice is present when the fire has already arisen. But before the fire has arisen, one should have it done by laypeople or novices using allowable terminology (kappiya-vohāra). When extinguishing with water, only water without living beings (appāṇaka) should be poured.
431:
## 
When receiving well-prepared, choice food in the houses of faithless families of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), one should not consume it oneself nor give it to others without careful investigation. This is because such families might even give alms-food mixed with poison. Even if one receives food or snacks that have become stale or smelly from such a house of wrong view, that should not be consumed. This is because such families might give alms-food or snacks that ought to be discarded, having been left uncovered and crawled over by snakes, scorpions, and so forth. Alms-food from such a house that is smeared with scents, turmeric, and so forth should also not be accepted. This is because those people consider even the rice used to wipe diseased parts of the body as fit to be given as an offering.

“Bhikkhus, there is no offense in a gift from a garden-keeper,” it was said. In that regard, what kind of gift from a garden-keeper is allowable, and what kind is not allowable? First, the Elder Mahāsumma said, “Whatever has been allotted and given to the garden-keeper, saying ‘Take this much every day,’ only that much is allowable; beyond that is not allowable.” However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said, “If the garden-keepers have been given the fruits by recording it or by making a sign, they become the owners (lords) of what has been relinquished into their hands; therefore, whatever they give, even if it is a lot, is allowable.” In the Kurundī Commentary, it is said, “Children guard the orchards or other various fruits of laypeople; what is given by those children is allowable, but one should not have it brought to oneself (by requesting). Regarding Sangha property or property belonging to a stupa (cetiya), the gift of one who guards it after having purchased the rights (keṇi) is alone allowable; if it is one who guards for a wage, only his own portion is allowable to be given.” In the Mahāpaccari, it is said, “What lay garden-keepers give to monks is also allowable. What garden-keepers of the Sangha’s orchard give by deducting it from their own wages is also allowable. One who guards an orchard for a half-share or guards certain trees for a wage is also allowed to give from his own trees; if he guards after having purchased the rights, he is allowed to give everything.” All of this, though different in phrasing, is the same in meaning; therefore, one should accept it after knowing the intention.

Furthermore, this decision should also be known here: in a monastery where the resident monks do not give to visiting monks, and when the time for fruit distribution arrives, seeing that no one else is there, they eat it themselves by way of theft; in that case, it is allowable for the visiting monks to strike the bell and distribute and consume the fruit. However, in a monastery where the resident monks guard the trees and, when the time for fruit distribution arrives, distribute and eat them, and properly manage the four requisites...
432:
Visiting monks have no authority in that monastery. Even regarding trees that have been designated and donated for the purpose of robes, visiting monks have no authority. The same principle should be understood for trees designated and donated for the purpose of other requisites. However, if resident monks protect and guard trees that have not been so designated, but consume their fruits through theft, they do not abide by the agreement of resident monks. Regarding trees donated for the purpose of consuming the fruit, if the resident monks protect and guard them and manage them properly, only in those trees do they abide by the agreement of resident monks.

In the Mahāpaccari, however, it is stated: "A monk who, with the intent to steal, consumes fruit designated for the four requisites, must have the property valued and be made to pay. For one who distributes and consumes by way of usage, the property must be compensated. Specifically, regarding fruit designated for the purpose of lodgings, for one who distributes and consumes it by way of usage alone, there is both a thullaccaya offense and the requirement to compensate for the property."

Fruit donated specifically for the purpose of robes should be applied only to robes. If a famine occurs and monks struggle for almsfood, but robes are easily obtainable, it is allowable to apply it to almsfood after performing an apalokanakamma (act of notification) according to the wish of the Saṅgha. If they struggle for lodgings or medicinal requisites, it is allowable to apply it for those purposes after performing an apalokanakamma according to the wish of the Saṅgha. The same principle applies to fruit donated specifically for the purpose of almsfood or medicinal requisites. However, fruit donated specifically for the purpose of lodgings is garubhaṇḍa (heavy property); it must be protected and guarded, and applied only for the purpose of those lodgings.

If a famine occurs and monks cannot subsist on almsfood, and in this situation, monasteries are falling into ruin and palmyra or coconut trees are being destroyed because monks are leaving for other places due to dangers from kings, diseases, or thieves, but it is possible to subsist by relying on the property of the lodgings; at such a time, the Blessed One has allowed the use of lodgings even by disposing of them for the sake of looking after the monastery. Therefore, it is allowable to keep one or two excellent lodgings and dispose of the remaining inferior ones for the sake of almsfood; however, one should not do so by destroying the original capital property.

Regarding an orchard (ārāma) donated specifically for the purpose of the four requisites, an apalokanakamma need not be performed. If there is a deficiency in any requisite, it is allowable to apply it for that purpose. The orchard should be maintained; it is allowable to have it maintained even by paying wages. If orchard-keepers who receive wages and live in houses built within the orchard itself protect it, and if they give coconuts or ripe palmyra fruits to arriving monks, the Saṅgha should allow them, saying, "Eat this much fruit every day."
433:
The orchard-keepers have the right to give only that permitted fruit. Even if the orchard-keepers give more than that, it is not allowable to accept it. However, if a person rents the orchard for a fee and gives only allowable items (kappiyabhaṇḍa) to the Saṅgha for the four requisites, that person has the right to give even a large amount of fruit. An orchard donated for the purpose of offering lamps to a shrine (cetiya) or for repairing broken and dilapidated parts must also be guarded; it must be guarded even by paying wages. In this case, it is allowable to pay the wages from either the shrine's property or the Saṅgha's property. Regarding such an orchard, the giving of fruit produced there by those who live and guard it for wages, or by those who rent it for a fee and donate allowable items, should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

A monk requesting lawful protection should not speak by referring to a specific person regarding past or future events. Regarding the past, there is speaking with reference to a specific person and speaking without reference to a specific person. Regarding the future, there is also speaking with reference to a specific person and speaking without reference to a specific person. How is there speaking with reference to a specific person regarding the past? In the monks' monastery, village boys, scoundrels, or anyone else may commit improper acts, cut down trees, take various fruits, or plunder requisites. The monk approaches the magistrates (vohārika) and says, "Such an act has been committed in our monastery." When asked, "Who did it?", he informs them, "This person and that person did it." In this way, speaking with reference to a specific person regarding the past is not allowable. If the magistrates hear that and punish those people, the entire responsibility for compensation lies on the monk's neck. Even if there is the intention that "they will be punished," the responsibility still lies on his neck. If he says, "Punish that person," and a punishment valued at five māsakas is taken, a pārājika offense is incurred. When asked, "Who did it?", it is not allowable for us to say, "This person did it"; you yourselves will know. We only request protection, please give us protection, and have the stolen property returned—this is all that should be said. Speaking in this way is speaking without reference to a specific person, and it is allowable. If the magistrates, having been told this, search for the perpetrators and punish them, even if all their property is seized, there is no responsibility for compensation on the monk, nor does an offense occur. Seeing those who are taking away requisites, it is also not allowable to shout "Thief! Thief!" with a mind wishing for their harm. If they are punished because of such speech, the entire responsibility for compensation lies on the monk's neck. However, to one who will listen to his words, he may say, "This person has taken my requisites, have those requisites returned, but do not [punish] him..."
434:
It is permissible to say, "Do it." They also engage in litigation (legal proceedings) for the sake of male and female slaves and so forth; this litigation is called unallowable litigation and is not permissible.

How does reporting with reference to a future matter occur? In the same manner as previously mentioned, when others commit improper conduct and so forth, a monk says to the officials (vohārika), "In our monastery, they do such and such; please provide us with protection so that it does not happen in the future." When asked, "Who did this?" he reports, "So-and-so and so-and-so did it." In this way, reporting occurs with reference to a future matter, and that too is not permissible. If those people are punished, all compensation is the responsibility of the monk, just as in the previous case; the rest is the same as before. If the officials, having proclaimed by drum, "We shall impose such-and-such a punishment on those who commit such improper conduct in the monks' monastery," search for and punish those who do not obey the order, there is no responsibility for the monk, nor is there an offense.

They take the billhooks, axes, and so forth of those who cut trees and such within the monastery boundary and strike them with stones; this is not permissible.
