If the blades are damaged, they must be repaired and returned. They run and take the requisites of those people; such taking should also not be done. This is because the mind changes quickly; if the intention to steal arises, it could even lead to a pārājika (defeat).

20. It is not permissible to discard or cause to be discarded feces, urine, rubbish, or food scraps over a wall or over a fence. For a monk who discards all four items with a single effort, there is only one dukkhaṭa offense; if he discards them separately, there are dukkhaṭa offenses according to the number of items. The same rule applies to commanding others. Discarding a tooth-stick also results only in a dukkhaṭa offense. There is no offense for a monk who discards feces and so forth after looking or in a place not used by people. Whether it be a cultivated field used by people or an orchard of coconuts and so forth, it is not permissible to discard these items in any place where there are planted green plants. For a monk who discards them, the different types of offenses should be understood as in the previous method. A monk who is sitting and eating in a field or an orchard, or a monk who is walking while eating sugarcane and so forth, if he discards mouth-rinsing water, dregs, and so forth in a place with green plants, or even if he drinks water and discards a coconut shell with the sprout removed, he incurs a dukkhaṭa offense. Even if seeds have been sown in a ploughed area, whether the sprouts have emerged or not, it is a dukkhaṭa offense. However, it is permissible to discard in the corners of fields where seeds have not yet been sown, or on the embankments of fields where crops are not planted, and it is also permissible in places where people discard rubbish.
435:
When people have harvested and removed the crops and left, it is called an abandoned field; in such a field, it is permissible to discard (mouth-rinsing water, etc.). However, in a field where they protect it, thinking, "Even though the early crops have been reaped, they will grow again," it is not permissible.

Because of the statement, "Monks, a monk who is bathing should not rub his body against a tree; for him who rubs it, there is a dukkhaṭa offense," a monk who is bathing should not rub his body against a tree, or against a post fixed at a bathing place, or against any wall among brick, stone, or wooden walls.

Because of the statement, "Monks, one should not bathe on an aṭṭāna; for him who bathes, there is a dukkhaṭa offense," it is also not permissible to bathe on an aṭṭāna. An aṭṭāna is a wooden plank that has been planed and carved with checkered patterns and fixed at a bathing place; people scatter powders there and rub their bodies.

Because of the statement, "Monks, one should not bathe with a gandhabba-hatthaka (wooden hand); for him who bathes, there is a dukkhaṭa offense," it is not permissible to bathe with that wooden hand kept at a bathing place, which people use to take powders and rub their bodies.

Because of the statement, "Monks, one should not bathe with a kuruvindakasutti; for him who bathes, there is a dukkhaṭa offense," it is also not permissible to bathe with a kuruvindakasutti. A kuruvindakasutti refers to a bundle of balls made by binding kuruvindaka stone powder with lac, which they hold at both ends and rub the body with.

Because of the statement, "Monks, one should not have a massage performed by rubbing against each other; for him who has it performed, there is a dukkhaṭa offense," it is not permissible to rub against each other's bodies.

Because of the statement, "Monks, one should not bathe with a mallaka; for him who bathes, there is a dukkhaṭa offense. Monks, I allow an akata-mallaka (unmade scrubber) for a sick monk," a mallaka is made by cutting a makara-daṇḍaka into a circular shape; this is not permissible even for a sick monk. An akata-mallaka is one made without cutting 'dog-teeth' (serrations); this is not permissible for a monk who is not sick (but is allowed for the sick). However, rubbing with a piece of brick or a piece of potsherd is permissible.

Because of the statement, "Monks, I allow the ukkāsika and the puthupāṇika," the ukkāsika and the puthupāṇika are permissible. An ukkāsika is a roll of cloth; therefore,
436:
A monk who is bathing is permitted to rub his back with a roll of bathing cloth. *Puthupāṇika* refers to manual massage; therefore, it is permitted for all monks to perform a back massage with their hands.

The procedure for bathing is as follows: Having gone to the bathing place, one should not jump into the water immediately while standing, after placing the robes here or there. Instead, one should look in all directions, and upon knowing it is secluded, identify stumps, bushes, creepers, etc. After coughing three times, while standing in a stooped position, one should remove and spread out the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*). The waistband (*kāyabandhana*) should be loosened and placed on top of the robe. If there is no bathing cloth (*udakasāṭikā*), one should sit in a crouching position at the water's edge, loosen the under-robe (*nivāsana*), and if there is a hollow spot, spread it out in the sun. If there is none, it should be folded and placed. When entering the water, one should descend slowly to navel depth, and without causing waves or making noise, dive while facing the direction from which one came. In this way, the robes are protected. When emerging, one should also emerge slowly without making noise. After bathing, one should sit in a crouching position at the water's edge, wrap the under-robe around, stand up, dress neatly, tie the waistband, and only then stand after donning the robe.

"Monks, ear-ornaments (*vallikā*) should not be worn... forehead-ornaments (*pāmanga*) should not be worn... necklaces (*kaṇṭhasuttaka*) should not be worn... waist-strings (*kaṭisuttaka*) should not be worn... bracelets (*ovaṭṭika*) should not be worn... anklets should not be worn... armlets and hand-ornaments should not be worn... finger-rings should not be worn. Whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)" (Cūḷavagga 245). Because of this word, any ornament such as ear-plugs is not permitted. In that context, *vallikā* is a name for pearl-pendants hanging from the ear, etc. Not only *vallikā*, but any ear-ornament, even a palm leaf, is not permitted. *Pāmanga* is any kind of pendant string. *Kaṇṭhasuttaka* is any ornament for the neck. *Kaṭisuttaka* is any ornament for the waist, even a mere thread. *Ovaṭṭika* is a bracelet. Anklets and others are well-known.

"Monks, long hair should not be worn. Whoever should wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow hair of two months' growth or two finger-breadths in length" (Cūḷavagga 246).
437:
According to the word regarding hair, if the hair reaches two finger-breadths within two months, it should be shaved within those two months; it is not permitted to let it exceed two finger-breadths. Even if it is not long, it is not allowed to exceed two months by even a single day. In both cases, the maximum limit is stated; there is no such thing as it being unallowable below that limit.

“Monks, hair should not be cut with scissors. Whoever should cut it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow hair to be cut with scissors in case of illness” (Cūḷavagga 275). Because of this word, except for illness, it is not permitted to cut hair with scissors.

“Monks, hair should not be smoothed with a bristle-comb (*koccha*)... hair should not be smoothed with a comb (*phaṇaka*)... hair should not be smoothed with a hand-comb (*hatthaphaṇaka*)... hair should not be smoothed with pomade (*sitthate laka*)... hair should not be smoothed with scented oil (*udakate laka*). Whoever should smooth it, there is an offense of wrong-doing” (Cūḷavagga 246). Because of this word, hair should not be smoothed with combs, etc., for the sake of adornment. However, for a monk whose hair stands up, he should moisten his hand and wipe his head so that it lies down. It is also permitted for monks oppressed by heat or those with dusty heads to wipe with a wet hand.

“Monks, one should not look at the reflection of one's face in a mirror or in a bowl of water. Whoever should look, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow one to look at the reflection of one's face in a mirror or in a bowl of water in case of illness” (Cūḷavagga 247). Because of this word, except for illness, one should not look at the face in a mirror or a bowl of water. Here, bronze bowls and such, in which a face reflection appears, all fall under the category of mirrors. Sour gruel and such also fall under the category of a bowl of water. Therefore, there is an offense of wrong-doing for a monk who looks into anything that shows a reflection. However, in case of illness, it is permitted for the purpose of knowing, “Has my wound healed, or not yet?” It is also said to be permitted for the purpose of reflecting on the nature of life, such as “Am I aged, or not?”

“Monks, the face should not be smeared... the face should not be massaged... the face should not be powdered... the face should not be marked with red arsenic (*manosilā*)... the body should not be dyed with vermilion, etc. (*aṅgarāga*)... the lips should not be reddened (*mukharāga*)... both body-dyeing and lip-reddening should not be done. Whoever should do so, an offense...”
438:
"Bhikkhus, I allow the face to be smeared because of an illness" (Cullavagga, 247). According to this word, one should not smear the face, etc., without an illness; if one does, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

"Bhikkhus, one should not go to see dancing, singing, or music; for whoever goes, there is an offense of wrongdoing" (Cullavagga, 248). According to this word, one should not go to see dancing, etc. In this context (Pācittiya-aṭṭhakathā, 835), "dancing" refers to the dancing of professional dancers, etc., or the dancing of drunkards, or even at the lowest, the dancing of peacocks, pigs, monkeys, etc.—all this is indeed dancing. Therefore, for a monk who goes to see even a peacock dancing, there is an offense of wrongdoing. If one dances oneself or makes another dance, there is also an offense of wrongdoing.

"Singing" refers to the singing of professional dancers, etc., or the celebratory singing associated with the virtues of the Triple Gem at the time of the Parinibbāna of Noble Ones, or the singing of undisciplined monks while preaching Dhamma, or even at the lowest, humming (buzzing) performed beforehand with the thought "I will sing"—all this is indeed singing. If one sings oneself or makes another sing, there is also an offense of wrongdoing.

"Bhikkhus, there are these five disadvantages for a monk who sings the Dhamma with a long, musical intonation. He himself becomes attached to that sound, others also become attached to that sound, householders criticize, the concentration of one who desires the modulation of the voice is broken, and future generations follow the example. Bhikkhus, these are the five disadvantages of singing the Dhamma with a long, musical intonation. Bhikkhus, the Dhamma should not be sung with a long, musical intonation; for whoever sings it, there is an offense of wrongdoing" (Cullavagga, 249).

According to this word, even the Dhamma should not be sung with a long, musical intonation. A "long musical intonation" is a sound that occurs by breaking the respective rhythm of recitation and destroying the syllables. In the Dhamma, however, there are the rhythms of reciting Suttas, Jātakas, and Gāthās; it is not proper to destroy those rhythms and make them excessively long. The syllables and phrases should be presented clearly with a complete rhythm.

"Bhikkhus, I allow intonation (sarabhañña)" (Cullavagga, 249). According to this word, it is proper to recite the Dhamma with intonation. In sarabhañña, it is said there are thirty-two rhythms such as taraṅga-vatta, dhotaka-vatta, and galita-vatta. Among those rhythms, one is permitted to use whichever one desires, without destroying any syllables or phrases...
439:
...without making distortions, and proceeding in a manner that is appropriate for a recluse and complete—this is the characteristic.

"Music" refers to instruments played by being strung, such as the lute, or the beating of a pot-drum, or even at the lowest, the beating of an overturned pot in water—all this is improper. However, if one snaps their fingers or claps their hands while sneezing or while standing in a place of suspicion (disgust), there is no offense in doing so. For one who sees while standing inside the monastery grounds, there is no offense in all cases of dancing and music. For a monk who goes from monastery to monastery with the intention "I will watch," there is indeed an offense. If one watches while sitting in the dining hall, there is no offense. For a monk who gets up and goes with the intention "I will watch," there is an offense. For one who stands on the road and turns their neck to watch, there is also indeed an offense. If one sees or hears while going for the sake of salāka-bhatta (food tickets), etc., or for any other business, there is no offense. If one enters a place of performance because of being oppressed by dangers or such calamities, and watches or listens while having entered thus, there is no offense.

One is not allowed to say, "Lay devotees, give an offering (upahāra) to the Cetiya," nor to accept it if they say, "We shall make an offering to your Cetiya." However, if they say, "We shall perform service (upaṭṭhāna) to your Cetiya," it is proper to say, "Performing service is indeed excellent."

"Bhikkhus, one's own organ should not be cut off; for whoever cuts it off, there is an offense of serious guilt (thullaccaya)" (Cullavagga, 251). According to this word, for a monk who cuts off his organ, there is a thullaccaya offense. If one cuts off any other part such as an ear, nose, or finger, or causes such pain, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). However, for a monk who lets blood or cuts because of a snake or insect bite, etc., or because of other illnesses, there is no offense.

"Bhikkhus, the miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya) that is beyond human state should not be shown to laypeople; for whoever shows it, there is an offense of wrongdoing" (Cullavagga, 252). According to this word, it is not proper to show the psychic power of transformation (vikkubbaniddhi) to laypeople. However, the psychic power of resolve (adhiṭṭhānaniddhi) is not prohibited.

"Bhikkhus, a bowl made of gold should not be carried... a bowl made of silver... a bowl made of gems... a bowl made of beryl... a bowl made of crystal... a bowl made of bronze... a bowl made of glass... a bowl made of tin... a bowl made of lead... a bowl made of copper should not be carried; for whoever carries one, there is an offense of wrongdoing" (Cullavagga, 252). According to this word...
440:
Alms-bowls made of gold and so forth are not allowable. Even if laypeople place side dishes in gold vessels and the like at a dining place and offer them, it is not allowable even to touch them. Vessels such as bowls made of crystal, glass, or bronze are not allowable for personal use; however, they are allowable if they are for communal use (Saṅghika) or if they are the property of laypeople. Only an alms-bowl made of copper is not allowable, but a dish (thālaka) is allowable. Because it was said, "Monks, I allow two kinds of bowls: an iron bowl and a clay bowl," only these two kinds of bowls are permitted.

Because it was said, "Monks, one should not go for alms with a gourd shell; for him who should go, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa)," it is not allowable to carry a gourd shell. However, if one obtains such a gourd shell, it is allowable to use it temporarily. The same rule applies to a pot-shard (ghaṭika-kaṭāha). Because it was said, "Monks, an alms-bowl made of a human skull should not be carried; for him who should carry it, there is an offense of wrong-doing," an alms-bowl made of a human skull is not allowable.

Because it was said, "Monks, I allow a bowl-stand," it is allowable to place the bowl on a ground-stand (bhūmi-ādhāraka) or a wooden-post stand (dāru-daṇḍa-ādhāraka) made of earth, wood, ivory, creepers, rattan, and so forth. In this regard, it is stated in the Kurundī: "It is allowable to stack three bowls on a ground-stand and two bowls on a wooden-post stand." However, in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, it is said: "There is no space to place three bowls on a ground-stand; it is only allowable to place two. The same rule applies to well-prepared wooden-post stands. A wooden stand similar to a lathe-turned piece is joined with three posts; there is no space even for a single bowl on such a post-stand. If placed there, one must sit while holding it with the hand. On the ground, however, only one bowl should be placed upside down."

Because it was said, "Monks, an alms-bowl should not be placed on the edge of an inner ledge (miḍḍhanta); for him who should place it, there is an offense of wrong-doing," it is not allowable to place it on the edge of inner ledges like those of a veranda. However, if it remains stable on that ledge even when turned around, it is allowable to place it on such a wide ledge. Because it was said, "Monks, an alms-bowl should not be placed on the edge of an outer ledge (paribhaṇḍanta); for him who should place it, there is an offense of wrong-doing," the same rule applies to a thin ledge made on the outer side. Because it was said, "Monks, I allow a coarse cloth (coḷaka)..."
441:
It is allowable to spread a coarse cloth and place the alms-bowl upon it. If such a coarse cloth is not available, it is allowable to place it on a mat (kaṭasāraka), a floor-mat, a place decorated with earth (smooth ground), or on sand where the bowl will not be damaged. However, for a monk who places it on dust, grit, or rough ground, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa).

“Monks, an alms-bowl should not be hung up; for him who should hang it up, there is an offense of wrong-doing” — because of this word (from the Cūḷavagga Pali), it is not allowable to hang it anywhere, such as on an ivory peg (nāgadanta) and so forth. It is also not allowable to tie and place it on a robe-line.

“Monks, an alms-bowl should not be placed on a couch; for him who should place it, there is an offense of wrong-doing” — because of this word, there is an offense of wrong-doing for a monk who places it anywhere on a couch (mañca) or a bench (pīṭha), whether they are made for storing goods or for sitting and sleeping. However, it is allowable to tie it together with other goods and place it, or to tie it to the frame (aṭani) of a couch and let it hang. Even if tied, it is not allowable to place it on top. If a couch or a bench is lifted and placed on a robe-line or similar place to serve as a shelf, it is allowable to place the bowl on such a couch or bench. It is allowable to sling the bowl over the shoulder with a strap and place it on the lap. It is not allowable to place an alms-bowl filled with food on an umbrella, nor a bowl slung over the shoulder. However, it is allowable to place an ordinary bowl on an umbrella that has been tied with a bundle of goods or made into a shelf.

“Monks, a monk with a bowl in hand should not push open a door-leaf; for him who should push it open, there is an offense of wrong-doing” — because of this word, a monk should not push open a door-leaf while having a bowl in hand. In this regard, “one with a bowl in hand” (patta-hattha) does not only mean one who has a bowl in the hand. It is not only that one is not permitted to push open a door-leaf; rather, if there is a bowl on any part of the body, whether in the hand or on the top of the foot, one is not permitted to push open a door-leaf, lift a bolt (ghaṭikā), or unlock a pin with a key using the hand, foot, head, or any part of the body. However, if the bowl is slung over the shoulder, one is permitted to open the door as one pleases.

“Monks, food scraps, bones, or mouth-rinse water should not be discarded with an alms-bowl; for him who should discard them, there is an offense of wrong-doing” — because of this word, it is not allowable to discard food scraps and so forth with an alms-bowl. In this context, “food scraps” (calakāni) refers to food remnants that have been chewed and spat out. “Bones” (aṭṭhikāni) refers to fish bones and meat bones. “Mouth-rinse water” (ucchiṭṭhodakaṃ) refers to water used for washing the mouth. For a monk who discards any of these with an alms-bowl, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Having used the alms-bowl as a receptacle, the hand...
442:
It is not allowed to use the alms-bowl as a basin for washing hands. One should not pour water used for washing hands or feet into the bowl and then throw it away. One should not touch a clean bowl that has no food remnants with a hand soiled by food. However, it is allowable to pour water into the bowl with the left hand, take a mouthful of water, and then hold the bowl with the soiled hand. By doing this much, that bowl becomes a bowl with food remnants (ucchiᙩᙩhapatta). One should touch the bowl only after washing the hand with external water. When eating fish, meat, or various fruits, if one wishes to discard bones or scraps from that food, one is not allowed to put them in the bowl. However, if one intends to eat them later, one may place them in the bowl. It is allowable to keep bones, thorns, etc., in the bowl itself and pull them out with the hand to eat. Anything taken out of the mouth should not be put back into the bowl even if one wishes to eat it again; however, pieces of raw ginger, coconut, etc., may be put back after being bitten.

According to the words, "Bhikkhus, one should not be a total paፁsukũlika (user of refuse-rag cloth); whoever should be so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaᙩa)" (Cũጷavagga 255), one should not be a total paፁsukũlika. In this regard, while it is allowable to use refuse-rag cloth for robes, beds, and chairs, for food, one should only accept what is given.

According to the words, "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is traveling on a long journey should not refuse to give a water filter when asked; whoever does not give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cũጷavagga 259), it is not allowable to refuse to give a water filter to one who asks because they lack one. However, if someone asks for a water filter even though they already have one in hand, it may be refused if one does not wish to give it. According to the words, "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should not set out on a long journey without a water filter; whoever sets out, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cũጷavagga 259), one should not travel without a water filter. If there is no water filter or a water-strainer (dhammakaraka), one should resolve upon the corner of the double-robe (saፅghāᙩi), thinking, "I will drink after filtering with this."

According to the words, "Bhikkhus, I allow a staff-filter (daፂጱaparissāvana)" (Cũጷavagga 259), a staff-filter is also allowable. A staff-filter is a type of filter where, like the lye-filter of dyers, a cloth is tied to a frame on four legs, and water is poured onto a staff in the middle, filling both sections and filtering through.
443:
According to the words, "Bhikkhus, I allow the ottharaka filter" (Cũጷavagga 259), the ottharaka filter is also allowable. An ottharaka filter is a type of filter that is submerged in water to draw water with a small pot. It is made by planting four sticks or posts in the water, tying a cloth to these posts so that the edges are above the water and the middle is submerged, and then drawing water with a pot. According to the words, "Bhikkhus, a naked monk should not salute a naked monk; whoever should salute, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cũጷavagga 261), etc., one should not salute while naked, nor should one be saluted, nor should one cause another to salute, nor should one perform services for a naked person, nor give anything, nor receive anything, nor chew, nor eat, nor lick, nor drink while naked.

According to the words, "Bhikkhus, I allow three coverings: the sauna-covering (jantāghara-paᙩicchādi), the water-covering (udaka-paᙩicchādi), and the cloth-covering (vattha-paᙩicchādi)" (Cũጷavagga 261), all three types of coverings are allowable. Here, the sauna-covering and the water-covering are allowable only for one performing services; they are not allowable for other matters such as saluting. The cloth-covering, however, is allowable for all activities.

According to the words, "Bhikkhus, one should not sleep on beds strewn with flowers; whoever should sleep, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cũጷavagga 264), one should not sleep on beds spread with flowers. However, it is allowable to take fragrant paste and make five-finger marks (pacaፅgulika) on door panels, or to take flowers and place them in a certain part of the monastery.

According to the words, "Bhikkhus, one should not eat while placing [food] in an āsittakũpadhāna; whoever should eat, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cũጷavagga 264), one should not eat by placing food in an āsittakũpadhāna. Āsittakũpadhāna is a name for a casket or a tray made of copper or silver; because it is prohibited, even one made of wood is not allowable.

According to the words, "Bhikkhus, I allow the maጷorika" (Cũጷavagga 264), it is allowable to eat by placing [the bowl] on a maጷorikā (bowl-stand or support). A maጷorikā refers to a support made with sticks or a bowl-stand. Supports made of bamboo strips, leaf-supports, baskets, chairs, etc., are also included here. From the general category of supports, whether they have holes or not, they are indeed allowable as long as they have the form of a bowl-stand.
444:
## 
“Monks, one should not eat together from the same vessel; for one who eats [thus], there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)” (Cūḷavagga 264). Based on this and other such statements, one should not eat together from the same vessel, nor should one drink together from the same cup. However, if one monk takes a fruit or a cake from the vessel and leaves, once he has departed, it is permissible for the remaining monk to eat what is left. It is also permissible for the other monk to take and eat it again at the moment it is given by that monk.

“Monks, one should not sleep on the same bed; for one who sleeps [thus], there is an offense of wrongdoing” (Cūḷavagga 264). Based on this and other such statements, one should not lie down together on the same bed, nor should one lie down on the same mat. However, if they lie down after placing a robe, a walking stick, or at least a waistband in the middle to show a boundary, there is no offense. One should not lie down with shared covers or shared mats and covers. ‘Shared mats and covers’ refers to monks who lie down by spreading one end of a sewn rug, mat, or grass mat and covering themselves with the other end.

“Monks, one should not step on a cloth mat; for one who steps [on it], there is an offense of wrongdoing” (Cūḷavagga 268). According to this statement, one should not step on a cloth mat. However, according to the statement, “Monks, I allow a monk who is requested by laypeople for the sake of a blessing to step on a cloth mat” (Cūḷavagga 268), if a woman has recently given birth or is heavily pregnant, it is permissible to step on it when requested for the sake of a blessing in such circumstances. According to the statement, “Monks, I allow stepping with washed feet” (Cūḷavagga 268), it is permissible to step on a mat spread for those with washed feet to step on at a foot-washing place.

“Monks, the foot scrubber known as a kataka should not be used; for one who uses [it], there is an offense of wrongdoing” (Cūḷavagga 269). According to this statement, a kataka is not permissible. A kataka is an object made with raised spikes like the filaments of a lotus for the purpose of scrubbing the feet. Whether it is round or square, it is prohibited as it is an indulgence in luxury; it is not permissible to accept or use it. According to the statement, “Monks, I allow three types of foot scrubbers: gravel, potsherds, and sea foam (cuttlebone)” (Cūḷavagga 269), scrubbing the feet with gravel and so on is permissible. ‘Sakkharā’ refers to gravel; a stone-foam (pumice) is also permissible.
445:
## 
“Monks, a yak-tail fan should not be carried; for one who carries [it], there is an offense of wrongdoing” (Cūḷavagga 269). According to this statement, a fan made from the tail-hair of a yak is not permissible. “Monks, I allow a mosquito fan. Monks, I allow three types of fans: those made of bark, those made of usīra-root, and those made of peacock feathers. Monks, I allow the square fan (vidhūpana) and the palm-leaf fan (tālavaṇṭa)” (Cūḷavagga 269). According to these statements, mosquito fans and others are permissible. In that context, ‘vidhūpana’ refers to a square fan. As for the palm-leaf fan, whether it is made of palm leaves, bamboo strips, ivory strips, peacock feathers, or special leather, every such fan is permissible. In the case of a mosquito fan, handles made of ivory or horn are also permissible. The term ‘bark fan’ also includes mosquito fans made from the flowers of the screw-pine (ketaka), palm leaves, and so on.

“Monks, an umbrella should not be carried; for one who carries [it], there is an offense of wrongdoing. Monks, I allow an umbrella for one who is sick” (Cūḷavagga 270). According to this statement, a monk who is not sick should not carry an umbrella. However, for a monk who has a burning sensation in the body, or a biliary disorder, or weak eyes, or if any other illness arises without an umbrella, it is permissible for him to carry an umbrella in a village or in the forest. In the rainy season, it is permissible for the sake of protecting the robes, or for the sake of self-protection against the dangers of wild beasts and thieves. An umbrella made of a single leaf is permissible in all places. According to the statement, “Monks, I allow even a monk who is not sick to carry an umbrella in the monastery and in the vicinity of the monastery” (Cūḷavagga 270), it is permissible for a non-sick monk to carry an umbrella within the monastery and its vicinity.

“Monks, long fingernails and toenails should not be kept; for one who keeps [them], there is an offense of wrongdoing. Monks, I allow the cutting of nails to the level of the flesh” (Cūḷavagga 274). According to this statement, long nails should be cut. “Monks, the twenty nails should not be polished; for one who has them polished, there is an offense of wrongdoing. Monks, I allow the removal of mere dirt” (Cūḷavagga 274). According to this statement, it is not permissible to scrape or polish the twenty nails; however, it is permissible to remove mere dirt from the nails.

“Monks, hair in the private parts should not be removed; for one who has it removed, there is an offense of wrongdoing. Monks, I allow the removal of hair in the private parts for the reason of an illness” (Cūḷavagga 275). According to this statement, it is not permissible to have hair in the private parts removed unless there is an illness such as a boil or a wound. “Monks, long nose hair should not be kept...”
446:
"If a monk carries [long nose hair], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṩa)" (Cullavagga, 275). According to these words, it is permissible to have nose hair removed with tweezers. There is no offense in having nose hair pulled with pebbles and such, but for the sake of protection [of the nose], the Buddha allowed tweezers, saying: "Monks, I allow tweezers" (Cullavagga, 275). "Monks, grey hair should not be plucked. Whoever has it plucked, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cullavagga, 275). According to these words, it is not permissible to have grey hair plucked. However, if hair grows on the eyebrows, forehead, or beard and stands out unsightlily, it is permissible to have such hair plucked, whether it is grey or not.

"Monks, one should not enter a village without a waistband. Whoever enters, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cullavagga, 278). According to these words, one should not enter a village without a waistband. A monk who has set out without tying his waistband should tie it wherever he remembers. It is permissible to go with the intention, "I will tie it at the rest house," but as long as he remembers and has not yet tied it, he should not wander for alms.

"Monks, one should not dress like laypeople. Whoever dresses so, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cullavagga, 280). According to this and other words, one should not dress like laypeople by letting the robe hang like an elephant's trunk, etc. One should not wrap oneself like laypeople by wearing white cloth, etc. One should not dress with the robe tucked up like laborers. It is not permissible for even a sick monk or a monk on a journey to dress in this way. While traveling, it is absolutely not permissible to lift one or both corners of the inner robe (antaravāsaka) and hook them above, or to wear one robe inside in that manner and another outside. A sick monk, however, is allowed to show the fold of the inner robe and wear another over it. A monk who is not sick and wishes to wear two robes should wear them layered together.

"Monks, a double-ended yoke should not be carried. Whoever carries one, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cullavagga, 281). According to these words, it is not permissible to carry a double-ended yoke. "Monks, I allow a single-ended yoke, a middle yoke, a head-load, a shoulder-load, a hip-load, and a hanging load." According to these words, it is permissible to carry a single-ended yoke and so on.

"Monks, a long tooth-stick should not be chewed. Whoever chews one, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cullavagga, 282). According to these words, a long tooth-stick should not be chewed. "Monks, ..."
447:
"...a tooth-stick of eight finger-breadths at most. Monks, I allow a tooth-stick of four finger-breadths at least" (Cullavagga, 282). According to these words, a tooth-stick should be chewed that is at most eight finger-breadths and at least four finger-breadths, measured by the finger-breadth of a man.

"Monks, a tree should not be climbed. Whoever climbs one, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow climbing a tree to the height of a man when there is a task to be done, and as much as needed in times of danger" (Cullavagga, 284). According to these words, a tree should not be climbed. However, if there is a task such as gathering dry wood, it is permissible to climb to the height of a man (one fathom). "Times of danger" means it is permissible to climb even a very high tree upon seeing wild beasts, etc., or if a monk who has lost his way wishes to look for directions, or upon seeing a forest fire or a flood coming.

"Monks, the Buddha's words should not be put into Sanskrit (Sakkata). Whoever puts them so, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow the Buddha's words to be learned in one's own language" (Cullavagga, 285). According to these words, it is not permissible to recite the Buddha's words in the Sanskrit language like the Vedas. They should be learned only in one's own Māgadha language.

"Monks, Lokāyata should not be learned. Whoever learns it, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Cullavagga, 286). According to this and other words, one should not learn the texts of sectarians called Lokāyata, which are associated with useless reasoning such as "Everything is a remnant, everything is not a remnant; the crow is white, the crane is black, because of this and that reason." Nor should one teach them to others. One should also not learn "lowly arts" (tiracchānavijjā) which obstruct the Path and Fruition, nor teach them to others.

"Monks, when someone sneezes, one should not say 'Live!' (Jīva). Whoever says it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow one to say 'Live long!' (Ciraṁ jīva) when laypeople say 'Venerable Sir, may you live!'" (Cullavagga, 288). According to these words, when someone sneezes, one should not say "Live!" However, if laypeople say "May you live!", it is permissible to reply "Live long!"

"Monks, garlic should not be eaten. Whoever eats it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow garlic to be eaten for the reason of illness" (Cullavagga, 289). According to these words,
448:
It is not allowable to eat garlic (lasuṇa) unless one is ill; however, it is allowable when added to the cooking of soup and so forth. It is allowable to eat it when added to any food or drink, such as in cooked mung bean soup and the like, various fish and meat dishes, oil, special foods made with jujube and the like, spicy dishes and the like, salads and the like, or at the very least, even in rice gruel (yāgu).

Based on the words, "Monks, one should not step on a lodging (senāsana) with unwashed feet; for him who steps on it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," one should not step on lodgings such as beds and chairs, or on a finished floor, with unwashed feet. Based on the words, "Monks, one should not step on a lodging with wet feet; for him who steps on it, there is an offense of wrong-doing," one should not step on a finished floor or a lodging with wet feet of such a nature that water is evident where one steps. However, if only the moisture of water is evident but not the water itself, it is allowable to step. It is certainly allowable to step on a foot-wiper even with wet feet. Based on the words, "Monks, one should not step on a lodging with sandals on; for him who steps on it, there is an offense of wrong-doing," it is not allowable to step with sandals on a place that should be stepped on with washed feet.

Based on the words, "Monks, one should not spit on a finished floor; for him who spits, there is an offense of wrong-doing," one should not spit on a finished floor. One should spit only in a spittoon (kheḷamalla), as permitted by the words, "Monks, I allow a spittoon." Based on the words, "Monks, I allow wrapping with a cloth," a monk placing a bed or chair on a plastered floor or a finished floor should wrap the legs of the bed or chair with cloth if there is no rug or mat. If such cloth is unavailable, it is allowable to spread even leaves. For him who places it without spreading anything, there is an offense of wrong-doing. However, if the resident monks there place them even on the bare floor without any covering and use them even with unwashed feet, it is allowable to use them in the same manner.

Based on the words, "Monks, one should not lean against a finished wall; for him who leans, there is an offense of wrong-doing," one should not lean against a finished wall, whether it is a white-plastered wall or a wall decorated with paintings. Not only the wall, but one is also not permitted to lean against a door, a window, a leaning-board, a stone pillar, or a wooden pillar without covering it with a robe or some kind of cloth. "I allow..."
449:
Based on the words, "Monks, I allow lying down after spreading a sheet (paccattharaṇa)" (Cullavagga, 325), one should step with washed feet. One should lie down only after spreading one's own sheet on a finished floor, a floor covering, a lodging, or a communal (saṅghika) bed or chair. If, while sleeping, the sheet bunches up and any part of the body touches the bed or chair, there is indeed an offense. If hairs touch, there are offenses according to the number of hairs. This same rule applies to one who leans for the purpose of use. However, it is allowable to touch or step with the palms of the hands or the soles of the feet. There is no offense if it touches the body of a monk who is carrying a bed or chair.

"Monks, these ten are not to be bowed to: one ordained earlier should not bow to one ordained later; a non-ordained person (layperson or novice) is not to be bowed to; an elder of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka) who speaks non-Dhamma is not to be bowed to; a woman is not to be bowed to; a eunuch (paṇḍaka) is not to be bowed to; one undergoing parivāsa is not to be bowed to; one deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassanāraha) is not to be bowed to; one deserving mānatta is not to be bowed to; one practicing mānatta is not to be bowed to; one deserving rehabilitation (abbhānāraha) is not to be bowed to" (Cullavagga, 312). Based on these words, it should be understood that these ten are persons not to be bowed to.

"One ordained later should bow to one ordained earlier; an elder of a different communion who speaks Dhamma is to be bowed to; the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One is to be bowed to" (Cullavagga, 312). Based on these words, these three persons are to be bowed to.

"Monks, I allow three kinds of stuffing (tūla): tree-cotton, creeper-cotton, and grass-cotton" (Cullavagga, 297). Based on these words, these three kinds of stuffing are allowable. In that context, 'tree-cotton' (rukkhatūla) refers to the cotton of any trees such as the silk-cotton tree and the like. 'Creeper-cotton' (latātūla) refers to the cotton of any creepers such as the milk-creeper and the like. 'Grass-cotton' (poṭakitūla) refers to the cotton of any kind of grass such as poṭaki grass or bonga grass; it even includes the cotton of sugarcane, reeds, and so forth. By these three terms, all plants (bhūtagāma) are included. For, excluding the species of trees, creepers, and grasses, there is no other thing called bhūtagāma. Therefore, the cotton of any bhūtagāma is allowable for a pillow (bimbohana). However, when it comes to a mattress (bhisi), all this is called unallowable stuffing. Not only is this cotton allowable for a pillow, but the feathers of all birds such as swans and peacocks, and the hair of all four-footed animals such as lions, are also allowable. However, any kind of flower, such as the khāra flower or the pīta flower, is not allowable. Tamāla leaves...
450:
Pure tamāla leaves are not allowable; however, if mixed, they are allowable. The five kinds of stuffing, such as wool, etc., allowed for bolsters (bhisi) are also allowable. According to the words, "Monks, I allow five kinds of bolsters: a wool bolster, a cloth bolster, a bark bolster, a grass bolster, and a leaf bolster," the five kinds of bolsters stuffed with the five kinds of filling, such as wool, etc., are allowed. The count of these bolsters is stated according to the count of the stuffing. Among those five kinds of stuffing, by the word 'uṇṇa' (wool), it is not only sheep's wool that is taken; rather, excluding human hair, the hair of any birds or four-footed animals, whether of species whose meat is allowable or unallowable, is all taken here by the word 'uṇṇa'. Therefore, it is allowable to make a bolster by making a bolster-cover with any of the six kinds of robes or the six kinds of supplementary robes (anuloma-cīvara) and stuffing all that hair into it. Even if sheep's wool is not stuffed, but a blanket is folded four or five times and inserted, it still falls under the category of a wool bolster.

Among the cloth bolsters and so forth, a bolster made by folding any kind of new cloth or old cloth and stuffing it inside is called a cloth bolster (coḷabhisi). A bolster made by stuffing any kind of bark is called a bark bolster (vākabhisi). A bolster made by stuffing any kind of grass is called a grass bolster (tiṇabhisi). It should be understood that a bolster made by stuffing any kind of leaves, excluding pure tamāla leaves, is called a leaf bolster (paṇṇabhisi). Tamāla leaves are allowable only when mixed with other things; they are not allowable alone. In the Kurundī, it is stated that the five kinds of stuffing, such as wool, etc., which are allowable for bolsters, are also allowable for masūraka bolsters. By saying this, it is established that it is allowable to use a masūraka bolster. There is no fixed measurement for a bolster; one should consider the appropriate condition for these bolsters—such as a bed bolster, a chair bolster, a floor bolster, a walkway bolster, or a foot-wiping bolster—and make the size according to one's preference. A pillow (bimbohana), however, is allowable only if it conforms to the proper measurement.

Having said, "Monks, half-body pillows should not be used; for him who uses one, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," the Buddha prohibited such half-body sized pillows which support from the waist up to the head. Then He allowed head-sized pillows, saying, "Monks, I allow a head-sized pillow." What is called a head-sized measurement is that, in terms of width, when measuring the distance between two of the three corners, it is one span (vidatthi) and four finger-breadths (aṅgula), and the center is a fist-span (muṭṭhiratana). In the Kurundī, it is stated, "In terms of length, it is one and a half cubits (ratana) or two cubits." This is the maximum limit for a head-sized pillow; beyond this, it is not allowable; below this...
451:
...it is allowable. For a monk who is not ill, only these two—a head pillow and a foot pillow—are allowable. For a monk who is ill, however, it is allowable even to lie down after spreading many pillows and placing a cover on top. The Elder Phussadeva said, "A pillow made with the five kinds of allowable stuffing permitted for bolsters (bhisi) is allowable even if it is large." The Vinaya-expert Elder Upatissa, however, said, "For a monk who makes a pillow by stuffing it with either allowable or unallowable filling, thinking 'I will make a pillow,' it is allowable only within the specified measurement."

According to the words, "Monks, I allow an āsandika (a square chair)," the āsandika, known as a four-cornered chair, is allowable. That āsandika is also allowable even if it has legs higher than eight finger-breadths (aṅgula), according to the words, "Monks, I allow even a high āsandika." Only a long chair (dīghapīṭha) that is long on one side is not allowable if it has legs higher than eight finger-breadths. Therefore, a square chair (caturassapīṭha) is allowable even if it exceeds the measurement. According to the words, "Monks, I allow a sattaṅga (a chair with a backrest)," a bed or chair made with backrests on three sides is also allowable. According to the words, "Monks, I allow even a high sattaṅga," this chair with a backrest is also allowable even if it exceeds the measurement. According to the words, "Monks, I allow a bhaddapīṭha," etc., the following are allowed in the Pali: a chair made of wicker (vettamaya-pīṭha), a chair woven with strips of old cloth (pilotikābaddha-pīṭha), a chair with curved legs like a ram's legs made by fixing legs onto a wooden plank like a dining table (eḷakapāda-pīṭha), a chair with many legs fixed with turned wood in the shape of an emblic myrobalan (āmaṇ္ဍကဝဋ္ဋိကပီဌ - āmaṇḍakavaṭṭika-pīṭha), a straw chair (palāla-pīṭha), and a wooden plank chair (phalaka-pīṭha). Any other kind of wooden chair, even if not directly mentioned in the Pali, is also allowable.

According to the words, "Monks, one should not sleep on a high bed; for him who sleeps on one, there is an offence of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," there is a dukkaṭa offence for a monk who sleeps on a bed that exceeds the measurement. For the monk who makes it or has it made, there is a Pācittiya offence involving cutting down (chedanaka pācittiya). If one obtains a bed made by another and wishes to use it, one should use it after cutting it down. If one does not wish to cut it, it is allowable to use it by burying it in the ground and showing the correct measurement above, or by turning it upside down, or by lifting it and placing it on the beams or rafters to use it as a loft. According to the words, "Monks, high bed-supports (mañcapaṭipādaka) should not be used; for him who uses them, there is an offence of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow a bed-support of at most eight finger-breadths," a bed-support is allowable only up to eight finger-breadths by the standard finger-breadth (pamaṇāṅgula) of humans; beyond that, it is not allowable.
452:
“Monks, high and luxurious beds and seats should not be used. What are they? They are: the long chair (āsandī), the couch (pallaṅka), the long-haired rug (gonaka), the variegated woolen cover (cittaka), the white woolen cover (paṭikā), the thick flowered woolen cover (paṭalikā), the cotton-stuffed mattress (tūlikā), the woolen cover variegated with figures of lions and tigers (vikatikā), the rug with hair on one side (uddalomi), the rug with hair on both sides (ekantalomi), the coverlet embroidered with gems and woven with silk and gold thread (kaṭṭissa), the silk coverlet embroidered with gems (koseyya), the woolen rug for dancers (kuttaka), the elephant rug (hatthatthara), the horse rug (assatthara), the chariot rug (rathatthara), the rug made of antelope skins (ajinapaveṇī), the excellent rug made of kadali-deer skin (kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇa), the rug with an upper canopy, and the bed with red pillows at both the head and the foot. Whosoever should use them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).” Because of these words, high and luxurious beds and seats are not allowable.

In that context, 'high bed' (uccāsayana) means a bed exceeding the prescribed measurements. 'Luxurious bed' (mahāsayana) means unallowable coverings. Among the items starting with āsandī: 'āsandī' is a seat exceeding the prescribed measurements. 'Pallaṅka' is a seat made with figures of beasts of prey on its legs. 'Gonaka' is a large rug with long hair; it is said that its hair is longer than four finger-breadths. 'Cittaka' is a woolen rug variegated with gems. 'Paṭikā' is a white rug made of wool. 'Paṭalikā' is a woolen rug with dense floral patterns; it is also called 'āmalakapaṭa'. 'Tūlikā' is simply a mattress stuffed with natural cotton or fluff. 'Vikatikā' is a woolen rug variegated with figures of lions, tigers, and so on. 'Uddalomi' is a woolen rug with hair rising on one side. 'Ekantalomi' is a woolen rug with hair rising on both sides. 'Kaṭṭissa' is a coverlet woven with silk and gold thread and embroidered with gems. 'Koseyya' is a silk coverlet embroidered with gems; however, a pure silk coverlet is allowable.

'Kuttaka' is a woolen rug suitable for sixteen dancers to stand and dance upon. 'Hatthatthara' and 'assatthara' are simply rugs spread on the backs of elephants and horses. The same principle applies to 'rathatthara' (chariot rug). 'Ajinapaveṇī' is a rug made by sewing antelope skins to the size of a bed. 'Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇa' means an excellent rug made from the skin of the animal called the kadali-deer; it is said that they make it by spreading and sewing the kadali-deer skin over a white cloth. 'Sauttaracchada' means a rug together with a red canopy fixed above. Even if it is a white canopy, it is not allowable if there is an unallowable rug beneath it; if there is no such rug, it is allowable. 'Ubhatolohitakūpadhāna' means having red pillows at both the foot and the head of the bed; such pillows are not allowable. However, if there is a single pillow, whether it be red, lotus-colored, or variegated, it is allowable if it is of the proper size; but a large pillow is rejected. Regarding gonaka and other such items, in a communal monastery...
453:
...or in a private monastery, it is not allowable to use them by spreading them on beds or stools. On a Dhamma-seat, however, they may be obtained if spread in the manner of laypeople; even then, it is not allowable to lie down upon them.

“Monks, I allow you to sit upon rugs that are the handiwork of laypeople, except for these three: the long chair (āsandī), the couch (pallaṅka), and the cotton-stuffed mattress (tūlikā); but I do not allow you to lie down upon them.” Because of these words, except for the three items like āsandī, it is allowable to sit on the remaining lay-style rugs such as gonaka, whether on a Dhamma-seat, in a dining hall, or inside a house; but it is not allowable to lie down. As for a bed or stool stuffed with cotton, it is allowable to sit on it in a dining hall or only inside a house; it is also allowable to lie down on such a cotton-stuffed bed or stool. However, for a monk who has a cotton-stuffed bed or stool made, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) involving the removal of the cotton.

“Monks, I allow a covered bed and a covered stool.” Because of these words, a bed or stool covered with leather and so on is allowable. “Monks, I allow a cloak (pāvāra). Monks, I allow a silk cloak. Monks, I allow a rug (kojava). Monks, I allow a woolen blanket (kambala).” Because of these words, cloaks and so on, whether they belong to the community or to an individual, are allowable to be used as one pleases in a monastery, inside a house, or anywhere else. In this context, regarding the rug (kojava), only an ordinary rug is allowable; a large rug used on an elephant's back is not allowable.

“Monks, I allow all palace-furnishings (pāsādaparibhoga).” Because of these words, all furnishings made elaborately, such as door-leaves, beds, stools, and fans variegated with gold and silver, as well as drinking-water pots and drinking-water cups made of gold and silver, are allowable as monastery furniture (senāsanaparibhoga). If people say, “We donate male and female servants, fields, lands, and cattle to the palace,” there is no need for a separate act of acceptance; once the palace is accepted, these are considered accepted as well.

“Monks, I allow a single-layered sandal... Monks, double-layered sandals should not be worn... triple-layered sandals should not be worn... multi-layered sandals should not be worn. Whosoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).” Because of these words, only a single-layered sandal is allowable; double-layered and triple-layered sandals are certainly not allowable. 'Multi-layered sandals' (guṇanguṇūpāhanā) refers to those with four layers or more; such sandals are not allowable only in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). “Monks, I allow multi-layered sandals in all the border regions (paccantima janapada).” Because of these words, in the border regions...
454:
Multi-layered sandals are allowable (in the border regions) whether they are new or used. However, in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), because of the word: "Monks, I allow multi-layered sandals that have been discarded. Monks, new multi-layered sandals should not be worn; for one who wears them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" (Mahāvagga, 247), only multi-layered sandals that have been worn and then taken off (used) are allowable; new ones that have not been used are indeed forbidden. Single-layered sandals, however, are allowable in all places, whether used or unused. In this matter, sandals made of any skin except human skin are allowable. The same rule applies to sandal-cases, knife-sheaths, and key-cases.

"Monks, all-blue sandals should not be worn. All-yellow sandals should not be worn. All-red sandals should not be worn. All-crimson sandals should not be worn... All-black sandals should not be worn. Sandals dyed with a dye the color of a centipede's back (mahāraṅgaratta) should not be worn. Sandals dyed with a dye the color of a withered leaf (mahānāmaratta) should not be worn. For one who wears them, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Mahāvagga, 246)—because of this word, sandals that are entirely blue, etc., are not allowable. Here, blue is the color of the flax flower (ummapuppha). Yellow is the color of the kaṇikāra flower. Red is the color of the jayasumana flower. Crimson is simply the color of madder (mañjiṭṭha). Black is the color of a fresh gall-nut (addāriṭṭhaka). Mahāraṅgaratta is the color of a centipede's back. Mahānāmaratta is a mixed color or the color of a withered leaf. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is said to be "the color of a lotus flower." If one obtains any of these, it is allowable to wear them after wiping the dye with a piece of cloth or breaking the color; even if the color is only slightly broken, it is indeed allowable.

"Monks, sandals with blue straps should not be worn. Sandals with yellow straps should not be worn. Sandals with red straps should not be worn. Sandals with crimson straps should not be worn. Sandals with black straps should not be worn. Sandals with straps the color of a centipede's back should not be worn. Sandals with straps the color of a withered leaf should not be worn. For one who wears them, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Mahāvagga, 246)—because of this word, sandals whose straps alone are blue, etc., are also not allowable; however, it is allowable to wear them after breaking the color.

"Monks, sandals with heel-covers (khallakabaddha) should not be worn. Sandals that are boot-shaped (puṭabaddha) should not be worn. Sandals that are wrapped around (pāliguṇṭhima) should not be worn. Sandals stuffed with cotton (tūlapuṇṇika) should not be worn. Sandals with straps like partridge wings (tittirapattika) should not be worn. ..."
455:
Sandals with straps shaped like ram horns should not be worn. Sandals with straps shaped like goat horns should not be worn. Sandals with straps shaped like scorpion tails should not be worn. Sandals stitched with peacock feathers should not be worn. Ornate sandals should not be worn. For the monk who wears them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (Mahāvagga, 246)—according to this statement, sandals with heel-covers and so forth are also not allowable.

Among those sandals, "heel-covering sandals" (khallakabaddha) refers to sandals made by binding a cover at the base to cover the heel. "Boot-shaped sandals" (puṭabaddha) refers to "Yonaka" (foreign) sandals, which cover the entire foot up to the calf. "Pāliguṇṭhima" sandals are those made by wrapping, covering only the top of the foot but not the calf. "Cotton-stuffed sandals" (tūlapuṇṇika) are sandals made by filling them with cotton wool. "Partridge-wing sandals" (tittirapattika) are sandals with ornate straps resembling the wings of a partridge. "Ram-horn shaped strap sandals" (meṇḍavisāṇavaddhika) are sandals made by attaching straps in the shape of ram horns at the point where the foot is inserted. The same method applies to goat-horn shaped straps and so on. "Scorpion-tail shaped strap sandals" (vicchikāḷika) are also made by attaching straps in the shape of a scorpion's tail (or claws) at that same insertion point. "Peacock-feather stitched sandals" (morapiñchaparisibbita) are sandals stitched on the soles or straps with peacock feathers that are like thread. "Ornate sandals" (citrā) are sandals that are variegated with various colors. If one obtains any of these sandals, they may be used if the heel-covers and so forth can be removed. If a monk uses them while those parts are still present, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

"Monks, sandals trimmed with lion skin should not be worn. Sandals trimmed with tiger skin should not be worn. Sandals trimmed with leopard skin should not be worn. Sandals trimmed with shaggy skin (ajina) should not be worn. Sandals trimmed with otter skin should not be worn. Sandals trimmed with cat skin should not be worn. Sandals trimmed with black squirrel skin should not be worn. Sandals trimmed with luva skin (luvakacamma) should not be worn. For the monk who wears them, there is an offense of wrong-doing" (Mahāvagga, 246)—according to this statement, sandals trimmed with lion skin and so forth are also not allowable. In this context, "trimmed with lion skin" means making the sandals by attaching lion skin around the edges, like the binding (anuvāta) of a robe. This method applies to all other skins. "Trimmed with luva skin" (luvakacamma) means trimming with the skin of a bird or a cat. If one obtains any of these, they should be worn after removing that skin.

"Monks, wooden clogs should not be worn. Palm-leaf clogs should not be worn. Bamboo-leaf clogs should not be worn. Grass clogs should not be worn. Muñja-grass clogs should not be worn. Babbaja-grass clogs should not be worn. Hintāla-leaf clogs should not be worn. Lotus-leaf clogs should not be worn. Woolen clogs should not be worn. Gold clogs should not be worn. Silver clogs should not be worn. Gem-studded clogs should not be worn. Beryl-studded clogs should not be worn. M..."
456:
Footwear made of crystal, footwear made of bronze, footwear made of glass, footwear made of tin, footwear made of lead, footwear made of copper, and so forth—any such removable footwear should not be worn. For a monk who wears them, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). According to this statement, any removable footwear made of grass or any other material should not be worn. 

'Monks, I allow three types of fixed, non-removable clogs: clogs for the toilet, clogs for the urinal, and clogs for rinsing (ācamana).' According to this statement, it is permissible to use these three types of clogs, such as those for the toilet and urinal, which are firmly fixed in the ground, immovable, and cannot be carried away.

'Monks, one should not enter a village wearing sandals. For one who enters, there is an offense of wrongdoing.' According to this statement, one should not enter a village wearing sandals. However, 'Monks, I allow a sick monk to enter a village wearing sandals.' According to this statement, for a monk who is ill—such as one whose soles are cracked, who has boils on the feet, or whose feet are painful, and who is unable to enter the village without sandals—it is permissible to enter the village wearing sandals. 'Monks, I allow the wearing of sandals, and the carrying of a torch, a lamp, and a staff within the monastery grounds (ārāma).' According to this statement, it is permissible to wear sandals within the monastery grounds even for one who is not ill.

'Monks, one should not walk up and down wearing sandals while teachers, those equal to teachers, preceptors, or those equal to preceptors are walking up and down without sandals. For one who walks so, there is an offense of wrongdoing.' According to this statement, one should not walk up and down wearing sandals while teachers and others are walking without them. In this context, the four types of teachers—the teacher for the novice ordination (pabbajjā-ācariya), the teacher for the full ordination (upasampadā-ācariya), the teacher who gives dependence (nissaya-ācariya), and the teacher who gives instruction (uddesa-ācariya)—are all considered 'teachers' here. For a monk with no seniority (vassa), a monk of six years' seniority is considered 'equal to a teacher.' This is because the monk with no seniority must live in dependence on the six-year monk until he reaches four years of seniority. In this same manner, for a one-year monk, a seven-year monk; for a two-year monk, an eight-year monk; for a three-year monk, a nine-year monk; and for a four-year monk, a ten-year monk are all considered 'equal to teachers.' The monk friends who are intimate with one's preceptor (upajjhāya), or any monks who are senior by ten years or more, are all called 'equal to preceptors.' For a monk who walks up and down wearing sandals while such monks are walking without sandals, there is an offense.
457:
'Monks, great skins such as lion skin, tiger skin, and leopard skin should not be worn. For a monk who wears them, there is an offense of wrongdoing. Monks, cow skin should not be worn. For a monk who wears them, there is an offense of wrongdoing. Monks, no skin of any kind should be worn. For a monk who wears them, there is an offense of wrongdoing.' According to these statements from the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pali, it is not permissible to take and use any skin, such as lion skin, in the Middle Country (Majjhima-desa). The prohibition is specifically against wearing or carrying lion skins and the like. However, as a floor covering, it is permissible to use any skin within the monastery, provided it is not taken outside.

'Monks, I allow the use of skins as rugs in all border regions (paccantima janapada), such as sheepskin, goatskin, and deerskin.' According to this statement, in border regions, it is permissible to lie down or sit on rugs made of sheepskin or goatskin. Among deerskins, only the skins of the eṇī-deer, the flying deer, the barking deer, the sambar deer, the migamātuka, and the rohita-deer are permissible. Others are not:

'The skins of monkeys, black bears, sarabha-beasts, kadalī-deer, and any wild beasts (vāḷamiga) are not permissible.'

In that verse, 'wild beasts' (vāḷamiga) refers to lions, tigers, bears, and hyenas. Not only these, but all other animals except those whose skins are explicitly allowed—down to cows, buffaloes, rabbits, and cats—should be understood as 'wild beasts' in this context. The skins of all these animals are not permissible.

'Monks, one should not travel by vehicle. For one who does, there is an offense of wrongdoing. Monks, I allow a vehicle for a sick monk.' According to this statement, a monk who is not ill should not travel by vehicle. Which vehicle is permissible and which is not? 'Monks, I allow a hand-cart pulled by men. Monks, I allow a palanquin (sivikā) and a litter (pāṭaṅki).' According to this statement, hand-carts pulled by men, palanquins, and litters are permissible. In this context, a vehicle pulled by men is permissible whether it is driven by a woman or a man. However, a vehicle pulled by a cow is not permissible. As for the hand-cart, it is permissible whether women push it or men push it.

'Monks, I allow a double outer robe (saṅghāṭi), a single upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and a single inner robe (antaravāsaka) made of new cloth or cloth as good as new. I allow a four-fold outer robe, a double upper robe, and a double inner robe made of old cloth that has been kept for a long time.' According to this statement, one should make a double outer robe, a single upper robe, and a single inner robe from new cloth or cloth washed only once. From worn-out cloth kept for a long time, one should make a four-fold outer robe, a double upper robe, and a double inner robe. For rag-robes (paṃsukūla), one may make as many layers as desired. One should also make an effort in seeking worn-out cloths dropped in the marketplace. There is no limit to the number of layers; even a hundred layers is permissible. All these points refer to a monk who is easily satisfied.
458: The Saṅghāṭi should be made fourfold, the Uttarāsaṅga twofold, and the Antaravāsaka twofold. In the case of rag-robes (paṃsukūla), they should be made with as many layers as desired. Based on the word [from the Mahāvagga]: 'Effort should be made in seeking worn-out cloths dropped in the market,' for unwashed cloths and cloths washed once, the Saṅghāṭi should be made twofold, and the Uttarāsaṅga and Antaravāsaka single-fold. For old cloths kept for a long season, the Saṅghāṭi should be made fourfold, and the Uttarāsaṅga and Antaravāsaka twofold. Regarding rag-robes, they may be made as desired. Effort and search should be made even for worn-out cloths dropped in the market; there is no limit to the number of layers, even a hundred layers is allowable. All this [regarding many layers] is said with reference to a monk who finds it agreeable. Among the three robes, two or one should be made by cutting. If there is not enough cloth, an additional layer (āgantukapatta) should be added. This is because an additional layer is permitted when there is insufficient cloth. It is said: 'Monks, I allow two cut robes and one uncut robe.' When two cut robes and one uncut robe were insufficient, they reported this matter to the Blessed One. He said: 'Monks, I allow two uncut robes and one cut robe.' When two uncut robes and one cut robe were also insufficient, they reported this matter to the Blessed One. He said: 'Monks, I allow even an extra strip (anvādhika) to be attached. But, monks, an entirely uncut robe should not be worn; whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).' Therefore, if it is sufficient with an additional layer, [leaving it uncut] is not allowable; it must be cut. 'Monks, a robe made of hemp (potthaka) should not be worn; whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, robes that are entirely blue should not be worn. Robes that are entirely yellow, entirely red, entirely crimson, entirely bronze-colored (mahāraṅgaratta) like the back of a beetle, or entirely yellowish-red (mahānāmaratta) like a withered leaf should not be worn. Robes with uncut fringes, long fringes, floral fringes, or fruit-like fringes should not be worn. A jacket (kañcuka), a bark garment (tirīṭaka), or a turban (veṭhana) should not be worn; whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.' Based on this word, robes made of hemp and so on should not be worn. In that context, 'potthaka' means a robe made of sunn-hemp (makaci). Cloths made of swallow-wort (akka), banana fiber (kadalī), or eraka-grass are also of the same class as potthaka. Robes that are entirely blue, etc., should be worn only after washing out the dye and re-dyeing them. If they cannot be washed, they should be made into floor coverings or placed in the middle of a triple-layered robe.
459: The distinction of colors for these robes is the same as mentioned regarding sandals. For cloths with uncut or long fringes, they should be worn after cutting the fringes. If a jacket is obtained, it is allowable to use it after tearing it, dyeing it, and [re-making it]. The same method applies to a turban. As for the bark garment, since it is made of tree bark, it is allowable to make it into a foot-wiper. 'Monks, an unrighteous legal act (adhammakamma) should not be performed; whoever should perform one, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, I allow you to protest when an unrighteous legal act is being performed.' According to this word, an unrighteous act should not be done, and if it is being done, it should be prevented. Regarding those who prevent it: 'Monks, I allow four or five to protest, two or three to make their view known, and one to resolve "This is not pleasing to me."' According to this word, a single monk should not protest in a place where they might cause harm to the protesting monk. If there are four or five, they should protest. If there are two or three, they should make their view known to another monk, saying, 'This act is unrighteous; this is not pleasing to me.' If there is only one, he should resolve, 'This is not pleasing to me.' All this is said for the sake of their safety. 'Monks, a monk should not be accused of an offense without having asked for permission; whoever should accuse, there is an offense of wrong-doing.' According to this word, a monk who wishes to accuse should ask for permission, saying, 'Venerable sir, give me leave; I wish to speak to you.' Herein, the variety of intentions should be understood. Intentions are of many kinds: the intention to make one fall [from the Sasana], the intention to abuse, the intention to perform a legal act, the intention to rehabilitate [from an offense], the intention to stop the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, the intention to investigate, and the intention to preach Dhamma. Among these, for the first four intentions, if one speaks without asking for permission, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Even after asking for permission, if one accuses him to his face of a groundless Pārājika, there is a Saṅghādisesa; if of a groundless Saṅghādisesa, a Pācittiya; if of a groundless failure in conduct (ācāravipatti), a Dukkaṭa. If one speaks with the intention to abuse, there is a Pācittiya. If one speaks behind his back regarding any of the seven classes of offenses, there is a Dukkaṭa. If one performs any of the seven types of legal acts behind his back, it is also a Dukkaṭa. In the Kurundī [Commentary], it is said: 'For a monk who speaks with the intention of rehabilitation, saying, "You have fallen into such-and-such an offense, atone for it," there is no need to ask for permission.' There is also no need to ask for permission for a monk who stops the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā. However, the time for stopping should be understood: one has the right to stop only before the syllable "re" in the text "suṇātu me bhante saṅgho... kare"; if it passes "te" and reaches "yya", there is no right to stop. The same applies to Pavāraṇā. For a Vinaya expert who investigates, when the case has been brought, there is no need to ask for permission when asking, 'Is this case mentioned by the accuser true of you?' A Dhamma-preaching monk sitting on the Dhamma-seat also does not need to ask for permission when preaching without referring to a specific person, saying, 'Whatever monk does such a thing, he is not a monk,' etc. However, if he wishes to speak referring [to a specific person], saying, 'Such-and-such a monk is not a monk, not a true monk,' he should descend from the Dhamma-seat, settle his own offense, and then go. 'Monks, those who are pure and without offense...'
460:
It is said that for a monk who says, "Atone for such-and-such an offense," there is no requirement for the formal request for permission (okāsa). For a monk who suspends the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, there is also no formal act of requesting permission; however, the time for suspension should be known as: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the fifteenth day Uposatha; if it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha."

In detail, the suspension is allowed only before the syllable "re" is passed; once the syllable "yya" is reached, it is no longer allowed. This same method applies to Pavāraṇā. For a Vinaya expert (anuvijjaka) who, when a case is presented, says with the intent of investigating, "This case of the accuser applies to you," there is no formal act of requesting permission. For a Dhamma preacher (dhammakathika) sitting on the Dhamma-seat, if he preaches the Dhamma without specifying anyone, saying, "Whichever monk does such-and-such, this monk is not a true recluse," and so forth, there is no formal act of requesting permission. However, if he specifies and identifies, "Such-and-such a monk and such-and-such a monk are not recluses, they are not followers," he must descend from the Dhamma-seat, confess his offense, and then depart.

Based on the words: "Monks, permission should not be made to be asked of pure monks who are without offense in a matter without cause and without reason; for him who makes them do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," permission should not be made to be asked of pure monks in a matter without cause. Based on the words: "Monks, I allow you to give permission after weighing the person," one should investigate, "Does he speak of a true offense or an untrue one?" and then give permission.

Based on the words: "Monks, a gift of faith (saddhādeyya) should not be wasted; for him who wastes it, there is an offense of wrong-doing," a gift of faith must not be wasted. A monk who gives to relatives other than his parents is indeed wasting it. However, even if parents are in the position of royalty, it should be given if they desire it.

Based on the words: "Monks, one should not enter a village with only the inner and upper robes (santaruttarena); for him who enters, there is an offense of wrong-doing," one should not enter a village with only the inner and upper robes.

Based on the words: "Monks, there are these five reasons for laying aside the outer robe (saṅghāṭi): he is ill, it is the rainy season boundary (vassikasanketa), he has gone to the other side of a river, it is a monastery secured with a bolt (aggaḷagutti), or the Kathina has been spread. These, monks, are the five reasons for laying aside the outer robe," a monk who is ill and unable to carry it, or when there is one of the reasons such as the rainy season boundary, etc.—in such circumstances, it is allowable to go with only the inner and upper robes, having left the outer robe in a secured monastery. In detail, in these five reasons, security with a door-bolt is the standard. It is allowable to go outside only after laying it aside in a secured monastery; it is not allowed in an unsecured monastery. For a forest-dwelling monk, if the monastery is not well-secured, he should place it in a robe-pot and hide it well in a rock crevice, a hollow tree, etc., and then go. These same five reasons should be understood for laying aside the upper robe and the inner robe. 

Based on the words: "Monks, surgical work or medical treatment should not be performed within two finger-breadths of the private parts (sambādha)," in the specified area, with any weapon, needle, thorn, or...
461:
...a monk who is ill and unable to carry the robe, or when there is one of the reasons such as the rainy season boundary, etc.—in such circumstances, it is allowable to go with only the inner and upper robes, having left the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) in a monastery secured with a bolt (aggaḷagutti). Indeed, in all these cases—illness, rainy season boundary, crossing a river, and the spreading of the Kathina—security with a bolt is the standard; it is allowable to go outside only after laying it aside in a secured monastery, not in an unsecured one. For a forest-dwelling monk, the monastery is often not well-secured; therefore, he should place the robe in a small pot and hide it well in a rock crevice, a hollow tree, and so forth, before going. These same five reasons should be understood for laying aside the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and the inner robe (antaravāsaka).

“Monks, surgical work (satthakamma) or medical treatment (vatthikamma) should not be performed within two finger-breadths of the private parts (sambādha); for him who performs it, there is an offense of grave guilt (thullaccaya).” According to these words, in the specified area, one should not perform cutting, splitting, piercing, or scratching with any weapon, needle, thorn, chisel, pebble, or fingernail; all this constitutes surgical work. One should also not perform medical treatment by pressing with any leather or cloth after applying medicine; all this constitutes medical treatment. Here, the phrase “within two finger-breadths of the private parts” is said only in reference to surgical work; medical treatment, however, is prohibited only on the private parts themselves. In that area, it is allowable to apply alkaline water or to bind with any string; if it is severed by that means, it is considered well-severed. Surgical work is not allowed even for the disease of swollen testicles (aṇḍavuḍḍhi); therefore, one should not act with the thought, “I will split the scrotum, remove the seeds, and make it free from disease.” However, there is no prohibition against heating with fire or applying medicinal ointments. In the rectal passage (vaccamagga), a cloth wick or a bamboo tube smeared with medicine is allowable; with that bamboo tube, they apply alkaline treatment or introduce oil.

“Monks, one who was formerly a barber should not carry a razor kit (khurabhaṇḍa); for him who carries it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.” According to these words, one who was formerly a barber is not allowed to carry and travel with a razor kit; however, it is allowable to cut hair with a razor belonging to another. If he cuts hair after taking a fee, it is not allowed. Only one who was not formerly a barber is allowed to carry a razor kit; it is also allowable for him to take his own or another’s razor and cut hair.
462:
"Monks, if seeds belonging to the Saṅgha are sown on private land, they should be consumed after giving a share (one-tenth). If private seeds are sown on land belonging to the Saṅgha, they should also be consumed after giving a share."
