According to these words, whether seeds belonging to the Saṅgha are sown on private land, or private seeds are sown on land belonging to the Saṅgha, they should be consumed after giving a tenth share. This is said to be an ancient custom in Jambudīpa; therefore, having made ten portions, one portion should be given to the landowners.

"Monks, there are difficult roads through the wilderness with little water and little food, which are not easy to travel without provisions. Monks, I allow you to seek provisions. One who needs rice should seek rice; one who needs mung beans, mung beans; one who needs black gram, black gram; one who needs salt, salt; one who needs molasses, molasses; one who needs oil, oil; and one who needs ghee, ghee." According to these words, a monk crossing such a wilderness is permitted to seek provisions. How should they be sought? If some people, knowing the need themselves, offer them, that is good. If they do not offer, they should be sought from the place of relatives or those who have given an invitation, or by the practice of going for alms. If they are not obtained in that way, they should be taken even by requesting from those who are not relatives or have not given an invitation. For a journey that can be made in one day, provisions should be sought for one meal. For a long journey, as much as is needed to cross the wilderness should be sought.

"Monks, whatever has not been rejected by me, saying, 'This is not allowable,' if it conforms with what is unallowable and goes against what is allowable, that is not allowable for you. Monks, whatever has not been rejected by me, saying, 'This is not allowable,' if it conforms with what is allowable and goes against what is unallowable, that is allowable for you. Monks, whatever has not been permitted by me, saying, 'This is allowable,' if it conforms with what is unallowable and goes against what is allowable, that is not allowable for you. Monks, whatever has not been permitted by me, saying, 'This is allowable,' if it conforms with what is allowable and goes against what is unallowable, that is allowable for you." The Blessed One spoke these Four Great Authorities for the sake of the monks grasping the method. Regarding those Great Authorities, the Elder Recorders of the Dhamma, taking the Sutta and comparing it, saw this matter: "Excepting the juice of grain fruits," the seven kinds of grain juice "are not allowable after noon"...
463:
By the phrase “except for the juice of grain fruits,” the juices of the seven kinds of grains are rejected as not allowable at night. These nine large fruits—palmyra, coconut, jackfruit, breadfruit, bottle gourd, pumpkin, and three types of cucumbers (tipusa, eḷāluka, and another variety)—as well as all kinds of pulses (aparanna), are just like grains. Although all of these are not explicitly rejected, they are not allowable at night because they conform to what is not allowable. Eight kinds of drinks are permitted. Other drinks made from small fruits such as rattan, tamarind, citron, wood-apple, rose-apple, and jujube are also like the eight permitted drinks. Although these small fruit drinks are not explicitly permitted, they are allowable because they conform to what is allowable. Indeed, except for grain juice and its equivalents, there is no other fruit juice that is not allowable; all are yāmakālika (allowable until dawn), as stated in the Kurundī.

The Blessed One said, “Monks, I allow six kinds of robes: linen (khoma), cotton (kappāsika), silk (koseyya), wool (kambala), hemp (sāṇa), and coarse hemp (bhaṅga),” thus permitting six kinds of robes. The Elders who conducted the Council also permitted six other kinds of robes that conform to those six: dukūla (fine cloth), pattunṇa (silk from the Pattunṇa region), cīnapṭṭa (Chinese silk), somārapaṭṭa (Somāra silk), iddhimaya (miraculous cloth), and devadattiya (cloth given by devas). Among these, pattunṇa is cloth produced from worms in the Pattunṇa region. Cīnapṭṭa and somārapaṭṭa are named after their regions. Three types of cloth conform to silk (koseyya). Dukūla conforms to hemp (sāṇa). The remaining two, iddhimaya and devadattiya, conform to cotton (kappāsika) or to all types of robes.

The Blessed One rejected eleven kinds of bowls and permitted only two kinds: the iron bowl and the clay bowl. Iron bowls, clay bowls, and copper bowls conform to these. The Blessed One permitted three kinds of pots: metal pots (lohatumba), wooden pots (kaṭṭhatumba), and fruit-shell pots (phalatumba). Water jars (kuṇḍikā), pitch-pots (kañcanaka), and water gourds (udakatumba) conform to these. In the Kurundī, however, it is said that these pots conform to water conchs and small water cups. Two kinds of waistbands were permitted: the flat type (paṭṭikā) and the “pig-tail” type (sūkaranta). Waistbands made of strips of cloth or rope conform to these. Three kinds of umbrellas were permitted: the white umbrella, the mat umbrella (kilañja), and the leaf umbrella. An umbrella made of a single leaf conforms to these. In this manner, having looked at the Pāḷi and the Commentaries, a Vinaya expert (Vinayadhara) should know other things that conform to what is allowable or not allowable.

A Vinaya expert attains the five benefits, six benefits, seven benefits, eight benefits, nine benefits, and ten benefits based on the mastery of the Vinaya.
464:
He obtains eleven kinds of benefits. Which five kinds of benefits does he obtain? He obtains the protection of his own aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), and so forth. Thus it was said:

“Monks, there are these five benefits for a person who is a bearer of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara). (1) His own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected. (2) He is a refuge for those who are remorseful (kukkucca). (3) He speaks confidently in the midst of the Saṅgha. (4) He well-subdues enemies in accordance with the Dhamma. (5) He is one who practices for the endurance of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma).”

How is the aggregate of virtue of that Vinaya bearer well-guarded and well-protected? In this Dispensation, some monks, when falling into an offense (āpatti), do so through six causes. They are: shamelessness (alajjitā), ignorance (aññāṇatā), remorsefulness (kukkuccapakatatā), perceiving the unallowable as allowable (akappiye kappiyasaññitā), perceiving the allowable as unallowable (kappiye akappiyasaññitā), and lapse of mindfulness (satisammosā).

How does one fall into an offense through shamelessness? Knowing that it is unallowable, one still violates it by disregarding the rule. Thus it was said: “He intentionally falls into an offense, conceals the offense, and follows a wrong course (agati); such a person is called a shameless person (alajjī).”

How does one fall into an offense through ignorance? An ignorant person, being deluded and foolish, does not know what should be done and what should not be done; he does what should not be done and fails to do what should be done. Thus one falls into an offense through ignorance.

How does one fall into an offense through remorsefulness? When remorse (doubt) arises regarding what is allowable or unallowable, one should ask a Vinaya bearer; if it is allowable, it should be done, and if it is unallowable, it should not be done. However, this person [decides for himself] “It is allowable,” and violates it by disregarding the rule. Thus one falls into an offense through remorsefulness.

How does one fall into an offense by perceiving the unallowable as allowable? He eats bear meat (acchamaṃsa) perceiving it as “pork” (sūkaramaṃsa); he eats leopard meat (dīpimaṃsa) perceiving it as “deer meat” (migamaṃsa); he eats unallowable food perceiving it as “allowable food”; he eats at the wrong time (after noon) perceiving it as the “right time”; he drinks an unallowable beverage perceiving it as an “allowable beverage.” Thus one falls into an offense by perceiving the unallowable as allowable.

How does one fall into an offense by perceiving the allowable as unallowable? He eats pork perceiving it as “bear meat”; he eats deer meat perceiving it as “leopard meat”; he eats allowable food perceiving it as “unallowable food”; he eats at the right time perceiving it as the “wrong time”; he drinks an allowable beverage perceiving it as an “unallowable beverage.” Thus one falls into an offense by perceiving the allowable as unallowable. How...
465:
How does one fall into an offense through lapse of mindfulness? One falls into an offense through lapse of mindfulness due to causes such as sleeping with one not fully ordained (sahasayya), being separated from the three robes (cīvaravippavāsa), and exceeding the time for medicine and robes. In this way, some monks in this Dispensation fall into offenses through these six causes.

A Vinaya bearer, however, does not fall into an offense through these six causes. How does he not fall into an offense through shame? That Vinaya bearer, guarding against the blame of others such as, "Look, sirs, this Vinaya bearer, even though he knows what is allowable and unallowable, still violates the regulation," does not fall into an offense. Thus, through shame, he does not fall into an offense; even if he should fall into an offense suddenly, if it is an offense that can be cleared by confession (desanāgāminī), he confesses it, and if it is an offense requiring rehabilitation (vuṭṭhānagāminī), he undergoes the procedures for rehabilitation and remains in a state of purity. Therefore—

“He does not intentionally fall into an offense, does not conceal an offense that has occurred, and does not go to a wrong course (agati); such a person is called a shameful person (lajjī)”—he remains established in this state of being a shameful person.

How does he not fall into an offense through knowledge? He knows what is allowable and unallowable; therefore, he does only what is allowable and does not do what is unallowable. Thus, through knowledge, he does not fall into an offense. How does he not fall into an offense through the absence of remorse? When remorse arises regarding what is allowable or unallowable, that Vinaya bearer examines the case, considers the Matrix (Mātikā), the Word-analysis (Padabhājaniya), the intermediate offenses (antarāpatti), and the non-offenses (anāpatti); if it is allowable, he does it, and if it is unallowable, he does not. Thus, through the absence of remorse, he does not fall into an offense. How does he not fall into an offense by [not] perceiving the unallowable as allowable and so forth? That Vinaya bearer knows what is allowable and unallowable; therefore, he does not perceive the unallowable as allowable, nor does he perceive the allowable as unallowable. His mindfulness is well-established; he performs the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) where it should be performed, and he performs the assignment (vikappanā) where it should be performed. Thus, through these six causes, he does not fall into an offense. A monk who does not fall into an offense is one whose virtue is unbroken and pure. In this way, the aggregate of virtue of that Vinaya bearer is well-guarded and well-protected.

How is he a refuge for those who are remorseful? Monks in other countries and other districts who have become remorseful, hearing that "A Vinaya bearer is residing in such-and-such a monastery," come to that Vinaya bearer from afar and ask about their remorse. That Vinaya bearer examines the facts of the act committed by those monks, notes the distinctions such as whether it is an offense or not, and whether it is grave (garuka) or light (lahuka). He then has them confess the offenses that can be cleared by confession, and has them undergo rehabilitation for the offenses requiring rehabilitation, thus establishing them in a state of purity. In this way, he is a refuge for those who are remorseful.
466:
It is true that he can speak confidently in the midst of the Saṅgha. When one who does not bear the Vinaya speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha, fear and hesitation overcome him; for the Vinaya-bearer, such fear does not occur. Why? Because he speaks knowing, "Speaking in this way is a fault; speaking in this way is not a fault," and thus all such hesitation and shrinking do not occur.

Regarding the statement that he well subdues enemies with reasons: here, 'enemies' are of two kinds—personal enemies and enemies of the Sāsana. Among these two, the monks Mettiya and Bhummajaka, and Vaddha the Licchavi, made accusations based on groundless Pārājika cases; these are called personal enemies. All others who are immoral and of evil conduct are also personal enemies. However, those with perverted views, such as the monk Ariṭṭha, the novice Kaṇṭaka, and the Vajjiputtaka monks residing in Vesālī, as well as the Mahāsaṅghika and other sects who present views such as "Arahants have emissions of semen, have ignorance, and have doubt," and who promote what is not the Buddha's Sāsana as the "Buddha's Sāsana," are called enemies of the Sāsana. He well subdues all those enemies with reasoned speech so that they cannot establish that unrighteous doctrine (adhamma).

Regarding the statement that he is one who practices for the longevity of the three types of Saddhamma: here, Saddhamma is of three kinds—Pariyatti, Paṭipatti, and Adhigama. Among them, the word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) consisting of the Tipitaka is called Pariyatti-saddhamma. The thirteen Dhutaṅga practices, the fourteen Khandhaka duties, and the eighty-two Mahā duties are called Paṭipatti-saddhamma. The four Paths and the four Fruits are called Adhigama-saddhamma.

Among these three types of Saddhamma, some elders say, "Pariyatti is the root of the Sāsana," based on this Sutta: "Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya I have taught and prescribed shall be your teacher after my passing." Some elders say, "Paṭipatti is the root of the Sāsana," based on this Sutta: "Subhadda, if these monks live rightly, the world will not be empty of Arahants," and they say, "As long as five monks are practicing rightly, the Sāsana remains established." Other elders, however, say, "If Pariyatti disappears, there can be no realization of the Dhamma even if one practices rightly," and they say, "If five monks guard the four Pārājikas, they will ordain faithful sons of good family as novices, grant them higher ordination in the border regions to complete a group of ten, and then perform higher ordination in the middle regions. By this means, they will complete a Saṅgha of twenty, perform their own Abbhāna kamma (rehabilitation), and make the Sāsana flourish..."
467:
...and reach expansion. In this way, this Vinaya-bearer is said to practice for the long-lasting of the three types of Saddhamma. Thus, it should be understood that this Vinaya-bearer first obtains these five benefits.

What are the six benefits he obtains? Performing Uposatha, performing Pavāraṇā, performing Saṅgha-kamma, granting novice ordination (Pabbajjā), and granting higher ordination (Upasampadā) are connected only with that Vinaya-bearer. That Vinaya-bearer gives dependence (nissaya) and trains novices. These nine types of Uposatha—Cātuddasī Uposatha, Pannarasī Uposatha, Sāmaggī Uposatha, Saṅgha Uposatha, Gaṇa Uposatha, Puggala Uposatha, Uposatha of reciting the Sutta (Suttuddesa), Pārisuddhi Uposatha, and Adhiṭṭhāna Uposatha—all these Uposathas are connected only with the Vinaya-bearer. These nine types of Pavāraṇā—Cātuddasī Pavāraṇā, Pannarasī Pavāraṇā, Sāmaggī Pavāraṇā, Saṅgha Pavāraṇā, Gaṇa Pavāraṇā, Puggala Pavāraṇā, Tevācika Pavāraṇā, Dvevācika Pavāraṇā, and Samānavassika Pavāraṇā—are also connected only with the Vinaya-bearer. These Uposathas and Pavāraṇās are the property of that Vinaya-bearer alone; he is the master of those Uposathas and Pavāraṇās.

These four types of Saṅgha-kamma—Apalokana-kamma, Ñatti-kamma, Ñattidutiya-kamma, and Ñatticatuttha-kamma—as well as acting as a preceptor (upajjhāya) to grant novice ordination and higher ordination to sons of good family, also rest only with the Vinaya-bearer. Even a person who bears two Pitakas, other than a Vinaya-bearer, is not entitled to act in this way. Only that Vinaya-bearer has the right to give dependence and train novices. Others are not allowed to give dependence or train novices. For this very reason, the Buddha prohibited it, saying, "Monks, one monk should not train two novices; whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," and then again, when allowing it, He said, "Monks, I allow a competent monk to train two novices, or as many as he is able to exhort and instruct," thus allowing only a competent monk to train novices. A monk who expects to train a novice is allowed to take a preceptor from a Vinaya-bearer and practice the major and minor duties. Here, giving dependence and training a novice are considered a single factor. Thus, among these six benefits, with one added to the previous five, there are six; with two, seven; with three, eight; with four, nine; with five, ten; and with all six, there are eleven. In this way, it should be understood that a Vinaya-bearer obtains five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven benefits.
468:
This is one factor. Thus, among these six benefits, the first five benefits together with the latter one factor make six. Together with the latter two benefits, they make seven. Together with three benefits, they make eight. Together with four, they make nine. Together with five, they make ten. Together with all those latter six benefits, they make eleven. Thus, it should be understood that such a person who is a Vinaya-holder (Vinayadhara) attains these five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven benefits.

In the manner stated above, a person who desires constant skill and proficiency in the Vinaya, which has great benefits, should repeatedly apply effort and strive in this Vinayasaṅgaha treatise.

## Thus, in the treatise which is a compendium of Vinaya decisions extracted from the Pali (Pāḷimuttaka-vinayavinicchaya-saṅgaha), the section concerning miscellaneous decisions is completed.
## The Compendium of Vinaya Decisions extracted from the Pali is also finished.
## Concluding Remarks (Nigamanakathā)

Requested by the Great King Parakkamabāhu, who illuminates the Sasana and desires the stability of the True Dhamma,

residing in this Jetavana monastery—which was built by that very king, adorned with hundreds of mansions, filled with various groups of trees, a dwelling for those delighted in meditation, and endowed with cool water—I have composed this Vinayasaṅgaha, which is the essence, for the welfare of practitioners (yogis).

By the merit achieved through composing this treatise and other merits I have accumulated, by this meritorious deed, in the second existence (the next life),

rejoicing in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, delighting in the qualities of virtue (sīla) and conduct (ācāra), without attachment to the five sensual pleasures, and having attained the first fruit (Sotāpatti-phala),

in the final existence, may I see the Noble Sage Metteyya, the Supreme Person among humans and gods, the Refuge, who delights in the welfare of all beings.

Having seen that Wise One and heard the teaching of the True Dhamma, having attained the highest fruit (Arahatship), may I glorify the Dispensation of the Conqueror (Jina-sāsana).

## The Vinayasaṅgaha Commentary is finished.
